subject: science
note: Descriptor text: Australian Curriculum v9 (ACARA, CC BY 4.0). Waypoints and prior knowledge: Learning Waypoints. Made by tools/import-curriculum.mjs; do not edit by hand.

descriptors.title: How people observe and question
descriptors.description: explore the ways people make and use observations and questions to learn about the natural world
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how people — including scientists, First Nations Australians and themselves — use their senses and tools to make observations, and use questions to guide their learning about the natural world.

nodes.label: People use observations and questions to learn about the natural world
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least two ways people make observations and explain that scientists (and others) ask questions about what they observe.
criteria: Describes at least two ways people make observations (using senses and/or tools)
Gives one example of a question a scientist or person might ask about nature

width.minimum: Students describe two ways people make observations and give one example of a question a scientist or person might ask.
width.typical: Students use senses to make observations; explore how scientists use both senses and equipment; view examples of observations (rock paintings, photographs, drawings, reports); engage with stories about scientists like Jane Goodall or Joseph Banks; and notice how they make observations and ask questions.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians gain knowledge about the land and its resources through observation — examining observation as a knowledge-building practice
Interact with stories or documentaries about scientists and notice the ways they make and record observations
Watch an age-appropriate documentary and notice how scientists, engineers and citizen scientists ask questions — then pose their own questions

modes.reason: First Nations land observation knowledge and documentary-style scientist stories provide culturally rich and varied contexts for the concept that observation and questioning are universal knowledge-building practices — not just school science activities.

descriptors.title: Questioning and predicting
descriptors.description: pose questions and make predictions based on experiences
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students pose simple questions about observed objects and phenomena and make predictions grounded in their personal experiences.

nodes.label: Questions and predictions come from experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose at least one question about an observed object or phenomenon and make one prediction based on their personal experience.
criteria: Poses at least one question about an observed object or phenomenon
Makes a prediction and can say what experience it is based on

width.minimum: Students pose one question about an observed object or phenomenon and make one prediction, explaining what experience it is based on.
width.typical: Students pose questions about everyday objects, materials and living things; make predictions before field work about what they will observe; make predictions about object movement; and explain what experience their prediction is based on.
wider: Pose questions about plant parts: 'What part of a plant is broccoli?'
Make predictions about how an unusually shaped object (egg, hexagonal block) might move down a slope — connecting shape observation to movement prediction
Make predictions about which plants and animals they might observe in the school grounds before field work

descriptors.title: Investigating safely and observing
descriptors.description: engage in investigations safely and make observations using their senses
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students engage in investigations following basic safety rules, make observations using appropriate senses and simple tools, and record observations in basic formats.

nodes.label: Investigations are conducted safely using the senses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow basic safety rules for investigations, make observations using at least three senses, and explain why we do not use taste to make science observations.
criteria: Follows at least two named safety rules during an investigation
Makes observations using at least three senses and explains why taste is not used in science

width.minimum: Students follow at least two safety rules during an investigation and make observations using at least three senses.
width.typical: Students discuss and follow safety rules (sun safe, no running, no tasting, following teacher instructions); explain safety considerations for touch, smell, sight and hearing; use tools (binoculars, magnifying glasses, digital cameras) to enhance observations; and record observations using numbers, dots, drawings, voice recordings or photos.
wider: Explore safety considerations for each sense — why we do not use taste in science investigations
Use magnifying glasses and digital cameras to observe plant and animal features in greater detail
Record observations using multiple formats: numbers, dots, drawings, voice recordings, digital photography

descriptors.title: Representing observations and identifying patterns
descriptors.description: represent observations in provided templates and identify patterns with guidance
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent observations in provided templates (tables, graphic organisers, displays) and identify simple patterns in sorted data with teacher guidance.

nodes.label: Observations are represented in provided formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a provided table or graphic organiser to record or sort observations, and contribute to a shared display.
criteria: Uses a provided template or graphic organiser to record or sort at least two observations
Contributes to a class display of sorted observations
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to identify patterns in sorted data — but if students cannot use a provided template to record or sort observations, they have no organised data in which to notice patterns. The pattern-identification task in Node 2 is only legible if Node 1 produces a usable representation.

width.minimum: Students record observations in one provided format and contribute one observation to a shared class display.
width.typical: Students use provided tables and graphic organisers to sort images of plants and animals by features; collaborate on floor or wall displays linking material images to object images; and represent observations through sorting, drawing and labelling in provided templates.
wider: Collaborate to create a floor or wall display linking material samples to images of objects made from them
Sort images of plants and animals into groups using a provided graphic organiser
Identify common features of familiar animal groups (fish, birds, reptiles) using a provided template

modes.reason: Students at Foundation need exposure to multiple representation formats — tables, graphic organisers, floor/wall displays — before they can reliably select and use one. Building a repertoire of recording forms prepares them to represent data in the format that surfaces patterns most clearly.

nodes.label: Simple patterns are identified with guidance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a simple pattern in sorted observations with teacher guidance.
criteria: Identifies at least one simple pattern in a set of sorted observations with guidance

width.minimum: Students identify one simple pattern in a set of sorted observations with guidance.
width.typical: Students identify patterns of movement in objects (balls roll in a straight line when pushed); identify patterns in material uses (wood, plastic, metal, glass objects); and name a simple repeating feature in a sorted group.
wider: Identify patterns of movement in objects — balls roll, cars move on wheels — examining what the pattern tells us
Identify patterns in uses of everyday objects made of similar materials
Connect identified patterns to predictions — 'if this is the pattern, what might happen next?'

descriptors.title: Comparing observations with predictions
descriptors.description: compare observations with predictions with guidance
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students revisit predictions after observing, compare them with what they actually observed, and — with guidance — identify whether they matched or differed.

nodes.label: Predictions are compared with observations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can revisit their prediction after an observation and say whether it matched, with teacher guidance.
criteria: States whether their prediction matched their observation
Describes at least one way the observation was the same as or different from the prediction

width.minimum: Students compare one prediction with one observation and state whether they matched.
width.typical: Students revisit predictions and with guidance identify whether they matched observations; use a provided table to draw or dictate their prediction and observation; compare field work observations with pre-field predictions; and describe what was the same and what was different.
wider: Use a provided table to draw or dictate prediction and observation side by side — comparing explicitly
Revisit predictions about plant or animal field work observations and compare with what was actually found
Explore what to do when a prediction does not match — 'what can we do to find out more?'

descriptors.title: Sharing questions, predictions and observations
descriptors.description: share questions, predictions, observations and ideas with others
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their science questions, predictions, observations and ideas with others using a range of forms — spoken, drawn, modelled, performed or displayed.

nodes.label: Science ideas are shared with others in varied forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share at least one science observation or idea with others using a chosen form (spoken, drawn, modelled, role-played or displayed).
criteria: Shares at least one science observation or idea with others
Uses at least one form beyond verbal — drawn, modelled, role-played or displayed

width.minimum: Students share one science observation or idea with others using at least one form.
width.typical: Students share questions, predictions and observations through discussions and circle groups; recount experiences observing nature; show or describe how objects move; role-play how scientists use equipment; represent plant and animal features using materials; and communicate using posters, collages, digital displays, drawings or storyboards.
wider: Acknowledge and explore First Nations Australians' ways of communicating information about anatomical features of plants and animals
Role-play or show how people use different equipment to make scientific observations
Represent external features of plants and animals using blocks, modelling clay, craft materials or paper

modes.reason: Foundation students sharing science ideas benefit from multiple communication forms — spoken, drawn, modelled, role-played, displayed. First Nations communication forms provide a culturally rich direction that expands what counts as valid scientific communication at this level.

descriptors.title: External features of plants and animals
descriptors.description: observe external features of plants and animals and describe ways they can be grouped based on these features
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed. Students bring everyday observations of living things from home and community contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students observe and name external features of plants and animals, describe similarities and differences between organisms, and sort living things into groups based on observable external features.

nodes.label: Plants and animals have observable external features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe and name external features of plants (roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds) and animals (eyes, body covering, legs, wings) using their senses and simple tools.
criteria: Names at least two external features of a plant and two of an animal
Recognises humans as animals and can describe at least two human external features
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (grouping by external features) requires students to apply feature observation as a sorting criterion. Students who cannot name and identify external features of plants and animals have no vocabulary or observational basis for constructing or explaining a grouping rule.

width.minimum: Students name at least two external features of a plant and two of an animal using observation.
width.typical: Students use magnifying glasses or digital cameras to observe and name features of plants and animals; identify humans as animals and describe external features of humans; compare features across organisms; and describe how features look and feel.
wider: Observe fruits and vegetables and identify them as parts of plants — roots, flowers, fruits or leaves
Recognise First Nations Australians' use of observable features to group living things — examining cultural classification knowledge
Explore how First Nations Australians' observations of external features are replicated in traditional dance

modes.reason: Naming external features across a range of organisms — including fruits and vegetables as plant parts, and First Nations classification practices — builds the observation vocabulary and range that Node 2 sorting requires. Width investment at this node serves both the cascade risk and the cultural enrichment opportunity.

nodes.label: Living things can be grouped by external features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort plants and animals into groups based on shared external features and explain the grouping rule they used.
criteria: Sorts a collection of living things into groups and states the feature used
Identifies at least one shared feature within a named animal group

width.minimum: Students sort a collection of plants or animals into two groups and explain one feature they used to sort them.
width.typical: Students sort collections of model animals using different feature-based grouping strategies; identify common features within familiar animal groups (fish, birds, reptiles); describe their grouping rule; and recognise that the same collection can be sorted in different ways.
wider: Sort collections of model animals and explain different grouping strategies — examining that multiple valid groupings are possible
Identify common features of familiar animal groups such as fish, birds or reptiles
Using a digital camera to collect plant and animal feature images on a nature scavenger hunt

descriptors.title: How objects move
descriptors.description: describe how objects move and how factors including their size, shape or material influence their movement
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed. Students bring everyday experience of moving objects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe different ways objects move, observe how size, shape and material affect movement, and make comparisons between objects based on how they move.

nodes.label: Objects move in different ways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can observe and describe different types of object movement (roll, slide, bounce, spin, swing) and group toys or objects by their movement type.
criteria: Describes at least three different ways objects can move
Groups at least two objects by movement type and explains the grouping
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 asks students to compare how factors (size, shape, material) affect movement — a comparison that requires movement vocabulary and prior observation of movement types. Students who cannot describe different movement types have no referent for 'how movement changed' when a factor is varied.

width.minimum: Students describe at least three different ways objects can move and give one example of each.
width.typical: Students observe how toys move; describe movement types (roll, slide, bounce, spin); group toys by movement type; describe unusually shaped objects (eggs, tubes) and predict how they might move; and explain what they observe.
wider: Explore how the size and shape of traditional instructive toys used by First Nations Australians influence their movement
Observe and describe ways unusually shaped objects (blocks, tubes, eggs) move when rolled down a slope
Group toys based on their movement and explain the grouping

modes.reason: Observing and naming multiple movement types (roll, slide, bounce, spin, swing) across varied objects — including First Nations instructive toys — builds the vocabulary and observation range needed to describe how factors alter movement in Node 2.

nodes.label: Size, shape and material affect how objects move
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how different-sized, shaped or material objects move and describe at least one factor that affects movement.
criteria: Compares two objects and describes how at least one factor (size, shape or material) affects how they move

width.minimum: Students compare two objects and describe how one factor (size, shape or material) affects how they move.
width.typical: Students compare different-sized similar-shaped objects (tennis balls, golf balls, marbles); explore how material affects movement (plastic, foam, cloth, rubber balls); observe how object shape affects rolling or bouncing; and explain the difference they observe.
wider: Compare how different-sized similar-shaped objects (tennis, golf, marble, basketball) roll and bounce
Explore how the material a ball is made from affects movement on a surface
Predict how an unusually shaped object such as an egg or hexagonal block might move down a slope then observe

descriptors.title: Materials and their properties
descriptors.description: recognise that objects can be composed of different materials and describe the observable properties of those materials
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed. Students bring everyday experience of handling objects and materials.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that objects are made of materials, identify the material(s) an object is made from, and describe observable properties of materials using appropriate vocabulary.

nodes.label: Objects are made of materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the material an object is made of and recognise that some objects are made of more than one material.
criteria: Identifies the material of at least three objects
Names at least one object made of more than one material and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (describing and sorting materials by observable properties) requires students to correctly identify what material an object is made of before they can describe that material's properties. Students who conflate the object with the material (e.g. 'the cup' rather than 'plastic') cannot direct their property observations to the right referent.

width.minimum: Students identify the material of at least three objects and name at least one object made of more than one material.
width.typical: Students observe and manipulate objects to identify their materials; recognise that some objects are made of more than one material type; use digital cameras on a materials scavenger hunt; and suggest why different parts of everyday objects (saucepan, clothing) are made from different materials.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians make utensils for different purposes by combining different materials — examining purposeful multi-material design
Use a digital camera to collect images of objects on a materials scavenger hunt
Suggest why different parts of everyday objects (saucepan handle vs base, clothing layers) are made from different materials

modes.reason: The object-material distinction — that objects are made of materials, not that they are those materials — is the conceptual move this node must make explicit. First Nations multi-material utensil examples provide a culturally grounded context in which the distinction between the object's purpose and the material's properties is visible.

nodes.label: Materials have observable properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe observable properties of materials using appropriate vocabulary (colour, hardness, texture, flexibility) and sort materials by those properties.
criteria: Describes at least two observable properties of each of three different materials
Sorts materials into groups by a named property and explains the rule

width.minimum: Students describe at least two observable properties of each of three materials using appropriate vocabulary.
width.typical: Students sort and group materials by properties (colour, hardness, texture, flexibility); create displays naming materials and exploring property language; describe and compare properties across materials; and recognise that tools like magnifying glasses enable more-detailed observations.
wider: Create a display of different materials, naming each and exploring language to describe properties
Sort materials by multiple properties — examining that materials can be grouped in different ways
Recognise that magnifying glasses enable more-detailed observations of material surfaces and textures

descriptors.title: Science in daily life
descriptors.description: describe how people use science in their daily lives, including using patterns to make scientific predictions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have not yet examined science as a human activity used in daily life or connected the idea of patterns to prediction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe examples of how people — including themselves, community members and First Nations Australians — use science knowledge and observed patterns to make decisions and predictions in everyday life.

nodes.label: People use science knowledge in everyday decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least two examples of how people use science knowledge in their daily lives, explaining what knowledge is being used and why.
criteria: Describes two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life
Identifies the science knowledge being used in each example
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's pattern-based prediction concept requires students to have first established that people use science knowledge in daily life — without this foundation, connecting patterns to prediction in N2 lacks meaningful grounding.

width.minimum: Students describe two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life, identifying the science knowledge used in each.
width.typical: Students identify and describe how farmers, gardeners, ecologists, engineers and families use science knowledge in daily decisions — plant care, weather planning, force use in cooking and tools, habitat design — and connect these examples to specific science concepts.
wider: Learning from farmers, bush care volunteers, gardeners or nursery owners about how they observe plant and animal needs and design habitats — examining professional science use
Investigating how First Nations Australians use science to meet needs including food, water supply and shelter
Exploring how engineers use knowledge of forces to create playground equipment or toys — connecting force concepts to design (AC9S1U03)

nodes.label: Patterns help people make scientific predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how observing patterns in nature (weather, seasons, animal behaviour) allows people to make predictions that guide decisions.
criteria: Describes one pattern in nature
Explains how observing that pattern helps people make a prediction or decision

width.minimum: Students describe one pattern in nature and one prediction that people make based on that pattern.
width.typical: Students describe multiple examples of pattern-based prediction — weather forecasting, seasonal resource gathering, animal behaviour prediction — and explain how the pattern is observed and used to make the prediction.
wider: Recognising how First Nations Australians use changes in the landscape and sky to answer questions about when to gather certain resources — examining long-term observational pattern knowledge
Sharing examples of how students have used science knowledge at home — weather forecasts, seasonal clothing, observing weather patterns before family events
Learning from local ecologists or wildlife carers about observing animal behaviour patterns to design habitat supports

modes.reason: First Nations pattern-based resource timing and personal home examples provide culturally rich and personally connected directions. Encountering pattern-based prediction across multiple contexts — ecological, cultural, domestic — builds a more complete and generalisable model.

descriptors.title: Questioning and predicting
descriptors.description: pose questions to explore observed simple patterns and relationships and make predictions based on experiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can ask questions about the world around them (F band). They now begin to pose questions about patterns and relationships specifically, and make predictions grounded in their experiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students pose simple investigable questions about observed patterns and relationships, and make experience-based predictions before observing or investigating.

nodes.label: Questions explore patterns and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a question about a simple pattern or relationship in an observed phenomenon, distinguishing it from a question about naming or describing.
criteria: Poses a question about a pattern or relationship (not just a naming question) for a given observation
Explains what the question is trying to find out
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's prediction-before-investigation sequence requires students to have a question to predict about. Without posing an investigable question, there is no anchor for making and checking an experience-based prediction.

width.minimum: Students pose at least one question about a pattern or relationship for a given observation context.
width.typical: Students pose questions about patterns (seasonal plant changes, weather patterns) and relationships (push strength and distance, plant care and growth) across Y1 science contexts, and explain what their question is trying to find out.
wider: Pose questions about how animals meet their needs in particular places — exploring habitat-need relationships
Pose questions about push and pull relationships: 'Does a toy car go further if it is pushed harder?' — examining force-motion relationships
Make predictions about types of animals and plants they might observe in a particular place — connecting habitat knowledge to prediction

nodes.label: Predictions are based on prior experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make a prediction before an observation or investigation and explain what experience the prediction is based on.
criteria: Makes a prediction before an observation or investigation
Explains what experience the prediction is based on

width.minimum: Students make one prediction and explain what experience it is based on.
width.typical: Students make predictions across Y1 science contexts (plant needs, force effects, seasonal changes) and explain the experience that grounds each prediction — distinguishing a prediction from a guess.
wider: Make predictions about patterns of observable phenomena such as seasonal plant changes or temperature patterns across seasons
Make predictions about plant needs: 'I think a plant will die if it does not get enough water' — grounding prediction in care experience
Consult with First Nations Australians to compare observations of animal tracks and evaluate identifications (AC9S1I05)

descriptors.title: Planning and conducting
descriptors.description: suggest and follow safe procedures to investigate questions and test predictions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have participated in guided investigations (F band). They now begin to suggest procedures — not just follow them — and contribute to safety planning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students suggest steps for safe investigation procedures and follow guided procedures — including age-appropriate safety measures — to investigate questions and test predictions.

nodes.label: Safe procedures are suggested and followed
nodes.checkpoint: Students can suggest at least one safety measure for a given investigation and follow teacher-guided steps to conduct an investigation safely.
criteria: Suggests at least one safety measure for a named investigation and explains why it is needed
Follows guided investigation steps to completion

width.minimum: Students suggest one safety measure for a given investigation and follow a guided procedure to completion.
width.typical: Students suggest safety measures (sun safety, goggles, aprons, careful equipment handling); follow steps in guided investigations; suggest ways to conduct observations safely; and contribute to setting up and packing away equipment.
wider: Explore different ways of investigating science questions through guided discussion — examining that there is more than one way to investigate
Suggest steps for setting up and packing away equipment — taking responsibility for the investigation environment
Discuss safe ways to observe the sun — applying safety reasoning to an important real investigation context

descriptors.title: Observing and measuring
descriptors.description: make and record observations, including informal measurements, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can make observations using their senses (F band). They now extend to making observations more systematically and recording them using informal measurements and digital tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students make and record observations using text, drawing, counts, informal measurements (cups, handspans, paces, blocks) and digital tools (photography, video) as appropriate.

nodes.label: Observations are made and recorded systematically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make observations using their senses and appropriate tools, record observations using at least two formats (drawing, count, informal measurement, digital photo), and explain what an observation is.
criteria: Makes and records observations in at least two different formats (e.g. drawing and informal measurement)
Explains what an observation is in their own words

width.minimum: Students make and record observations in two different formats for a given investigation.
width.typical: Students explore what an observation is through guided discussion; make observations using senses and tools; use informal measurements (cups, handspans, paces, blocks, string) to record quantities; photograph or video observations; and organise recorded observations in tables or drawings.
wider: Use informal measurements such as blocks to measure plant growth or paces to measure how far an object has moved — applying informal measurement to quantify observations
Record observations through text, drawing, counts, informal measurements and digital photography — building a repertoire of recording formats
Explore how digital photography can capture observations that are hard to record by hand — comparing recording tools

descriptors.title: Processing and representing data
descriptors.description: sort and order data and information and represent patterns, including with provided tables and visual or physical models
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sort objects by observable features (F band). They now extend to sorting and ordering scientific data and identifying patterns in provided formats.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sort and order data using provided tables, graphic organisers and visual models, and identify simple patterns in sorted data.

nodes.label: Data is sorted and ordered to show patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort and order data into provided categories, use a provided table or graphic organiser to organise their data, and identify one pattern from the organised data.
criteria: Sorts data into at least two categories using a provided organiser
Identifies one pattern from the organised or ordered data

width.minimum: Students sort data into two categories using a provided organiser and identify one pattern from the sorted data.
width.typical: Students use pictographs, tables and graphic organisers to sort data (plants vs animals, push vs pull objects, seasonal changes across the year); order data (sequential images of plant growth, seasonal changes); and identify patterns in organised data.
wider: Use pictographs with drawings or digital photographs to document patterns of plant growth
Order images of seasonal changes across the year — examining time-ordered pattern representation
Use graphic organisers to sort objects that need a push vs pull force to work

descriptors.title: Evaluating
descriptors.description: compare observations with predictions and others' observations, consider if investigations are fair and identify further questions with guidance
descriptors.knowledge: Students have made observations and predictions (F band). They now begin to compare these with others and consider fairness — guided by the teacher.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare their observations with predictions and with others' observations, consider with guidance whether an investigation was fair, and identify further questions prompted by their observations.

nodes.label: Observations are compared with predictions and others
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare their observation with their prediction (did it match?) and compare their observation with another student's observation, identifying at least one similarity or difference.
criteria: Compares observation with prediction and states whether it matched
Compares observation with at least one other student's and identifies a similarity or difference

width.minimum: Students compare their observation with their prediction and with one other student's observation.
width.typical: Students compare observations with predictions across investigations; compare observations with others (bird counts, plant growth, object movement); consider whether differences might be due to an unfair investigation; and identify one further question prompted by an unexpected observation.
wider: Consult with First Nations Australians to compare observations and evaluate identifications of animal tracks — examining how knowledge of Country informs observation comparison
Explore if making weather observations at different times of day makes a difference — considering fairness of comparison
Compare how far an object travels with different students pushing and discuss how to make the investigation fairer

descriptors.title: Communicating
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate observations, findings and ideas, using everyday and scientific vocabulary
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share ideas informally (F band). They now begin to create texts — written, drawn, modelled or role-played — that communicate observations and ideas using both everyday and scientific vocabulary.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write and create texts to communicate science observations and ideas, using scientific vocabulary alongside everyday language and selecting from a range of forms (drawing, model, label, role-play, sequential representation).

nodes.label: Texts communicate science observations using scientific vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a text (written, drawn, modelled or performed) that communicates a science observation or idea, using at least two science vocabulary terms correctly.
criteria: Creates a text communicating a science observation in at least one form (drawing, model, labels, role-play)
Uses at least two science vocabulary terms correctly in the text

width.minimum: Students create a text communicating a science observation and use at least two science vocabulary terms.
width.typical: Students explore the difference between everyday and scientific vocabulary; create models, drawings, labels, arrows or role-plays to represent observations (habitats, seasonal changes, force effects); represent sequential changes using drawings or photographs; and describe their representations using both everyday and scientific vocabulary.
wider: Acknowledge and learn about First Nations Australians' ways of representing and sharing observations — examining diverse communication forms for scientific knowledge
Represent push and pull forces using role-play, labels, arrows or time-lapse drawings — applying multiple representation forms to the same concept
Role-play or recount how people use patterns to make predictions at work or in daily life (AC9S1H01)

descriptors.title: Basic needs of plants and animals
descriptors.description: identify the basic needs of plants and animals, including air, water, food or shelter, and describe how the places they live meet those needs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can observe and describe features of living things and their environments (AC9SFU01, F band). They have not yet systematically identified needs of living things or described how habitat features meet those needs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the basic needs of plants and animals (air, water, food, shelter) and describe how features of the places they live meet those needs — connecting habitat features to specific survival requirements.

nodes.label: Living things have basic needs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the basic needs of plants and animals — air, water, food and shelter — and explain that all living things must have their needs met to survive.
criteria: Names the four basic needs of living things (air, water, food, shelter)
Gives at least one example of each need being met for a named plant or animal
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to understand what basic needs are before they can describe how habitat features meet those needs. Without knowing what air, water, food and shelter mean as needs, students cannot reason about which habitat features are relevant or why.

width.minimum: Students name the basic needs of plants and animals and give one example of each need being met for a named living thing.
width.typical: Students identify and compare the needs of a variety of plants and animals including humans; explain that different living things have the same basic needs even if they meet them differently; and connect their own experiences (caring for pets, watering plants) to need-meeting.
wider: Recognise how First Nations Australians care for living things — examining how traditional ecological knowledge addresses the needs of plants and animals on Country
Explore why caring for plants and animals matters beyond the individual — as sources of food, fibre and ecological balance
Learning from farmers, bush care volunteers or nursery owners about how they observe plant and animal needs and design habitats to meet them

nodes.label: The places living things live meet their needs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how features of a named habitat meet the basic needs of a plant or animal that lives there.
criteria: Identifies a named habitat and describes how at least two features of it meet the needs of a living thing found there
Explains why those features matter for the living thing's survival

width.minimum: Students identify one place a named plant or animal lives and describe how at least two features of that place meet its needs.
width.typical: Students identify multiple habitats (pond, garden, forest, home) and describe how each provides for the needs of the living things found there; create dioramas or models showing need-meeting features; and explain why a living thing removed from its habitat may struggle to survive.
wider: Identify ways local gardens or parks could better meet the needs of native animals — connecting habitat features to design decisions
Learn from local ecologists or wildlife carers about native animals' needs and how they observe behaviour to design supports (frog hotels, nesting boxes)
Exploring how First Nations Australians use science to meet their needs — food, water supply and shelter — through understanding of local habitats

modes.reason: Students commonly think only of one or two familiar habitats (garden, home). Encountering a range of habitat types — aquatic, terrestrial, domestic, wild — and the different ways each meets living thing needs builds a more complete and generalisable model of habitat-need matching.

descriptors.title: Daily and seasonal changes
descriptors.description: describe daily and seasonal changes in the environment and explore how these changes affect everyday life
descriptors.knowledge: Students can observe and describe features of their local environment (F band). They have not yet described daily and seasonal change patterns or connected those patterns to effects on living things and human decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe observable daily changes (weather, temperature, day length) and seasonal patterns, and explain how these changes affect plants, animals and human daily life — including clothing, activity planning and habitat use.

nodes.label: The environment changes daily and across seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe observable daily changes (weather, temperature, daylight) and identify seasonal patterns across the year.
criteria: Describes at least two observable daily changes in the environment
Names at least two seasons and describes one observable environmental change for each
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to have identified daily and seasonal change patterns before they can reason about how those changes affect people, plants and animals. Without an established pattern model, N2 explanations reduce to isolated anecdotes rather than pattern-based reasoning.

width.minimum: Students describe at least two daily changes in the environment and name at least two seasons with one observable change for each.
width.typical: Students make and record observations of daily weather changes and seasonal patterns in plants (leaf colour, flowering, dropping leaves) and weather; identify patterns across days and seasons; and explain what makes one season different from another using observable evidence.
wider: Recognise the extensive knowledges of daily and seasonal change held by First Nations Australians — examining how traditional seasonal calendars describe environmental patterns beyond the four-season European model
Explore how First Nations Australians' concepts of time and weather patterns explain how things happen in the world around them
Investigate how seasonal changes affect animals including hibernation and migration — connecting seasonal pattern to animal behaviour

modes.reason: First Nations seasonal calendars and animal behaviour directions broaden the pattern model beyond the European four-season framework, providing culturally rich and ecologically grounded encounters with seasonal change that deepen the concept before N2 applies it.

nodes.label: Daily and seasonal changes affect everyday life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how daily weather and seasonal changes affect decisions people make and how plants and animals respond to these changes.
criteria: Describes at least one way daily weather change affects a human decision
Describes at least one way seasonal change affects a plant or animal

width.minimum: Students describe at least one way daily weather changes affect human decisions and one way seasonal change affects a plant or animal.
width.typical: Students explain how daily weather indicators and seasonal patterns help people plan activities and clothing choices; investigate how seasonal changes affect animals (hibernation, migration) and plants; and connect their own experiences of responding to weather and season to the broader pattern.
wider: Explore how people make clothing choices using weather predictions or seasonal knowledge — connecting observable pattern to everyday decision-making
Investigate how changes in weather affect plants and animals including humans
Recognising how First Nations Australians use changes in landscape and sky to answer questions about when to gather certain resources

modes.reason: Students readily connect seasonal change to their own clothing choices but miss the broader effects on other living things and on planning decisions. Encountering multiple ways daily and seasonal change affects daily life — human, plant and animal — builds a more complete model of environmental change and response.

descriptors.title: Pushes and pulls
descriptors.description: describe pushes and pulls in terms of strength and direction and predict the effect of these forces on objects' motion and shape
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally experienced pushing and pulling objects. They have not yet described forces in terms of strength and direction or predicted their effects on motion and shape.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe pushes and pulls in terms of strength (stronger/weaker) and direction, predict how push and pull forces affect the motion and shape of objects, and represent forces using simple labels, arrows or role-play.

nodes.label: Pushes and pulls have strength and direction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a force is a push or a pull, describe its direction, and compare the strength of forces (stronger/weaker).
criteria: Identifies at least three objects requiring a push or pull and names the direction of each force
Compares the strength of forces needed for at least two objects
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to apply strength and direction concepts when predicting force effects. Without being able to characterise a force by its direction and relative strength, students cannot reason about why changing the force changes the outcome for motion or shape.

width.minimum: Students identify at least three everyday objects that require a push or pull, describe the direction of each force, and compare the strength needed.
width.typical: Students observe and manipulate everyday objects (playground equipment, toys, doors, windows); identify the push or pull required; describe direction and strength; and explain that changing strength or direction changes the outcome for the object.
wider: Investigate the push and pull movements of traditional First Nations Australians' children's instructive toys — examining how force direction and strength produce different play outcomes
Explore how traditional Asian toys and games (kendama, Daruma Otoshi, shuttlecock) are played using push or pull forces
Identify how we use pushes and pulls when preparing meals and the tools that help us push or pull objects

modes.reason: Traditional toys from First Nations and Asian cultural contexts provide culturally rich and hands-on directions that ground force concepts in diverse real-world objects, building a more complete model of strength and direction before students apply these to prediction in N2.

nodes.label: Forces affect motion and shape
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and describe how pushes and pulls affect the motion (start, stop, change direction, speed) and shape (squash, stretch) of objects.
criteria: Predicts the effect of a push or pull on an object's motion or shape before observing
Describes how changing force strength or direction changes the outcome for the object

width.minimum: Students describe how a push or pull affects the motion of one object and the shape of one object, and make a prediction before observing.
width.typical: Students investigate how push and pull forces start or stop motion, change direction of travel, or change the shape of materials (playdough, soft objects); make and check predictions about force effects; and represent forces using labels, arrows or role-play.
wider: Investigate how the design of sporting equipment (paddles, plastic bats, racquets) produces stronger pushes and pulls — connecting force concepts to design
Design playground equipment, toys or games and represent push and pull forces using models, digital drawings or role-play
Explore how engineers use knowledge of forces to create new playground equipment or toys (AC9S1H01)

modes.reason: Students readily observe that pushing makes things move but need explicit scaffolding to predict effects before observing and to connect force strength/direction to specific motion or shape outcomes. The prediction-then-observe sequence is the primary scaffold at this year level.

descriptors.title: Earth in the solar system
descriptors.description: recognise Earth is a planet in the solar system and identify patterns in the changing position of the sun, moon, planets and stars in the sky
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe daily and seasonal changes in the environment (AC9S1U02). They have not yet placed Earth within the solar system or examined patterns in the changing position of celestial objects as a systematic phenomena.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise Earth as a planet in the solar system, identify observable patterns in the changing position of the sun, moon and stars across days and months, and make predictions based on those patterns.

nodes.label: Earth is a planet in the solar system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe Earth as a planet in the solar system, name other planets and the sun, and describe the shape of Earth using images from space.
criteria: Names Earth as a planet in the solar system and identifies at least two other planets
Describes the shape of Earth using evidence from space images
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to know what celestial objects are and that Earth is positioned within a solar system — without this, students cannot distinguish patterns in celestial object positions from generic environmental change (already covered in Y1). The solar system framework is the necessary context for sky pattern investigation.

width.minimum: Students name Earth as a planet in the solar system, name at least two other planets, and describe the shape of Earth.
width.typical: Students explore representations of the solar system; identify Earth and other planets; describe Earth's shape from space images; distinguish celestial objects visible during the day (sun) from those visible at night (moon, stars, planets); and name the sun as the central body.
wider: Explore how cultural stories of First Nations Peoples of Australia describe patterns in the changing positions of the sun, moon and stars — comparing with Western astronomical frameworks
Create a class model of the solar system and name the sun and planets — representing scale and position relationships
Distinguish between regular sky events (full moon cycle) and irregular events (blood moon, blue moon) — examining the difference between predictable patterns and rare phenomena

modes.reason: First Nations astronomical knowledge and solar system modelling broaden students' encounter with sky objects beyond a single framework — building the richer conceptual model of Earth's position that N2 pattern observation requires.

nodes.label: Celestial objects show observable patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe patterns in the changing position of the sun across a day and the changing appearance of the moon across a month, and use these patterns to make predictions.
criteria: Describes the pattern of the sun's movement across a day (direction and shadow change)
Describes the pattern of moon shape change across a month and makes one prediction based on this pattern

width.minimum: Students describe the pattern of the sun's position across a day and describe at least two phases of the moon, using these to make one prediction.
width.typical: Students observe and record how shadow length changes with the changing position of the sun; create a moon diary across a month identifying the pattern of changing moon shape; observe and describe short-term and longer-term sky patterns; and make predictions based on identified patterns.
wider: Observe the changing appearance of the moon across a month and make predictions about future phases — connecting pattern observation to scientific prediction
View time-lapse video of sun, moon, stars or satellite movement across the sky — using digital tools to observe patterns invisible at normal timescales
Explore how First Nations Peoples use patterns in the night sky for navigation and timekeeping — examining practical applications of astronomical pattern knowledge

modes.reason: Students see sky events as random rather than patterned. Making the pattern explicit — sun position changes predictably across each day; moon shape changes predictably across each month — and using those patterns to make and check predictions is the core reasoning scaffold at this year level.

descriptors.title: Sound
descriptors.description: explore different actions to make sounds and how to make a variety of sounds, and recognise that sound energy causes objects to vibrate
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally experienced sound. They have not yet investigated the relationship between actions, vibration and sound production, or explored how sound can be varied (louder, softer, higher, lower).
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how different actions (striking, blowing, plucking, scraping, shaking) produce sounds, explain that sound energy causes objects to vibrate, and investigate how to vary sound properties including loudness and pitch.

nodes.label: Sound is produced by different actions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe different actions that produce sound, classify instruments or objects by the action used to produce their sound, and explain that all sound production involves some form of action on an object.
criteria: Names at least four different actions that produce sound with an example of each
Classifies at least three instruments or objects by the action used to produce their sound

width.minimum: Students name at least four different sound-producing actions and give one example of each.
width.typical: Students explore different ways to produce sound (striking, blowing, scraping, plucking, shaking); classify instruments by action type; explore how traditional musical instruments used by First Nations Australians produce their characteristic sounds; and design and make simple instruments that produce sounds.
wider: Explore how traditional musical instruments used by First Nations Australians produce their characteristic sounds — examining action-to-sound relationships in culturally specific instruments
Design and make instruments that produce different sounds — applying sound production knowledge in a design context
Explore how voices have a unique sound and investigate voice-activated tools — connecting voice pattern recognition to everyday technology

modes.reason: First Nations instrument direction and instrument design provide culturally rich and creative directions that build a broader repertoire of action-to-sound relationships, enriching the concept before N2 applies the vibration mechanism across those same contexts.

nodes.label: Sound energy causes objects to vibrate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that sound energy causes objects to vibrate, observe and describe vibrations produced by sound-making objects, and connect the speed or strength of vibration to sound properties.
criteria: Describes vibrations in a named sound-making object
Explains that the object vibrates because of sound energy

width.minimum: Students describe vibrations in at least one sound-making object and explain that the object is vibrating because of sound energy.
width.typical: Students observe vibrations from a twanged ruler, tuning fork or music speaker; explain that sound energy causes vibrating; investigate how the speed or strength of vibration relates to loudness or pitch; and describe how sound travels through different materials — connecting vibration to hearing.
wider: Investigate which materials best muffle sound — examining how different materials absorb or block vibrations
Discuss situations where students have heard echoes and explore how animals (dolphins, bats) use echolocation — connecting sound vibration to navigation
Explore how music can be understood as patterns of sounds — connecting vibration to the structured organisation of sound in music (AC9S2H01)

modes.reason: Students commonly believe sound is simply noise rather than energy that causes physical vibration. Making the vibration mechanism explicit — sound energy → object vibrates → vibration travels through medium → detected as sound — is the key conceptual scaffold before students can explain how sound behaves in different materials or conditions.

descriptors.title: Physical changes to materials
descriptors.description: recognise that materials can be changed physically without changing their material composition and explore the effect of different actions on materials including bending, twisting, stretching and breaking into smaller pieces
descriptors.knowledge: Students can observe and describe properties of materials (AC9SFU03, F band). They have not yet distinguished between changing the form of a material and changing its composition, or systematically explored multiple physical change actions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that physical actions (bending, twisting, stretching, folding, cutting, crushing) change the shape or size of a material without changing what it is made of, and explore how different materials respond differently to the same physical action.

nodes.label: Physical changes alter shape without changing composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that physically changing a material (bending, twisting, stretching, breaking) changes its shape or size but not what it is made of.
criteria: Applies at least two physical changes to a material and names each action
Explains that the material is still the same substance after a physical change — only its shape or size has changed
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to accept that physical action changes form but not composition before they can reason about why different materials respond differently to the same action. Without the composition-vs-form distinction, students conflate different physical outcomes with different materials — blocking the comparison at N2.

width.minimum: Students demonstrate at least two physical changes to a material and explain that the material is still the same substance after the change.
width.typical: Students manipulate materials (paper, fabric, playdough, wool); apply multiple physical changes (scrunching, twisting, bending, cutting, tearing, folding); explain that the material is still the same even though its shape has changed; and compare the properties of the original and changed material.
wider: Crush a stick of chalk into powder — comparing properties of the stick and powder and discussing whether it is still the same material
Explore how First Nations Australians make physical changes to natural materials to produce objects such as bowls, baskets and fibre crafts — examining purposeful physical transformation
Create an 'odd one out' game using samples of the same material changed in different ways plus one different material — applying composition knowledge to a classification challenge

modes.reason: Students commonly believe that dramatically changing the shape of a material (crushing chalk, folding paper into a plane) creates a different material. Making the composition-vs-form distinction explicit — the shape changes, what it is made of does not — is the essential conceptual scaffold before students can correctly distinguish physical from chemical change in later years.

nodes.label: Different actions affect materials differently
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore and describe how different physical actions affect different materials and explain how physical changes can be purposeful.
criteria: Compares how the same physical action affects two different materials
Describes at least one physical change that is purposeful — explaining why the change is useful

width.minimum: Students compare how the same action affects two different materials and describe the result of each.
width.typical: Students investigate how different materials respond to the same actions (twisting cotton wool vs paper vs fabric); explore how physical changes can be purposeful (twisting strands of cotton to make thread stronger, folding paper to make it fly); and describe multiple ways the same material can be physically changed.
wider: Explore how materials can be physically changed to suit a particular purpose — twisting cotton to make thread stronger, folding paper to make it fly
Learn from people who work with materials (woodworkers, fibre artists, sculptors) about how they learn about material properties and use creativity when manipulating them (AC9S2H01)
Explore how physically changing materials helps us re-use them — connecting physical change to waste reduction

modes.reason: Material worker perspectives (AC9S2H01) and purposeful change directions provide authentic real-world connections that show physical transformation as intentional and contextually meaningful — enriching the concept beyond classroom manipulation tasks.

descriptors.title: Data and scientific explanations
descriptors.description: examine how people use data to develop scientific explanations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how people use science in daily life and use patterns to make scientific predictions (AC9S1H01, 1-2 band). They have not yet examined the specific role of data in developing scientific explanations or how the scientific community shares and evaluates explanations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how scientists and other knowledge-holders use data to develop and support scientific explanations, identifying what data is, how it is collected, and how it supports — rather than simply produces — an explanation.

nodes.label: Data is recorded evidence from observations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish data from explanation — identifying what counts as data (recorded observations, measurements, survey results) and what counts as an explanation (an account of why or how).
criteria: Distinguishes data from explanation given a mixed set of statements from a scenario
Explains that data is collected through observation or measurement, and that the scientist uses the data to construct an explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: The data/explanation distinction is the foundational concept for the entire standard. Students who cannot separate what was recorded from what it means cannot examine the data-to-explanation pathway in Node 3, and will conflate evidence and conclusion in all subsequent inquiry work.

width.minimum: Students identify examples of data and examples of explanations from a given scenario and describe the difference between the two.
width.typical: Students explain that data is collected through systematic observation or measurement, and that data supports (but does not automatically produce) an explanation — the scientist interprets the data.
wider: Examine a simple scientific journal article or report and identify the data section and explanation/conclusion section — exploring why scientists communicate this way

Explore how First Nations Australians develop and test predictions through systematic observation — for example, observing landscape features or seasonal indicators — and discuss what makes this a form of data collection
Investigate the difference between reliable and unreliable data (one observation vs many observations, careful vs careless measurement)

modes.reason: The data/explanation distinction is non-obvious at Year 4. Students tend to treat observations and explanations as the same kind of thing — 'I saw X therefore X happens'. Making the distinction explicit (data describes what was recorded; explanation accounts for why it happened using the data) is a necessary scaffold before students can examine how scientists move from data to explanation.

nodes.label: Scientists collect data to answer questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how scientists or knowledge-holders collect data in response to a question, including the type of data collected and why that data is relevant to the question.
criteria: Describes a specific example of how a named person or group collected data to answer a question
Explains how the data collected connects to the question being answered

width.minimum: Students describe how a scientist or knowledge-holder collected data to answer a specific question, naming the type of data and explaining how it connects to the question.
width.typical: Students examine two contrasting contexts for scientific data collection (e.g. ecologist counting species; hydrologist measuring rainfall) and explain how each type of data connects to the explanations those scientists develop.
wider: Examine documentary or news content featuring researchers and identify how they describe their data collection — what they count, measure or observe, and what question they are trying to answer

Investigate how First Nations Australians test predictions and gather data in the development of technologies and processes — for example, testing plant properties or observing animal behaviour patterns

Compare data collection for ecological questions (food chains, species populations) with data collection for physical questions (force, material properties) — what kinds of data suit different types of questions

modes.reason: Students tend to have a narrow image of 'scientist with a test tube' for data collection. Varied authentic contexts — ecologists, hydrologists, First Nations knowledge-holders — broaden the concept of what counts as scientific data collection and who engages in it, preventing a narrow stereotype from limiting students' understanding.

nodes.label: Data supports the development of explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a real-world case where data was used to develop a scientific explanation, tracing the connection between the data collected and the explanation produced.
criteria: Identifies what data was collected and what explanation it supported in a given real-world case
Explains that data supports an explanation rather than automatically producing one — the scientist interprets the data

width.minimum: Students describe a real-world case where data was used to develop a scientific explanation, identifying what data was collected and what explanation it supported.
width.typical: Students examine how ecologists use food chain data to explain population decline of native species and develop management strategies, connecting data type to explanation quality — more data, better explanation.
wider: Investigate how hydrologists use rainfall and water use data to explain seasonal river flow variation (AC9S4U02 connection) — showing how the same data type supports multiple explanations
Examine a case where limited data produced an incomplete explanation, and discuss what additional data would be needed to improve it
Research how First Nations Australians use accumulated observational knowledge — passed across generations — as a form of long-term data that supports explanations about ecological patterns

modes.reason: Students tend to see data as simply 'proving' an explanation rather than as evidence that supports it — missing the interpretive step and the idea that more varied data produces stronger explanations. Examining multiple real-world cases (ecology, hydrology) where the same kind of data work is done in different contexts helps students develop a more general understanding of how data functions in science.

descriptors.title: Scientific explanations meet needs
descriptors.description: consider how people use scientific explanations to meet a need or solve a problem
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how science knowledge has changed peoples' lives (AC9S3H02, 3-4 band). They have not yet examined the specific link between a scientific explanation and the design of a solution — the mechanism by which understanding produces application.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how scientific explanations about natural phenomena are applied by people to meet needs or solve problems, and identify the explanation-to-application pathway in real-world examples including First Nations knowledge applications.

nodes.label: Scientific explanations can be applied to solve problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a scientific explanation (an account of how or why something happens) and an application (a solution that uses that explanation to meet a need), and identify examples of each.
criteria: Identifies the scientific explanation and the problem it addresses for a given application example
Describes how the scientific explanation was used to design or improve the solution
nodes.hinge_reason: The explanation-to-application pathway is the analytical frame for the entire standard. Students who cannot separate the explanation from the application cannot analyse real-world cases in Node 2, and will default to describing applications as isolated inventions without connecting them to underlying scientific knowledge.

width.minimum: Students identify a scientific explanation and the problem-solving application it enabled for at least one example, describing the connection between them.
width.typical: Students describe the pathway from explanation to application for two contrasting examples, explaining what the scientific knowledge was and how it was used to design or improve a solution.
wider: Compare how the same scientific explanation (e.g. friction) has been applied in multiple different contexts — vehicle safety, sport, manufacturing — and discuss how the application differs while the underlying explanation remains the same
Examine historical examples where a scientific explanation changed how a problem was approached — e.g. germ theory changing medicine, decomposer knowledge enabling composting at industrial scale
Research how First Nations Australians apply deep knowledge of plant biology or ecological relationships to develop sustainable solutions

modes.reason: The explanation-to-application pathway is not intuitive — students tend to see applications as separate from science rather than as science knowledge in action. Making the chain explicit (what is the explanation? → what problem does it address? → how is the explanation used in the solution?) scaffolds students' ability to analyse new application examples independently.

nodes.label: Examining real applications of science knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine real-world cases where scientific knowledge was applied to meet a need, identifying the specific knowledge used and the problem or need it addressed.
criteria: Identifies the specific scientific knowledge (not just 'science') that enabled a named application
Explains the problem or need the application was designed to address

width.minimum: Students examine at least two real-world application cases from different contexts (e.g. one ecological, one materials-based) and identify the scientific explanation behind each.
width.typical: Students examine applications across the Y4 science concepts — decomposers in composting, magnetic force in recycling sorting, friction in car safety, properties of plastic in consumer choices — and describe the explanation-to-application pathway for each.
wider: Investigate how knowledge of friction is used to improve safety on wet and icy roads — examining tyre design, road surfacing, and braking systems
Research how knowledge of magnetic force is applied in recycling, mining and food processing — tracing how one scientific explanation supports multiple industries
Investigate how First Nations Australians of arid regions use scientific knowledge to manage water resources — including evaporation management and water source identification

modes.reason: Students tend to see science applications as isolated inventions rather than as a repeated pattern of explanation-to-application. Examining multiple cases across the Y4 concepts — each following the same pathway structure — helps students recognise the pattern and build a more generalisable understanding of how science knowledge is applied.

nodes.label: Science knowledge influences decisions and practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how scientific knowledge has influenced how people make decisions or change their practices — not only in designed solutions but in everyday choices and policy.
criteria: Describes an example where scientific knowledge changed how people make decisions or behave, identifying the knowledge and the change
Distinguishes between an engineered application (a designed product) and a behavioural or practice change as two different ways science knowledge is used

width.minimum: Students describe at least one example where scientific knowledge changed how people behave or make decisions (e.g. plastic disposal, water conservation), explaining what the knowledge was and what changed.
width.typical: Students examine how knowledge of plastic properties has influenced purchasing, use and disposal practices, and how this differs from engineered applications — connecting scientific knowledge to individual and community decision-making.
wider: Research a community or policy response to a scientific finding (e.g. water restrictions based on hydrological data; species protection based on ecological knowledge) and explain the knowledge-to-decision pathway

Compare two decisions influenced by different scientific knowledge — one where the knowledge led to a designed solution, one where it changed behaviour — and discuss the different ways science knowledge shapes human action
Examine how knowledges of plant biology enable First Nations Australians to sustainably harvest and use plants — tracing how deep ecological knowledge shapes sustainable practice decisions

modes.reason: This node asks students to integrate the explanation-to-application framework with a new dimension — behavioural and policy change — alongside designed solutions. Students must coordinate the same underlying idea (knowledge informs action) across a broader range of outcomes than engineered solutions alone.

descriptors.title: Questioning and predicting
descriptors.description: pose questions to explore observed patterns and relationships and make predictions based on observations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can pose simple questions and make predictions based on their experiences (AC9S1I01, 1-2 band). They have not yet posed questions that target patterns or relationships specifically, or made predictions that are explicitly grounded in prior observations rather than intuition.
descriptors.endpoint: Students pose investigable questions that target patterns and relationships in observed phenomena, and make predictions that are explicitly grounded in prior observations, distinguishing between questions that can be tested and those that cannot.

nodes.label: Questions target patterns and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose investigable questions that go beyond naming or describing — targeting a pattern (what changes when X changes?) or relationship (how does X affect Y?) in an observed phenomenon.
criteria: Poses a question that targets a relationship or pattern (not just a description) for a given observation
Explains what observable pattern or relationship the question is designed to explore
nodes.hinge_reason: A relationship question is the prerequisite input to investigation planning (AC9S3I02). Students who cannot distinguish relationship questions from descriptive questions will design descriptive observation tasks rather than fair tests, collapsing the planning scaffold in the next standard.

width.minimum: Students reframe a descriptive question into a relationship question for a given observation context, and explain what distinguishes the two.
width.typical: Students pose their own relationship questions for two different science contexts (biological, physical or materials-based) and explain what observable pattern or relationship each question targets.
wider: Examine how ecologists pose questions about population patterns — e.g. 'What happens to prey populations when predators are removed?' — and compare to descriptive questions about the same topic
Explore how First Nations Australians pose questions about patterns in Country — observing landscape and seasonal indicators to predict resource availability
Investigate the difference between a question that can be tested in a classroom and one that requires field observation or a longer time scale

modes.reason: The shift from descriptive ('what is this?') to relationship ('how does X affect Y?') questioning is non-obvious and requires explicit modelling. Students need to see the structural difference between question types before they can generate relationship questions independently. Without this scaffold, students default to description questions that do not guide investigation design.

nodes.label: Predictions are grounded in prior observations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make predictions that are explicitly linked to prior observations or patterns they have noticed, and distinguish between a prediction (grounded in evidence) and a guess.
criteria: Makes a prediction that is explicitly linked to a prior observation or identified pattern
Distinguishes their prediction from a guess by explaining the observational basis

width.minimum: Students make a prediction for a given investigation scenario and explain what prior observation or pattern their prediction is based on.
width.typical: Students make predictions for two contrasting investigation contexts, explain the observational basis for each, and revise a prediction when additional information is provided.
wider: Investigate how predictions about food chains (e.g. what happens when a predator is removed) are grounded in observations about feeding relationships

Consult with, or explore resources about, how First Nations Australians predict the location of water sources from landscape feature observations — examining what constitutes an observation-based prediction
Make predictions about magnetic force at different distances based on a pattern identified from initial observations, then test them

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate predictions with guesses or wishes ('I predict the magnet will pick it up because I want it to'). Encountering prediction-making across varied science contexts — biological, physical, ecological — helps students build a more general understanding of what makes a prediction observation-based rather than arbitrary.

descriptors.title: Planning and conducting
descriptors.description: use provided scaffolds to plan and conduct investigations to answer questions or test predictions, including identifying the elements of fair tests, and considering the safe use of materials and equipment
