descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow instructions to conduct investigations safely and make observations (AC9S1I02, 1-2 band). They have not yet identified the elements of a fair test or used a provided scaffold to plan an investigation, as opposed to following a given procedure.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use provided scaffolds to plan investigations that test a prediction, identify and control the elements of a fair test (variable to change, variable to measure, variables to keep the same), and conduct investigations safely with appropriate materials and equipment.

nodes.label: Fair tests control variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the variable being changed, the variable being measured, and the variables that must be kept the same in a fair test, and explain why controlling variables makes a test fair.
criteria: Identifies the variable being changed, the variable being measured, and at least two variables kept the same in a given investigation
Explains why keeping variables the same makes the test fair (not just states the rule)
nodes.hinge_reason: Variable identification is the prerequisite for completing an investigation scaffold (Node 2). Students who cannot identify what to change, measure and keep the same cannot populate the planning scaffold meaningfully — they produce a scaffold with blanks or incorrect entries that make the planned investigation unworkable.

width.minimum: Students identify the independent, dependent and control variables in a given investigation scenario using the terms 'what I change', 'what I measure' and 'what I keep the same'.
width.typical: Students explain why each variable must be treated as described — connecting the rationale for keeping variables the same to the reliability of the result — and identify what would make a test unfair.
wider: Analyse an investigation scenario with a flaw (an uncontrolled variable) and explain specifically how the flaw affects the reliability of any conclusion drawn
Examine how simulations (food chain role-play, virtual habitat models) control variables in ways that real investigations cannot — what are the trade-offs
Compare fair test design for different investigation types from Y4 science contexts (friction, magnetic force, material properties) and discuss how the variables differ across contexts

modes.reason: The variable control logic is non-obvious. Students understand 'only change one thing' as a rule without understanding why — they do not connect uncontrolled variables to unreliable conclusions. Making the reasoning chain visible (if we change two things at once → we cannot tell which one caused the result → our conclusion is unreliable) is the scaffold that allows students to identify fair test elements purposefully rather than mechanically.

nodes.label: Using a scaffold to plan an investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a provided investigation scaffold to plan a fair test that answers a given question, including identifying variables, selecting materials and outlining a procedure.
criteria: Completes a provided scaffold with all required elements: question, prediction, variable to change, variable to measure, variables to keep the same, and procedure steps
Procedure steps are described clearly enough that another student could follow them

width.minimum: Students complete a provided investigation scaffold for a given question, correctly identifying variables and describing the steps of the procedure.
width.typical: Students use a provided scaffold to plan a fair test for a question they have generated, evaluate whether their plan addresses all elements of a fair test, and identify any gaps.
wider: Plan and build a prototype to test a prediction (e.g. toy or game design predicting force interactions) using a provided scaffold — connecting design thinking to fair test planning
Compare two student-generated plans for the same question and evaluate which is the fairer test, identifying specific improvements

Explore how professional investigation protocols in science (lab procedures, field survey protocols) serve the same function as classroom scaffolds — standardising what is changed, measured and controlled

modes.reason: Students tend to transfer fair test planning mechanically to new investigation contexts — repeating a familiar procedure rather than adapting the scaffold to the new question. Encountering the scaffold across varied investigation types (friction, materials, food chains, magnetic force) builds flexible application of the planning framework.

nodes.label: Safe and appropriate use of materials and equipment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify safety considerations relevant to a planned investigation and demonstrate safe behaviour when using materials and equipment, including field site considerations.
criteria: Identifies at least two safety considerations relevant to a specific investigation
Demonstrates correct safety behaviour when conducting an investigation (PPE use, equipment handling)

width.minimum: Students identify at least two safety considerations relevant to a given investigation and explain the safe procedure for each.
width.typical: Students apply safety rules appropriately in practice — wearing PPE correctly, using equipment according to guidelines, and identifying and managing risks in a field site or biological specimen investigation.
wider: Compare safety requirements across different investigation contexts — classroom (chemical or physical), field (biological specimens, outdoor sites) — and explain why contexts require different safety measures
Research how professional scientists manage safety in their investigation contexts — lab safety protocols, field site risk assessments

Limited width — safety procedure following is a compliance and precision skill. Extensions exist (risk assessment design, professional safety protocols) but these go beyond the Y4 band. The key demand at this year level is applying given safety rules correctly, not designing safety protocols.

modes.reason: Safe equipment use and PPE compliance require consistent accurate practice, not broader conceptual understanding. Students need repeated application of safety procedures across different investigations to build reliable safe behaviour. This is a precision-required procedural skill where practice is the primary lever.

descriptors.title: Observing and measuring
descriptors.description: follow procedures to make and record observations, including making formal measurements using familiar scaled instruments and using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can make and record observations using their senses and simple tools (AC9S1I03/I04, 1-2 band). They have not yet used scaled instruments with formal measurement conventions or discussed the effect of scale size on measurement accuracy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students follow procedures to make and record systematic observations, use familiar scaled instruments accurately (including reading scales and applying rounding conventions), and use digital tools where appropriate to record observations.

nodes.label: Reading scaled instruments accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read a value from a familiar scaled instrument (ruler, thermometer, measuring cylinder, balance) and apply rounding conventions when the reading falls between scale divisions.
criteria: Reads a value from a familiar scaled instrument to the nearest marked division
Applies rounding correctly when a reading falls between two scale divisions
Identifies a more or less accurate instrument for a given measurement task based on scale size
nodes.hinge_reason: Instrument reading accuracy is a prerequisite for data quality in all subsequent inquiry work. Systematic reading errors (wrong end of ruler, meniscus ignored) propagate into every data set students produce, making conclusions from those data unreliable. Students who cannot read instruments correctly cannot produce usable data for AC9S3I04 or AC9S3I05.

width.minimum: Students read values from at least two types of scaled instruments and correctly apply rounding (up or down) when a value falls between scale markings.
width.typical: Students explain the effect of scale size on measurement accuracy — a ruler with 1mm divisions is more accurate than one with 1cm divisions for the same measurement — and select an appropriate instrument for a given measurement task.
wider: Investigate how the choice of scale increments affects the conclusions that can be drawn — can a difference between two objects be detected if the scale is too coarse?
Compare digital and analogue instruments for the same measurement — what are the trade-offs in accuracy, ease of use and recording?
Explore how ecologists use specific instruments for field identification — pitfall traps, call identification equipment, GPS — and what each measures

modes.reason: Accurate scale reading requires precision and consistent application of rounding conventions. Errors are common (reading from the wrong end of a ruler, ignoring the meniscus in a measuring cylinder, not aligning the instrument correctly) and affect all subsequent data recording. Repeated accurate practice with feedback is the primary remedy — not broader context variation.

nodes.label: Systematic observation and recording
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a procedure to make observations systematically — recording what is observed in an organised way (table, graphic organiser, labelled diagram) so that it can be used for analysis.
criteria: Records all required observations in a consistent, organised format (table, graphic organiser or diagram as appropriate)
Recording is complete and legible enough that another student could use it for analysis

width.minimum: Students follow a provided procedure to make and record observations in a table or graphic organiser, recording all required observations in a consistent format.
width.typical: Students select an appropriate recording format for a given observation task, explain why that format suits the data type, and complete the recording consistently across multiple observations.
wider: Compare different recording formats for the same data set — table vs graphic organiser vs labelled diagram — and evaluate which is clearest for the type of observations being made
Use digital tools (camera, voice recorder, data logger) to record observations and discuss what digital tools add (timestamping, precision, replayability) compared to written recording
Examine how scientists use field notebooks and digital tools in combination for ecological observations — exploring professional observation recording practice

modes.reason: Students tend to default to one recording format (usually a list or informal notes) regardless of the observation type. Encountering systematic recording across varied observation types — counts, measurements, field identifications, material properties — helps students build a more flexible understanding of how recording format should match data type.

descriptors.title: Processing and representing data
descriptors.description: construct and use representations, including tables, simple column graphs and visual or physical models, to organise data and information, show simple relationships and identify patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent observations in provided templates and identify simple patterns with guidance (AC9SFI03, F band; AC9S1I04, 1-2 band). They have not yet constructed representations independently or used representations specifically to identify patterns and relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students construct and use tables, column graphs, visual models and physical models to organise data, show simple relationships between variables, and identify patterns in data.

nodes.label: Tables organise data for comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a table with appropriate headings to organise data from an investigation, and use the table to make comparisons between observations.
criteria: Constructs a table with appropriate column headings including units where relevant
All required data is recorded in a consistent, complete format
Identifies at least one comparison or pattern from the completed table
nodes.hinge_reason: Table construction accuracy is a prerequisite for column graph work in Node 2 — students typically construct their graph from their table. A table with incorrect headings, missing units, or inconsistent rows produces an ungraphable or misleading data set that collapses Node 2 work.

width.minimum: Students construct a table with correct headings for a given data set and use it to make at least one comparison between rows or columns.
width.typical: Students explain why a table is an appropriate format for their data type, construct the table independently, and identify a pattern or comparison directly from the table.
wider: Compare two different table structures for the same data (e.g. results organised by material type vs by property) and discuss which reveals patterns more clearly
Examine how data tables in scientific reports or textbooks are structured — column headers, units, consistent formatting — and apply professional conventions
Construct a table to record food chain data across multiple habitats and use it to compare structural features of chains across habitats

modes.reason: Table construction requires precision: correct headings, consistent units, all cells filled. Common errors include missing units in column headers, inconsistent recording across rows, and unorganised headings that make comparison difficult. Deliberate practice with feedback on table quality is more productive at this stage than encountering many different data types.

nodes.label: Column graphs display and compare quantities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a column graph with appropriate axes, title and labels for a given data set, and use the graph to identify and describe a pattern.
criteria: Constructs a column graph with labelled axes (including units), a title, and correctly scaled bars
Describes the pattern shown in the graph and connects it to the investigation question

width.minimum: Students construct a column graph with labelled axes and a title for a given data set, and describe what the graph shows.
width.typical: Students select an appropriate scale for the y-axis, construct the graph accurately, and describe the pattern shown — including identifying which condition produced the highest or lowest value and explaining what this means.
wider: Compare the same data displayed as a table vs a column graph — what does the graph make visible that the table does not?
Construct a column graph for friction investigation data (distances moved under different surface conditions) and use it to draw a conclusion about surface friction
Explore when column graphs are and are not appropriate — the difference between categorical data (materials) and continuous data (temperature over time), and why bar graphs suit the former

modes.reason: Column graph construction requires precision across multiple conventions: axis labels with units, appropriate scale, bars at the correct height, title. Errors in any of these undermine the representation's reliability. Consistent accurate practice across multiple data sets is more productive than breadth of data types at this stage.

nodes.label: Visual and physical models represent relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct or use a visual or physical model to represent a scientific relationship, explain what the model shows, and identify its limitations.
criteria: Constructs or interprets a model and explains what relationship or process it represents
Identifies at least one element of the model and explains what it stands for in the real phenomenon
Describes at least one way the model simplifies or differs from the real phenomenon

width.minimum: Students construct or use a given visual or physical model (food chain diagram, force arrow diagram, water cycle model) and explain what relationship or process it represents.
width.typical: Students construct a model for a relationship from Y4 science content, explain what each element of the model represents, and describe at least one thing the model simplifies or leaves out.
wider: Use force arrows to model forces on objects in a range of scenarios — stationary, moving, floating — and discuss how the model shows the relationship between forces
Use a virtual food chain simulation to explore the effects of changing producer or consumer numbers, comparing model predictions with real-world examples
Evaluate a physical model of the water cycle (water cycle in a bag, terrarium) — what does it show accurately, and what does it simplify?

modes.reason: Students tend to treat models as pictures rather than as representations of relationships — they describe what the model looks like rather than what it shows about how things interact. Encountering models across varied science contexts (food chains, forces, water cycle) helps students develop a more general understanding of what models are for and how to read them as representations of relationships.

descriptors.title: Evaluating
descriptors.description: compare findings with those of others, consider if investigations were fair, identify questions for further investigation and draw conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare observations with predictions with guidance, and identify unexpected results (AC9S1I05, 1-2 band). They have not yet systematically evaluated fairness of investigations, drawn evidence-based conclusions, or posed further questions from findings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare their findings with others, evaluate whether their investigation was fair, draw conclusions that are grounded in their data, and identify questions for further investigation arising from their findings or unexpected results.

nodes.label: Conclusions are grounded in data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw a conclusion from an investigation that is directly grounded in the data collected, and distinguish between a conclusion supported by data and a claim that goes beyond the data.
criteria: States a conclusion that accurately reflects the data (does not overclaim)
Identifies at least one piece of data that supports the conclusion
nodes.hinge_reason: Data-grounded conclusion drawing is the payoff of the entire inquiry sequence and feeds directly into AC9S3H01. Students who cannot distinguish a supported conclusion from an overclaim produce unreliable conclusions that undermines the purpose of investigation — and carry this pattern into all subsequent inquiry work.

width.minimum: Students draw a conclusion from a given data set and explain how the data supports the conclusion.
width.typical: Students identify the difference between a conclusion that accurately reflects the data and one that overclaims, and revise an overclaiming conclusion to match the data.
wider: Examine a scenario where two data sets lead to different conclusions — what does this suggest about the investigation?

Evaluate conclusions drawn from food chain simulations (virtual or role-play) against what would actually happen in a real habitat — what does the simulation's simplification mean for the conclusion's validity?
Compare how conclusions are presented in a scientific article (hedged, data-referenced) versus how they appear in a news report (often more absolute) — and discuss why scientists are cautious

modes.reason: The data-to-conclusion chain requires explicit scaffolding. Students commonly draw conclusions that go well beyond what the data shows, or that contradict the data, without recognising the mismatch. Making the chain explicit (what did the data show → what can I conclude from that data → what would I need to be able to say something stronger?) supports more disciplined conclusion-drawing.

nodes.label: Comparing findings and evaluating fairness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare their investigation findings with those of other students or groups, identify differences and suggest reasons for them, and evaluate whether differences are attributable to unfair testing.
criteria: Identifies at least one difference between their findings and another student's findings
Suggests a specific reason for the difference — distinguishing between an unfair test element and a legitimate source of variation

width.minimum: Students compare their findings with at least one other student's findings, identify at least one difference, and suggest a reason for the difference.
width.typical: Students identify whether differences between findings are likely due to an unfair test element (uncontrolled variable) or natural variation, and explain their reasoning.
wider: Compare findings of water use surveys across different homes or contexts and discuss what the differences reveal — and what cannot be concluded without knowing more about the context
Examine findings from the same investigation run multiple times and discuss what repeated results increase confidence in vs what a single result cannot support
Research how scientists handle inconsistent results between research groups — replication, peer review, reporting methods — as the professional version of the same evaluation activity

modes.reason: Students readily identify that someone 'did it wrong' as the reason for different findings, without considering legitimate sources of variation (natural variation, measurement precision, context differences). Varied comparison contexts — water surveys, material tests, force investigations — where different findings are legitimate help students develop a more nuanced understanding of what differences between findings mean.

nodes.label: Identifying questions for further investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify at least one question for further investigation arising from their findings, unexpected results, or limitations of the investigation.
criteria: Identifies at least one question for further investigation that arises specifically from the findings or an unexpected result
Explains what in the investigation prompted the further question

width.minimum: Students identify at least one question arising from their investigation findings or an unexpected result, and explain what prompted the question.
width.typical: Students identify questions arising from both expected and unexpected results, and distinguish between questions they could investigate further in the classroom and questions requiring a different approach (longer time, larger scale, different equipment).
wider: Examine a scenario with unexpected findings and generate two further investigation questions — one that tests whether the unexpected finding is reliable, and one that explores a possible explanation for it
Explore how unexpected findings in real science have led to significant discoveries — connecting the habit of posing further questions to the way science progresses
Connect to AC9S3H01: scientists use unexpected findings and the questions they generate as part of developing scientific explanations

modes.reason: Students who generate further questions only from expected results miss the richer direction — unexpected findings. Encountering varied scenarios where unexpected results prompted real scientific discoveries broadens students' understanding of how further questions function in science practice.

descriptors.title: Communicating
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate findings and ideas for identified purposes and audiences, using scientific vocabulary and digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share questions, predictions, observations and ideas with others in simple forms (AC9S1I06, 1-2 band). They have not yet written or created texts that are explicitly structured for a purpose and audience, or used scientific vocabulary deliberately for communicative effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write and create texts to communicate science findings and ideas for identified purposes and audiences, selecting appropriate text forms and scientific vocabulary, and using digital tools where appropriate.

nodes.label: Texts have purpose, audience and appropriate vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a science text, its intended audience, and how purpose and audience influence the vocabulary and structure of the text.
criteria: Identifies the purpose and audience of a given science text
Explains at least one way the text's vocabulary or structure is shaped by its purpose or audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Purpose-audience awareness is the prerequisite for deliberate text construction in Node 3. Students who have not internalised how purpose and audience shape vocabulary and structure default to a single writing style regardless of the task, making Node 3's selection-and-creation demand impossible to meet.

width.minimum: Students identify the purpose and audience of a given science text and explain at least one way the text is shaped by those factors.
width.typical: Students compare two texts communicating similar science content for different purposes or audiences (e.g. an informative report vs a persuasive poster) and identify structural and vocabulary differences.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians share information about water sources or ecological knowledge using different forms — oral, visual, spatial — and discuss what each form communicates that others don't
Explore a range of text forms used in science communication (journal abstract, news article, infographic, documentary) and identify what purpose and audience each serves
Discuss how digital tools change what is possible in science communication — interactivity, multimedia, global reach

modes.reason: The purpose-audience-vocabulary relationship is non-obvious. Students default to a single writing style regardless of purpose or audience without scaffolding. Making the relationship explicit (who will read this → what do they need to understand → what vocabulary suits them → what structure helps them?) supports more deliberate text construction.

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary in writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate scientific vocabulary in their writing to communicate about science findings, selecting terms that are precise and appropriate for the purpose and audience.
criteria: Uses at least four science vocabulary terms accurately and in context (not just listed)
At least one use of scientific vocabulary achieves precision that an everyday word could not

width.minimum: Students use at least four science vocabulary terms accurately in a piece of written science communication.
width.typical: Students use scientific vocabulary purposefully — not just inserted, but used to communicate precise meaning that everyday words would not achieve — and explain the choice of at least one term.
wider: Produce an informative text using scientific vocabulary to explain the impact of introduced predators on food chains — applying U-strand vocabulary in an HE context
Construct a report using scientific vocabulary to explain which materials are best suited for particular products — connecting vocabulary from U04 to a written analytical task
Investigate how vocabulary use differs between a formal science report and a community-facing poster about the same topic — which terms stay, which are replaced, and why

modes.reason: Students tend to use scientific vocabulary as decoration rather than for precision — inserting terms without using them to carry meaning. Writing across multiple science contexts (food chains, water cycle, forces, materials) in different text forms helps students build a working sense of when scientific vocabulary adds precision and when simpler language suffices.

nodes.label: Selecting form and creating a text for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate text form for a given science communication purpose and audience, and create a text in that form that communicates findings or ideas clearly.
criteria: Creates a text in the specified or selected form that communicates the required science findings or ideas
Uses at least two science vocabulary terms accurately in the text
Text is structured appropriately for the identified purpose and audience

width.minimum: Students create a text in a given form (informative text, poster, report, model) that communicates science findings for a specified purpose and audience.
width.typical: Students select and justify a text form for a given science communication purpose, create the text using appropriate vocabulary and structure, and evaluate whether the text achieves its purpose.
wider: Create a poster, song, slideshow or performance to encourage the school community to save water — choosing and justifying the form for the purpose and audience
Represent feeding relationships in multiple forms (written explanation, labelled diagram, physical model, oral presentation) and compare what each communicates most effectively
Use digital tools to create a multi-modal science text and discuss what the digital form allows that a written or drawn form cannot

modes.reason: Creating a science text for purpose and audience requires students to simultaneously apply vocabulary knowledge, form knowledge, purpose-audience reasoning, and their science content knowledge. All four dimensions must be coordinated in a single product. Students who have each element separately must now deploy them together — this is the integration challenge of the node.

descriptors.title: Life cycles
descriptors.description: compare characteristics of living and non-living things and examine the differences between the life cycles of plants and animals
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and describe features of living things and group them based on observable characteristics (AC9SFU01, F band; AC9S1U01, 1-2 band). They have not yet formally compared living and non-living things using a characteristic framework, or examined the different structural forms life cycles can take (metamorphic vs non-metamorphic).
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare characteristics of living and non-living things using observable evidence, and examine how plant and animal life cycles differ in structure — distinguishing metamorphic from non-metamorphic cycles and connecting the physical characteristics of organisms to their life stage.

nodes.label: Living, once living and non-living things have distinct characteristics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify objects as living, once living or non-living and explain their reasoning using observable characteristics (growth, reproduction, response to environment, need for nutrients).
criteria: Classifies at least five objects as living, once living or non-living with characteristic-based reasoning
Correctly classifies at least one ambiguous case (e.g. seed, dead leaf, fire) with explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: The characteristic-based classification framework is the prerequisite for examining life cycles in Nodes 2 and 3. Students who classify by appearance or familiarity rather than characteristics cannot reason about what changes at each life stage, because they lack a principled definition of what being 'living' involves at any stage.

width.minimum: Students classify a collection of objects as living, once living or non-living and explain the reasoning for at least three classifications using observable characteristics.
width.typical: Students explain the characteristics that distinguish living from non-living things, correctly classify ambiguous cases (dead leaves, fire, crystals, seeds) with reasoning, and distinguish between 'once living' and 'never living'.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians understand and classify the relationships between living things, Country and non-living elements — comparing with the living/non-living framework
Examine edge cases that challenge the classification (viruses, crystals that 'grow', fire that 'spreads') and discuss what characteristic evidence is used to decide
Research how scientists classify single-celled organisms and discuss whether the living/non-living distinction applies at the microscopic level

modes.reason: Students commonly classify by appearance or familiarity rather than by characteristics — dead wood is 'non-living' because it looks dead, seeds are 'non-living' because they aren't moving. Making the characteristic evidence explicit (what does living mean? → growth, reproduction, response, needs nutrients) is the scaffold that makes classification reliable across ambiguous cases.

nodes.label: Life cycles describe stages of growth and change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the life cycle of a named plant and a named animal, identifying the stages in sequence and explaining what changes occur at each stage.
criteria: Names the stages of one plant and one animal life cycle in sequence
Describes the key change that occurs at each stage for both organisms

width.minimum: Students describe the life cycle of one plant and one animal, naming the stages in sequence and describing the key change at each stage.
width.typical: Students describe and represent the life cycle stages of a plant and an animal, explain what happens at each stage (growth, reproduction, development), and identify similarities and differences between the two cycles.
wider: Represent stages of a plant or animal life cycle using drawings, digital photographs, graphic organisers or physical models — choosing a format that best shows the cyclic nature of the sequence
Investigate how First Nations Australians understand and utilise the life cycles of certain species — examining how knowledge of life stage behaviour guides sustainable harvesting
Compare the life cycle of a plant with that of a single-celled organism (e.g. yeast budding) — exploring what 'life cycle' means across very different living things

modes.reason: Students commonly have a narrow life cycle model based on one familiar animal (butterfly or frog). Comparing plant and animal cycles, and examining cycles with different structural forms, builds a more general understanding of what a life cycle is and prevents students from treating one example as universal.

nodes.label: Metamorphic and non-metamorphic cycles differ in structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between metamorphic life cycles (dramatic change in body form between stages) and non-metamorphic cycles (gradual growth without structural transformation), and give examples of each.
criteria: Distinguishes metamorphic from non-metamorphic life cycles with at least one example of each
Explains what 'metamorphosis' means in terms of change in body form between life stages

width.minimum: Students describe one metamorphic and one non-metamorphic life cycle, explaining the key structural difference between them.
width.typical: Students compare metamorphic and non-metamorphic life cycles across multiple examples (butterflies, beetles, frogs as metamorphic; humans, birds, lizards as non-metamorphic), explain why the physical characteristics of an organism differ across life stages in metamorphic cycles, and represent the comparison.
wider: Compare complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult) with incomplete metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult) — examining why insects have evolved different developmental strategies
Investigate the physical characteristics of a frog or moth at different life stages and explain how each stage's characteristics suit its role in survival
Research how Maria Sibylla Merian's careful observation across life stages was the first to document metamorphosis — connecting systematic data collection to scientific explanation (AC9S3H01)

modes.reason: Students commonly know butterfly metamorphosis as the only metamorphic example and are unaware that beetles, flies, and frogs also undergo metamorphosis. Encountering multiple metamorphic examples across insect and amphibian groups — and contrasting with non-metamorphic examples — builds a more accurate and generalisable concept of metamorphic change.

descriptors.title: Soils, rocks and minerals
descriptors.description: compare the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals and investigate why they are important Earth resources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can observe and describe properties of natural and made materials (AC9SFU03, F band). They have not yet systematically compared soil types, distinguished rocks from minerals, or examined Earth materials as resources that living things depend on.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals using appropriate vocabulary, understand that minerals are components of rocks, and explain why soils, rocks and minerals are important resources for living things including humans.

nodes.label: Soils have observable properties and components
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the observable components of soil samples (pebbles, sand, clay, plant matter, living things) and compare the properties of different soils using observable evidence.
criteria: Identifies at least three components in a soil sample using observation
Compares two soil samples using at least two property terms with observable evidence

width.minimum: Students examine at least two soil samples, identify their components, and describe at least two observable differences between them.
width.typical: Students examine soils from different local contexts, describe components and properties (particle size, colour, texture, water retention, presence of organic matter), compare soils systematically, and explain how soil properties affect its suitability for plant growth.
wider: Investigate how farmers use soil tests to monitor and manage farm health — connecting observable soil properties to agricultural decision-making (AC9S3H01)
Examine information on plant tags and explore vocabulary used to describe soil requirements — applying property knowledge to real plant care contexts
Explore how First Nations Australians observe soil and landscape characteristics to make decisions about resource availability and land management

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate accurate observations across multiple soil samples using consistent property vocabulary before they can compare or explain differences. Without a shared property vocabulary, comparisons are vague ('this soil is better') rather than evidence-based ('this soil has finer particles and holds more water').

nodes.label: Rocks and minerals have observable properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and compare observable properties of rocks and minerals (colour, texture, grain size, crystal size, hardness, lustre), and explain that minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
criteria: Describes at least two observable properties for each of three rock or mineral samples
Explains that minerals are the building blocks of rocks

width.minimum: Students describe at least two observable properties of each of three different rock or mineral samples, and state that minerals are components of rocks.
width.typical: Students compare rocks and minerals systematically using property vocabulary, explain that rocks are composed of one or more minerals, identify similarities and differences between samples from local and non-local sources, and recognise common uses of minerals.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of different rock and mineral types and how they were used — for stone blades, grindstones and pigments — examining how deep property knowledge guided material selection
Explore the school grounds or local area to observe and collect different rock types and construct a comparative display showing property differences
Research which rocks or minerals are quarried or mined locally and how they are used — connecting local geology to community resources

modes.reason: Students commonly have a narrow rock concept (grey, hard, outdoor) and miss the diversity of rock and mineral types in their environment. Encountering a range of samples — including minerals with vivid colour, crystal structure, or varied hardness — builds a more accurate and complete model of what rocks and minerals are.

nodes.label: Soils, rocks and minerals are important Earth resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why soils, rocks and minerals are important resources for living things — including how living things depend on soils and how humans use rocks and minerals — and give specific examples of each.
criteria: Gives at least two examples of how living things depend on soil with explanation
Gives at least two examples of human use of rocks or minerals, connecting the use to a property of the material

width.minimum: Students give at least two examples of how living things depend on soil and at least two examples of how humans use rocks or minerals, explaining why each is important.
width.typical: Students explain the multiple ways living things depend on soils (food production, plant growth, habitat, water filtration) and describe how humans use specific rocks and minerals in everyday objects and the built environment, connecting specific properties to specific uses.
wider: Investigate which rocks or minerals are quarried or mined locally or regionally and examine how those resources are used — tracing the resource from extraction to use
Research how humans depend on soils for food production and examine what happens when soil quality degrades — connecting soil health to food security
Examine how First Nations Australians' use of rocks, minerals and soils reflects a deep understanding of their properties and sustainable use within Country

modes.reason: Students commonly think of soil as 'dirt' and miss its ecological and agricultural importance. Encountering the multiple roles of soil — habitat, water filtration, food production, plant support — and varied uses of rocks and minerals across the built environment and everyday objects builds a more complete understanding of Earth materials as resources.

descriptors.title: Heat energy and transfer
descriptors.description: identify sources of heat energy and examine how temperature changes when heat energy is transferred from one object to another
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how objects move and respond to pushes and pulls (1-2 band). They have informally experienced heat and cold but have not yet identified heat as a form of energy, distinguished temperature from heat, or examined heat transfer between objects systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify sources of heat energy in everyday and natural contexts, explain that heat energy transfers from warmer to cooler objects, use thermometers to measure temperature change, and identify how materials vary in their ability to conduct or insulate heat.

nodes.label: Heat energy comes from identifiable sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and classify sources of heat energy in everyday and natural contexts (sun, fire, electrical devices, geothermal, friction, body heat) and explain that heat is a form of energy.
criteria: Identifies at least four sources of heat energy across at least two categories
Explains that heat is a form of energy that can be transferred and measured

width.minimum: Students identify at least four sources of heat energy from different categories (natural, electrical, combustion) and explain that heat is a form of energy.
width.typical: Students identify and classify heat sources across natural (sun, geothermal, fire) and human-made (electrical devices, friction) categories, explain that heat is a form of energy that can be sensed and measured, and distinguish between a heat source and an object that has been warmed by a source.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians developed fire-starting techniques — examining the heat sources involved and the knowledge required to produce and maintain fire
Investigate geothermal heat as a less familiar heat source — examining how geothermal springs, geysers and geothermal power use heat from within the Earth
Research how different cooking methods (boiling, frying, roasting, solar cooking) use different heat sources and heat transfer mechanisms (AC9S3H02)

modes.reason: Students tend to list only familiar heat sources (sun, fire, electric heater) and miss friction and geothermal sources. Encountering a wider range — including culturally grounded contexts like First Nations fire-starting and geothermal phenomena — builds a more complete understanding of what counts as a heat source.

nodes.label: Heat transfers from warmer to cooler objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that heat energy transfers from a warmer object to a cooler object when they are in contact, describe what happens to the temperature of each object during the transfer, and use temperature measurements to support their explanation.
criteria: Explains that heat transfers from warmer to cooler objects, not from cold to warm
Describes what happens to the temperature of both objects during heat transfer (warm cools, cool warms) until they reach the same temperature
Uses thermometer observations to support the explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: The direction of heat transfer — warm to cool, never the reverse — is the conceptual prerequisite for understanding conduction and insulation in Node 3. Students holding the 'cold flows in' misconception will systematically misexplain why insulators work and produce inverted reasoning about conductor/insulator selection.

width.minimum: Students describe what happens to the temperature of a warm and a cold object when they are placed in contact, and explain the direction of heat transfer using observations.
width.typical: Students observe and measure temperature change when objects of different temperatures are placed in contact, explain that heat flows from warmer to cooler until temperatures equalise, and use thermometer readings to support their explanation.
wider: Investigate how 18th-century physicists Jean Ingenhousz and Benjamin Thompson collected temperature data to determine best conductors and insulators — connecting systematic observation to scientific explanation (AC9S3H01)
Model heat transfer using drawings, role-play or arrows to show the direction of energy movement — applying a representation to make the invisible visible
Explore how heat transfer from warm ocean water to cooler air drives weather patterns — extending the object-to-object transfer concept to environmental scale

modes.reason: Students commonly believe cold 'flows into' a warm object (a cold drink makes your hand cold) rather than heat flowing from the warm hand to the cold drink. Making the direction of transfer explicit — heat always moves from warmer to cooler, never the reverse — and supporting this with thermometer evidence is the key conceptual scaffold before students can understand insulation.

nodes.label: Materials differ in how well they conduct or insulate heat
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that some materials (conductors) transfer heat quickly and others (insulators) transfer heat slowly, give examples of each, and connect material selection to everyday uses for keeping things hot or cold.
criteria: Identifies at least two conductors and two insulators with examples
Explains the difference between a conductor and an insulator in terms of how quickly heat transfers
Gives at least one everyday example where conductor or insulator properties determine material selection

width.minimum: Students identify at least two conductors and two insulators, explain the difference between them, and give one everyday example of each being used for its heat transfer properties.
width.typical: Students investigate heat transfer through different materials (metals, plastics, ceramics, fabrics), classify them as better or worse conductors using evidence, explain why conductors and insulators are selected for specific uses, and connect material properties to everyday objects (saucepan handles, oven mitts, thermos flasks, building insulation).
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians developed clothing from animal skins (possum fur cloaks, kangaroo skin) that trap heat close to the body — examining how insulation properties guided material selection
Investigate how engineers test insulation properties of materials and how this information is used to design food packaging, building insulation or cold-weather clothing (AC9S3H02)
Plan and conduct a fair test to determine which material is the best insulator for keeping a substance cold — applying conductor/insulator knowledge to an investigation (AC9S3I02)

modes.reason: Students commonly know metals are conductors and fabrics are insulators without understanding why different materials are selected in different contexts. Encountering conductor/insulator properties across varied everyday contexts — cooking, building, clothing, food storage — helps students develop a more flexible understanding of how material properties determine use.

descriptors.title: Solids, liquids and change of state
descriptors.description: investigate the observable properties of solids and liquids and how adding or removing heat energy leads to a change of state
descriptors.knowledge: Students can observe and describe properties of materials and sort them by observable features (AC9SFU03, F band). They have not yet formally defined solid and liquid using observable properties, investigated change of state, or connected heat energy addition/removal to state transitions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the observable properties that distinguish solids from liquids, explain that adding or removing heat energy causes changes of state (solid ↔ liquid), and give examples of state change in everyday and cultural contexts — including how state change enables recycling of materials.

nodes.label: Solids and liquids have distinct observable properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish solids from liquids using observable properties — solids hold their shape, liquids take the shape of their container and flow — and correctly classify materials including ambiguous cases.
criteria: Classifies at least five materials as solid or liquid using property evidence
States at least two observable properties that distinguish solids from liquids
nodes.hinge_reason: The property-based definition of solid and liquid is the prerequisite for understanding change of state in Node 2. Students who classify by appearance rather than by the defining property criteria cannot correctly describe what changes when a solid melts — they see 'ice' becoming 'water' as a substance change rather than a state change.

width.minimum: Students classify at least five materials as solid or liquid using observable properties and explain the reasoning for each classification.
width.typical: Students describe the observable properties that define solids (hold shape, fixed volume) and liquids (take shape of container, fixed volume, flow), correctly classify materials including ambiguous cases (toothpaste, slime, honey, cornflour mixture), and explain the evidence for each classification.
wider: Investigate substances that are difficult to classify as solid or liquid — toothpaste, slime, hair gel, cornflour in water — and discuss what properties are used to decide and what limitations the binary classification has
Explore gases as a third state of matter — comparing their properties with solids and liquids and discussing what the three states have in common
Examine how properties of solids and liquids are used in everyday design decisions — why a container for liquid must be rigid and sealed, why a cutting tool must be solid

modes.reason: Students commonly classify by appearance (sugar is a solid because it looks like sand; honey is a solid because it moves slowly) rather than by the defining property criteria. Making the property definitions explicit — does it hold its shape without a container? does it flow? — and applying them to ambiguous cases is the scaffold that makes classification reliable.

nodes.label: Adding or removing heat causes change of state
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that adding heat energy causes a solid to melt (become liquid) and removing heat energy causes a liquid to freeze (become solid), and describe what is observed during each change.
criteria: Names the change of state when heat is added to a solid (melting) and when heat is removed from a liquid (freezing)
Describes at least two observable changes that occur during a state change

width.minimum: Students describe what happens when heat is added to a solid and when heat is removed from a liquid, naming the change of state in each case.
width.typical: Students explain that adding heat energy causes melting and removing heat energy causes freezing; describe observable changes during state change (shape lost, flows, hardens); investigate melting or freezing in a sealed container and explain that the substance itself (mass) does not change even though the state does.
wider: Investigate the melting of different substances (ice, butter, chocolate, wax) and compare how quickly each melts — exploring whether all solids melt at the same temperature
Investigate how changes of state in materials used by First Nations Australians — such as beeswax or resins — are important for their practical use in tools and artefacts
Explore how changes from solid to liquid and back enable recycling of materials such as glass and plastics — connecting state change to sustainability

modes.reason: Students commonly think of melting and freezing as applying only to ice and water. Encountering state change in butter, chocolate, wax, beeswax and industrial materials (glass, plastic) builds a more generalisable understanding of state change as a property of all materials, not just water.

nodes.label: State change is reversible and conserves the substance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that state changes are reversible (a melted solid can be refrozen), that the substance itself does not change during a state change (only its form changes), and use evidence from an investigation (mass before and after in a sealed container) to support this.
criteria: Explains that state change is reversible and that the substance does not change — only its form
Predicts that the mass of a substance will be the same before and after melting in a sealed container
Distinguishes between a substance changing state and a substance changing into a different substance

width.minimum: Students explain that melting and freezing are reversible and that the substance does not change — only its state — giving at least one example.
width.typical: Students investigate ice melting or water freezing in a sealed container, explain that the mass does not change even though the state does, describe how the change can be reversed, and distinguish state change (reversible, substance unchanged) from chemical change (new substance formed).
wider: Explore how the reversibility of state change is used to recycle materials — glass, metals, plastics — examining which materials can be returned to a liquid state and reformed
Investigate whether mass changes when a substance changes state by predicting and then measuring mass before and after melting in a sealed container — applying measurement skills to test a prediction
Examine a case where state change appears irreversible (burning) and discuss why — introducing the distinction between physical and chemical change informally

modes.reason: Students commonly believe that melting changes what the substance is — ice becomes water, which is different. The reasoning chain — same substance, same particles, just different arrangement → mass unchanged → change is reversible → this is different from a chemical change — is the conceptual foundation for all later chemistry work on physical vs chemical change (AC9S8U07).

descriptors.title: Food chains and habitats
descriptors.description: explain the roles and interactions of consumers, producers and decomposers within a habitat and how food chains represent feeding relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare characteristics of living and non-living things and explain differences between plant and animal life cycles (AC9S3U01). They have not yet examined feeding relationships between organisms or the role of decomposers in a habitat.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers within a habitat — including how each group obtains energy and contributes to the habitat — and construct food chains to represent feeding relationships between named organisms across different habitats.

nodes.label: Producers make their own food
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify producers as living things that make their own food using sunlight and explain why this makes them the starting point of a food chain.
criteria: Identifies at least two producers from a named habitat and explains that they make their own food using sunlight
Explains why producers are placed at the start of a food chain
nodes.hinge_reason: Producers are the definitional starting point of a food chain. Students who overgeneralise 'plants' as the only producers, or who cannot explain the sunlight-energy link, will construct incorrect chains in Node 4 and fail to understand why food chains always begin with a producer.

width.minimum: Students identify plants as producers and explain that they use sunlight to make food, giving one or two habitat examples.
width.typical: Students identify producers across different habitat types (terrestrial, aquatic) and explain the role of sunlight as the energy source for the whole food chain.
wider: Examine producers beyond flowering plants — algae, phytoplankton, and aquatic grasses — and discuss what makes something a producer regardless of its form
Connect to First Nations Australians' deep knowledge of productive plants in local habitats and how this knowledge guided sustainable use
Explore edge cases: fungi are not producers — where do they fit? (seeds a question that connects to the decomposer node)

modes.reason: Students frequently overgeneralise 'plants' as the only producers and miss aquatic or microscopic producers. Exposure to producers across varied habitat types (forest floor, reef, wetland) builds a more robust concept of what a producer is and prevents the food-chain construction errors that follow from this misconception.

nodes.label: Consumers eat other organisms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify animals as consumers, distinguish between herbivores, carnivores and omnivores, and explain that consumers obtain energy by eating producers or other consumers.
criteria: Classifies at least three animals from a named habitat as herbivore, carnivore or omnivore with reasoning
Explains that consumers get their energy from eating other living things, not from sunlight directly

width.minimum: Students classify animals from a named habitat as consumers and sort examples into herbivore, carnivore or omnivore categories with justification.
width.typical: Students explain how energy moves from producers to consumers and identify multiple levels of consumers (primary, secondary) in a habitat without using that terminology explicitly.
wider: Examine consumers that are difficult to classify — omnivores that shift diet by season, scavengers, parasites — and discuss where they fit
Explore how First Nations Australians classify animals and their feeding relationships, and compare with the producer/consumer framework
Investigate how the removal of one consumer from a habitat affects others — connects to food chain disruption in the next node

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'consumer' with 'animal that eats meat' and struggle with omnivores and scavengers. Varied examples across habitats and feeding types help students build a working classification that holds up under edge cases and prepares them for accurate food chain construction.

nodes.label: Decomposers break down waste and remains
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify decomposers as living things that break down dead organisms and waste, and explain why decomposers are important to a habitat.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of decomposers and explains that they break down dead matter
Explains why decomposers are important to the habitat (nutrients returned to soil for producers)

width.minimum: Students identify examples of decomposers (worms, fungi, bacteria) and explain that they break down dead organisms, returning nutrients to the soil.
width.typical: Students explain the role of decomposers in cycling nutrients through a habitat and describe why removing decomposers would affect other organisms.
wider: Research the diversity of decomposers — bacteria, fungi, detritivores — and compare how each contributes to breakdown
Examine how knowledge of decomposers has been applied in composting systems (connects to AC9S4H02)
Explore how First Nations Australians understand the role of decomposers in Country management and ecological cycles

modes.reason: The decomposer role is non-obvious — students do not intuitively connect decomposers to nutrient cycling or see them as part of the food chain. Making the logic explicit (dead matter accumulates → decomposers break it down → nutrients return to soil → producers can grow) supports accurate understanding before students encounter food web models.

nodes.label: Food chains show feeding sequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a food chain for a named habitat using correct notation (arrows showing energy flow) and label each organism as producer, consumer or decomposer.
criteria: Constructs a food chain with arrows pointing in the direction of energy flow (not toward predator)
Correctly labels each organism in the chain as producer, consumer or decomposer
Explains what the arrows in a food chain represent
nodes.hinge_reason: Arrow direction errors (pointing toward predator rather than in the direction of energy flow) are prerequisite errors that propagate into Node 5 — students who cannot construct accurate chains cannot reason about what happens when an organism is removed, because they lack a correct model of energy flow sequence.

width.minimum: Students construct a simple food chain (3–4 links) for a given habitat using arrow notation and label each organism correctly.
width.typical: Students construct food chains for two different habitats, explain what the arrows represent (energy flow, not just 'eats'), and compare the chains to identify structural similarities.
wider: Compare food chains across markedly different habitats — arid desert, tropical rainforest, reef — and explain what determines chain length
Represent the same habitat's feeding relationships as both a food chain and an informal food web, and discuss what a food chain can and cannot show
Construct food chains from First Nations ecological knowledge of a local habitat and compare to textbook examples

modes.reason: Arrow direction errors are common and persistent — students draw arrows toward the predator ('what eats what') rather than in the direction of energy flow. Accurate notation requires deliberate practice with feedback, not more examples of different habitats.

Food chain construction requires coordinating the three roles (producer, consumer, decomposer) into a single representation. Students who have each role as a separate idea must now apply all three simultaneously while observing notation conventions.

nodes.label: Habitat disruption affects food chains
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how removing or adding an organism to a habitat affects the feeding relationships in a food chain, using examples of introduced species or habitat change.
criteria: Predicts the effect on at least one other organism when a named organism is removed from a food chain and explains the reasoning
Identifies at least one real-world example where a food chain was disrupted and describes the cause

width.minimum: Students predict and explain what would happen to one organism in a food chain if another organism were removed, using a given habitat example.
width.typical: Students explain how the removal of a producer or key consumer cascades through a food chain, and describe at least one real-world example of food chain disruption in Australia.
wider: Investigate a specific case of introduced predator impact on Australian native species (e.g. foxes and small mammals) and explain the cascading effects through the food chain
Research how First Nations Australians use food chain knowledge to manage Country, including controlled burning and its effects on food chains
Explore the ecological role of decomposers in recovery after disruption — what happens to dead matter when predator populations crash

modes.reason: Students struggle to extend their reasoning beyond the immediately removed organism — they see one step of the chain affected rather than cascading effects. Varied disruption scenarios (producer loss, consumer loss, introduced predator) and Australian contexts help students develop a more flexible and accurate model of chain interdependence.

descriptors.title: Water cycle
descriptors.description: identify sources of water and describe key processes in the water cycle, including movement of water through the sky, landscape and ocean; precipitation; evaporation; and condensation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe observable properties of solids and liquids and explain how adding or removing heat energy causes changes of state (AC9S3U04). They can compare properties of soils, rocks and minerals as Earth resources (AC9S3U02). They have not yet connected state changes to the movement of water through the environment as a continuous cycle.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the key processes of the water cycle — evaporation, condensation and precipitation — trace the movement of water through sky, landscape and ocean, and identify sources of water including how First Nations Australians and others understand and manage water resources.

nodes.label: Water exists in different forms and locations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sources of water in the environment — sky, landscape, ocean, underground — and recognise that water exists as liquid, vapour and solid depending on conditions.
criteria: Identifies at least three sources of water in the environment across different locations (sky, landscape, underground or ocean)
Connects each source to a state of water (liquid, solid or vapour)

width.minimum: Students name at least three sources of water in the environment and connect each to a state of water (liquid rain, solid snow/ice, vapour in air).
width.typical: Students describe where water is found across sky, landscape and ocean, and explain that the same water moves between these locations over time.
wider: Map local water sources — creeks, reservoirs, stormwater drains — and trace where water comes from and where it goes
Explore First Nations Australians' knowledge of water sources and landscape reading (identifying water from topographic and vegetation cues)
Investigate underground water (groundwater, aquifers) as a less visible but important water source

modes.reason: Students tend to think of water only in visible, surface forms (rain, rivers, taps). Mapping local water sources and exploring First Nations knowledge of water reading broadens this to include underground, atmospheric and landscape-embedded water — supporting the more complete model needed for the full cycle in Node 5.

nodes.label: Evaporation — liquid water becomes vapour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain evaporation as the process by which liquid water becomes water vapour and identify everyday examples of evaporation occurring.
criteria: Describes evaporation using an everyday example and explains that liquid water becomes water vapour
Identifies at least one condition that affects how quickly evaporation occurs
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaporation is the entry point for the water cycle. Students who do not understand that liquid water becomes invisible vapour — and particularly those who restrict evaporation to heating/drying contexts — cannot correctly explain how water enters the atmosphere or why the cycle operates at all, breaking Node 5 integration.

width.minimum: Students describe evaporation using an everyday example (wet washing drying, puddle disappearing) and explain that liquid water becomes water vapour that enters the air.
width.typical: Students explain that heat energy drives evaporation and identify conditions that speed it up (warmth, wind, exposed surface area), connecting to their prior knowledge of heat energy and state change.
wider: Investigate how evaporation rate changes with temperature and surface area using a simple investigation
Explore how First Nations Australians' knowledge of evaporation is applied to conserve water — covering surfaces to reduce evaporative loss
Connect ocean evaporation to the global scale of the water cycle — most water vapour in the atmosphere comes from the ocean

modes.reason: Students often have a narrow concept of evaporation tied to drying or heating — they miss large-scale evaporation from oceans and lakes, and evaporation in cool conditions. Varied everyday examples help students generalise beyond heat-drying to a broader concept of liquid-to-vapour transition.

nodes.label: Condensation — vapour becomes liquid water
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain condensation as the process by which water vapour becomes liquid water and identify everyday examples where condensation is visible.
criteria: Describes condensation using an everyday example and explains that water vapour becomes liquid water when cooled
Does not describe condensation as water passing through a container wall (misconception check)
Connects cloud formation to condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere
nodes.hinge_reason: The condensation misconception (water 'sweats through' a container rather than forming from vapour in the air) directly corrupts students' model of cloud formation and precipitation in Node 4 and Node 5. Students holding this misconception cannot construct a coherent water cycle.

width.minimum: Students describe condensation using an everyday example (water droplets on a cold drink bottle, bathroom mirror fogging) and explain that water vapour in the air becomes liquid water when cooled.
width.typical: Students explain that cooling drives condensation, connect the formation of clouds to condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere, and describe what conditions are needed for clouds to form.
wider: Observe a 'cloud in a bottle' or fog-formation demonstration and explain the conditions that produced it
Investigate dew formation — when and where does dew form, and why? Connect to First Nations knowledge of collecting dew as a water source
Explore how condensation forms rain droplets — water vapour condenses around tiny particles (dust, pollen) in the atmosphere

modes.reason: Students commonly believe condensation is water 'sweating through' a container rather than water vapour from the air cooling on a cold surface. Making the reasoning explicit — air contains invisible water vapour → cold surface cools nearby air → vapour loses energy and becomes liquid → droplets form on the surface — is necessary before students can correctly explain cloud formation or dew.

nodes.label: Precipitation — water falls from clouds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain precipitation as water falling from clouds in different forms (rain, snow, hail) and describe the conditions that determine which form precipitation takes.
criteria: Explains that precipitation occurs when water falls from clouds and names at least two forms
Describes at least one condition that determines what form precipitation takes

width.minimum: Students explain that precipitation occurs when water droplets in clouds combine and fall, and name two forms of precipitation.
width.typical: Students describe conditions that determine precipitation form (temperature at different altitudes determines rain vs snow vs hail) and give examples of each from different climates or seasons.
wider: Explore how rainfall data is collected and used — rain gauges, Bureau of Meteorology data — connecting to how hydrologists use this data (AC9S4H01)
Investigate seasonal rainfall patterns in different Australian regions and connect to First Nations seasonal calendars
Examine hail formation as an example of precipitation with a more complex mechanism — water droplets carried upward by air currents, freezing in layers

modes.reason: Students commonly think of precipitation only as rain and miss the variety of forms and the conditions that determine them. Exploring rainfall data collection and First Nations seasonal calendars broadens students' understanding of precipitation as a varied, data-rich phenomenon embedded in real knowledge systems.

nodes.label: The water cycle — continuous movement through Earth's systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace the movement of water through the complete cycle — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff and collection — and explain that the water cycle is continuous.
criteria: Traces the path of water through at least three named stages of the water cycle, correctly labelling the process at each transition
Explains that the water cycle is continuous and driven by solar energy
Identifies at least two locations where water is stored (e.g. ocean, atmosphere, groundwater, ice)

width.minimum: Students trace a water molecule through at least three stages of the water cycle, naming the processes at each transition and identifying where the water is at each stage.
width.typical: Students describe the complete water cycle including the movement of water through sky, landscape and ocean, explain that solar energy drives the cycle, and represent it in a labelled diagram or model.
wider: Explore how hydrologists use rainfall and water use data to explain river flow and seasonal variation (AC9S4H01) — connecting the abstract cycle to real data
Examine how land use changes (deforestation, urbanisation) affect the water cycle at local and regional scales
Consider how First Nations Australians' water resource management practices are grounded in understanding the water cycle, including seasonal variation

modes.reason: The water cycle integrates evaporation, condensation and precipitation — three processes students have encountered separately — into a single continuous system. Students must now coordinate these components and understand that the same water moves repeatedly through the cycle, driven by solar energy.

Students tend to model the water cycle as a simple loop (rain falls, evaporates, becomes rain again) without accounting for groundwater, ocean reservoirs, or long-term storage in ice. Varied representations — local creek, ocean, underground — help students build a more complete model of the cycle.

descriptors.title: Forces and motion
descriptors.description: identify how forces can be exerted by one object on another and investigate the effect of frictional, gravitational and magnetic forces on the motion of objects
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe pushes and pulls in terms of strength and direction and predict their effects on motion and shape (AC9S1U03). They have not yet encountered named force types (friction, gravity, magnetism) or the concept that forces are exerted by one object on another, including at a distance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how forces are exerted between objects — including contact and non-contact forces — and describe the effects of friction, gravity and magnetism on the motion of objects, using force arrows to represent direction and magnitude.

nodes.label: Forces are exerted by one object on another
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a force is an interaction between two objects — one exerting, one receiving — and distinguish between contact forces (objects touching) and non-contact forces (acting at a distance).
criteria: Identifies the two objects involved in a force interaction for a given example
Distinguishes between a contact force example and a non-contact force example with justification
nodes.hinge_reason: The two-object interaction framing is the conceptual prerequisite for correctly identifying friction, gravity and magnetism in Nodes 2–4. Students who attribute force to one object ('the magnet pulls') without identifying the receiving object cannot accurately describe force pairs and will misidentify contact vs non-contact situations throughout the sequence.

width.minimum: Students identify the two objects involved in a force interaction for at least two examples, and distinguish between contact and non-contact examples.
width.typical: Students explain that forces require an interaction between objects and that some forces (gravity, magnetism) act without physical contact, using examples from their experience.
wider: Investigate traditional First Nations Australians' toys and games and identify the forces involved in each — connecting cultural artefacts to the force concept
Explore the idea that even 'stationary' objects have forces acting on them (a book on a table — gravity pulling down, table pushing up) — introducing force balance informally
Examine how force arrows are used to show direction and magnitude, and draw force arrow diagrams for simple scenarios

modes.reason: The concept that force requires two objects — an exerter and a receiver — is non-obvious to Year 4 students who tend to think of force as a property of one object ('the magnet pulls'). Making the two-object interaction explicit, and distinguishing contact from non-contact, is a necessary conceptual scaffold before students can correctly identify friction, gravity and magnetism as force types.

nodes.label: Friction slows motion between surfaces
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that friction is a force that acts between two surfaces in contact, describe its effect on motion (slowing or stopping), and identify factors that affect friction strength.
criteria: Explains that friction is a force between surfaces and describes its effect on motion
Gives one example where friction is helpful and one where it is a problem
Identifies at least one factor that affects how strong the friction force is

width.minimum: Students explain that friction acts between surfaces and slows or stops moving objects, giving two everyday examples.
width.typical: Students explain positive and negative effects of friction in everyday contexts (friction needed for gripping; friction causes wear and slows machines) and identify how surface texture affects friction strength.
wider: Investigate how shoe sole design uses friction principles — examining patterns and materials for different surface conditions
Test friction between different surface combinations and represent results in a column graph (connects to AC9S4I04)
Research how friction reduction is used in engineering contexts (lubricants, ball bearings, aerodynamics) and examine trade-offs

modes.reason: Students readily identify friction as 'slowing things down' but struggle to see it as a force exerted by one surface on another. They also miss contexts where friction is desirable (braking, gripping, writing). Varied contexts — shoe grip, playground slides, bike brakes, wet roads — help students build a more complete model of friction as a surface interaction with both beneficial and detrimental effects.

nodes.label: Gravity pulls objects toward Earth
