nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that gravity is a force that pulls all objects toward the centre of Earth, acts on objects regardless of whether they are moving or stationary, and explain why objects fall when dropped.
criteria: Explains that gravity pulls all objects toward the centre of Earth
Confirms that gravity acts on objects whether they are moving or stationary (does not restrict gravity to falling objects)
Gives a correct example of gravity's effect on a stationary object

width.minimum: Students explain that gravity pulls objects toward Earth and that it acts on all objects, giving examples of gravity's effect on moving and stationary objects.
width.typical: Students explain that gravitational force acts continuously on objects (a held object, a stationary object, a falling object) and describe what would change if gravity were weaker — connecting to astronauts on the moon.
wider: Watch footage of astronauts on the moon or dropping objects in a vacuum and describe the force they are observing — connecting to the idea that gravity varies with planetary mass
Investigate the pushing force of a liquid (buoyancy) and discuss how it can counteract gravity, allowing objects to float
Explore how gravity acts on objects in free fall — using slow-motion footage of falling objects to describe the motion

modes.reason: Students commonly believe gravity only acts when objects are falling or moving, not on stationary objects. They also conflate gravity with 'weight' as a fixed property. Varied contexts — a stationary book, a falling apple, an astronaut on the moon, a floating boat — help students see gravity as a continuous force that acts regardless of motion state.

nodes.label: Magnetic forces attract and repel
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that magnets exert forces on other magnets and on some metals, describe attraction and repulsion, and identify that magnetic force acts at a distance.
criteria: Distinguishes between magnetic and non-magnetic materials with examples (does not claim all metals are magnetic)
Explains that magnetic force can act at a distance without the objects touching
Describes both attraction (opposite poles) and repulsion (same poles) between magnets

width.minimum: Students explain that magnets attract some metals and can attract or repel other magnets, give examples of magnetic and non-magnetic materials, and confirm that this force acts without contact.
width.typical: Students explain the conditions under which magnets attract (opposite poles) or repel (same poles), identify which common metals are magnetic, and describe practical uses of magnetic force.
wider: Investigate how magnetic force strength changes with distance and represent findings graphically
Explore how magnetic forces are used in sorting metals in recycling and food safety (metal detection) — connecting to AC9S4H02
Examine how compasses work and how the Earth's magnetic field is a large-scale example of magnetism

modes.reason: Students commonly believe all metals are magnetic and struggle with the at-a-distance nature of magnetic force. Varied materials testing (iron, steel, aluminium, copper) and distance investigations resolve both misconceptions more effectively than re-explaining the rule.

nodes.label: Force arrows represent forces on objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw and interpret force arrow diagrams showing the direction and relative magnitude of forces acting on an object, and use these to describe the overall effect on motion.
criteria: Draws force arrows with the correct direction for at least two forces acting on an object
Sizes arrows to indicate relative magnitude (larger force = longer arrow) where two forces are compared
Explains what the force arrows in a given diagram indicate about the object's motion

width.minimum: Students draw force arrows on a simple diagram to show the direction of at least two forces on an object and describe the effect of those forces on motion.
width.typical: Students draw force arrow diagrams for familiar scenarios (a falling object, a car braking, a floating boat) showing multiple forces with arrows sized to show relative magnitude, and explain what the overall forces mean for motion.
wider: Represent forces in traditional First Nations instructive toys and games using force arrow diagrams — applying the representation to culturally grounded scenarios
Explore how force diagrams are used in engineering and design to analyse structures and moving objects
Investigate balanced forces (two equal, opposite arrows) and informally describe why the object doesn't move — a preview of Y7 force concepts

modes.reason: Force arrow direction errors are common — students draw arrows showing the direction of motion rather than the direction of the force, or place arrows incorrectly on objects. Accurate diagramming requires deliberate practice with feedback on placement and direction. This is a precision-required representation skill.

Force arrow diagrams require students to simultaneously represent multiple forces (gravity, friction, magnetic, applied) in a single diagram and interpret their combined effect. Coordinating the three named force types with correct arrow conventions is the integration challenge at this node.

descriptors.title: Properties of materials
descriptors.description: examine the properties of natural and made materials including fibres, metals, glass and plastics and consider how these properties influence their use
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that objects are made of materials and describe observable properties of those materials (AC9SFU03). They can recognise that physical actions change the shape of materials without changing their composition (AC9S2U03). They have not yet systematically compared material classes (fibres, metals, glass, plastics) or connected material properties to selection for specific uses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine properties of natural and made materials across fibres, metals, glass and plastics, use property vocabulary to describe and compare materials, and explain how specific properties determine why materials are selected for particular uses.

nodes.label: Materials have observable and testable properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use property vocabulary to describe and compare materials, making observations and using appropriate terms (hardness, flexibility, transparency, conductivity, texture, absorbency).
criteria: Uses at least four property terms accurately when describing a given material
Distinguishes between properties that can be observed without testing (colour, transparency) and properties that require testing (hardness, absorbency)
nodes.hinge_reason: Property vocabulary is the language for all subsequent nodes. Students who lack accurate property terms produce vague selection rationales ('it's good because it's strong') in Nodes 3 and 4, making the property-to-demand reasoning chain impossible to complete correctly.

width.minimum: Students use at least four property terms to describe and compare two materials, making observations to justify each term.
width.typical: Students systematically describe a range of materials using property vocabulary, distinguishing between properties they can observe directly and properties they need to test.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians use material properties to select appropriate natural materials for tools, clothing, shelter and musical instruments
Investigate how property vocabulary is used in materials science and engineering — product datasheets, material specifications
Compare how the same material can have different properties in different forms (e.g. glass as flat sheet vs glass fibre vs tempered glass)

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a working vocabulary of property terms through applying them to varied materials before they can use these terms reliably in comparative and explanatory tasks. Rushing to selection-for-use before property vocabulary is established produces vague explanations ('it's good because it's strong').

nodes.label: Material classes: fibres, metals, glass, plastics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify examples of fibres, metals, glass and plastics, and describe characteristic properties of each class that distinguish it from others.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples from each of the four material classes (fibres, metals, glass, plastics)
Names at least two characteristic properties of each class that distinguish it from others

width.minimum: Students identify at least two examples from each of the four material classes and name two characteristic properties of each class.
width.typical: Students compare the four material classes using a property framework, identify natural vs made materials within each class, and give examples of where each class is typically used based on its characteristic properties.
wider: Investigate natural vs synthetic versions within a class (natural fibres: wool, cotton; synthetic: nylon, polyester) and compare properties
Research how glass is made from natural materials (silica sand) — connecting to the idea that 'made' materials are often processed from natural sources
Examine how plastics are classified by resin code and how these different types have different properties and recycling outcomes

modes.reason: Students tend to have narrow prototypes for each class — 'metal' means iron/steel, 'fibre' means string. Exposure to the full range within each class (metals including aluminium, copper, gold; fibres including natural and synthetic; glass including safety glass and optical fibre) builds a more robust class concept and prevents selection-for-use errors based on prototype thinking.

nodes.label: Properties determine material selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a specific material is used for a particular purpose by connecting one or more of its properties to the demands of that use.
criteria: Names the relevant property and explains how that property meets the demands of the use for a given material-object pair
Explains why a different material would be less suitable for the same use (naming the missing property)

width.minimum: Students explain the selection of a material for a given object by naming the relevant property and explaining why it matters for that use.
width.typical: Students explain how the combination of properties of a material determines its suitability for a specific use, and recognise that no material is universally 'best' — selection depends on the demands of the use.
wider: Examine familiar objects made from combinations of materials (shoes: rubber sole, leather/synthetic upper, foam insole) and explain the property rationale for each component
Investigate how knowledge of material properties has influenced people's decisions about plastic use and disposal (AC9S4H02)
Research a case where material selection failed — a product that used the wrong material for its purpose — and analyse the property mismatch

modes.reason: Students frequently explain material selection with generic justifications ('glass is used for windows because it's see-through') without articulating the property-to-demand connection ('transparency allows light in while the hardness and weather resistance keep the elements out'). Making the reasoning chain explicit — demand → required property → material that has that property — produces better explanatory quality.

nodes.label: Objects often combine materials with different properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a multi-material object, identify the different materials present, and explain why each material was selected based on its properties and the specific demands it meets in that object.
criteria: Identifies at least two different materials in a named object and names at least one property of each
Explains the specific property-to-function connection for each identified material in the object
Identifies at least one property that would make a substitute material unsuitable for one component

width.minimum: Students identify two different materials in a familiar object and explain the property rationale for each.
width.typical: Students systematically examine a multi-material object (shoe, lunchbox, tent, backpack), map each material to its location and function, and explain the property rationale for each material choice.
wider: Design and build a test object for a specific purpose (tent, bird feeder, lunchbox) selecting materials based on property analysis — connects to AC9S4I02 (fair testing of designs)
Investigate which materials in a chosen object can be recycled and research alternatives for materials with poor sustainability properties
Consider how First Nations Australians combine natural materials in traditional objects — e.g. spears combining wood, sinew, stone — and analyse the property rationale for each component

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate material identification, property vocabulary, and the selection rationale framework — applying all three simultaneously to a complex multi-material object. Students who have each component as a separate skill must now deploy them together in a single analytical task.

descriptors.title: Science collaboration and building on others' work
descriptors.description: examine why advances in science are often the result of collaboration or build on the work of others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine how data is used to develop scientific explanations (AC9S3H01, 3-4 band). They have not yet examined the collaborative and cumulative nature of science — the idea that advances typically require multiple people, disciplines and prior discoveries.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine real examples of scientific advances that required collaboration across disciplines, institutions or cultures, or that built on the prior work of others — explaining why scientific knowledge advances more effectively through collective effort than individual work alone.

nodes.label: Scientific advances build on prior work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least one example where a scientific advance built on the prior work of others, explaining what earlier knowledge was required and how the new discovery extended or depended on it.
criteria: Describes one example of a scientific advance that built on prior work
Identifies the earlier knowledge that was required and explains how the new contribution depended on it
nodes.hinge_reason: The cumulative-science concept is foundational to the H strand at Y5 — students who retain the 'eureka individual' model will be unable to meaningfully engage with Node 2's collaboration framing, and will misread H01-linked cross-strand references throughout U and I nodes.

width.minimum: Students describe one example where a scientific discovery built on the prior work of others, identifying the earlier work and the new contribution.
width.typical: Students examine multiple examples where scientific understanding developed cumulatively — including the history of optics (Plato, Euclid, Ibn al-Haytham, Bacon) — explaining how each contribution added to or refined what came before, and why no single scientist could have made all contributions alone.
wider: Explore how understanding of light and optics developed through contributions from Plato, Euclid, Ptolemy, Ibn al-Haytham and Roger Bacon — examining how ideas from different cultures and centuries built a cumulative scientific understanding

Investigate how contemporary soil erosion management adapts and builds on First Nations Australians' fire management and agricultural practices — examining how traditional ecological knowledge informs current scientific practice
Research why European naturalists initially rejected the platypus as a faked animal and how ongoing collaborative research has continued to reveal its features and behaviours

modes.reason: Students tend to think of science as a series of individual 'eureka' moments rather than as a cumulative process where each advance depends on prior work. Making the dependency chain explicit — what prior knowledge was required → what new contribution was made → what it made possible for others — is the scaffold that produces genuine understanding of science as a cumulative human endeavour.

nodes.label: Collaboration across disciplines and institutions advances science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why complex scientific questions often require collaboration across disciplines, institutions or countries, and describe at least one example where such collaboration produced an advance.
criteria: Describes one example of collaboration across at least two disciplines or groups
Explains what each contributor brought to the collaboration and why a single discipline could not have answered the question alone

width.minimum: Students describe one example of scientific collaboration across at least two disciplines or groups, explaining what each contributed and why collaboration was necessary.
width.typical: Students examine multiple collaboration examples — including ecologists collaborating with engineers and computer scientists for remote sensing, and geologists/hydrologists/farmers collaborating on erosion mitigation — explaining what each discipline contributes and why the question could not be answered by one discipline alone.
wider: Explore how developing erosion mitigation techniques (contour banks, strip cropping) requires collaboration across geologists, hydrologists and farmers — examining what each brings to the problem

Research how the discovery of biofluorescent mammals (flying squirrel → wombats, bilbies, echidnas) led to international scientific collaboration across fields — examining how one discovery opened a line of collaborative inquiry
Examine why international collaboration is necessary for questions about climate, ecosystems and space — exploring the scale and complexity that require distributed scientific effort

modes.reason: Students tend to imagine scientists as lone individuals working in isolation. Encountering collaboration at different scales — across disciplines within a project, across institutions nationally, across countries internationally — builds a more accurate and complete model of how science actually operates.

descriptors.title: Scientific knowledge used by communities
descriptors.description: investigate how scientific knowledge is used by individuals and communities to identify problems, consider responses and make decisions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine how scientific explanations are used to meet needs or solve problems (AC9S3H02, 3-4 band). They now extend to examining how knowledge is used by communities — not just to design solutions, but to identify problems, evaluate responses and make collective decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate examples where scientific knowledge enables individuals and communities to identify problems, evaluate possible responses and make decisions — examining what knowledge was used, what options were considered, and how decisions were reached.

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge helps identify and define problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how scientific knowledge enables people to identify and precisely define a problem — distinguishing between a symptom (what is observed) and a cause (what the knowledge explains).
criteria: Describes one example where scientific knowledge enabled a problem to be identified
Explains what the knowledge was and how it transformed an observation into a defined problem with a cause

width.minimum: Students describe one example where scientific knowledge helped identify a problem, explaining what the knowledge was and how it enabled the problem to be recognised.
width.typical: Students examine how knowledge of erosion processes enables identification of at-risk landscapes, and how knowledge of light properties enables identification of light pollution as a problem — explaining in each case how scientific knowledge transforms an observable phenomenon into a defined problem with a cause.
wider: Examine how park rangers use knowledge of erosion to identify and define problems in fragile environments — distinguishing natural and human-caused erosion and predicting risk locations
Investigate how knowledge of light pollution and its effects on ecosystems enables communities to identify artificial lighting as a problem requiring management
Research how First Nations Australians use ecological knowledge to identify problems in Country — examining how deep observational knowledge enables early problem recognition

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge informs decisions and responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how communities use scientific knowledge to evaluate options and make decisions — explaining what knowledge was used, what options were considered, and why a particular response was chosen.
criteria: Describes one example where a community used scientific knowledge to make a decision
Explains what knowledge was used, what options were considered, and why the chosen response was selected

width.minimum: Students describe one example where a community used scientific knowledge to make a decision, identifying the knowledge used and the decision made.
width.typical: Students examine multiple examples where communities use scientific knowledge to make decisions — farming decisions based on habitat knowledge, erosion mitigation design, light pollution reduction strategies — explaining the knowledge-to-decision pathway and evaluating the trade-offs involved.
wider: Research how communities have used knowledge of light pollution to design and implement solutions — covered streetlights, automated systems, motion sensors — and evaluate each response's effectiveness
Examine how people use properties of light to design signal lamps for Morse code communication — tracing the knowledge-to-application pathway for a historical and ongoing technology

Consider how communities in different regions make decisions about which crops or animals to farm based on local habitat conditions — examining how biological knowledge shapes agricultural decision-making

modes.reason: Students tend to see science as producing one correct answer rather than informing a decision among multiple options. Encountering varied decision contexts — where different communities make different but scientifically informed choices — builds a more accurate model of how scientific knowledge functions in community decision-making.

descriptors.title: Questioning and predicting
descriptors.description: pose investigable questions to identify patterns and test relationships and make reasoned predictions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can pose questions targeting patterns and relationships and make observation-grounded predictions (AC9S3I01, 3-4 band). They now extend to posing questions that test causal relationships and making reasoned predictions — predictions that are explicitly justified with prior knowledge, not just prior observation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students pose investigable questions that target patterns and test causal relationships, make reasoned predictions that are explicitly justified with prior scientific knowledge, and distinguish between questions that can and cannot be scientifically investigated.

nodes.label: Investigable questions test relationships between variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose investigable questions that specifically target a relationship between two variables — framed as 'Does X affect Y?' or 'How does X change when Y changes?' — and explain what makes a question investigable.
criteria: Poses a question that targets a relationship between two named variables
Explains why the question is investigable — what would be changed and what would be measured
nodes.hinge_reason: Posing a well-formed relationship question is the entry point for I02 planning — students who cannot frame a question around two identifiable variables cannot independently decide what to change and measure. Thin treatment here means I02 planning defaults to teacher-supplied questions rather than student-generated ones.

width.minimum: Students pose one investigable question targeting a relationship between two variables and explain why it is investigable.
width.typical: Students pose investigable relationship questions across two or more Y5-6 science contexts (biological, geological, physical), explain what makes each question investigable (variables identifiable, testable by observation or measurement), and distinguish from questions that cannot be scientifically investigated.
wider: Pose questions about landscape features and how they were changed by weathering, erosion or deposition — examining what observation or measurement would test the relationship

Use information from First Nations Australians to formulate investigable questions about structural features and behaviours of living things — examining how traditional knowledge can guide scientific question formulation

Compare the structure of relationship questions in different science domains (biological: survival features; geological: erosion rates; physical: light behaviour) and identify what makes each type investigable

nodes.label: Reasoned predictions are justified with prior scientific knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make reasoned predictions that are explicitly justified using prior scientific knowledge — distinguishing a reasoned prediction from an observation-based prediction by the nature of the justification.
criteria: Makes a prediction and explicitly states the prior scientific knowledge (not just prior observation) that justifies it
Identifies what outcome would confirm or challenge the prediction

width.minimum: Students make a reasoned prediction for a named investigation scenario and explicitly state the prior scientific knowledge that justifies it.
width.typical: Students make reasoned predictions across two or more science contexts, explicitly linking each prediction to a scientific principle or prior knowledge (not just a prior observation), and explain what outcome would confirm or challenge the prediction.
wider: Make reasoned predictions about habitat survival: 'Will animals in desert habitats all have water conservation adaptations?' — justifying with knowledge of natural selection and habitat demands
Make reasoned predictions about erosion: 'Will steeper slopes show more erosion?' — justifying with knowledge of water velocity and transport capacity
Make reasoned predictions about light: 'Will light reflecting off a curved mirror behave differently from a flat mirror?' — justifying with knowledge of straight-line travel and angle of reflection

descriptors.title: Planning and conducting
descriptors.description: plan and conduct repeatable investigations to answer questions, including, as appropriate, deciding the variables to be changed, measured and controlled in fair tests; describing potential risks; planning for the safe use of equipment and materials; and identifying required permissions to conduct investigations on Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use provided scaffolds to plan fair tests (AC9S3I02, 3-4 band). They now take greater ownership — deciding variables independently, planning for repeatability, and considering field site permissions and risks without a provided scaffold.
descriptors.endpoint: Students independently plan repeatable investigations — deciding variables, describing risks, planning safe equipment use and identifying required permissions — and conduct investigations that could be reproduced by another person from the recorded method.

nodes.label: Repeatable investigations require a recorded, reproducible method
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and record an investigation method in sufficient detail that another person could repeat it, and explain why repeatability is important for reliable findings.
criteria: Records an investigation method in sufficient detail for another student to repeat it
Explains why repeatability is important for the reliability of findings

width.minimum: Students record an investigation method for a given question in enough detail that another student could follow it, and explain why repeatability matters.
width.typical: Students plan investigations across different approaches (experimental testing, field observation, research, virtual simulation), record methods in sufficient detail for reproduction, and explain that repeatable findings are more reliable than single-trial results.
wider: Compare different investigation approaches for the same question (experimental vs field observation vs simulation) and evaluate the trade-offs in repeatability, control and ecological validity
Plan a field excursion to collect erosion data — using maps or aerial photographs to predict sites, planning observation methods and recording a method that could be repeated by another group
Consult with First Nations Australians to identify local areas that require permission before accessing — examining the intersection of scientific investigation and cultural protocols on Country

nodes.label: Variables, risks and permissions are identified in planning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can independently decide which variables to change, measure and control in a fair test, describe potential risks, plan safe equipment use, and identify any permissions required for field investigations.
criteria: Independently identifies variables to change, measure and control without a provided scaffold
Describes at least one potential risk and the planned safety measure to address it
nodes.hinge_reason: Independent variable identification is the prerequisite for all subsequent fair test work at Y5-6 — students who cannot decide variables without scaffolding cannot meaningfully engage with I03 precision measurement or I05 error analysis, both of which assume a validly planned investigation.

width.minimum: Students independently identify the variable to change, variable to measure and at least two variables to control for a given investigation question, and describe one potential risk.
width.typical: Students independently plan fair tests across Y5-6 investigation contexts (light, erosion, survival features); decide all variables without scaffolding; describe multiple potential risks and planned safety measures; identify any permissions required for field investigations on Country/Place.
wider: Evaluate an investigation plan for completeness — identifying any uncontrolled variables, unaddressed risks or missing permissions, and explaining the consequence of each gap
Plan for and navigate the practical challenge of conducting field erosion observations — identifying what permissions, safety equipment and observation methods are required
Consult with First Nations Australians to guide investigation planning, including safety considerations and culturally appropriate approaches to field sites

modes.reason: Students at this band must transfer the fair test planning skill to investigation types beyond the classroom bench test — field observations, simulations, research-based investigations. Encountering planning across these varied investigation types builds the flexible, context-independent planning capability the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Observing and measuring
descriptors.description: use equipment to observe, measure and record data with reasonable precision, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can read familiar scaled instruments and record observations systematically (AC9S3I03, 3-4 band). They now extend to selecting equipment for precision, using standard units with prefixes, and recording data electronically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select equipment appropriate to the precision required, measure and record data using standard units and prefixes, discuss why precision matters for investigation findings, and use digital tools where appropriate.

nodes.label: Equipment is selected for the precision the investigation requires
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why different equipment gives different levels of precision, select appropriate equipment for a given measurement task, and describe the effect of low precision on investigation findings.
criteria: Selects appropriate equipment for a given measurement task and explains the reasoning
Records data using standard units with appropriate metric prefixes
Explains how low precision could affect the conclusions of an investigation
nodes.hinge_reason: Precision measurement with appropriate equipment is a prerequisite for I04 data representation and I05 error analysis — students who do not measure with adequate precision cannot construct meaningful representations or identify measurement error as a specific error source. Imprecision at I03 propagates as systematically poor data through all downstream inquiry nodes.

width.minimum: Students compare the precision of two instruments for the same measurement and select the more appropriate one, explaining their reasoning.
width.typical: Students select appropriate equipment across investigation types, explain why precision matters for investigation conclusions, use standard units with metric prefixes (kilo-, milli-) consistently, and record data in tables, diagrams or digital formats.
wider: Explore which equipment gives the most appropriate precision for different investigation contexts — comparing cup vs measuring jug vs digital scale for mass measurement
Use digital tools (digital photography, spreadsheets) to record and organise observation data — examining what digital recording adds in accuracy and reproducibility
Investigate how the precision of measurement equipment affects whether a difference between two conditions can be detected

modes.reason: Precise measurement with standard units requires consistent accurate practice across investigation types. Students at this band must apply precision reasoning independently — not just follow instructions — which requires encountering precision decisions across varied measurement contexts.

descriptors.title: Processing and representing data
descriptors.description: construct and use appropriate representations, including tables, graphs and visual or physical models, to organise and process data and information and describe patterns, trends and relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct tables and column graphs and use visual/physical models (AC9S3I04, 3-4 band). They now extend to selecting appropriate representations independently, constructing a wider range of types (ray diagrams, annotated field sketches, maps, physical landscape models), and using representations to identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships — not just to display data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and construct appropriate representations for a given data type or relationship, and use those representations to identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships — treating construction and interpretation as two distinct phases of data processing.

nodes.label: Representations are selected and constructed for a given data type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate representation type for a given data set or relationship and construct it accurately — with correct labels, conventions and structure.
criteria: Selects a representation type appropriate to the data or relationship and explains why it suits the purpose
Constructs the representation with correct labels, units and conventions for the chosen type
nodes.hinge_reason: Constructing a valid representation is the prerequisite for Node 2 interpretation — students cannot extract patterns from a malformed or wrong-type representation. A student who defaults to column graphs regardless of data type will be unable to use maps or ray diagrams to identify the patterns those representations are designed to reveal.

width.minimum: Students select and construct one appropriate representation for a given data set and explain why that representation type suits the data.
width.typical: Students select and construct representations across Y5-6 science contexts — annotated field sketches for structural features, column graphs for simulation outcomes, physical landscape models for erosion, labelled ray diagrams for light behaviour, maps for erosion pattern distribution — and justify the representation type chosen in each case.
wider: Compare two different representation types for the same data set and explain what each communicates that the other does not — examining representation as a deliberate choice
Construct labelled ray diagrams for light reflection and refraction scenarios — applying a new representation convention to Y5 physical science content
Use maps or aerial photographs to represent spatial data on erosion site locations — examining how spatial representation suits geographically distributed data

modes.reason: Students at this band encounter a wider range of representation types than at 3-4 band — ray diagrams, annotated photographs, physical landscape models and maps are all new. Building fluency in selecting the right type for the data, and constructing each accurately, requires encountering varied representation types across different science contexts. Without breadth, students default to familiar formats (tables, column graphs) regardless of data type.

nodes.label: Representations are used to identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a completed representation to identify a pattern, trend or relationship in the data and describe what it means in the context of the investigation question.
criteria: Identifies at least one pattern, trend or relationship in a completed representation
Describes what the pattern or relationship means in the context of the investigation question — not just what the graph shows, but what it tells us
nodes.hinge_reason: Pattern identification from representations is directly required by I05 evaluating — students must select evidence from data to draw conclusions. A student who cannot identify what a representation shows cannot distinguish evidence from noise, and cannot draw a reasoned conclusion at I05.

width.minimum: Students use one completed representation to identify and describe one pattern or relationship, connecting it to the investigation question.
width.typical: Students use representations across Y5-6 science contexts to describe patterns and relationships — predation and camouflage outcomes from column graphs, erosion patterns from maps, force interactions from ray diagrams, structural feature distributions from annotated sketches — and explain what each pattern or relationship means for the investigation question.
wider: Construct column graphs from repeated simulation data (predation and camouflage outcomes) and explain why using values across multiple runs gives a more reliable pattern than a single run
Use a representation to distinguish a clear pattern from a noisy or ambiguous result — examining what makes a pattern reliable enough to support a conclusion
Connect an identified pattern directly to a prediction made before the investigation — evaluating whether the pattern confirms, partially confirms or contradicts the prediction

modes.reason: Students readily describe what a representation shows at surface level ('the column graph shows group A had more') without identifying a pattern or connecting it to the investigation question. Encountering the interpretation move across varied representation types and science contexts — where 'what does this show?' requires different reasoning for a ray diagram vs a map vs a column graph — builds a more generalisable interpretation capability.

descriptors.title: Evaluating
descriptors.description: compare methods and findings with those of others, recognise possible sources of error, pose questions for further investigation and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare findings, evaluate fairness and draw data-grounded conclusions (AC9S3I05, 3-4 band). They now extend to recognising specific error sources, selecting evidence from data, and drawing reasoned conclusions — not just grounded ones.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare methods and findings with peers, recognise specific sources of error in methods and measurements, select appropriate evidence from data to support reasoned conclusions, and pose further questions arising from method limitations or unexpected findings.

nodes.label: Errors are identified and their effect on findings is explained
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific sources of error in an investigation method (uncontrolled variables, measurement errors, environmental changes) and explain how each error could affect the findings and conclusions.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific sources of error in an investigation method
Explains how each identified error could affect the findings or conclusion
nodes.hinge_reason: Error identification is prerequisite for Node 2 evidence selection — students who cannot recognise what made their data unreliable cannot make principled decisions about which data counts as valid evidence for a conclusion. Thin treatment here produces conclusions that ignore data quality.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two specific sources of error in a given investigation and explain how each could affect the findings.
width.typical: Students identify error sources across types (uncontrolled variable, misreading of measurements, changed environmental factors); explain the specific effect of each error on the data; compare methods with peers to identify whether different methods produced different findings due to error differences; and distinguish error from natural variation.
wider: Examine the difference between data and evidence — discussing how the same data can be interpreted differently depending on what counts as relevant evidence for a conclusion
Compare proposed reasons for findings in a group — explaining reasoning, identifying disagreements and posing further questions about what additional evidence would resolve them
Reflect on inferences made during analysis and evaluate whether the inference is supported by the data or goes beyond it

nodes.label: Evidence is selected to draw reasoned conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select relevant evidence from a data set, use it to draw a reasoned conclusion, and explain why the selected evidence supports the conclusion while other data does not.
criteria: Distinguishes between data and evidence for a given investigation
Selects at least two pieces of evidence that support a named conclusion and explains why each is relevant
Draws a reasoned conclusion that does not overclaim beyond the selected evidence

width.minimum: Students identify at least two pieces of evidence from a data set that support a named conclusion and explain why each piece is relevant.
width.typical: Students distinguish between data (all recorded observations) and evidence (data selected because it is relevant to the question); select evidence to support a reasoned conclusion; explain why the conclusion is reasoned (evidence-based, not overclaiming); and pose at least one further question arising from the limitations of the investigation.
wider: Examine a scenario where two groups selected different evidence from the same data set and drew different conclusions — discussing how evidence selection affects conclusions
Evaluate an inference made from observational data — determining whether it follows from the evidence or goes beyond it
Research and discuss how scientists in different fields manage the data-to-evidence selection process — examining how peer review and replication address this challenge

modes.reason: The data-vs-evidence distinction and the scenario of two groups drawing different conclusions from the same data are genuinely enriching directions that connect to epistemological thinking about science. These go well beyond what the minimum band requires.

descriptors.title: Communicating
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas and findings for specific purposes and audiences, including selection of language features, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can write and create science texts for identified purposes and audiences using scientific vocabulary (AC9S3I06, 3-4 band). They now extend to selecting specific language features (vocabulary, sentence structure) deliberately to shape meaning, and co-authoring scientific reports with standard conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write and create texts that use deliberately selected language features to serve specific scientific communication purposes — including persuasive texts, scientific reports and digital presentations — selecting vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Language features are selected deliberately to shape meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how vocabulary and sentence structure contribute to the meaning and effectiveness of a science text, and make deliberate language choices in their own writing to serve their communication purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two language features in a science text and explains how each contributes to meaning
Makes at least two deliberate language choices in their own writing and explains the reasoning

width.minimum: Students identify at least two language features in a given science text and explain how each contributes to the text's meaning or effectiveness.
width.typical: Students explain how vocabulary, sentence structure and text organisation shape a science text; deliberately select scientific vocabulary for precision; use appropriate sentence structures for their genre (active/passive voice, present/past tense); and justify language choices in terms of their communication purpose.
wider: Acknowledge and explore First Nations Australians' ways of representing and communicating information about anatomical features — comparing with written scientific text conventions
Explore whether there is a 'correct' way to represent particles — examining how different representational choices in an animation communicate different aspects of the particle model
Compare language features across scientific genres (report vs persuasive text vs digital presentation) and explain how each genre's conventions serve its purpose

nodes.label: Science texts serve specific purposes with appropriate conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and create science texts in at least two different forms (scientific report, persuasive text, digital presentation) with appropriate conventions for each form, tailored to a specific purpose and audience.
criteria: Produces a science text in a given form using appropriate conventions
Selects vocabulary appropriate to the purpose and audience
Justifies at least one language choice in terms of how it serves the communication purpose

width.minimum: Students produce a science text in a given form using appropriate conventions for that form and with vocabulary suited to the purpose and audience.
width.typical: Students produce science texts across multiple forms — a co-authored scientific report with standard conventions (prediction, method, results, conclusion, discussion of errors), a persuasive text for a local authority, and a digital presentation for information sharing — selecting and justifying language choices for each.
wider: Construct a persuasive text for local council arguing for an erosion mitigation strategy — applying scientific knowledge to a genuine civic communication purpose
Co-author a scientific report on a light investigation using standard scientific report conventions and appropriate vocabulary, data representations and sentence structures
Develop a digital presentation on structural features of animals in a specific habitat — selecting language and visual representations appropriate for the intended audience

modes.reason: Students at this band must produce texts across genuinely different forms — each with different conventions and purposes. Encountering report, persuasive and digital presentation forms in different science contexts builds flexible communication capability rather than a single-genre template.

descriptors.title: Structural features and survival
descriptors.description: examine how particular structural features and behaviours of living things enable their survival in specific habitats
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers in a habitat and describe food chains (AC9S4U01). They can identify physical conditions of habitats at a surface level but have not yet examined the specific structural and behavioural adaptations that enable individual organisms to survive in those conditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine structural features (physical characteristics) and behaviours of plants and animals that enable survival in specific habitats, explain the function of each feature or behaviour in terms of the survival challenge it addresses, and connect these to the physical conditions of the habitat.

nodes.label: Structural features are physical characteristics that aid survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify structural features of plants and animals and explain how each feature addresses a specific survival challenge in the organism's habitat.
criteria: Identifies at least three structural features of a named organism
Explains how each feature addresses a specific survival challenge in the organism's habitat
nodes.hinge_reason: The feature-function-habitat reasoning chain is prerequisite for Node 2 and Node 3 — students who only list features without explaining their survival function cannot explain behavioural adaptations (N2) or connect features to specific habitat conditions (N3). The descriptor requires explanation, not identification, and thin treatment at N1 produces a feature-listing habit that persists through the unit.

width.minimum: Students identify at least three structural features of a named organism and explain how each feature enables survival in its specific habitat.
width.typical: Students examine structural features across multiple organisms from different habitats, explain the function of each feature in terms of the survival challenge it addresses (obtaining food, conserving water, avoiding predators, regulating temperature), and compare how different organisms solve the same survival challenge in different ways.
wider: Use physical or digital simulations to explore how beak shape in birds influences food-finding success — examining the relationship between structural feature and habitat resource availability
Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of structural features of certain species and how those features can be identified and exploited sustainably
Examine how biofluorescence in mammals (wombats, bilbies, platypus) was discovered through scientific collaboration — connecting structural feature discovery to scientific practice (AC9S5H01)

modes.reason: Students commonly describe structural features without explaining their function — 'the camel has a hump' without 'the hump stores fat that can be metabolised for water and energy in a desert habitat where food and water are scarce'. Making the feature-to-function-to-habitat-condition chain explicit is the scaffold that produces genuine biological reasoning rather than a list of facts.

nodes.label: Behaviours also enable survival in specific habitats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify behavioural adaptations of organisms and explain how each behaviour addresses a specific survival challenge — distinguishing behavioural from structural adaptations.
criteria: Identifies at least two behavioural adaptations of a named organism and explains the survival function of each
Distinguishes between a structural feature and a behavioural adaptation for the same organism

width.minimum: Students identify at least two behavioural adaptations of a named organism and explain how each behaviour aids survival in its habitat.
width.typical: Students explain behavioural adaptations (nocturnal activity, migration, camouflage behaviour, social grouping, hibernation) across multiple organisms, explain the survival function of each behaviour, and distinguish between structural features (physical) and behavioural adaptations (actions).
wider: Investigate how camouflage functions as both a structural (colour, pattern) and behavioural (stillness, movement timing) adaptation — examining how the two work together
Explore features and behaviours of living things in Australia's desert environments — bottle trees, water-holding frogs, thorny devils — and explain how each addresses water scarcity
Use simulations to model how camouflage affects predation rates — examining the relationship between behavioural adaptation and survival probability

modes.reason: Students commonly think of adaptation only in terms of physical features (sharp claws, thick fur) and overlook behavioural adaptations, or they treat behaviours as choices rather than as evolved survival strategies. Encountering behavioural adaptations across varied organisms and habitat types builds a more complete model of how living things are suited to their environments.

nodes.label: Features and behaviours match the challenges of specific habitats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect the structural features and behaviours of an organism to the specific physical conditions and challenges of its habitat — explaining why this organism is well-suited to this habitat and less suited to a different one.
criteria: Connects at least two features or behaviours to specific physical conditions of a named habitat
Predicts at least one challenge an organism would face if placed in a different habitat, with reasoning

width.minimum: Students explain why a named organism is well-suited to its specific habitat by connecting at least two features or behaviours to the physical conditions of that habitat.
width.typical: Students compare two organisms from different habitats, explain how each is suited to its own habitat's conditions, and predict what challenges each would face if placed in the other's habitat — using this to demonstrate that adaptation is habitat-specific, not universally 'better'.
wider: Pose and investigate questions about survival: 'Do all animals living in desert habitats have ways to survive without water?' — examining whether habitat challenges predict adaptation patterns
Examine how decisions are made to farm particular crops or animals based on local habitat conditions — connecting biological adaptation knowledge to agricultural decision-making (AC9S5H02)
Research how introduced species that lack local adaptations affect native species — examining what happens when organism-habitat matching breaks down

modes.reason: This node requires students to integrate structural feature knowledge, behavioural adaptation knowledge and habitat condition knowledge in a single explanatory account. Students must coordinate all three to explain organism-habitat fit and predict mismatch consequences — this is the synthesis challenge of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition
descriptors.description: describe how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition cause slow or rapid change to Earth's surface
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare observable properties of soils and rocks and explain their importance as Earth resources (AC9S3U02). They have not yet distinguished weathering from erosion, examined the agents driving each, or connected these processes to landscape change over time.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how weathering breaks down rock material and how erosion, transportation and deposition move and redistribute that material to change Earth's surface — across both slow geological and rapid event-driven timescales — and examine human impacts on these processes.

nodes.label: Weathering breaks down rocks in place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish weathering from erosion — explaining that weathering breaks down rock material in place through mechanical and biological means — and identify agents of weathering with examples.
criteria: Explains that weathering breaks down rock material in place without moving it
Names at least two weathering agents and explains the mechanism by which each breaks down rock
nodes.hinge_reason: The weathering/erosion distinction is definitionally prerequisite for Node 2 — students who conflate the two processes cannot accurately describe the erosion → transportation → deposition sequence, and will describe all surface change as 'erosion'. This conflation is a known persistent misconception that causes systematic errors across N2 and N3.

width.minimum: Students explain that weathering breaks down rock material in place, name at least two types of weathering (mechanical, biological) and give one example of each.
width.typical: Students describe mechanical weathering (wind abrasion, freeze-thaw cycles, thermal expansion) and biological weathering (plant roots, organisms), explain how each breaks down rock without moving the material, and distinguish this from erosion which involves movement.
wider: Investigate how freeze-thaw weathering operates by modelling water expanding in cracks — examining the mechanical force that splits rock without chemical change
Examine how biological weathering by tree roots and organisms operates at a timescale invisible to observation but visible in landscape features
Connect weathering to rock cycle processes (AC9S8U04) — examining how weathered material becomes sediment in the rock cycle

modes.reason: Students consistently conflate weathering and erosion, treating them as synonyms or as sequential steps in the same process. The distinction — weathering breaks down in place, erosion moves material — is fundamental to understanding how landscapes change and must be established explicitly before students can accurately describe the full sequence.

nodes.label: Erosion, transportation and deposition move and redistribute material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that erosion picks up and moves weathered material, transportation carries it, and deposition lays it down in a new location — describing the agents involved (water, wind, ice, gravity) and the landforms each process produces.
criteria: Explains the three-stage sequence: erosion (picks up) → transportation (carries) → deposition (lays down)
Names at least two agents of erosion and identifies a landform feature produced by each

width.minimum: Students explain the sequence of erosion → transportation → deposition with one agent (water or wind), naming the agent and describing what happens at each stage.
width.typical: Students describe erosion, transportation and deposition by multiple agents (water, wind, ice, gravity), identify the landforms each produces (river deltas, sand dunes, alluvial fans, cliffs), compare fast and slow timescales of these processes, and give local or regional examples.
wider: Use aerial photographs or maps to identify patterns in erosion site locations at local or regional scale — examining how topography and land cover influence erosion distribution
Model landscape erosion using sand, gravel, soil and water to explore factors that affect erosion rates — connecting model behaviour to real landscape processes
Examine the effects of significant rainfall (monsoon, flood events) on transportation and deposition of river sediments in the Asia-Pacific region — exploring rapid event-driven change

modes.reason: Students typically think of erosion only as water cutting into riverbanks, missing wind erosion, glacial erosion, gravity-driven mass movement and coastal erosion. Encountering erosion agents across varied landform contexts builds a more complete and accurate model of how landscapes change.

nodes.label: Human activity changes erosion rates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how human activity alters natural erosion rates and predict the consequences of specific land use changes on local landscapes.
criteria: Explains at least one mechanism by which human activity increases erosion rates
Describes at least one strategy that mitigates erosion and explains how it reduces the rate

width.minimum: Students describe at least one way human activity increases erosion rates and explain the likely consequence for the landscape.
width.typical: Students examine how human activities (deforestation, urbanisation, agriculture, construction) change natural erosion rates, explain the mechanisms involved (removal of vegetation cover, increased run-off, disturbed soil), and describe strategies that reduce erosion in fragile environments.
wider: Examine how erosion mitigation strategies — contour banks, strip cropping, revegetation — adapt and build on First Nations Australians' fire management and agricultural practices (AC9S5H01)
Consider how First Nations Australians are impacted by rapid erosion of sand dunes and the resulting effect of saltwater on culturally significant freshwater swamps
Research how park rangers use knowledge of erosion processes to design rules and built features that protect fragile environments and heritage sites (AC9S5H02)

modes.reason: Students commonly think of erosion as a purely natural process and are not aware of how dramatically human land use accelerates it. Encountering multiple contexts where human activity changes erosion rates — and where mitigation strategies have been designed in response — builds a more complete and practically useful understanding.

descriptors.title: Light
descriptors.description: identify sources of light, recognise that light travels in a straight path and describe how shadows are formed and light can be reflected and refracted
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally encountered light and shadows in earlier years. They have not yet examined light as travelling in straight paths, distinguished natural from artificial sources, or described reflection and refraction as distinct interactions between light and matter.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify natural and artificial light sources, explain that light travels in straight paths from a source, describe shadow formation and the conditions that affect shadow size and shape, explain reflection and refraction as different interactions of light with surfaces and media, and represent these using ray diagrams.

nodes.label: Light travels in straight paths from sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify natural and artificial light sources, explain that light travels in straight paths (rays) from a source, and use this to explain why objects cast shadows.
criteria: Names at least two natural and two artificial light sources
Explains that light travels in straight paths (rays) from a source
Uses straight-line travel to explain why an object casts a shadow
nodes.hinge_reason: Straight-line travel of light is the foundational model for all subsequent nodes — Node 2 shadow formation and Node 3 reflection/refraction both depend on the ray model. Students who do not hold this model cannot construct valid ray diagrams or predict shadow and reflection behaviour.

width.minimum: Students distinguish natural from artificial light sources with examples, and explain that light travels in straight paths from a source.
width.typical: Students classify light sources as natural (sun, stars, fire, bioluminescence) and artificial (light globes, LEDs, candles), explain that light travels in straight lines from a source in all directions, and use straight-line travel to explain why we can see objects and why shadows form where light is blocked.
wider: Investigate bioluminescent organisms (glow worms, deep sea creatures, fireflies) as natural light sources — examining how living things produce light and why
Explore how understanding of light and optics has developed historically — comparing ideas of Plato, Euclid, Ibn al-Haytham and Roger Bacon about the nature of light and how we see (AC9S5H01)
Research how First Nations Australians use shimmering body paint as an application of light reflection properties — connecting cultural practice to light behaviour

modes.reason: The historical development of optics (AC9S5H01) provides a rich cross-strand direction that connects the science content to how scientific understanding is built over time. Bioluminescence offers a genuinely interesting natural light source that broadens students' concept beyond sun and lamps — and breadth of light source examples reinforces the straight-line travel model across varied phenomena, addressing the hinge risk.

nodes.label: Shadows form when light is blocked
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how shadows form when an opaque object blocks light, describe how shadow size and shape change with the position and distance of the light source, and represent shadow formation using ray diagrams.
criteria: Explains shadow formation using the straight-line travel of light being blocked by an object
Predicts how shadow size will change when the light source or object position changes, with reasoning
Draws a ray diagram showing shadow formation

width.minimum: Students explain that shadows form when an object blocks light, and describe how changing the position of a light source changes the shadow.
width.typical: Students explain shadow formation using the straight-line travel of light; describe how shadow size relates to the position and distance of the light source and object; investigate shadow formation using sundials or shadow puppets; and draw ray diagrams showing how light from a source is blocked to create a shadow.
wider: Investigate how sundials use shadow position to indicate time — examining the relationship between sun position, Earth's rotation and shadow direction across the day
Explore how shadow puppets use controlled light blocking to create effects — examining how puppet distance, light distance and screen distance affect shadow size and sharpness
Examine partial shadows (penumbra) produced by extended light sources — exploring why the edge of a shadow is sometimes sharp and sometimes fuzzy

modes.reason: Students commonly describe shadows as 'the dark side of an object' rather than as a region where light is blocked. Making the ray diagram reasoning explicit — light travels in straight lines → object blocks some rays → region behind object receives no light → shadow forms there — is the scaffold that allows students to predict shadow behaviour under different conditions.

nodes.label: Light reflects off surfaces and refracts when changing medium
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain reflection as light bouncing off a surface in a predictable direction, describe refraction as the bending of light when it passes between different media, give everyday examples of each, and draw ray diagrams for reflection.
criteria: Explains reflection using a ray diagram showing light bouncing off a surface
Explains refraction as the bending of light when it passes between different media, with an everyday example
Distinguishes reflection from refraction as different interactions of light with matter

width.minimum: Students explain reflection using an everyday example and draw a ray diagram showing reflection; explain that refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another.
width.typical: Students explain reflection from flat and curved surfaces with ray diagrams; describe practical applications of reflection (periscopes, mirrors, mirror mazes); explain refraction using prisms or water examples; describe the rainbow spectrum produced by refraction; and distinguish reflection from refraction as different light-surface interactions.
wider: Recognise First Nations Australians' understanding of refraction as experienced in spearfishing — examining how refraction causes objects underwater to appear at a different position than they actually are
Explore how 'holograph' videos use refractive properties of light to create apparently 3-dimensional images — connecting refraction to contemporary optical technology
Investigate how signal lamps use reflection of light to communicate via Morse code — examining how reflection principles are applied in communication (AC9S5H02)

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse reflection and refraction or reduce both to 'what mirrors do'. Encountering reflection across multiple surface types (flat mirror, curved mirror, water surface, shiny objects) and refraction across multiple media (prism, water, glass) — with distinct explanations for each — builds an accurate and differentiated understanding of the two phenomena.

descriptors.title: Particle model of matter
descriptors.description: explain observable properties of solids, liquids and gases by modelling the motion and arrangement of particles
descriptors.knowledge: Students can classify materials as solids or liquids by observable properties and explain changes of state using heat energy (AC9S3U04). They have not yet used a particle model to explain why solids, liquids and gases behave as they do, or examined gases as a third state of matter with distinct properties.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use a particle model — describing the arrangement, spacing and motion of particles — to explain the observable properties of solids, liquids and gases, and connect state changes to changes in particle behaviour when heat energy is added or removed.

nodes.label: Gases have observable properties distinct from solids and liquids
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe observable properties of gases — including that gases have mass, can be compressed, and take the shape and volume of their container — and distinguish these from the properties of solids and liquids.
criteria: States at least two observable properties of gases that distinguish them from solids and liquids
Provides evidence that gases have mass
nodes.hinge_reason: The empirical foundation for gas properties must precede the particle model — students who believe gases have no mass or cannot be compressed will reject the particle model explanation at Node 2 because it contradicts their existing framework. Thin treatment here produces a particle model that students apply by rote without understanding what it explains.

width.minimum: Students describe at least two observable properties of gases and explain how these differ from the properties of solids or liquids.
width.typical: Students classify substances as solids, liquids and gases; describe the characteristic properties of each state including compressibility, fixed vs variable shape and volume; demonstrate that gases have mass; and explain what is different about gases compared with the other two states.
wider: Investigate examples demonstrating that gases have mass — using a balance to compare an empty balloon with one filled with air, or blowing air through a straw to move objects
Explore what is between gas particles — guided discussion about the nature of 'empty space' between particles and what this means for compression

Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of gases and their applications — including the extraction of oils, medical therapies and cooking — connecting practical knowledge to particle-level understanding

modes.reason: Students commonly believe gases have no mass ('air is nothing') and cannot be compressed ('there is nothing to compress'). Encountering multiple demonstrations of gas mass and compressibility — and discussing what is between particles — builds an accurate empirical foundation before the particle model is introduced.

nodes.label: Particle arrangement and motion explain state properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a particle model to explain the observable properties of each state — describing how particle arrangement (close/far apart) and motion (vibrating/flowing/moving freely) differ across solids, liquids and gases.
criteria: Describes particle arrangement and motion for each of the three states
Uses the particle model to explain at least two observable properties — one for solids and one for gases
nodes.hinge_reason: The particle model as an explanatory tool is directly required for Node 3 state change explanation — students must describe particle behaviour changing during melting, evaporation and condensation. Without the model internalised as explanatory (not just diagrammatic), state change explanations collapse to observable descriptions with no particle-level reasoning.

width.minimum: Students describe the particle arrangement and motion for each of the three states and connect each to at least one observable property of that state.
width.typical: Students explain all major observable properties of solids, liquids and gases using particle arrangement and motion — fixed shape (particles tightly packed, vibrating in place), liquid flow (particles close but able to move past each other), gas compression (particles far apart, moving freely) — and represent these models using diagrams or role-play.
wider: Use role-play to model particle arrangement and motion in solids, liquids and gases — examining how collective behaviour of particles produces the observable properties of each state
Observe a virtual demonstration of coloured gases being compressed and explain the change in colour intensity using the particle model — applying the model to predict observable outcomes
Explore whether there is a 'correct' way to represent particles — examining different representations (diagrams, models, animations) and what each communicates and omits

modes.reason: The particle model is the first time students are asked to explain observable properties using an invisible underlying structure. The reasoning chain — particles have arrangement and motion → arrangement and motion determine macroscopic behaviour → observable properties are evidence of particle-level structure — is the scaffold that makes the model genuinely explanatory rather than decorative labelling of diagrams.

nodes.label: State changes are explained by changes in particle behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain state changes (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation) using the particle model — describing how adding or removing heat energy changes particle motion and the transitions between states.
criteria: Explains at least one state change using particle arrangement and motion — describing what happens to particles when heat is added or removed
Explains why mass is conserved during a state change using the particle model

width.minimum: Students explain melting using the particle model — describing how adding heat energy increases particle motion until particles can move past each other.
width.typical: Students explain all common state changes (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation) using the particle model, connecting heat energy addition/removal to changes in particle motion; explain why mass is conserved during state change (same particles, different arrangement); and connect this to their prior knowledge of observable state change (AC9S3U04).
wider: Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of state changes in beeswax and resins — connecting particle-model explanation to culturally significant material use
Investigate how changes of state in materials enable recycling — explaining at the particle level why glass and metals can be returned to liquid state and reformed
Connect particle model state change to the water cycle (AC9S4U02) — explaining evaporation and condensation as particle-level processes that drive the macroscopic cycle

modes.reason: State change explanation using the particle model requires students to integrate observable state change knowledge (AC9S3U04), particle model knowledge, and heat energy concepts in a single explanatory account. This is the synthesis move of the descriptor — applying the model to explain a familiar phenomenon at a new level of explanation.

descriptors.title: Physical conditions and survival
descriptors.description: investigate the physical conditions of a habitat and analyse how the growth and survival of living things is affected by changing physical conditions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how structural features and behaviours enable survival in specific habitats (AC9S5U01). They have not yet systematically investigated physical conditions as variables, examined how changes in conditions affect growth and survival, or analysed the impact of human-caused condition changes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify physical conditions in habitats (temperature, light, salinity, soil type, moisture), investigate how changes in those conditions affect the growth and survival of living things, and analyse how human-caused condition changes affect organisms — including predicting impacts and examining responses.

nodes.label: Habitats have measurable physical conditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the physical conditions of an aquatic or terrestrial habitat — including temperature, light availability, salinity, soil type, moisture and pH — and explain how these conditions vary over time.
criteria: Identifies at least three physical conditions of a named habitat
Explains how at least one physical condition varies over time in the habitat
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying physical conditions as named, measurable variables is prerequisite for Node 2 analysis — students who think of habitat only as 'where an animal lives' cannot analyse how a change in a specific condition (e.g. salinity, temperature) affects growth or survival. This vocabulary and conceptual shift must precede any investigation or analysis work.

width.minimum: Students identify at least three physical conditions of a named habitat and describe how at least one condition changes over time.
width.typical: Students identify the full range of physical conditions in a habitat, measure or gather data on those conditions, describe how conditions vary seasonally or in response to events, and explain why these conditions determine which organisms can survive in the habitat.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of the physical conditions necessary for the survival of certain plants and animals — examining how deep observational knowledge of conditions guides land and resource management
Use digital sensors (soil moisture probes, digital thermometers) to collect physical condition data over time and identify patterns in condition variation
Compare physical conditions across two contrasting habitats and predict which organisms could survive in each, and which could not

modes.reason: First Nations knowledge of condition-organism relationships provides a sophisticated and culturally grounded direction. Digital sensor data collection over time introduces a richer data-gathering approach that connects to real ecological monitoring practice. Breadth of habitat examples reinforces the named physical conditions vocabulary across varied contexts, addressing the hinge risk.

nodes.label: Changing physical conditions affect growth and survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how changes in physical conditions affect the growth and survival of living things — using investigation data or case study evidence to support their analysis.
criteria: Describes how a change in a named physical condition affects the growth or survival of a named organism
Uses evidence (investigation data or case study) to support the analysis
