nodes.hinge_reason: Condition-change analysis (mechanism + evidence) is the direct prerequisite for Node 3 — students must be able to explain how a specific condition change affects an organism before they can analyse human-caused condition changes and predict organism impacts. Without this analytical move, N3 reduces to listing human impacts without explanatory depth.

width.minimum: Students describe how a change in one physical condition (e.g. temperature, salinity, light) affects the growth or survival of a named organism, using evidence.
width.typical: Students investigate how changes in physical conditions (salinity, soil type, sunlight, temperature) affect plant growth; examine how temperature, light and rainfall changes affect animals; explain the mechanism by which each condition change affects the organism; and use data to support their analysis.
wider: Investigate how changes in physical conditions affect the growth of bread mould colonies in sealed bags — examining temperature, moisture and light as variables in a controlled investigation
Examine how changes in physical conditions (temperature, light availability, acidity) affect corals, honey bees or flying foxes — connecting condition change to real threatened species
Recognise how environmental conditions affect life stages — ponds drying up preventing tadpole development, seeds requiring water to germinate, temperature affecting egg hatching

modes.reason: Students commonly understand that extreme conditions kill organisms but miss the subtler effects of condition change on growth rates, reproductive success and life stage completion. Encountering condition-response relationships across plant and animal examples, and across different physical variables, builds a more complete analytical model.

nodes.label: Human activity changes physical conditions and affects living things
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how human-caused changes to physical conditions affect living things, examine community and scientific responses, and predict the impact of specific condition changes on named organisms.
criteria: Describes a human-caused change to a physical condition and its effect on a named organism, with the mechanism explained
Describes at least one scientific or community response to a human-caused condition change

width.minimum: Students describe one example of how human activity changes physical conditions and explain the effect on at least one organism.
width.typical: Students examine multiple examples of human-caused condition change (urban lighting affecting nocturnal animals, pollution changing water chemistry, habitat clearing changing temperature and moisture), explain the mechanism by which each change affects organisms, and describe scientific or community responses.
wider: Research the impacts of light pollution and how communities have used scientific knowledge to reduce it — examining covered streetlights, automated systems and motion sensors as evidence-based responses (AC9S6H02)
Investigate how changes in physical conditions caused by human activity affect aquatic organisms — examining noise pollution, temperature change, chemical runoff
Examine international scientific collaboration in Antarctica to understand how extreme physical conditions affect living thing survival — connecting to global climate condition change (AC9S6H01)

modes.reason: Students are often aware of dramatic habitat destruction but miss less visible human-caused condition changes (light pollution, noise pollution, temperature increase from urban heat islands). Varied examples help students see human impact as operating through physical condition change — a more analytical and generalisable framework than 'humans damage habitats'.

descriptors.title: Earth, sun and solar system
descriptors.description: describe the movement of Earth and other planets relative to the sun and model how Earth's tilt, rotation on its axis and revolution around the sun relate to cyclic observable phenomena, including variable day and night length
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally observed day/night cycles and seasons. They have not yet modelled Earth's rotation and revolution as the mechanical causes of these cycles, or connected Earth's axial tilt to variable day length and seasons.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the movement of Earth and planets in the solar system relative to the sun, model how Earth's rotation causes day and night, explain how Earth's axial tilt causes variable day length and seasons across hemispheres, and connect these movements to cyclic observable phenomena.

nodes.label: Earth and planets orbit the sun; gravity keeps them in orbit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the relative positions and movements of the sun and planets in the solar system, explain that gravity keeps planets in orbit, and appreciate the scale of distances involved.
criteria: Describes the movement of Earth and at least two other planets relative to the sun
Explains that gravity keeps planets in orbit around the sun

width.minimum: Students describe the movement of Earth and at least two other planets relative to the sun, and explain that gravity is the force keeping planets in orbit.
width.typical: Students describe the solar system including the relative positions and orbital paths of planets, explain that gravity keeps planets in orbit around the sun, use simulations to appreciate the scale of distances between bodies, and describe Earth's position and orbital period.
wider: Explore simulations of the solar system to appreciate the distances and size relationships between the sun and planets — examining why the solar system is mostly empty space

Construct a timeline showing how contributions of scientists, mathematicians and astronomers from many cultures have advanced our understanding of the solar system — examining how models were refined by accumulating evidence (AC9S6H01)
Research how astronauts and scientists from many countries have collaborated in the International Space Station program — connecting space science to international collaboration (AC9S6H01)

modes.reason: The multi-cultural history of solar system understanding (AC9S6H01) is directly elaboration-grounded and provides substantive enrichment that connects the science content to how knowledge was built through collaboration and evidence.

nodes.label: Earth's rotation causes day and night
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a model to explain how Earth's rotation on its axis causes day and night, and explain why different places on Earth experience daylight at different times.
criteria: Explains that day and night are caused by Earth's rotation on its axis
Uses a model or diagram to show that the side of Earth facing the sun has day and the side facing away has night
nodes.hinge_reason: The geocentric misconception (sun moves around Earth) must be resolved at Node 2 before Node 3 axial tilt reasoning can proceed — students who believe the sun moves cannot model or understand why tilt causes different hemispheres to receive different sunlight amounts at different orbital positions. The model-building at N2 is the conceptual foundation for the more complex N3 spatial reasoning.

width.minimum: Students explain that day and night are caused by Earth rotating on its axis, using a model or diagram to show the mechanism.
width.typical: Students use 3D models or role-play to model Earth's rotation causing day and night; explain why it appears that the sun moves across the sky (it is Earth rotating, not the sun moving); explain why different regions on Earth are in daylight or darkness at the same moment; and connect rotation to the 24-hour day length.
wider: Research First Nations Australians' understandings of the night sky and its use for timekeeping — examining how sky observation was used to track time and seasons before mechanical clocks
Use real-time views of Earth from space to observe which regions are in daylight and darkness at a given moment — connecting the model to live observation
Examine how different cultures have tracked day length for agricultural and ceremonial purposes — connecting observable sky phenomena to human timekeeping systems

modes.reason: Students commonly believe the sun moves around Earth rather than that Earth rotates — geocentric intuition is persistent. The model-based reasoning chain (Earth rotates on its axis → the side facing the sun has day → the side facing away has night → one rotation = one day) must be established clearly using physical models before students can explain variable day length.

nodes.label: Earth's tilt and revolution cause variable day length and seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how Earth's axial tilt, combined with its revolution around the sun, causes different hemispheres to receive different amounts of sunlight at different times of year — producing variable day length and seasons.
criteria: Explains that Earth's axial tilt causes one hemisphere to receive more sunlight than the other at different times of year
Uses a model or diagram to show why the Southern and Northern hemispheres have opposite seasons
Explains why day length varies between summer and winter at the same location

width.minimum: Students explain that Earth's axial tilt causes one hemisphere to receive more sunlight than the other at different times of year, and connect this to longer days in summer and shorter days in winter.
width.typical: Students use 3D models or simulations to demonstrate how Earth's tilt points one hemisphere toward the sun at one point in its orbit and away six months later; explain why the Southern and Northern hemispheres have opposite seasons; describe how day length varies with latitude and season; and connect variable day length to light intensity and temperature.
wider: Use virtual simulations or real-time views from space to explore why polar regions experience periods of continuous sunlight or darkness — examining extreme cases of the tilt effect

Research First Nations Australians' understandings of seasonal change as evidenced in rock paintings, oral traditions and stone arrangements — examining how cyclic sky observations encode ecological knowledge
Create an imaginative text about a future in which humans live on planets with different axial tilts — exploring the social implications of very different day length variation cycles

modes.reason: Students commonly explain seasons as caused by Earth being closer to the sun in summer — missing the axial tilt mechanism and unable to explain why Australia's summer coincides with Southern Hemisphere tilt toward the sun. Modelling the tilt across multiple orbital positions, including the polar extreme cases, builds the correct spatial reasoning.

descriptors.title: Electrical circuits
descriptors.description: investigate the transfer and transformation of energy in electrical circuits, including the role of circuit components, insulators and conductors
descriptors.knowledge: Students know that heat energy moves from warmer to cooler objects and can sort materials into conductors and insulators of heat (AC9S3U03). They have met sound as energy that makes objects vibrate (AC9S2U02) and explored light from different sources (AC9S5U03). They have not yet examined electrical circuits, circuit components or electrical conductors and insulators.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the requirements for a working electrical circuit, identify the role of each component, distinguish electrical conductors from insulators, construct and represent circuits using standard conventions, and explain how electrical energy is transferred and transformed within a circuit.

nodes.label: A circuit requires a complete conducting path and energy source
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what is required for an electrical circuit to work — a complete conducting path from and back to the energy source — and identify what happens to the circuit when the path is broken.
criteria: Explains that a circuit requires a complete conducting path and an energy source
Explains what happens to the circuit when the path is broken and why
nodes.hinge_reason: The complete-circuit model is prerequisite for Nodes 2 and 3 — students who believe electricity is consumed at the load cannot reason about why conductors and insulators matter (N2) or how energy is transferred through the whole circuit (N3). The 'electricity used up' misconception produces systematic errors in all subsequent circuit reasoning.

width.minimum: Students explain that a circuit requires a complete path and an energy source, and describe what happens when the path is broken.
width.typical: Students construct real or virtual circuits, identify the necessary components (energy source, conducting material, load), explain that electricity flows only in a complete circuit, explore the role of switches in opening and closing the circuit, and explain why a broken path stops the circuit.
wider: Explore electrical hazards in the home and identify safety measures — fuses, circuit breakers, insulation — that prevent dangerous current flow (AC9S6H02)
Investigate why underground power cables were developed and how scientific knowledge about electrical safety informs infrastructure decisions (AC9S6H02)
Examine how the development of electrical circuits has required collaboration across science and engineering — connecting circuit science to the broader history of electrical technology

modes.reason: Students commonly believe electricity 'comes out' of one terminal of a battery and is used up, rather than flowing continuously in a complete loop. Making the complete-circuit logic explicit — electricity must flow from the source, through the circuit, and back to the source — is necessary before students can explain why breaks stop circuits or why components in series all stop when one fails.

nodes.label: Conductors allow electricity to flow; insulators do not
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish electrical conductors from insulators, classify common materials, explain why conductors and insulators are used in specific components, and connect this to safe electrical design.
criteria: Classifies at least four materials as electrical conductors or insulators
Explains why a wire has a metal core with a plastic coating — connecting conductor and insulator properties to a real design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: The conductor/insulator distinction is directly required for Node 3 component analysis — students must understand material properties to explain why specific components transform energy as they do, and why circuit design places conductors and insulators in specific roles. Without this, N3 energy transformation explanations lack material-level grounding.

width.minimum: Students classify at least four materials as electrical conductors or insulators with examples, and explain why this distinction matters in electrical devices.
width.typical: Students investigate different electrical conductors and insulators; explain that conductors allow electrons to move freely while insulators restrict flow; classify metals as conductors and most plastics, rubber and ceramics as insulators; explain why wires are metal with plastic coating; and connect conductor/insulator selection to safety.
wider: Use an ammeter to compare conductivity of different materials — examining how current measurement reveals conductor quality rather than just a binary conductor/insulator distinction
Examine how knowledge of electrical conductors and insulators informs the design of electrical safety guidelines for children (AC9S6H02)
Connect electrical insulation to heat insulation studied in Y3 (AC9S3U03) — examining what these two types of insulation have in common and what is different

modes.reason: Students know metals conduct electricity but often do not understand why the distinction matters in circuit design and safety. Encountering conductor/insulator properties across circuit components, safety equipment, and everyday objects builds a more complete understanding of how material properties are applied in electrical engineering.

nodes.label: Electrical energy is transferred and transformed by circuit components
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how electrical energy is transferred through a circuit and transformed by components into light, heat and sound, and represent circuits using standard conventions.
criteria: Explains how at least two different circuit components transform electrical energy into other forms
Draws a circuit diagram using standard symbols
Connects electrical energy transformation in a circuit to the general concept that energy changes form

width.minimum: Students explain that at least one named component (globe, buzzer, motor) transforms electrical energy into another form, and draw a circuit diagram using standard symbols.
width.typical: Students explain how electrical energy is transferred through the circuit and transformed by different components (globes → light and heat, buzzers → sound, motors → kinetic energy); represent circuits using accepted conventions; examine the purpose of different components including switches, bulbs and ammeters; and connect electrical energy transformation to the general concept of energy transformation (AC9S8U05).
wider: Design a product that uses electrical circuits for a specific purpose and present a case for its use — applying circuit knowledge in a design context (AC9S6I06)
Explore how electricity is used in the home and identify where each energy transformation occurs — tracing electrical energy from source through appliances
Investigate how aquatic noise pollution is related to energy transformation in underwater electrical devices — connecting circuit energy transformation to environmental impact (AC9S6H02)

modes.reason: Circuit energy transformation requires students to coordinate component function knowledge, circuit diagram conventions, and energy transformation concepts from the energy strand. Students who have each as separate knowledge must now apply them together in circuit design and analysis tasks.

descriptors.title: Reversible and irreversible changes
descriptors.description: compare reversible changes, including dissolving and changes of state, and irreversible changes, including cooking and rusting that produce new substances
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain changes of state using the particle model (AC9S5U04) and distinguish solids, liquids and gases (AC9S3U04). They have informally encountered dissolving. They have not yet formally compared reversible and irreversible changes or connected irreversibility to the production of new substances.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare reversible changes (dissolving, state changes — same substances, no new matter produced) with irreversible changes (cooking, rusting — new substances produced), explain what makes a change reversible or irreversible at the substance level, and describe methods for recovering dissolved substances.

nodes.label: Reversible changes do not produce new substances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that reversible changes — including dissolving and state changes — do not produce new substances, describe how dissolved substances can be recovered, and give examples of reversible changes used in recycling.
criteria: Explains that dissolving is reversible — the dissolved substance can be recovered
Describes at least one method for recovering a dissolved substance
Explains that reversible changes do not produce new substances
nodes.hinge_reason: The new-substance criterion is the definitional basis for the reversible/irreversible distinction at Node 3 — students who believe dissolving is irreversible because the substance visually disappears cannot correctly classify changes at N3, and cannot distinguish reversible from irreversible in ambiguous cases like dissolving. The misconception must be resolved here before systematic comparison is possible.

width.minimum: Students explain that dissolving and state changes are reversible, give one method for recovering a dissolved substance, and name one reversible change used in recycling.
width.typical: Students explain why dissolving and state changes are reversible (same substances, no new matter produced); describe evaporation, filtration and distillation as methods for reclaiming dissolved substances; explain how state change reversibility enables recycling of glass and metals; and use particle-level reasoning to explain why these changes are reversible.
wider: Investigate how dissolved substances are reclaimed from solutions — comparing evaporation, filtration and crystallisation as recovery methods
Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of reversible processes such as the application of adhesives — exploring how reversibility is a deliberately selected property in traditional material use
Explore how reversible changes are exploited in industrial recycling — examining which materials can be returned to their original state and reformed

modes.reason: Students commonly believe dissolving is irreversible ('the salt is gone') because the change is visually dramatic. The reasoning chain — dissolved particles are still present in the solution → they can be recovered by removing the water → the original substance is unchanged → this is reversible — requires explicit scaffolding before students can consistently distinguish dissolving from chemical change.

nodes.label: Irreversible changes produce new substances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that irreversible changes produce new substances with different properties, identify observable evidence of new substance formation, and give examples of common irreversible changes.
criteria: Explains that irreversible changes produce new substances with different properties
Names at least two observable indicators that an irreversible change has occurred
Distinguishes an irreversible change from a reversible change by the presence or absence of new substance formation
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding irreversibility as caused by new substance formation (not just visual change) is required for Node 3 systematic classification — students who identify irreversibility by appearance alone will fail on ambiguous cases, especially those where visual change is subtle. The substance-change criterion must be established here before it can be applied systematically.

width.minimum: Students explain that cooking and rusting produce new substances with different properties, and identify at least two observable indicators that an irreversible change has occurred.
width.typical: Students examine the substances produced in cooking and rusting and compare them with original substances (different colour, texture, composition); explain that irreversible changes cannot be undone because new substances have formed; identify observable indicators of new substance formation; and compare energy requirements for reversible vs irreversible changes.
wider: Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of irreversible processes such as the use of fuels for torches — exploring how controlled combustion has been used purposefully across generations
Compare how the amount of heat energy added determines whether a reversible state change or an irreversible change occurs — examining the threshold between melting and burning for different materials
Connect irreversible changes to chemical change indicators studied in Y8 (AC9S8U07) — tracing how this foundational distinction develops into formal chemistry

modes.reason: Students often identify cooking as irreversible ('you can't uncook an egg') without understanding why — that new proteins have formed with different properties. Encountering multiple irreversible changes (rusting, burning, cooking, digestion) with evidence of new substance formation builds a more principled understanding of irreversibility grounded in substance change rather than visual appearance.

nodes.label: Reversible and irreversible changes are compared systematically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare reversible and irreversible changes systematically — using the criterion of new substance formation — classify a range of everyday changes correctly, and explain how this distinction is used in practical contexts.
criteria: Classifies at least four everyday changes as reversible or irreversible using the new-substance criterion
Correctly classifies at least one ambiguous case (e.g. dissolving) with reasoning
Explains how the reversible/irreversible distinction is applied in a practical context

width.minimum: Students classify at least four everyday changes as reversible or irreversible using the new-substance criterion, with reasoning for each.
width.typical: Students compare reversible and irreversible changes using a systematic framework (new substances formed? properties changed? change undoable?); classify a range of changes including ambiguous cases (dissolving, digestion, melting, burning, rusting, baking); explain their reasoning; and describe how this distinction is applied in practical contexts such as cooking, recycling and manufacturing.
wider: Discuss what makes a change reversible or irreversible using a range of everyday examples — including ambiguous cases that challenge the classification
Construct a poster or slideshow comparing everyday examples of reversible and irreversible change — selecting representations that clearly show the before/after substance comparison
Examine how knowledge of reversibility influences material and process selection in manufacturing and product design — connecting the science concept to real industrial decision-making

modes.reason: Systematic comparison requires students to apply the new-substance criterion consistently across varied examples — including ambiguous cases — coordinating substance properties knowledge, change observation, and reversibility reasoning. This is the synthesis move that transforms a collection of examples into a generalisable chemical classification framework.

descriptors.title: Evidence changes knowledge
descriptors.description: explain how new evidence or different perspectives can lead to changes in scientific knowledge
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine why scientific advances depend on collaboration and building on prior work (AC9S5H01). They have not yet explained how specific new evidence or perspectives cause established scientific knowledge to change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how new evidence or different perspectives can lead to changes in scientific knowledge.

nodes.label: Scientific knowledge is based on evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that scientific knowledge is built from evidence and that the type and quality of evidence matters
criteria: States that scientific knowledge is based on evidence
Gives one correct example of evidence supporting a scientific idea
Does not confuse evidence with opinion or belief

width.minimum: State that scientific knowledge is based on evidence; give one example of evidence that supports a scientific idea
width.typical: Distinguish between types of evidence (observational, experimental, technological) and explain why some evidence is more convincing than others
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' ecological observations constitute evidence that informs scientific understanding
Compare evidence from different fields (e.g. fossil record vs DNA analysis) that supports the same scientific idea
Research how al-Battani's astronomical calculations provided new evidence that refined earlier models of the solar year

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of evidence types and examples — observational, experimental, technological, cultural — before they can reason about what makes evidence convincing or how it drives change. A single example of evidence is not enough to generalise the concept; breadth of examples builds the repertoire needed for Node 2.

nodes.label: New evidence changes scientific understanding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how new evidence — from new technology, methods or discoveries — has led to changes in scientific understanding
criteria: Names a specific example where scientific understanding changed due to new evidence
Explains what the new evidence was and how it caused the change
Does not describe the change as science being 'wrong before'

width.minimum: Identify one example of how scientific understanding has changed over time as new evidence or methods became available; explain what changed and why
width.typical: Investigate how scientific understanding in at least two content areas has developed through new evidence or technology; explain the role of evidence in each case
wider: Explore how scientists are re-examining organism relationships using new genetic evidence to refine classification
Investigate how aeronautical engineers' evolving understanding of forces in flight led to changes in aircraft design
Research how improvements in microscopy led to changes in biological classification systems

modes.reason: Students commonly treat changed scientific knowledge as a sign of unreliability rather than a feature of the evidence-based process. Seeing multiple examples across different content areas (classification, astronomy, forces) helps students recognise the pattern — that change is how science works, not a flaw. Single-example teaching reinforces the misconception; breadth resolves it.

nodes.label: Different perspectives shape knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how different perspectives — including cultural, historical and disciplinary — contribute to the development of scientific knowledge
criteria: Names a specific example where a different perspective contributed to scientific knowledge
Explains the contribution rather than just naming the perspective
Recognises that multiple perspectives can coexist and contribute to understanding

width.minimum: Identify one example where a different perspective contributed new understanding to a scientific field; explain the contribution
width.typical: Compare how two different perspectives (e.g. First Nations ecological knowledge and Western ecology) approach the same phenomenon; explain what each contributes
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' land management practices inform contemporary environmental management to protect biodiversity
Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional ecological knowledges inform sustainable harvesting practices of species such as dugongs and turtles
Research how perspectives from different scientific disciplines (e.g. genetics and palaeontology) together changed understanding of a phenomenon

modes.reason: Students commonly name a different perspective without explaining the contribution — they describe the perspective rather than reasoning through what it adds to scientific knowledge. Scaffolding the reasoning explicitly (what did this perspective see that others missed, and what did science gain from including it?) is what moves students from description to explanation.

nodes.label: Evidence and perspectives together refine knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the interplay of new evidence and different perspectives leads to ongoing refinement of scientific knowledge
criteria: Explains how both new evidence and different perspectives contributed to a knowledge change
Identifies that scientific knowledge refinement is an ongoing process

width.minimum: Explain how both new evidence and different perspectives contributed to a change in scientific knowledge in one case; identify that this process is ongoing
width.typical: Construct an explanation tracing how a specific area of scientific knowledge (e.g. classification, astronomy) has been refined through multiple rounds of new evidence and perspective shifts
wider: Evaluate whether a specific change in scientific knowledge was driven primarily by new evidence, new perspectives, or both — justify with examples
Investigate a current area where scientific knowledge is being refined by new evidence or perspectives and explain what is changing and why
Compare two cases of knowledge change — one driven primarily by technology (new evidence) and one driven primarily by cultural perspective — and explain what each reveals about how science works

modes.reason: This node brings together the evidence strand (Node 2) and the perspectives strand (Node 3) into a coordinated explanation of knowledge refinement. Students who can explain each separately but cannot articulate their interplay have not met the descriptor's full demand — the integration of both into a coherent account of how science develops is the learning.

The evaluative tasks in the wider tier — judging whether a change was driven by evidence or perspective, or both — require explicit reasoning scaffolding. Students need to be supported in constructing the argument structure: claim, evidence strand, perspective strand, and how they interact. Without this scaffold, students produce description rather than evaluation.

descriptors.title: Culture shapes scientific knowledge
descriptors.description: investigate how cultural perspectives and world views influence the development of scientific knowledge
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine why scientific advances depend on collaboration and building on prior work (AC9S5H01). They have not yet investigated how cultural perspectives and world views specifically shape which questions are asked and how knowledge develops.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how cultural perspectives and world views influence the development of scientific knowledge.

nodes.label: Scientists bring perspectives to their work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that scientists' personal beliefs, cultural backgrounds and societal contexts influence the questions they pursue
criteria: Names a specific example where perspective influenced a scientific question or approach
Explains the connection between the perspective and the scientific work
Does not treat perspective as automatically introducing bias or error

width.minimum: Identify one example where a scientist's personal beliefs or cultural background influenced the questions they chose to investigate
width.typical: Compare two scientists whose different perspectives led them to pursue different questions or approaches; explain how perspective shaped each
wider: Explore how Richard Levins' political views led him to focus on population ecology, or how Joseph Rotblat refused to work on atomic bomb science
Investigate how David Unaipon used cultural knowledge of boomerang aerodynamics to conceptualise early flight technology
Research how a scientist's disciplinary training shapes the questions they see as worth investigating

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of scientist examples — across gender, culture, discipline, era — to see that perspective-shaping of scientific questions is a general phenomenon, not a biographical curiosity. Two examples (Levins, Rotblat; Unaipon) give different dimensions: political values, cultural knowledge, disciplinary lens. Each adds a distinct facet to the repertoire.

nodes.label: Cultural knowledge systems contribute to science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how knowledge systems from different cultures contribute to scientific understanding
criteria: Names a specific cultural knowledge contribution to scientific understanding
Explains what the contribution is rather than just naming the culture
Does not frame cultural knowledge as inferior to or separate from science

width.minimum: Identify one example where cultural knowledge has contributed to scientific understanding; explain the contribution
width.typical: Investigate First Nations Australians' classification systems and explain how they differ in context and purpose from Linnaean taxonomy; identify what each contributes
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have developed sustainable harvesting practices and cultural protocols based on deep ecological understandings
Explore the work of Wang Zhenyi, including her experiments on lunar eclipses, as an example of non-Western scientific contribution
Compare how different cultural knowledge systems approach the same natural phenomenon and what each reveals

modes.reason: Students commonly hold a deficit view — that cultural knowledge is either 'real science' or 'not science' — rather than understanding that different knowledge systems ask different questions and contribute different insights. Investigating multiple cultural contexts (First Nations classification, Wang Zhenyi, sustainable harvesting) helps students see that contributions are genuine and varied, not tokenistic. Single-context teaching reinforces the deficit view; breadth resolves it.

nodes.label: Different perspectives on science-society issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why different people hold different perspectives on science-related issues and why recognising this matters
criteria: Identifies a science-society issue with multiple perspectives
Explains why different groups hold different views
Recognises that considering multiple perspectives improves decision-making

width.minimum: Identify one science-society issue where different groups hold different perspectives; explain why the perspectives differ
width.typical: Analyse a science-society issue (e.g. biological controls for invasive species) from at least two stakeholder perspectives; explain why each perspective exists and why recognising multiple perspectives matters
wider: Consider why it is important to recognise different perspectives on the introduction of biological controls to eradicate an invasive species
Investigate a local science-society issue and map the different stakeholder perspectives, explaining the values behind each
Evaluate whether a scientific decision-making process adequately considered diverse perspectives and explain what was missing

modes.reason: Students commonly describe different perspectives without explaining why the perspectives differ — they list viewpoints rather than reasoning through the values, knowledge systems, and stakes that produce them. Scaffolding the reasoning (what does this group know, what do they value, what are they protecting?) moves students from perspective inventory to perspective analysis.

nodes.label: Culture shapes the development of scientific knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural perspectives and world views have influenced the development of scientific knowledge across multiple examples
criteria: Explains how a cultural perspective influenced the development of specific scientific knowledge
Connects the perspective to the knowledge outcome rather than just describing each separately

width.minimum: Explain how cultural perspectives influenced the development of scientific knowledge in one specific case, connecting the perspective to the knowledge outcome
width.typical: Compare two cases where cultural perspectives shaped scientific knowledge differently; explain the mechanism of influence in each
wider: Investigate how First Nations ecological knowledge has shaped contemporary conservation science in a specific region
Research how cultural context shaped scientific priorities in a historical case (e.g. space race, colonial-era natural history) and evaluate the consequences
Construct an argument about why diversity of perspectives strengthens scientific knowledge overall

modes.reason: This node integrates the personal perspective thread (Node 1), the cultural knowledge systems thread (Node 2), and the science-society thread (Node 3) into a coherent explanation of how culture shapes scientific knowledge development. Students who can address each thread separately but cannot synthesise them into a general explanatory account have not met the descriptor's investigative demand.

The argument-construction direction — why diversity of perspectives strengthens scientific knowledge — requires explicit scaffolding of the claim-evidence-reasoning structure. Students need support connecting the empirical examples from earlier nodes to the general claim, not just listing them.

descriptors.title: Science responses impact society
descriptors.description: examine how proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues may impact on society and explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate how individuals and communities use scientific knowledge to identify problems and make decisions (AC9S5H02). They have not yet examined how proposed scientific responses to issues carry ethical, environmental, social and economic trade-offs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues may impact on society and explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations.

nodes.label: Scientific responses to contemporary issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues and describe the intended impact
criteria: Identifies a proposed scientific response and the contemporary issue it addresses
Describes the intended impact of the response
Distinguishes the scientific response from a political or social response

width.minimum: Identify one example of a proposed scientific response to a contemporary issue; describe the problem it addresses and the intended impact
width.typical: Compare two proposed scientific responses to the same or related issues; explain how each addresses the problem differently
wider: Investigate how laboratory-grown meat is proposed as a response to ecosystem impacts of livestock farming
Examine how desalination plants are proposed as a response to freshwater scarcity
Research how ecological reserves are proposed as a response to biodiversity loss and competing land use interests

modes.reason: Students need a repertoire of scientific response examples across different issue types — food production, water scarcity, biodiversity — to be able to reason about impacts across contexts in later nodes. A single example limits the range of consideration types students can encounter; multiple examples build the conceptual library needed for the four-lens analysis in Node 3.

nodes.label: Impacts can be positive and negative
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine both intended and unintended impacts of a scientific response on society and the environment
criteria: Identifies both an intended and an unintended impact of a scientific response
Explains why the unintended impact occurs
Does not frame the response as simply good or bad

width.minimum: Identify one intended and one unintended impact of a proposed scientific response; explain why the unintended impact occurs
width.typical: Analyse the impacts of a scientific response across environmental and social dimensions; explain how an intended benefit in one area can create an unintended cost in another
wider: Examine how desalination plants produce fresh water but impact marine ecosystems at discharge sites
Investigate how changes in aircraft design improved safety and efficiency but introduced environmental considerations
Research how the introduction of biological controls solved one problem but created new ecological impacts

modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate scientific responses as simply 'good' or 'bad' rather than examining trade-offs. Seeing multiple examples where the same response produces both positive and negative impacts — desalination, aircraft design, biological controls — across different contexts helps students develop nuanced evaluation rather than binary judgement. Single-context teaching entrenches the binary view.

nodes.label: Ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations associated with a proposed scientific response
criteria: Identifies at least two types of consideration relevant to a specific response
Explains why each consideration matters for that response
Distinguishes between the consideration types rather than conflating them

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of consideration (from ethical, environmental, social, economic) relevant to a proposed scientific response; explain why each matters
width.typical: Analyse a proposed scientific response across all four consideration types; explain why stakeholders may hold different views depending on which consideration they prioritise
wider: Investigate the ethical, environmental, social and economic implications of others using First Nations Australians' knowledges of medicinal properties of endemic plants
Investigate ethical and economic implications of cross-cultural partnerships that build on First Nations Australians' land management techniques
Research how properties of gases were used in WWI gas warfare and the subsequent development of international arms control treaties — examine the ethical implications

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate the four consideration types or address only one (usually environmental). Examining the same response through all four lenses across different contexts — medicinal plants, land management, gas warfare — helps students distinguish the considerations and understand why different stakeholders prioritise differently. Breadth across contexts is what builds the four-lens thinking habit.

The four-lens analysis requires an explicit reasoning scaffold — students need to be supported in applying each consideration type systematically rather than defaulting to whichever lens feels most prominent. Without structure, students describe one consideration in depth and mention others superficially.

nodes.label: Evaluating scientific responses with multiple considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a proposed scientific response by weighing multiple considerations and explaining why stakeholders may reach different conclusions
criteria: Examines a scientific response using at least two consideration types
Explains why different stakeholders evaluate the response differently
Connects stakeholder conclusions to their priorities rather than framing disagreement as ignorance

width.minimum: Examine one proposed scientific response using at least two consideration types; explain why different stakeholders may evaluate it differently
width.typical: Compare how two different stakeholder groups evaluate the same scientific response; explain how their different priorities lead to different conclusions
wider: Evaluate a proposed ecological reserve by analysing competing interests — conservation scientists, landowners, First Nations communities, local government — and explain what each prioritises
Analyse the development of laboratory-grown meat from the perspective of farmers, environmentalists, consumers and ethicists
Construct an evidence-based argument for or against a proposed scientific response, explicitly addressing counter-arguments from stakeholders with different priorities

modes.reason: This node integrates the response identification (Node 1), trade-off analysis (Node 2), and four-lens framework (Node 3) into a coordinated stakeholder evaluation. Students who can apply each element separately but cannot coordinate them into a multi-stakeholder analysis have not met the descriptor's full evaluative demand.

The argument-construction direction — arguing for or against a response while addressing counter-arguments — requires explicit scaffolding of the claim-evidence-counterargument structure. Students need support both in selecting and weighting considerations and in representing opposing stakeholder positions fairly rather than as straw men.

descriptors.title: Science communication shapes policy
descriptors.description: explore the role of science communication in informing individual viewpoints and community policies and regulations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate how individuals and communities use scientific knowledge to identify problems and make decisions (AC9S5H02). They have not yet explored how the communication of science — not just the knowledge itself — shapes viewpoints and drives policy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore the role of science communication in informing individual viewpoints and community policies and regulations.

nodes.label: Science communication takes many forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different forms of science communication and recognise that how science is communicated affects what people understand
criteria: Identifies at least two forms of science communication
Explains how each form reaches a different audience
Recognises that communication choices affect what people understand

width.minimum: Identify at least two forms of science communication (e.g. media reports, scientific publications, public campaigns); explain how each reaches a different audience
width.typical: Compare how the same scientific finding is communicated differently for different audiences; explain what is emphasised, simplified or omitted in each
wider: Reflect on the role of contemporary First Nations Australians scientists, such as Wiradjuri astrophysicist Kirsten Banks, in communicating science to diverse audiences
Compare how a scientific finding was communicated in a peer-reviewed journal vs a news article vs social media — what changes and why?
Investigate how science communicators choose what to include and exclude and how this shapes public understanding

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of communication forms — journals, news, social media, public campaigns, two-way Indigenous knowledge communication — to see that the form-audience-content relationship is general, not specific to one medium. Each form in the repertoire demonstrates a different set of communication choices and trade-offs.

nodes.label: Communication informs individual viewpoints
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication informs and changes individual viewpoints on science-related issues
criteria: Names a specific example where science communication changed viewpoints
Explains what was communicated and how viewpoints changed
Distinguishes the role of communication from the knowledge itself

width.minimum: Identify one example where science communication changed individual viewpoints on an issue; explain what was communicated and how viewpoints changed
width.typical: Analyse how science communication about two different issues (e.g. conservation, waste) informed individual viewpoints; explain the mechanisms by which communication influenced understanding
wider: Explore how Dame Jane Goodall's communication of her research changed individual viewpoints about primate conservation
Investigate how science communication about waste materials changed individual behaviour around household waste
Analyse how science communication can both inform and misinform — compare an effective and an ineffective example

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'communication' with 'the science itself' — treating viewpoint change as automatic once knowledge exists, rather than understanding that how science is communicated determines whether and how viewpoints shift. Seeing multiple examples where the same knowledge was communicated differently with different viewpoint outcomes (Goodall, waste communication) helps resolve this conflation.

nodes.label: Communication shapes community policies and regulations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication leads to changes in community policies and regulations
criteria: Names a specific example where science communication led to a policy or regulation change
Explains the pathway from communication to policy outcome
Distinguishes the policy change from the underlying scientific knowledge

width.minimum: Identify one example where science communication led to a policy or regulation change; explain the connection between the communication and the policy outcome
width.typical: Analyse how science communication across two contexts led to specific policy or regulation changes; explain the pathway from communication to policy
wider: Examine how science communication of endangered species has led to fishing catch and hunting limits
Examine how global reporting on high-impact weather events has led to warning systems and evacuation policies
Investigate how First Nations Australians are using two-way approaches such as Caring for Country initiatives to influence policies

modes.reason: Students commonly name a policy change without tracing the pathway from communication to policy outcome — they establish correlation (communication happened, policy changed) without explaining the causal mechanism. Scaffolding the reasoning explicitly (what was communicated, to whom, through what channels, and how did this reach policy makers?) is what moves students from correlation to explanation.

nodes.label: The role of science communication in society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how science communication plays an ongoing role in informing viewpoints and shaping policies across different contexts
criteria: Explains how communication choices connected to both viewpoint and policy outcomes
Identifies what made the communication effective or ineffective

width.minimum: Explain how science communication informed viewpoints and shaped policy in one case, connecting communication choices to outcomes
width.typical: Compare two cases where science communication had different impacts — one primarily on viewpoints, one primarily on policy — and explain what made each effective
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of a science communication campaign — what worked, what didn't, and what could be improved?
Investigate how science communication of the impact of waste materials led to both changed viewpoints and community recycling policies
Construct an argument about what makes science communication effective at driving both viewpoint change and policy change

modes.reason: This node integrates the communication forms thread (Node 1), the viewpoints thread (Node 2), and the policy thread (Node 3) into a coordinated account of science communication's role in society. Students who can address each separately but cannot connect them into a coherent explanation of how communication choices produce viewpoint and policy outcomes have not met the descriptor's exploratory demand.

The effectiveness evaluation direction — what made communication work or not work — requires explicit criteria scaffolding. Students need support in identifying what 'effective' means across the viewpoint and policy dimensions, not just narrating what happened. Without this scaffold, evaluations default to impressionistic judgements.

descriptors.title: Explore models and test relationships
descriptors.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to explore scientific models, identify patterns and test relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can pose investigable questions to identify patterns and test relationships and make predictions based on experiences (AC9S5I01). They have not yet developed hypotheses with explicit variable-outcome-reasoning structure or generated questions to explore scientific models.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to explore scientific models, identify patterns and test relationships.

nodes.label: Investigable vs non-investigable questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions and explain what makes a question investigable
criteria: Correctly classifies at least 3 questions as investigable or non-investigable
States at least two features that make a question investigable
Does not confuse 'interesting' with 'investigable'

width.minimum: Identify whether a given question is investigable or not; state at least two features that make a question investigable
width.typical: Discuss features of investigable and non-investigable questions; evaluate their own and others' questions for investigability; refine a non-investigable question into an investigable one
wider: Limited width — distinguishing investigable from non-investigable questions is a judgement skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. More question sets provide practice volume, not genuine breadth. Extensions such as evaluating questions from First Nations ecological knowledge contexts add cultural dimension but don't change the underlying criteria being practised.

modes.reason: Distinguishing investigable from non-investigable questions is a judgement skill that students commonly get wrong in both directions — either accepting untestable questions or rejecting testable ones. The concept does not vary meaningfully across contexts; what helps is repeated practice classifying and refining questions until the criteria become automatic.

Students commonly apply the label 'investigable' or 'not investigable' without being able to articulate why. Scaffolding the reasoning — what feature of this question makes it testable or untestable, and what would need to change — builds the explicit criteria that consolidation practice then reinforces.

nodes.label: Developing investigable questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop investigable questions to explore scientific models or test relationships between variables
criteria: Develops an investigable question that identifies variables or a model to explore
The question is testable with available methods and resources
Explains how the question connects to the model or relationship being investigated

width.minimum: Develop one investigable question to explore a model or test a relationship; identify the variables involved
width.typical: Develop investigable questions for two different purposes — one to explore a model and one to test a relationship; explain how the question connects to the model or relationship
wider: Develop investigable questions to explore scientific models such as 'How does particle theory explain the properties of substances?'
Develop investigable questions to test relationships such as 'How does the volume of a balloon change as it is heated and cooled?'
Develop multi-variable investigable questions where the relationship between variables is not immediately obvious

modes.reason: Students commonly write questions that are too broad ('What affects plant growth?') or too narrow ('Does water help plants?') to be genuinely investigable. Developing questions across different science contexts — models, patterns, relationships — helps students calibrate the right scope and specificity. Each new context forces fresh calibration rather than pattern-matching a single example.

Question development is not intuitive — students need an explicit reasoning scaffold: what is the model or relationship I'm exploring, what would change, and what would I measure? Without this scaffold, students produce questions that sound investigable but don't actually specify the variables or connect to the phenomenon. The scaffold is what makes breadth across contexts productive rather than just generating more poorly-formed questions.

nodes.label: Predictions and hypotheses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate reasoned predictions and hypotheses that include a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
criteria: Develops a hypothesis that includes a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
Distinguishes a prediction from a hypothesis
The reasoning in the hypothesis is scientifically plausible

width.minimum: Use a provided scaffold to develop a hypothesis for a given investigation; distinguish a prediction from a hypothesis
width.typical: Formulate hypotheses independently, identifying the key elements — variable, predicted outcome, reasoning; discuss the relationship between a reasoned prediction and a hypothesis
wider: Limited width — the if...then...because hypothesis structure does not vary across investigation contexts. Formulating hypotheses for more complex investigations and evaluating student hypotheses are both practice volume on the same three-part structure, not genuinely broader contexts.

modes.reason: Writing well-structured hypotheses is a precision skill — students commonly omit the reasoning component or confuse predictions with hypotheses. The three-part structure (if... then... because...) does not vary across contexts; what helps is practice writing and refining hypotheses until the structure becomes fluent.

The 'because' component is what distinguishes a hypothesis from a prediction, and students consistently drop it. Explicit scaffolding of the reasoning component — why do you expect this outcome, what scientific principle or model supports it — is what makes the structure meaningful rather than a formula to fill in. Consolidation practice without structured reasoning produces fluent but hollow hypotheses.

descriptors.title: Plan reproducible investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying variables and assumptions and, as appropriate, recognising and managing risks, considering ethical issues and recognising key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct repeatable fair-test investigations, identifying variables (AC9S5I02). They have not yet planned for reproducibility, identified assumptions about controlled variables, or considered ethical issues and heritage site protocols.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct reproducible investigations, identifying variables and assumptions, recognising and managing risks, considering ethical issues and recognising heritage site considerations.

nodes.label: Variables and assumptions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify independent, dependent and controlled variables and recognise assumptions about controlled variables
criteria: Correctly identifies independent, dependent and controlled variables in a given method
Names at least one assumption about a controlled variable
Explains why controlling variables matters for the investigation

width.minimum: Identify variables and at least one assumption in a provided investigation method; explain why controlling variables matters
width.typical: Identify independent, dependent and controlled variables and assumptions in a given method; explain what happens if an assumption is wrong; discuss why identifying variables and assumptions is important
wider: Identify assumptions relating to variables assumed to be constant, such as ambient temperature, material properties or substance purity
Compare two methods for the same investigation and evaluate which better controls variables
Design an investigation where an assumption about a controlled variable is deliberately tested

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the three variable types or fail to recognise that controlled variables involve assumptions. These errors propagate directly into method design and evaluation. Seeing variable identification across different investigation contexts — forces, particles, ecosystems — helps students generalise the skill rather than memorising one example. Each new context forces fresh variable identification without the scaffold of familiarity.

nodes.label: Planning reproducible methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a method that another person could reproduce to obtain comparable results
criteria: Plans a method with sufficient detail for another person to reproduce
Method logically tests the stated hypothesis
Peer review confirms the method is followable

width.minimum: Identify the features that make an investigation reproducible; compare a method with its hypothesis and assess whether it reasonably tests the hypothesis
width.typical: Plan a reproducible investigation method for a given hypothesis; have another student review it and identify gaps; revise based on feedback
wider: Limited width — writing reproducible methods is a precision skill that does not vary meaningfully across investigation types. All wider directions (multiple trials, peer review, explicit variable statements) are more practice on the same reproducibility criteria, not broader contexts.

modes.reason: Writing reproducible methods is a precision task — students commonly write methods that are too vague for someone else to follow. The skill does not vary meaningfully across contexts; what helps is practice writing, peer-testing and refining methods until sufficient detail becomes habitual. More investigation contexts don't help; more writing-and-feedback cycles do.

nodes.label: Risks, ethics and heritage considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and manage risks, consider ethical issues and recognise heritage site protocols when planning investigations
criteria: Identifies at least one risk and suggests how to manage it
Identifies at least one ethical consideration relevant to the investigation
Recognises that heritage sites and artefacts require specific protocols

width.minimum: Identify at least one risk in a given investigation and suggest how to manage it; identify one ethical consideration relevant to the investigation
width.typical: Identify risks and ethical considerations including interactions with living things; recognise state and territory laws relating to First Nations Australians' heritage sites and artefacts; integrate these into investigation planning
wider: Collaborate with First Nations Australians communities to plan investigations about ecosystems, ensuring mutually beneficial outcomes and following cultural protocols
Recognise First Nations Australians' artefacts and heritage sites and understand obligations not to harm or disturb sites
Design an investigation that explicitly addresses ethical issues relating to interactions with living organisms and justifies decisions made

modes.reason: Students commonly identify risks as a checklist item without reasoning through consequences — they name the risk without explaining what harm could occur or why the management strategy addresses it. Similarly, heritage considerations require explicit reasoning about obligation, not just recognition of existence. Scaffolding the reasoning (what could go wrong, who is affected, what is the protocol and why) builds genuine risk literacy rather than tick-box compliance.

descriptors.title: Select equipment and record data
descriptors.description: select and use equipment to generate and record data with precision, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow safe procedures to investigate questions and use basic measurement tools (AC9S5I02). They have not yet selected equipment based on measurement range or precision requirements, or used digital tools to improve data quality.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use appropriate equipment to generate and record data with precision, using digital tools as appropriate.

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate equipment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select equipment appropriate to an investigation's measurement needs and justify the choice
criteria: Selects equipment appropriate to the measurement task
Justifies the choice based on measurement range or precision
Does not select equipment that cannot measure the expected values

width.minimum: Select appropriate equipment for a given investigation; explain why the selected equipment suits the measurement task
width.typical: Select and use equipment appropriate to the investigation's measurement range; explain why a thermometer, measuring cylinder or force meter was chosen based on the expected measurement range
wider: Select equipment for an investigation where the expected measurement range is not given — estimate the range first, then choose
Compare two pieces of equipment for the same measurement task and justify which is more appropriate
Design a data collection system for a multi-variable investigation, justifying equipment selection

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of equipment types and their appropriate contexts — thermometers for temperature ranges, measuring cylinders for volumes, force meters for force ranges, digital sensors for abiotic factors — before they can make justified selection decisions in novel contexts. More equipment examples in varied investigation contexts build the selection vocabulary.

nodes.label: Recording data with precision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record data in organised formats using correct units and appropriate precision
criteria: Records data using correct standard units
Precision is appropriate to the equipment used
Data table is organised with clear headings and units

width.minimum: Record data in a provided table using correct units; use appropriate precision for the equipment used
width.typical: Construct tables or spreadsheets to collect data; use standard units and perform simple unit conversions; record data to the precision of the equipment
wider: Limited width — recording data with correct units and consistent precision is a mechanical skill that does not vary across investigation contexts. Designing tables and evaluating recording errors are practice volume on the same conventions, not genuinely broader contexts.

modes.reason: Recording data with correct units and consistent precision is a mechanical skill where students commonly make careless errors — missing units, inconsistent decimal places, unlabelled columns. The skill does not vary across contexts; what helps is repeated practice with feedback on recording quality until correct habits are automatic.

nodes.label: Using digital tools for data generation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools to generate more precise or efficient data and explain the advantage over manual methods
criteria: Identifies a digital tool appropriate for a given investigation
Explains the advantage of the digital tool over a manual alternative
Uses the tool to generate data with appropriate precision

width.minimum: Identify one digital tool that improves data precision or efficiency in a given investigation; explain the advantage
width.typical: Use digital tools such as sensors to measure abiotic factors and apps for field identification; compare precision of digital and analogue methods
wider: Evaluate how digital tools such as stopwatches and digital scales improve data precision compared to analogue equivalents
Use field identification apps that use image or call recognition during ecosystem investigations
Design a comparison between digital and manual data collection for the same investigation and analyse which produces more reliable data

modes.reason: Students need to encounter a range of digital tools — sensors, apps, spreadsheets, identification tools — across different investigation types to understand that 'digital tool' is a broad category with varied precision advantages. Each tool type adds a different dimension to the repertoire and prevents the overgeneralisation that digital is always more precise.

descriptors.title: Select tables, graphs and models
descriptors.description: select and construct appropriate representations, including tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships, to organise and process data and information
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct and use tables, graphs and models to describe patterns, trends and relationships (AC9S5I04). They have not yet selected between representation types based on data characteristics or constructed mathematical relationships from data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and construct appropriate representations, including tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships, to organise and process data and information.

nodes.label: Choosing appropriate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate representation type for a given data set based on data characteristics
criteria: Selects a representation type appropriate for the data characteristics
Explains why the chosen representation suits the data
Does not default to one representation type regardless of data

width.minimum: Construct one type of data representation (table, graph or diagram) from collected data; explain why it is appropriate for that data
width.typical: Distinguish between discrete and continuous data; select appropriate representations for each; explain why a bar chart suits discrete data and a line graph suits continuous data
wider: Evaluate a mismatched representation (e.g. a pie chart for continuous data) and explain why it is misleading
Compare two representations of the same data and explain what each reveals and conceals
Select representations for a multi-variable data set where different variables require different representation types

modes.reason: Students commonly default to one representation type (usually a bar chart) regardless of data characteristics. Understanding that representation choice depends on data type is prerequisite for all subsequent analysis. Seeing different data types across science contexts — populations, forces, particles, astronomical data — helps students generalise the selection criteria rather than associating one type with one topic.

nodes.label: Constructing representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct tables, graphs, food webs, dichotomous keys and other models to organise data and information
criteria: Constructs a representation with correct labels, scales and conventions
Representation accurately reflects the source data
Uses the representation to describe at least one pattern

width.minimum: Construct a representation from collected data with correct labels, scales and conventions; use it to describe a pattern
width.typical: Construct food webs, dichotomous keys, graphs and tables; use spreadsheets to aid presentation and analysis; apply correct conventions for each representation type
wider: Code a simple program to represent a dichotomous key as an interactive tool
Acknowledge, analyse and interpret data from First Nations Australians' astronomical observations using appropriate representations
Construct representations of data from multiple sources and synthesise findings across representations

modes.reason: Constructing representations with correct conventions — axis labels, scales, titles, units — is a precision skill. Students commonly make procedural errors that undermine the representation's usefulness. Practice and feedback on conventions is what helps, not more representation types or contexts.

nodes.label: Processing data through representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use representations including mathematical relationships to process and analyse data
criteria: Uses a representation to identify and describe a pattern
Description is supported by specific reference to the data
Does not over-interpret the data beyond what the representation shows

width.minimum: Use a constructed representation to identify a pattern and describe what it shows
width.typical: Analyse secondary data to determine mathematical relationships such as tidal variation over a lunar cycle; use spreadsheets to process and analyse data; draw conclusions supported by the representation
wider: Analyse data from multiple representations to build a more complete picture of a phenomenon
Investigate mathematical relationships in data sets such as qualitative relationships between planet mass and gravity
Evaluate whether a representation adequately supports the conclusion drawn from it

modes.reason: Students commonly describe what a representation shows without reasoning from it to a conclusion — they read the pattern without connecting it to the scientific question. Scaffolding the reasoning step explicitly (what does this pattern mean in terms of the variables, and what conclusion does it support?) is what moves students from data reading to data processing.

descriptors.title: Identify patterns and anomalies
descriptors.description: analyse data and information to describe patterns, trends and relationships and identify anomalies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare methods, recognise sources of error and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions (AC9S5I05). They have not yet systematically analysed data to describe patterns and relationships or identified and explained anomalies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse data and information to describe patterns, trends and relationships and identify anomalies.

nodes.label: Describing patterns and trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe patterns and trends in data sets
criteria: Identifies a pattern or trend in a data set
Describes the pattern using appropriate language
Does not confuse correlation with a single data point

width.minimum: Identify a pattern or trend in a provided data set; describe what the pattern shows
width.typical: Identify patterns and trends across multiple data types; describe patterns using appropriate scientific language (e.g. 'as X increases, Y decreases')
wider: Analyse data to identify patterns in the proportions of a day spent in sunlight and darkness and relate these to seasons
Collaborate with First Nations Australians communities to create a seasonal calendar representing patterns and relationships
Compare patterns across two related data sets and explain whether they support the same or different conclusions

modes.reason: Describing patterns using appropriate language ('as X increases, Y decreases') is a precision skill that students commonly approximate — they describe direction without precision, or use vague language that doesn't commit to the relationship. Practice with feedback on language precision is what helps here, not more data contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying relationships in data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse data to identify and describe relationships between variables
criteria: Identifies a relationship between two variables
Describes the relationship type (positive, negative or non-linear)
Connects the relationship to the variables involved, not just the trend direction

width.minimum: Identify a relationship between two variables in a data set; describe whether the relationship is positive, negative or non-linear
width.typical: Identify relationships across multiple data types including qualitative relationships such as the relationship between planet mass and gravity; explain what the relationship means in scientific terms
wider: Analyse change in predator and prey numbers over time to identify predator-prey cycles
Investigate a complex multi-variable data set where relationships are non-obvious
Compare patterns across multiple secondary data sets, evaluating consistency of findings

modes.reason: Students commonly describe patterns without identifying the underlying relationship between variables — they say 'it goes up' without connecting the independent and dependent variables. Analysing relationships across different science contexts (forces, ecosystems, astronomy) helps students practise the variable-linking skill rather than just pattern-spotting. Each new context requires fresh variable identification.

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining anomalies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify anomalies in data and investigate their effect on observed patterns or relationships
criteria: Identifies an anomaly in a data set
Explains why the anomaly does not fit the observed pattern
Does not automatically discard anomalies without considering whether they are meaningful
