width.minimum: Identify an anomaly in a provided data set; explain why it does not fit the pattern
width.typical: Identify anomalies in data and investigate their effect on observed patterns; distinguish between anomalies caused by error and those that reveal genuine phenomena
wider: Investigate anomalies in data and evaluate whether they should be excluded, explained, or investigated further
Analyse a data set where an anomaly changes the interpretation of the pattern and explain the implications
Evaluate whether removing an anomaly from a data set changes the conclusion and justify the decision

modes.reason: Students commonly either ignore anomalies or automatically discard them without reasoning through whether they represent error or genuine phenomena. Scaffolding the decision process explicitly — is this measurement error, equipment error, or a real data point? what would I need to know to decide? — builds genuine anomaly literacy rather than reflexive exclusion or retention.

descriptors.title: Analyse methods and claims
descriptors.description: analyse methods, conclusions and claims for assumptions, possible sources of error, conflicting evidence and unanswered questions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare methods, recognise sources of error and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions (AC9S5I05). They have not yet analysed conclusions and claims for assumptions, conflicting evidence and unanswered questions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse methods, conclusions and claims for assumptions, possible sources of error, conflicting evidence and unanswered questions.

nodes.label: Identifying sources of error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify possible sources of error in an investigation method and suggest improvements
criteria: Identifies a specific source of error (not just 'human error')
Explains how the error affects the data or results
Suggests a specific improvement to reduce the error

width.minimum: Identify one possible source of error in an investigation method; suggest how it could be reduced
width.typical: Identify multiple sources of error in a method; suggest specific improvements with reasoning; consider the spread of repeated measurements and observations
wider: Limited width — identifying specific sources of error and connecting them to consequences is a precision skill that does not vary meaningfully across investigation types. Applying evaluative criteria across more investigations and distinguishing random from systematic errors are more practice on the same skill, not broader contexts.

modes.reason: Identifying sources of error is a skill students often apply superficially — naming 'human error' without specifying what the error was or how it affected results. The concept does not vary across contexts; what helps is repeated practice identifying specific errors and connecting them to specific consequences in the data, until the specificity becomes habitual.

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and assumptions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate an investigation method by identifying assumptions about controlled variables and assessing whether the method tests the hypothesis
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption about a controlled variable
Explains why the assumption matters for the investigation's validity
Assesses whether the method tests the stated hypothesis

width.minimum: Identify at least one assumption in a given method about a variable that should be controlled; explain why the assumption matters
width.typical: Evaluate a method by identifying assumptions about controlled variables; suggest improvements with reasoning; assess whether the method adequately tests the hypothesis
wider: Evaluate a method where an assumption about a controlled variable is likely wrong and explain the consequences for results
Compare two methods for testing the same hypothesis and evaluate which is more rigorous
Analyse conclusions and claims to identify facts or premises taken for granted and evaluate their relevance

modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate methods by checking procedural steps rather than examining underlying assumptions. The misconception that a method is 'good' if the steps are followed correctly persists unless students see — across multiple investigation contexts — that hidden assumptions can invalidate even well-executed procedures. Different investigation types surface different categories of assumption.

Identifying an assumption requires students to reason backward from the method — 'for this method to work, what must be true about the controlled variables?' — which is a non-obvious reasoning move. Explicit scaffolding of this backward reasoning helps students find assumptions rather than just evaluate ones they're told about.

nodes.label: Evaluating conclusions and claims
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse conclusions and claims for conflicting evidence and unanswered questions
criteria: Identifies evidence that both supports and conflicts with a claim
Identifies at least one unanswered question arising from the evidence
Does not treat a conclusion as proven simply because some evidence supports it

width.minimum: Identify one piece of evidence that supports and one that conflicts with a given claim; identify one unanswered question
width.typical: Evaluate conclusions against the quality of evidence; identify the evidence cited to support a claim; evaluate conflicting evidence; identify unanswered questions that arise from the investigation
wider: Evaluate conflicting evidence from multiple sources and assess which more strongly supports a conclusion
Analyse a published scientific claim — identify the evidence, assumptions and potential sources of error
Evaluate a conclusion by systematically assessing whether the evidence is sufficient, relevant and unambiguous

modes.reason: Students commonly treat a conclusion as proven once any supporting evidence exists, without weighing conflicting evidence or identifying what remains unanswered. Scaffolding the evaluation structure — what supports this, what conflicts, what would need to be true for the conclusion to hold, and what is still unknown — builds systematic evaluative thinking rather than binary accept/reject judgement.

descriptors.title: Construct evidence-based arguments
descriptors.description: construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare methods, recognise sources of error and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions (AC9S5I05). They have not yet constructed arguments with explicit evidence-reasoning structure or considered ethical issues around using secondary data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims, considering ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions from evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw a conclusion from evidence that supports or rejects a hypothesis and identify the evidence used
criteria: Draws a conclusion that is consistent with the evidence
Identifies the specific evidence that supports the conclusion
States whether the evidence supports or rejects the hypothesis

width.minimum: Draw a conclusion from evidence that supports or rejects a hypothesis; identify the evidence used
width.typical: Draw a logical conclusion considering the method of data collection, quality of evidence and limitations or significance of a claim
wider: Draw conclusions from an investigation where the evidence is ambiguous and explain why the conclusion is uncertain
Compare two investigations that reach different conclusions about the same question and explain what accounts for the difference
Evaluate whether a conclusion is justified by the evidence or whether it over-reaches

modes.reason: Students commonly state conclusions without identifying the specific evidence that supports them, or over-reach beyond what the evidence shows. Scaffolding the conclusion-drawing process — what evidence do I have, what does it show, does it support or reject the hypothesis, and what are its limits — builds the explicit connection between evidence and conclusion that the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Constructing evidence-based arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct an argument supported by evidence and reasoning to support a conclusion or evaluate a claim
criteria: Constructs an argument that links evidence to a conclusion through reasoning
The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the conclusion
Does not simply list evidence without connecting it to the conclusion

width.minimum: Construct an argument that links evidence to a conclusion with reasoning; evaluate one claim by assessing the evidence behind it
width.typical: Construct arguments supported by evidence and reasoning to support or reject a hypothesis; evaluate the credibility of sources; assess whether cited evidence is sufficient to support a claim
wider: Evaluate a contested scientific claim by systematically assessing the credibility, relevance and sufficiency of evidence from multiple sources
Investigate cultural, historical and archaeological evidence used in the scientific debate about the role of early First Nations Australians in the extinction of Australian megafauna
Construct competing arguments for and against a claim and evaluate which is better supported

modes.reason: Students commonly state conclusions and list evidence without connecting them through reasoning — the 'because' is missing. Constructing arguments across different science content areas (ecology, forces, classification, megafauna extinction) helps students practise the evidence-reasoning-conclusion structure rather than relying on the familiarity of one context to carry the argument.

nodes.label: Ethics of using secondary data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can consider ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information
criteria: Identifies an ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to using secondary data
Explains why the issue matters for the integrity of the argument
Recognises that cultural knowledge requires specific protocols for use and citation

width.minimum: Identify one ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to using secondary data; explain why it matters
width.typical: Consider ethical issues and cultural protocols when using secondary data from First Nations Australians or other culturally sensitive sources; evaluate the credibility and appropriateness of citing secondary sources
wider: Research the development of commercial products founded on traditional knowledges of First Nations Australians and discuss ethical considerations around biopiracy and intellectual property rights
Evaluate a case where secondary data was used without appropriate cultural protocols and explain the consequences
Develop a set of criteria for ethically using and citing secondary data from culturally sensitive sources

modes.reason: Students commonly identify ethical issues as abstract principles without reasoning through the specific consequences — they name 'biopiracy' without explaining what harm occurs, to whom, and why the protocol exists. Scaffolding the reasoning (whose knowledge is this, what are the ownership rights, what protocol applies, and what happens if it's violated?) makes the ethical consideration concrete and actionable.

descriptors.title: Communicate ideas and arguments
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments for specific purposes and audiences, including selection of appropriate language and text features, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can write and create texts to communicate ideas and findings for specific purposes and audiences (AC9S5I06). They have not yet selected language and text features strategically for purpose and audience or produced multi-modal scientific communications.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments for specific purposes and audiences, selecting appropriate language and text features and using digital tools as appropriate.

nodes.label: Purpose, audience and text type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose and audience of scientific texts and select an appropriate text type
criteria: Identifies the purpose and target audience of a scientific text
Explains how the text type suits the audience
Does not assume all scientific communication uses the same format

width.minimum: Identify the purpose and target audience of a given scientific text; explain how the text type suits the audience
width.typical: Examine a range of scientific texts; infer purpose and audience from language and text features; select appropriate text types for different communication purposes
wider: Compare how the same scientific finding is communicated in a journal article, a news report and a social media post — explain what changes and why
Evaluate a scientific text that is poorly matched to its audience and explain what should change
Analyse how First Nations Australians scientists communicate science to diverse audiences and what text features they use

modes.reason: Students commonly write for a generic audience rather than making deliberate choices about language, detail level and text features for a specific reader. Examining multiple text types across different purposes — journal, news, social media, letter to editor, animation — helps students see that communication is a design decision, not a fixed format. Each new text type reveals different choices and trade-offs.

nodes.label: Language and text features for science communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use appropriate language and text features including diagrams, graphical representations and data
criteria: Includes at least one diagram or graphical representation
Representation is referenced in the text, not just appended
Language is appropriate for the stated audience

width.minimum: Report on a scientific investigation using at least one diagram or graphical representation; communicate findings to a known audience
width.typical: Produce a scientific report incorporating diagrams, graphical representations and data; examine accuracy and reproducibility of data; select language features appropriate to purpose
wider: Create an informative text for a younger audience explaining a science concept (e.g. seasons, particle theory) — adapt language and representations appropriately
Write a letter to the editor expressing a science-informed view about a local environmental issue
Create an animation explaining a science concept to a peer audience using digital tools

modes.reason: Incorporating diagrams, data and scientific language into written reports is a precision skill. Students commonly include representations without integrating them into the text — diagrams are decorative, not referenced in the writing. Practice producing reports where text and representations are explicitly connected is what helps, not more communication contexts.

nodes.label: Communicating for specific purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and create texts that communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for a specific purpose and audience
criteria: Produces a communication for a specific purpose and audience
Text type and language features are appropriate to the purpose
Communication includes ideas, findings or arguments — not just description

width.minimum: Produce a scientific communication for a specific purpose and audience; select text type and language features appropriate to that purpose
width.typical: Produce communications for two different purposes or audiences; explain and justify the choices made about text type, language and representations in each
wider: Develop a prototype dichotomous key app to enable community members to classify organisms in a local park or reserve
Create a multi-modal scientific communication (e.g. video, poster, interactive tool) and evaluate its effectiveness for the target audience
Produce a scientific communication that integrates findings from multiple investigations into a coherent argument

modes.reason: This node integrates purpose/audience awareness (Node 1), language and representation skills (Node 2), and argument construction from AC9S7I07 into a coordinated communication product. Students who can address each element separately but cannot produce a text that coordinates all three have not met the descriptor's full communicative demand.

descriptors.title: Classification and biodiversity
descriptors.description: investigate the role of classification in ordering and organising the diversity of life on Earth and use and develop classification tools including dichotomous keys
descriptors.knowledge: Students can group living things by their external features (AC9SFU01), compare living and non-living things and the life cycles of plants and animals (AC9S3U01), and explain how structural features and behaviours help living things survive in their habitats (AC9S5U01). They have not studied formal taxonomy or constructed classification tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate why classification systems are used, apply and construct dichotomous keys, and evaluate how classification tools order and organise biodiversity.

nodes.label: Purpose of classification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why classification is useful for organising and communicating about living things
criteria: Names at least two reasons why classification is useful (e.g. identification, communication)
Gives a correct everyday example of classification
Does not confuse classification with simple sorting or listing

width.minimum: State at least two reasons why scientists classify living things (e.g. identification, communication); give one example of classification in everyday life
width.typical: Compare two different classification systems; explain which is more useful for a given purpose and why
wider: Investigate how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples classify living things on Country and compare with Linnaean taxonomy — what does each system prioritise?
Research how classification systems have changed over time through improvements in microscopy; explain what this reveals about scientific knowledge
Consider how classification supports identification and communication in a real scientific or practical context (e.g. biosecurity, medicine)

modes.reason: The wider tier offers genuine breadth through multiple distinct lenses — cultural classification systems (First Nations vs Linnaean), historical change through microscopy, and practical contexts (biosecurity, medicine). Each adds a different dimension to why classification exists and what any system reveals about the priorities of those who made it. More contexts here help students see classification as purposeful and constructed rather than natural and fixed.

nodes.label: Taxonomy: major groups and kingdoms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can place organisms into major taxonomic groups using observable features and justify their classification
criteria: Correctly places 5 familiar organisms into kingdoms with observable feature justification
Identifies at least one organism that is difficult to classify and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably assign organisms to kingdoms using observable features cannot select discriminating features when constructing keys in Node 4 — the feature-selection skill that underpins both using and constructing keys depends on having a working taxonomy foundation.

width.minimum: Name the major kingdoms; correctly place 5 familiar organisms into their kingdom with justification using observable features
width.typical: Sort a set of 12 organisms into kingdoms; identify one organism that is difficult to classify and explain why
wider: Name and classify species using Linnaean hierarchy (kingdom → species); explain what each level represents
Research a boundary case (e.g. Euglena, virus) — does it fit the kingdom model? What does this reveal about classification systems?
Observe and identify similarities and differences of particular features within and between groups of organisms using provided specimens or images

modes.reason: Correctly placing organisms into kingdoms is a classification skill that improves through accumulated examples. Students need to build a repertoire of familiar organisms across kingdoms so the feature-based judgement becomes reliable — a single set of 5 organisms is not enough to generalise the skill. More varied organism sets, including boundary cases, build the pattern recognition needed for confident classification.

nodes.label: Using dichotomous keys
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a dichotomous key to identify organisms by applying binary decisions based on observable features
criteria: Follows all decision points in a provided key to reach correct identifications
Names the observable feature used at each decision point
Explains why an incorrect path leads to a wrong outcome
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not internalise the binary decision logic of using a key cannot construct one in Node 4 — key construction requires students to reverse the process, selecting features that produce clean binary splits. Procedural key-following without conceptual understanding of why each decision point works produces key constructions that are structurally broken.

width.minimum: Use a provided dichotomous key to correctly identify at least 5 organisms; explain how each decision point works
width.typical: Use two different keys for the same organism set; identify where they agree and disagree and explain why
wider: Use a provided dichotomous key to identify organisms surveyed on a field trip or from local environment
Evaluate a flawed dichotomous key — identify the error, explain its consequence, and propose a correction
Compare a scientific dichotomous key with a First Nations classification system for the same organisms — what features does each prioritise?

modes.reason: Using a key requires students to apply binary logic to observable features — a prerequisite for constructing keys. Misconceptions about feature selection cluster here and propagate directly into Node 4. More varied organism sets and key types (field trip keys, flawed keys, comparative keys) force students to apply binary decision logic across contexts rather than pattern-matching a single worked example.

Students commonly follow key steps procedurally without understanding the binary decision logic underlying each step. Explicit scaffolding of the reasoning — 'at this decision point, what observable feature am I checking, and what are the two possible outcomes?' — helps students internalise the logic rather than just follow arrows. This is prerequisite for constructing their own keys in Node 4.

nodes.label: Constructing dichotomous keys
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a dichotomous key that correctly classifies a set of organisms using observable features
criteria: Constructs a key that correctly classifies all organisms in a given set
Key uses binary observable features at each decision point
Peer testing confirms key produces correct identifications

width.minimum: Construct a simple dichotomous key for a set of 6 organisms using observable features; test it with a peer
width.typical: Construct and refine a key for 10 organisms; document one revision made after peer testing and explain the improvement
wider: Create and modify a dichotomous key to classify organisms into groups and subgroups; evaluate its effectiveness
Design a key for a novel organism set (e.g. everyday objects or invented creatures); reflect on what makes a feature scientifically useful
Construct a key based on First Nations classification criteria for local organisms and compare its structure with a Linnaean key

modes.reason: Students commonly select non-discriminating features or features that work for one organism set but fail for another. Constructing keys across more varied organism sets forces students to confront what makes a feature genuinely discriminating — resolving the misconception through breadth rather than repetition on a single set.

Constructing a key integrates binary decision logic (Node 3), feature selection from taxonomy (Node 2), and understanding of classification purpose (Node 1). The construction task is where these components come together — students who can use a key but cannot construct one are missing the integrated understanding. Peer testing is a key part of this integration: it surfaces whether the key works across the full organism set, not just for the constructor.

nodes.label: Classification systems change over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how classification systems change in response to new evidence and evaluate what this reveals about scientific knowledge
criteria: Names a real reclassification event and the evidence that caused it
Explains whether reclassification weakens or strengthens confidence in science

width.minimum: Give one example of a reclassification event; explain what new evidence caused the change
width.typical: Trace the reclassification of one organism — what evidence existed before, what changed, and how did the scientific community respond?
wider: Examine how biological classification has changed through improvements in microscopy and DNA analysis
Evaluate: is reclassification a sign that science is unreliable, or a sign that it works? Construct an evidence-based argument
Investigate how First Nations classification knowledge has contributed to or challenged scientific classification in specific cases

modes.reason: Students commonly describe reclassification events without connecting them to the nature of scientific knowledge — they report what changed without explaining what it means that science changes. Scaffolding the reasoning explicitly (what was the old classification, what new evidence emerged, what changed, and what does this reveal about how science works) helps students reach the evaluative claim rather than stopping at description.

descriptors.title: Food webs and ecosystems
descriptors.description: use models, including food webs, to represent matter and energy flow in ecosystems and predict the impact of changing abiotic and biotic factors on populations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers in a habitat and construct simple food chains (AC9S4U01), and know that a habitat's physical conditions affect the growth and survival of living things (AC9S6U01). They have not studied energy flow quantitatively or modelled multi-factor ecosystem changes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use food web models to represent matter and energy flow, and predict the impact of changes to abiotic and biotic factors on populations.

nodes.label: From food chains to food webs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a food web and identify the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers including microorganisms
criteria: Correctly places all organisms in a food web into producer, consumer or decomposer roles
Arrows show direction of energy flow, not just feeding relationships
Includes microorganisms in the decomposer role
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot construct food webs with correct arrow direction and role assignment cannot represent matter and energy flow in Node 2 — the web structure is the scaffolding all later modelling depends on.

width.minimum: Construct a food web from a given organism list; identify producers, primary and secondary consumers, and decomposers including microorganisms
width.typical: Compare a food chain and food web for the same ecosystem — explain what information is lost in the simpler model
wider: Analyse food webs to show feeding relationships including the role of microorganisms in decomposition
Critique a published food web diagram — what is it missing, what assumptions does it make?
Investigate First Nations Australians' food webs in a specific region and compare with a scientific representation of the same ecosystem

modes.reason: Students need to construct food webs across multiple ecosystem types — aquatic, terrestrial, Australian — to build a reliable mental model of web structure. A single ecosystem example may be memorised rather than understood; multiple examples build the structural pattern recognition needed for prediction tasks in later nodes.

nodes.label: Matter and energy flow
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the direction and loss of energy through trophic levels and distinguish energy flow from matter cycling
criteria: States that energy is lost at each trophic level
Correctly distinguishes energy flow from matter cycling in an explanation
Traces the direction of energy through at least 3 trophic levels
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate matter cycling with energy flow make systematic errors in all population prediction nodes — they predict energy recovery rather than loss, producing confidently wrong cascade explanations in Nodes 3 and 4.

width.minimum: Explain the direction of energy flow in a food web; state that energy is lost at each trophic level; distinguish energy flow from matter cycling
width.typical: Use a given energy pyramid to explain why top predators are rare; connect to food web structure
wider: Model how energy flows into and out of an ecosystem via food web pathways; represent quantitatively using the 10% rule
Compare energy flow in two different ecosystems (e.g. rainforest vs desert); explain structural differences
Analyse a real dataset of biomass at each trophic level; explain the pattern using energy flow principles

modes.reason: Energy flow direction and loss is the conceptual engine behind all population prediction tasks. Students who conflate matter cycling with energy flow make systematic errors in Nodes 3 and 4. Seeing energy flow across multiple ecosystem types — rainforest, desert, aquatic — forces students to apply the principle in new contexts rather than recall a single worked example, resolving the conflation misconception.

nodes.label: Abiotic factors and population effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and explain how a change to an abiotic factor cascades through populations in a food web
criteria: Correctly defines abiotic factor and gives 3 examples
Predicts the effect of one abiotic change on one population with reasoning
Identifies at least one other population affected by the cascade

width.minimum: Define abiotic factor; give three examples; explain how one abiotic change would affect one population in a given food web
width.typical: Trace the cascade effect of one abiotic change (e.g. drought, temperature rise) through at least 3 populations with reasoning at each step
wider: Examine how seasonal changes or habitat destruction impact abiotic factors and cause population changes
Compare cascade effects of two different abiotic changes on the same ecosystem — which is more destabilising and why?
Investigate First Nations Australians' fire management practices and their effect on abiotic factors and flora/fauna distribution

modes.reason: Students commonly predict only the immediate effect of an abiotic change without tracing the cascade through the web. Scaffolding the multi-step reasoning explicitly — what changes first, what does that affect next, and what follows from that — builds the chain-of-reasoning habit needed for genuine prediction, not just first-order effect identification.

nodes.label: Biotic factors and population effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can predict and explain how a change to a biotic factor cascades through populations in a food web
criteria: Correctly defines biotic factor and gives 3 examples
Predicts the effect of removing one species with food web reasoning
Traces at least one cascade effect beyond the immediate population
nodes.hinge_reason: Predicting biotic cascade effects requires holding the whole food web in mind simultaneously — the same multi-step reasoning skill required in AC9S9U03 (Carbon Cycle and Earth's Spheres), where students must trace carbon flow through biotic and abiotic ecosystem components. Students who haven't secured biotic cascade reasoning here will treat carbon flow as a simple transfer rather than a web of interdependent pathways.

width.minimum: Define biotic factor; give three examples; predict the effect of removing one species from a given food web with reasoning
width.typical: Analyse a trophic cascade case study (e.g. wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone); explain the chain of biotic effects with evidence
wider: Predict effects on local ecosystems when pollinators or predators are removed or introduced
Investigate First Nations Australians' responses to invasive species and their effect on food webs communities depend on
Evaluate an invasive species scenario — construct food webs before and after, predict population effects, and propose a management response

modes.reason: Students commonly predict only the immediate effect of species removal without tracing the cascade through the web. Seeing more biotic change scenarios across different ecosystem types — predator removal, invasive species, pollinator loss — forces students to practise multi-step reasoning through food web structure rather than applying a single memorised cascade pattern.

nodes.label: Models, limitations and predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of food web models and explain how these affect the reliability of predictions
criteria: Identifies at least one limitation of food web models
Explains how that limitation affects the reliability of a specific prediction

width.minimum: Identify one limitation of food web models; explain how this affects the reliability of predictions made from them
width.typical: Compare a simple and complex model of the same ecosystem — explain what each can and cannot predict
wider: Evaluate a real scientific food web model used in a conservation decision — what did it predict, what did it miss?
Consider how introduction of a species impacts abiotic and biotic factors beyond immediate food web effects
Research how First Nations ecological knowledge has improved or challenged scientific food web models in a specific case

modes.reason: Students commonly identify model limitations as abstract statements ('it doesn't include everything') without reasoning through how a specific limitation affects a specific prediction. Scaffolding the connection — what is missing from this model, and what prediction would be wrong as a result — builds genuine model evaluation rather than generic limitation-listing.

descriptors.title: Earth-Sun-Moon system
descriptors.description: model cyclic changes in the relative positions of the Earth, sun and moon and explain how these cycles cause eclipses and influence predictable phenomena on Earth, including seasons and tides
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify patterns in the changing positions of the sun, moon and stars in the sky and observe moon phases (AC9S2U01), and can relate Earth's tilt, rotation and revolution around the sun to day and night and day length (AC9S6U02). They have not modelled the Earth, sun and moon together as one system or explained eclipses, seasons and tides mechanistically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students model and explain how cyclic changes in Earth-sun-moon positions cause eclipses, seasons and tides.

nodes.label: Earth's rotation, revolution and axial tilt
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish Earth's rotation from revolution and explain how axial tilt relates to observable changes across a year
criteria: Correctly distinguishes rotation from revolution
Links rotation to day/night and revolution to the year
Identifies that Earth's axis is tilted
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish rotation from revolution and build the 3D spatial model cannot explain eclipses or seasons in Nodes 3-4 — both require coordinating Earth's axial tilt with its orbital position simultaneously.

width.minimum: Distinguish rotation from revolution; link rotation to day/night and revolution to the year; identify that Earth's axis is tilted
width.typical: Use a physical or digital model to demonstrate both cycles simultaneously; explain what an observer on Earth would experience across a year
wider: Use physical models or virtual simulations to explain how Earth's tilt and position relative to the sun causes differences in light intensity
Investigate First Nations Australians' calendars and how they are used to predict seasonal changes
Explain why the length of daylight changes across a year at different latitudes using a model

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse rotation and revolution or understand each separately without being able to explain their combined observable effects. Scaffolding the spatial reasoning — what does an observer on Earth experience as a result of each cycle, and how do the two cycles combine — builds the 3D mental model that is prerequisite for eclipse and season explanations in later nodes.

nodes.label: Moon phases and the lunar cycle
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain moon phases as a result of the moon's position relative to Earth and sun and sequence them correctly
criteria: Correctly sequences all 8 moon phases
Explains phases as caused by the moon's position, not Earth's shadow
Does not confuse moon phases with eclipses
nodes.hinge_reason: The shadow misconception — phases caused by Earth's shadow — persists directly into eclipse explanation in Node 3. Students who hold it will explain lunar eclipses as moon phases and cannot correctly distinguish the two phenomena.

width.minimum: Correctly sequence all 8 moon phases; explain that phases result from the moon's position relative to Earth and sun, not Earth's shadow
width.typical: Model moon phases using a light source and spheres; predict the phase visible from Earth at a given moon position
wider: Analyse a month of real moon phase data — identify the pattern, calculate the period, identify anomalies
Research knowledges held by First Nations Australians regarding the phases of the moon and the lunar cycle
Investigate how lunar calendars from different cultures use moon phases differently and why

modes.reason: Sequencing all 8 moon phases correctly and explaining the position-based cause is a precision task that students commonly get partially right. The common error — confusing phases with Earth's shadow — is persistent and needs targeted correction through repeated modelling practice, not more contexts.

nodes.label: Eclipses: solar and lunar
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the conditions required for solar and lunar eclipses and why eclipses do not occur every month
criteria: States the conditions required for both solar and lunar eclipses
Correctly distinguishes umbra from penumbra
Explains why eclipses don't occur every month

width.minimum: Explain the conditions required for a solar and lunar eclipse; correctly distinguish umbra from penumbra; explain why eclipses don't occur every month
width.typical: Model both eclipse types using a light source; explain the role of the moon's orbital tilt in eclipse frequency
wider: Use physical models or virtual simulations to explain cyclic patterns of lunar and solar eclipses
Research First Nations Australians' oral traditions and cultural recordings of solar and lunar eclipses; compare with contemporary understandings
Analyse historical eclipse records — explain why ancient cultures found eclipses unpredictable and what understanding was missing

modes.reason: Eclipse explanation requires 3D spatial reasoning about three bodies simultaneously — the hardest conceptual step in this standard. Students who rely on 2D diagrams alone consistently misexplain why eclipses are rare. Broader contexts — historical records, cultural accounts, simulation — help students build the 3D mental model that 2D diagrams cannot provide.

nodes.label: Seasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain seasons as caused by axial tilt and correctly relate tilt to solar angle and day length at different latitudes
criteria: Explains seasons as caused by axial tilt, not distance from the sun
Links tilt to solar angle and day length
Correctly identifies opposite seasons in Northern and Southern hemispheres
nodes.hinge_reason: The distance misconception — seasons caused by proximity to the sun — is explicitly noted as assessed and extremely persistent. Students who hold it produce confidently wrong season explanations and cannot correctly account for opposite hemispheric seasons.

width.minimum: Explain that seasons are caused by Earth's axial tilt, not distance from the sun; correctly link tilt to solar angle and day length
width.typical: Use a model to demonstrate why the Southern and Northern hemispheres experience opposite seasons simultaneously
wider: Compare seasonal patterns at the equator, temperate zones, and poles — explain differences using the tilt model
Investigate First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars (e.g. six-season calendars) and compare with the four-season European model
Analyse real insolation data for two locations at different latitudes across a year; explain the patterns using the tilt model

modes.reason: The distance misconception — seasons caused by proximity to the sun — is extremely persistent and directly assessed. Without resolving it here, students produce confidently wrong answers. High width investment across multiple latitude contexts (equator, temperate, polar) and cultural calendar comparisons forces students to confront the misconception repeatedly until the tilt explanation displaces it.

nodes.label: Tides
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain tides as caused by the moon's gravitational pull and distinguish spring from neap tides by moon position
criteria: Explains tides as caused by the moon's gravitational pull
Correctly identifies spring and neap tides
Links spring and neap tides to moon positions

width.minimum: Explain that tides are caused by the moon's gravitational pull; identify spring and neap tides and the moon positions that cause them
width.typical: Analyse a tide chart for a coastal location — identify spring and neap cycles and connect them to the lunar calendar
wider: Examine the gravitational attraction of the moon and sun on Earth's oceans; explain how relative positions result in tidal variations
Research how First Nations Australians used tidal patterns and connection between lunar cycle and ocean tides for resource management
Investigate how tidal patterns differ between locations and explain using the moon-sun-Earth model

modes.reason: Tides integrate the lunar cycle (Node 2), the Earth-moon-sun positional model (Node 3), and gravitational force concepts from AC9S7U04 into a single explanatory account. Students who understand each component separately but cannot coordinate them into a tidal explanation have not reached this node's checkpoint. Analysing tide charts requires all three components to work together.

descriptors.title: Forces and motion
descriptors.description: investigate and represent balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravitational force, acting on objects, and relate changes in an object's motion to its mass and the magnitude and direction of forces acting on it
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify pushes and pulls as forces and have investigated how frictional, gravitational and magnetic forces affect the motion of objects (AC9S4U03). They have not represented forces as vectors, analysed balanced and unbalanced forces, or related changes in motion to an object's mass and the size and direction of the forces on it.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent and explain how balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravity, relate to changes in an object's motion in terms of mass, magnitude and direction.

nodes.label: Forces as vectors: magnitude and direction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent forces on an object as vectors showing correct magnitude and direction and name the forces
criteria: Represents at least 2 forces on an object with correct arrow direction and relative size
Names each force represented
Diagram is consistent with the described scenario
nodes.hinge_reason: Force diagram errors — wrong arrow direction, omitted forces, incorrect relative sizes — propagate into every subsequent node. Nodes 2-5 all require accurate force diagrams as reasoning tools; students with imprecise diagrams cannot correctly identify balanced/unbalanced states.

width.minimum: Represent at least two forces on an object using arrows with correct relative size and direction; name the forces
width.typical: Draw force diagrams for 4 different scenarios (stationary, accelerating, decelerating, falling); justify arrow choices
wider: Measure the magnitude of forces using a force meter; represent magnitude and direction using force arrow diagrams
Analyse a real photograph of an object in motion — identify all forces acting and represent them in a diagram
Investigate forces acting on boomerangs and how First Peoples of Australia designed an aerofoil profile — represent forces involved

Limited width — representing forces as vectors is a precision skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. More scenarios build fluency but the conceptual content is fixed. The genuine width comes at later nodes where force diagrams are used as reasoning tools.

modes.reason: Representing forces as vectors — correct arrow direction, relative size, and force naming — is a precision skill students commonly approximate. They confuse spacing and direction, or omit forces (e.g. normal force). Repeated practice with feedback on diagram completeness and accuracy is what helps, not broader contexts.

nodes.label: Balanced forces and equilibrium
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether forces on an object are balanced or unbalanced and predict the resulting motion state
criteria: Correctly identifies balanced vs unbalanced forces in a given diagram
States that balanced forces mean no change in motion — not that no forces are acting
Predicts the motion state from a force diagram
nodes.hinge_reason: The misconception that balanced forces mean no forces acting propagates directly into Node 3 — students who hold it cannot correctly predict motion states or explain why objects at constant velocity have balanced forces.

width.minimum: Define balanced forces; correctly identify whether forces are balanced in a given diagram; state that balanced forces mean no change in motion
width.typical: Analyse 6 scenarios — classify each as balanced or unbalanced; predict the motion state for each with reasoning
wider: Analyse the effect of balanced and unbalanced forces on an object's motion including starting, stopping and changing direction
Investigate a real engineering structure (e.g. bridge, building) — identify how balanced forces are maintained and what happens if equilibrium is disturbed
Investigate how simple machines such as levers and pulleys change the magnitude of force needed — represent forces involved and identify whether forces are balanced

modes.reason: The misconception that balanced forces mean no forces — rather than equal and opposite forces — is extremely common and propagates into every subsequent node. Students who hold this misconception cannot correctly predict motion states or apply Newton's First Law. Working across multiple scenario types (stationary, moving at constant velocity, engineering structures) exposes and resolves the misconception — more contexts, not more repetition of the same scenario.

nodes.label: Unbalanced forces and changes in motion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion and represent this with force diagrams
criteria: States that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion
Gives 2 examples with correct force diagrams
Identifies both speed and direction as possible changes

width.minimum: Explain that unbalanced forces cause a change in motion (speed or direction); give two examples with force diagrams
width.typical: Analyse motion scenarios — identify the unbalanced force, predict the change in motion, draw the force diagram
wider: Investigate the effects of applying different forces to familiar objects of the same and different mass — identify the pattern between force magnitude and rate of motion change
Design a fair test to investigate how the magnitude of an unbalanced force affects the rate of motion change

Investigate forces through the application of traditional tools such as spearthrowers used by First Peoples of Australia — analyse the forces involved and how tool design optimises the unbalanced force

modes.reason: Students frequently apply unbalanced force reasoning only to obvious acceleration scenarios (car speeding up) and miss direction changes (turning, projectile) or deceleration as force-caused changes. Multiple motion-change contexts — starting, stopping, turning, falling — build the generalised understanding that any change in motion requires an unbalanced force.

nodes.label: Gravitational force and mass
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish mass from weight, explain gravitational force as dependent on mass, and calculate weight from mass
criteria: Correctly distinguishes mass from weight with definitions
Calculates weight correctly given mass and g
Explains gravitational force as dependent on mass — not just Earth's pull
nodes.hinge_reason: Mass/weight confusion propagates directly into AC9S10U05 (Newton's Laws of Motion) — F=ma is meaningless if students conflate mass and weight, and gravitational force scenarios in Newton's Laws require the distinction to be functional. Students who hold this misconception produce systematically wrong force calculations three years later.

width.minimum: Distinguish mass from weight; explain gravitational force as dependent on mass; calculate weight given mass and gravitational field strength
width.typical: Compare gravitational force on the same object on Earth, the Moon, and Mars — explain differences using gravitational field strength; represent using force diagrams
wider: Investigate how Earth's gravitational force pulls objects to the centre of Earth and how its magnitude relates to mass
Examine how gravity affects objects in space including moons, planets, stars, galaxies and black holes — explain patterns in terms of mass and distance
Evaluate a common misconception (e.g. 'objects fall at different rates based on mass') using experimental evidence; construct a refutation using force diagrams and particle reasoning

modes.reason: Mass/weight confusion is the most persistent misconception in this standard — students who conflate the two make systematic errors in force calculations and cannot correctly explain gravitational scenarios. Encountering gravitational force across multiple contexts (Earth, Moon, Mars, space) where mass stays constant but weight changes forces the distinction to become functional rather than definitional.

nodes.label: Relating force, mass and motion change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration and interpret data from force investigations
criteria: States the qualitative relationship between force, mass and acceleration
Correctly predicts which object accelerates more under the same force
Identifies the pattern in data from a force investigation

width.minimum: State the relationship between force, mass and acceleration qualitatively; predict whether a heavier or lighter object will accelerate more under the same force
width.typical: Analyse data from a force investigation — identify the pattern between force, mass and acceleration; represent graphically
wider: Evaluate a real-world application (e.g. vehicle safety, rocket launch) — explain how engineers manipulate force and mass to achieve desired acceleration outcomes
Investigate how simple machines change force magnitude for a task; analyse the trade-offs between force and distance involved
Analyse the forces acting on a boomerang in flight — explain how design variables (aerofoil shape, mass, throwing force) affect the motion outcome

modes.reason: This node integrates force vector representation (Node 1), balanced/unbalanced force reasoning (Nodes 2-3), and gravitational force (Node 4) into a qualitative account of how force, mass and motion change relate. Students who can handle each component separately but cannot reason about which of two objects accelerates more under the same force have not integrated the model.

descriptors.title: Particle theory and properties
descriptors.description: use particle theory to describe the arrangement of particles in a substance, including the motion of and attraction between particles, and relate this to the properties of the substance
descriptors.knowledge: Students know that matter exists as solids, liquids and gases, can describe observable properties, and know that adding or removing heat energy changes state (AC9S3U04) and changes temperature (AC9S3U03). They have used a simple particle model of motion and arrangement to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases (AC9S5U04). They have not included attraction between particles, or used the model to explain a wider range of properties such as compressibility, density and diffusion, or energy in changes of state.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use particle theory to describe the arrangement, motion and attraction of particles in substances and relate this to observable physical properties, including changes of state.

nodes.label: Introducing the particle model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can match particle diagrams to states of matter and state the key ideas of particle theory
criteria: Matches particle diagrams to correct states of matter
States the 4 key ideas of particle theory
Identifies differences in arrangement, motion and attraction across states
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably reproduce the four-component particle model (particles, spacing, motion, attraction) cannot use it as an explanatory framework in Node 2 onwards — they treat diagrams decoratively rather than as reasoning tools.

width.minimum: State the key ideas of particle theory (particles, spacing, motion, attraction); correctly match particle diagrams to solid, liquid and gas
width.typical: Explain three observable properties of a substance using particle theory language; draw and annotate particle diagrams
wider: Use and construct models, diagrams or virtual simulations to represent particle arrangement in different states
Evaluate the particle model as a model — what does it explain well, what does it not explain, and what evidence supports it?
Compare the particle model with how materials properties are described in Design and Technologies contexts

modes.reason: Matching particle diagrams to states and stating the four key ideas is a precision task that students commonly approximate — they confuse spacing and motion, or omit attraction. Practice with feedback on the four-component structure (particles, spacing, motion, attraction) until the model is reliably reproduced is what helps here.

nodes.label: Particle arrangement, motion and attraction in each state
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe particle arrangement, motion and attraction for each state and explain observable properties using this model
criteria: Describes particle arrangement, motion and attraction for each state
Explains why solids hold shape and gases fill containers using particle theory
Does not treat particle diagrams as decorative — uses them to support reasoning
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat particle diagrams as decorative rather than explanatory cannot apply the model to property explanation in Node 3. The pattern-recognition built across multiple substances in this node is what enables the explanatory move — without it, Node 3 collapses to labelling.

width.minimum: Describe particle arrangement, motion and attraction for each state; explain why solids hold shape and gases fill containers
width.typical: Compare particle diagrams for 6 substances — rank by particle spacing and predict relative density; check against data
wider: Relate motion and energy of particles to distances between particles in different states of the same substance
Compare attractive forces in solid, liquid and gaseous states and relate to relative position and movement of particles
Investigate an anomalous case (e.g. ice floating on water) — explain using particle theory and evaluate whether the basic model needs refinement

modes.reason: Particle arrangement is the foundation of all property explanations. Students who treat particle diagrams as decorative rather than explanatory cannot use the model to reason. More substances and state comparisons force students to use diagrams as reasoning tools rather than illustrations — the misconception resolves through breadth of application, not repetition on the same substance.

nodes.label: Explaining physical properties using particle theory
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances including compressibility, viscosity and density
criteria: Uses particle theory to explain at least 2 physical properties of a given substance
Explanation references arrangement, motion or attraction — not just state labels
Correctly links a named property to the relevant particle behaviour
nodes.hinge_reason: Using particle theory explanatorily — not just descriptively — is directly prerequisite for AC9S7U06 (Pure Substances and Mixtures), the immediate downstream standard. Selecting and justifying separation techniques requires students to explain property differences at the particle level; students who can only label diagrams cannot access the property-technique reasoning that underpins every node in U06.

width.minimum: Use particle theory to explain at least two physical properties (e.g. compressibility, viscosity, density) of a given substance
width.typical: Compare the physical properties of three substances using particle theory; explain why properties differ in terms of arrangement, motion and attraction
wider: Investigate properties of materials such as density, melting point and compressibility and explain in terms of particle arrangement
Explain the process of diffusion in a liquid and a gas in terms of particle motion
Predict the properties of an unfamiliar substance given only its particle diagram; justify predictions and test against published data

modes.reason: This is the key application node — using the model to explain rather than just describe. Each new property context (compressibility, viscosity, density, diffusion) forces a fresh application of the particle model, resolving the misconception that particle theory is a recall task rather than an explanatory framework. The prediction direction — properties from diagram — is particularly effective at exposing whether students can actually use the model.

nodes.label: Changes of state and energy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain changes of state using particle theory and correctly identify energy input or output for each change
criteria: Explains melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation using particle theory
Correctly identifies energy input or output for each change
Does not confuse temperature change with state change during plateau regions

width.minimum: Explain melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation using particle theory; correctly identify energy input/output for each change
width.typical: Analyse a heating/cooling curve — identify each state change, explain plateau regions using particle theory, connect to energy changes
wider: Examine how changing motion and energy of particles is affected by heat energy absorbed or released
Model changes in particle arrangement as substances change state using diagrams or virtual simulations
Investigate sublimation or a non-standard state change — explain using particle theory and evaluate whether the basic model is sufficient

modes.reason: Changes of state integrate particle arrangement (Node 2), property explanation (Node 3), and energy input/output into a coordinated account of what happens during state change. Students who understand each element separately but cannot explain why temperature plateaus during melting — why energy input doesn't raise temperature but does change state — have not integrated the model components.

nodes.label: Particle theory as a model: scope and limits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the scope and limitations of the particle model and explain what evidence supports it
criteria: Identifies one phenomenon particle theory explains well and one it does not
Gives a reason for each based on the model's assumptions

width.minimum: Identify one phenomenon particle theory explains well and one it does not explain; give a reason for each
width.typical: Compare particle theory with an alternative model — explain what each is designed to explain and why scientists use multiple models
wider: Research a historical development of particle theory — how did evidence change the model over time?
Analyse how characteristics and properties of materials are used in Design and Technologies to create solutions — connect to particle-level explanations
Evaluate published claims about a material's properties using particle theory as a critical lens

modes.reason: Students commonly describe model limitations abstractly without reasoning through why the model fails for a specific phenomenon. Scaffolding the reasoning — what does the model assume, and what does this phenomenon require that the model doesn't provide — builds genuine model evaluation rather than generic limitation-listing.

descriptors.title: Pure substances and mixtures
descriptors.description: use a particle model to describe differences between pure substances and mixtures and apply understanding of properties of substances to separate mixtures
descriptors.knowledge: Students know how the properties of materials influence their use (AC9S4U04), have compared reversible changes including dissolving and changes of state (AC9S6U04), and have an introductory particle model from AC9S7U05. They have not formally distinguished pure substances from mixtures at the particle level or applied separation techniques systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use a particle model to describe the difference between pure substances and mixtures, and select and apply appropriate separation techniques based on properties of substances.

nodes.label: Pure substances vs mixtures at the particle level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish pure substances from mixtures using particle diagrams and classify familiar materials correctly
criteria: Correctly distinguishes pure substance from mixture using particle diagrams
Classifies 5 familiar materials correctly with justification
Does not confuse homogeneous mixtures (e.g. solutions) with pure substances
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish pure substances from mixtures at the particle level cannot select appropriate separation techniques in Nodes 3-5 — technique selection requires knowing what type of mixture is present.

width.minimum: Distinguish pure substance from mixture using particle diagrams; classify 5 familiar materials correctly with justification
width.typical: Draw particle diagrams for a pure substance, a homogeneous mixture and a heterogeneous mixture; explain the key differences
wider: Use representations of particles to show the difference between samples of pure substances and mixtures; identify examples of each in everyday contexts
Examine different solutions and identify the solvent and solute; represent at the particle level
Investigate a borderline case (e.g. alloy, saltwater at different concentrations) — is it pure or a mixture? What does this reveal about the definition?

modes.reason: The pure/mixture distinction at the particle level is prerequisite for all separation technique selection. Students who cannot make this distinction select inappropriate techniques and cannot explain their choices. Seeing the distinction across multiple material types — solutions, alloys, everyday materials — forces students to apply the particle-level definition rather than relying on visual appearance.

nodes.label: Properties as the basis for separation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that separation techniques exploit differences in physical properties and match property differences to techniques
criteria: States that separation exploits differences in physical properties
Correctly matches at least 3 property differences to separation techniques
Explains why a chosen technique would work for a given mixture
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot map property differences to techniques apply techniques by rote and cannot justify choices or adapt when scenarios change. This mapping is the conceptual engine for all technique selection nodes.

width.minimum: State that separation techniques exploit differences in physical properties; match at least three property differences to a separation technique
width.typical: Analyse a mixture — identify relevant property differences and justify which technique is most appropriate, including why others would not work
wider: Analyse how physical properties of substances in mixtures (particle size, density, volatility) determine the separation technique used
Explore and compare separation methods used in a variety of situations such as in the home, recycling industries and water purification
Evaluate a separation scenario with multiple possible techniques — rank by efficiency, cost and practicality

modes.reason: Understanding that techniques exploit property differences (not just 'removing things') is the conceptual key. Without this, students apply techniques by rote and cannot explain or adapt when scenarios change. Seeing the property-technique connection across multiple real-world contexts — home, industry, water purification — forces students to apply the principle rather than memorise a technique-mixture pairing.

nodes.label: Filtration and evaporation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform or describe filtration and evaporation and justify their use for appropriate mixtures
criteria: Correctly describes or performs filtration and evaporation
Identifies a mixture appropriate for each technique with property reasoning
Explains why the chosen technique works using property differences

width.minimum: Correctly perform or describe filtration and evaporation; identify a mixture each technique is appropriate for and explain why using property differences
width.typical: Design a procedure to separate a given mixture using filtration and/or evaporation; predict and explain the result at the particle level
wider: Investigate and use filtration and evaporation in a range of practical contexts; evaluate effectiveness
Investigate separation techniques used by First Nations Australians such as hand-picking, sieving, winnowing and filtering — explain the property differences each exploits
Investigate the effect of a variable (e.g. filter paper grade, temperature) on separation efficiency; analyse results using particle theory

modes.reason: Performing or describing filtration and evaporation correctly requires procedural precision — students commonly describe steps in the wrong order, omit key steps, or confuse the two techniques. Practice with feedback on procedural accuracy is what helps, not more separation technique contexts.

nodes.label: Distillation and chromatography
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the principles of distillation and chromatography and identify mixtures each technique is appropriate for
criteria: Describes the principle of distillation and chromatography
Identifies a mixture appropriate for each technique
Distinguishes when distillation is preferred over evaporation

width.minimum: Describe the principle of distillation and chromatography; identify a mixture each is appropriate for and explain why
width.typical: Compare distillation and evaporation — explain when each is appropriate and why, using particle theory and property differences
wider: Investigate crystallisation, chromatography and distillation; explain the property differences each exploits
Investigate separation techniques used by First Nations Australians such as yandying, cold-pressing and steam distilling — connect to property principles
Analyse a chromatography result — calculate Rf values, identify components, evaluate what the result reveals about mixture composition

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse distillation with evaporation — both involve heat and phase change — without reasoning through the key difference: distillation collects the vapour, evaporation does not. Scaffolding the comparison explicitly (same property exploited, different outcome sought, different equipment needed) is what resolves the confusion.

nodes.label: Selecting and justifying separation techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and justify an appropriate separation technique for an unfamiliar mixture using property differences
criteria: Selects an appropriate technique for an unfamiliar mixture
Justifies the choice using property differences
Identifies at least one technique that would not work and explains why

width.minimum: Given an unfamiliar mixture, select an appropriate technique and justify the choice using property differences
width.typical: Design a multi-step separation procedure for a mixture with three components; justify each step and predict the outcome
wider: Evaluate a real-world separation process (e.g. water purification, mining, food processing) — identify techniques used and property differences exploited
Compare industrial and First Nations separation techniques for the same type of mixture — analyse efficiency, sustainability and cultural significance
Design and evaluate an original separation procedure for a novel mixture; assess against criteria of efficiency, cost and practicality

modes.reason: This node integrates pure/mixture distinction (Node 1), property-technique mapping (Node 2), and procedural knowledge of all four techniques (Nodes 3-4) into a coordinated selection and justification task for unfamiliar mixtures. Students who can handle each technique separately but cannot select and justify for a novel mixture have not integrated the property-based framework.

descriptors.title: Cells as basic units
descriptors.description: recognise cells as the basic units of living things, compare plant and animal cells, and describe the functions of specialised cell structures and organelles
descriptors.knowledge: Students can group living things by external features (AC9SFU01), compare living and non-living things and life cycles (AC9S3U01), explain how structural features enable survival (AC9S5U01), and classify organisms using dichotomous keys (AC9S7U01). All prior learning is at the organism level — external structures, observable features, habitat relationships. There is no prior curriculum treatment of internal cell structure, cellular scale, or sub-organism organisation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that all living things are made of cells, compare plant and animal cells identifying structures present in each, and describe the functions of key organelles including nucleus, cell membrane, cell wall, cytoplasm, chloroplasts and vacuoles.

nodes.label: Cellular scale — why cells are invisible and require magnification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the scale of cells relative to organisms and explain why microscopes are required to observe them.
criteria: States that cells are microscopic and not visible to the naked eye
Explains that microscopes were necessary to discover and observe cells
Gives an approximate size comparison between a cell and a familiar object

width.minimum: Students state that cells are microscopic and explain that the microscope was necessary to discover them.
width.typical: Students compare cell size to familiar objects using scale diagrams; explain that a human body contains trillions of cells; describe how light microscopes magnify; explain that single-celled organisms are complete living things at microscopic scale; connect the invention of the microscope to cell discovery.
wider: Trace the historical development of cell discovery — Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Schleiden, Schwann — and explain what each contribution added to the emerging cell theory
Use a digital microscope or photomicrographs to observe prepared slides and describe what is visible at different magnifications

modes.reason: Students enter with entirely organism-level biology. The shift to cellular scale is the entry point for all subsequent nodes — students who do not grasp why cells are invisible cannot make sense of microscopy as a tool or understand why cell theory required new technology to discover.

nodes.label: Cell theory — all living things are made of cells
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state that all living things — including plants, fungi and single-celled organisms — are made of cells, and distinguish single-celled from multicellular organisms.
criteria: States that all living things are made of cells
Includes plants and single-celled organisms explicitly in this claim
Distinguishes single-celled from multicellular organisms with examples from each
nodes.hinge_reason: Cell theory universality is the prerequisite for the plant-animal comparison in N4. Students who believe only animals (or only complex organisms) have cells cannot make sense of the plant cell structures in N3 or explain why plant cells have additional organelles. This misconception is documented and persistent.

width.minimum: Students state cell theory and give one example each of a single-celled and multicellular organism.
width.typical: Students apply cell theory universally — explicitly including plants, bacteria and single-celled organisms that students may not intuitively expect to have cells; explain that cells carry out all life processes; describe that multicellular organisms are organised collections of cells; connect to AC9S3U01's living/non-living distinction — cells are what makes something living.
wider: Examine photomicrographs of cells from bacteria, yeast, leaf tissue and human cheek — compare visible structures and discuss what 'cell' means across such different organisms
Investigate which organisms are single-celled vs multicellular and discuss what this implies about the minimum requirements for life

modes.reason: The misconception that plants do not have cells, or that only animals have 'real' cells, must be explicitly addressed. Students need to encounter plant cells, fungal cells and bacterial cells as cells before organelle differences are introduced — otherwise the plant-animal comparison in N4 has no foundation.

nodes.label: Cell structures shared by plant and animal cells — nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the function of structures present in both plant and animal cells: nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm.
criteria: States the function of nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm
Explains at least one structural feature of each that relates to its function
Identifies these three as structures present in both plant and animal cells
nodes.hinge_reason: The three shared structures are the foundation for the plant-animal comparison in N4. Students who cannot correctly assign functions to nucleus, membrane and cytoplasm cannot identify what is additional in plant cells or explain why those additions exist.

width.minimum: Students state the function of nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm.
width.typical: Students describe nucleus as the genetic control centre containing DNA; cell membrane as a selectively permeable barrier controlling what enters and exits; cytoplasm as the aqueous medium in which chemical reactions occur; explain that these three structures are universal — present in essentially all cells; connect nucleus to heredity (DNA) in anticipation of AC9S10U01.
wider: Investigate what happens when the nucleus is removed from a cell — what does this reveal about its role as control centre?
Compare the cell membrane to a security checkpoint — what analogy works and where does it break down?

modes.reason: Structure-function pairing for organelles is most securely learned by connecting physical properties to function. The nucleus contains DNA and directs cell activity; the membrane is a boundary with selectivity; cytoplasm is the medium for chemistry. Learning functions as a list without this reasoning produces rapid forgetting.

nodes.label: Plant-specific structures — cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify cell wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole as plant-specific structures and explain the functional significance of each.
criteria: Identifies cell wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole as plant-specific structures
Explains the function of each plant-specific structure
Connects each plant-specific structure to an organism-level need that animal cells do not have

width.minimum: Students identify the three plant-specific structures and state the function of each.
width.typical: Students explain cell wall as rigid structural support (plants lack a skeleton); chloroplasts as sites of photosynthesis (plants are autotrophs); large central vacuole for turgor pressure and storage; explain why animal cells lack these — animals have skeletons, obtain food rather than making it, lack turgor requirements; examine prepared slides or photomicrographs of plant and animal cells; design a physical or digital model justified by function.
wider: Compare cells from different plant tissues — why do root cells lack chloroplasts while leaf mesophyll cells have many? What does this reveal about cell specialisation within a plant?
Design and justify a cell model — for each modelling choice, explain what it represents accurately and what it simplifies

modes.reason: Plant-specific structures are most meaningfully understood as solutions to organism-level problems: no skeleton → need rigid wall; autotrophic → need photosynthesis machinery; osmotic needs → need vacuole. This organism-level reasoning connects to prior survival/adaptation knowledge and prepares the structure-function analysis in AC9S8U02.

Cell modelling, tissue comparison within plants, and microscopy each apply the plant-animal comparison in a different representational context. Each reveals different aspects of the structural differences.

nodes.label: Additional organelles — mitochondria, ribosomes and cell specialisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the roles of mitochondria and ribosomes as organelles present in both cell types, and recognise that cells are specialised — different cells have different organelle complements.
criteria: States the function of mitochondria and ribosomes
Explains why a named specialised cell has more or fewer of a particular organelle
Describes cell specialisation as variation in organelle complement reflecting cell function

width.minimum: Students state the function of mitochondria (energy release) and describe one example of a specialised cell whose organelle complement reflects its function.
