width.typical: Students describe mitochondria as the site of cellular respiration (energy release for cell activity); ribosomes as protein synthesis sites; explain that the number and type of organelles varies with cell function — muscle cells have many mitochondria, secretory cells have many ribosomes, root hair cells have no chloroplasts; connect organelle complement to the cell's role in the organism; introduce the concept that specialisation is built on the same DNA base.
wider: Investigate a cell disorder that results from organelle malfunction — e.g. mitochondrial disease — and explain how failure at the organelle level affects cell, tissue and organism function
Explore how augmented or virtual reality tools allow 'zooming in' to explore organelle scale within cells

modes.reason: This node integrates the structure-function principle established in N3 and N4 into the broader concept of cell specialisation — different organelle complements for different functions. This is the bridge to AC9S8U02's tissue and organ system analysis, where specialisation is the mechanism enabling tissue formation.

descriptors.title: Structure, function and organ systems
descriptors.description: analyse the relationship between structure and function of cells, tissues and organs in a plant and an animal organ system and explain how these systems enable survival of the individual
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe organelle functions and cell specialisation (AC9S8U01) and explain how structural features enable survival at the organism level (AC9S5U01). They have not yet encountered the tissue or organ as organisational levels, or analysed how structure at sub-organism levels enables system-level survival functions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse structure-function relationships across the cell → tissue → organ → organ system hierarchy in one plant and one animal system, explaining how integrated system function enables individual survival.

nodes.label: Cell specialisation — same DNA, different structure and function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how cells with the same genetic information become specialised for different functions, and describe structural features of two or more specialised cell types.
criteria: Describes at least two structural features of a specialised cell and explains how each serves the cell's function
Explains that cells with the same DNA can be specialised for different functions
Connects organelle complement to cell specialisation for at least one cell type
nodes.hinge_reason: Cell specialisation is the conceptual mechanism that explains tissue formation. Students who cannot explain why cells differ structurally cannot understand why similar cells group into tissues in N2, and cannot analyse organ structure in N3 in terms of the specialised cells that compose it.

width.minimum: Students describe two structural features of one specialised cell type and explain how each feature serves the cell's function.
width.typical: Students analyse: red blood cells (biconcave, no nucleus — maximises haemoglobin, flexible for capillaries); xylem cells (hollow, thick walls — water transport); nerve cells (long axon, many dendrites — signal transmission over distance); muscle cells (elongated, many mitochondria — contraction); explain that specialisation means organelle complement and shape are matched to function; connect to N5 of AC9S8U01.
wider: Compare the organelle complement of a secretory cell (many ribosomes, large Golgi) to a muscle cell (many mitochondria) — explain each difference using function
Investigate how an artificial organ mimics real cell specialisation — what cell-level properties does the artificial version replicate or approximate?

modes.reason: The structure-function reasoning method must be practised at the cell level before it is applied at the tissue and organ level. Students who learn specialised cell features as a list without the reasoning framework ('this feature enables this function') cannot transfer the analysis to novel cell types or to tissues.

nodes.label: Tissues — groups of specialised cells performing a shared function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define a tissue as a group of similar specialised cells performing a shared function, and give examples from plant and animal systems.
criteria: Defines a tissue as a group of similar specialised cells performing a shared function
Names at least one animal and one plant tissue with the function of each
Explains how tissue function emerges from the collective action of its component cells

width.minimum: Students define tissue and give one plant and one animal tissue example with the shared function of each.
width.typical: Students describe: muscle tissue (muscle cells — contraction); epithelial tissue (epithelial cells — lining/protection); xylem tissue (xylem cells — water transport); phloem tissue (sieve tube cells — sugar transport); explain that tissues perform functions individual cells cannot perform at scale; explain that tissue identity is defined by cell type and function, not just location.
wider: Examine prepared slides of muscle, epithelial and plant vascular tissue — describe how the arrangement of cells in each tissue reflects its function
Research how a tissue disorder (e.g. fibrosis — abnormal connective tissue) affects the function of the organ it composes

modes.reason: The tissue concept extends specialisation to the collective level — similar cells acting together. Students need to understand that tissue function emerges from cell arrangement and cooperation, not just from individual cell properties. This is the building block for organ composition in N3.

nodes.label: Organs — tissues working together for an integrated function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe an organ as a structure composed of multiple tissue types, each contributing to the organ's overall function.
criteria: Names at least two tissue types in a named organ and explains the contribution of each
Explains why organs require multiple tissue types
Analyses how a tissue-level change affects organ function
nodes.hinge_reason: The organ-as-multi-tissue-structure concept is the prerequisite for organ system analysis. Students who think of organs as single-tissue structures cannot explain why organ function depends on the coordination of component tissues, and cannot analyse how organ failure propagates from tissue disorder.

width.minimum: Students name two tissue types in one organ and explain how each contributes to the organ's function.
width.typical: Students analyse: the heart (cardiac muscle tissue, epithelial lining, connective tissue — contraction, smooth flow, structural integrity); a leaf (epidermis, mesophyll, vascular tissue — gas exchange, photosynthesis, water/sugar transport); explain that organs require multiple tissue types because no single tissue can perform all the functions an organ needs; compare 2D and 3D representations of organs to understand spatial relationships.
wider: Compare 2D and 3D representations of the same organ — what spatial relationships are visible in 3D that flat diagrams cannot show?
Investigate how a disorder at the tissue level affects organ function — e.g. how atherosclerosis (connective tissue thickening in arteries) impairs the circulatory organ's function

modes.reason: Students commonly think of organs as single things rather than integrated multi-tissue structures. Making the tissue composition of organs explicit — and explaining why multiple tissue types are required — is the conceptual move that connects tissue-level analysis to organ-level function.

nodes.label: Organ systems — coordinated organs enabling survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how organs within a system coordinate to perform a survival function, applying this to one animal and one plant system.
criteria: Names the organs of one animal and one plant system and explains the function of each
Explains how the coordinated system enables a specific survival function
Compares one plant and one animal system as solutions to a shared survival problem

width.minimum: Students describe the organs of one system and explain how the system as a whole enables a named survival function.
width.typical: Students analyse one animal system (circulatory — heart, blood vessels, blood; or digestive — mouth, stomach, intestines, liver) and one plant system (vascular — xylem, phloem, roots, leaves); explain how each organ's structure contributes to the system's survival function; explain that the system fails if any organ fails; connect system function to individual survival (oxygen delivery, nutrient transport, water uptake).
wider: Compare the vascular system of a plant to the circulatory system of an animal as analogous solutions to the same survival problem — what structural differences reflect different organism constraints?
Investigate how an artificial organ (dialysis machine, pacemaker) mimics or augments the function of a real organ — what structural principles does it replicate?

modes.reason: Applying the organ system analysis to both a plant and an animal system — and comparing them as analogous solutions — builds the generalised structure-function analytical capability the descriptor's 'analyse' demand requires.

descriptors.title: Plate tectonics
descriptors.description: investigate tectonic activity including the formation of geological features at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and describe the scientific evidence for the theory of plate tectonics
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe observable properties of rocks and minerals (AC9S3U02) and explain how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition change Earth's surface (AC9S5U02). Prior learning is entirely surface-level — there is no curriculum treatment of Earth's interior at any prior year level. Earth-Sun-Moon cycles (AC9S7U03) address celestial geometry, not geological interior. Students have no prior exposure to Earth's internal structure, plates, or tectonic processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the formation of geological features at divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and explain the scientific evidence — including seafloor spreading, continental fit, fossil distribution and earthquake/volcanic patterns — that supports the theory of plate tectonics.

nodes.label: Earth's internal structure — layers, states and the lithosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe Earth's layered internal structure, identify the state and composition of each layer, and explain that the lithosphere is the rigid outer layer.
criteria: Names Earth's main internal layers and describes the state (solid/liquid) of each
Explains that the lithosphere is the rigid outer layer (crust + upper mantle)
States that temperature and pressure increase with depth
nodes.hinge_reason: The lithosphere concept is the prerequisite for the plate model in N2. Students who do not understand that there is a rigid outer layer sitting on a semi-fluid asthenosphere cannot grasp why plates can move independently, or why they behave as they do at boundaries in N3–N5.

width.minimum: Students name Earth's main layers, state whether each is solid or liquid, and identify the lithosphere as the rigid outer layer.
width.typical: Students describe crust (thin, solid, oceanic vs continental), mantle (mostly solid but flows slowly over geological time, convection occurs in upper mantle), outer core (liquid iron/nickel), inner core (solid); explain that temperature and pressure increase with depth; describe the lithosphere as crust plus rigid upper mantle; explain that Australia's ancient craton reflects a long history of tectonic stability.
wider: Investigate how we know about Earth's interior without direct observation — what does seismic wave behaviour reveal about layer boundaries and states?
Compare the relative thickness of the crust to Earth's radius using a scale model — why is the lithosphere described as like the skin of an apple?

modes.reason: Students have no prior mental model of Earth's interior. The layered structure with varying states — particularly the mantle as solid yet able to flow over geological time — is counterintuitive. This node must build the interior model explicitly before any tectonic mechanism is introduced.

nodes.label: Tectonic plates and the driving mechanism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates and describe mantle convection as the mechanism driving plate movement.
criteria: Explains that the lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates that move
Describes mantle convection as the mechanism driving plate movement
States that plates move at rates of centimetres per year
nodes.hinge_reason: The plate-as-moving-unit concept is the structural prerequisite for all three boundary types. Students who do not understand that plates are distinct rigid units that move relative to each other cannot explain why different boundary types produce different features — the feature depends entirely on the direction of relative plate motion.

width.minimum: Students state that the lithosphere is divided into moving plates and identify convection in the mantle as the driving mechanism.
width.typical: Students describe plates as large rigid sections of lithosphere; explain that heat from Earth's core drives convection currents in the mantle; describe how convection creates slab pull and ridge push forces; explain that plates move at rates of centimetres per year (fingernail growth rate); describe the major plates; connect the extreme age and stability of the Australian craton to its position away from active plate boundaries.
wider: Investigate the relative significance of slab pull, ridge push and mantle convection — which force dominates and what evidence supports this?
Research First Nations Australians' cultural accounts of earthquakes and volcanic events — what geological record do these accounts preserve?

modes.reason: The plate model requires students to reconceptualise Earth's surface from a fixed landscape to a dynamic system of moving pieces. The convection mechanism must be established before boundary types — without a driving mechanism, plate movement appears arbitrary and boundary feature formation cannot be explained causally.

nodes.label: Divergent boundaries — plates moving apart
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geological features formed where plates diverge and explain the process producing each.
criteria: Explains that diverging plates produce tension and allow magma to rise
Describes mid-ocean ridges and seafloor spreading as products of divergent boundaries
States that oceanic crust is youngest at ridges and ages with distance

width.minimum: Students describe seafloor spreading and mid-ocean ridges as the result of diverging plates.
width.typical: Students explain that diverging plates create tension in the crust; magma rises to fill the gap — forming new oceanic crust (seafloor spreading) and mid-ocean ridges; on continents, divergence produces rift valleys; explain that rock at mid-ocean ridges is youngest and age increases with distance from the ridge; describe volcanic activity along ridges.
wider: Investigate Marie Tharp's topographic mapping of the Atlantic Ocean floor — how did her maps reveal the mid-ocean ridge system and what resistance did she face in getting her findings accepted?
Model divergent boundary interactions using physical materials — evaluate the model's accuracy and identify what it cannot show

modes.reason: Each boundary type is most clearly understood through the plate movement direction → stress type → feature chain. Divergent = tension → crust thins → magma rises → new crust. Making this causal chain explicit for each type builds a transferable reasoning framework rather than a list of boundary features.

nodes.label: Convergent boundaries — plates colliding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geological features formed at convergent boundaries and distinguish ocean-continent from continent-continent convergence.
criteria: Describes subduction as the process at ocean-continent convergent boundaries
Explains the formation of ocean trenches and volcanic arcs at ocean-continent boundaries
Explains why continent-continent convergence produces mountain ranges rather than subduction

width.minimum: Students describe subduction and explain one feature (trench or volcanic arc) that results from ocean-continent convergence.
width.typical: Students explain ocean-continent convergence: denser oceanic plate subducts under continental → trench, volcanic arc, earthquakes; continent-continent convergence: neither subducts → folding and uplift → mountain ranges (Himalayas); explain why continental crust doesn't subduct (less dense); describe the Ring of Fire as a product of convergent boundaries around the Pacific; evaluate engineering solutions to tectonic hazards.
wider: Investigate engineering solutions designed to reduce tectonic event impacts — what assumptions about plate forces do these solutions embed?
Analyse earthquake and volcanic activity distribution maps and identify which patterns correspond to convergent vs divergent boundaries

modes.reason: Convergent boundaries are more complex than divergent — the outcome depends on the density of the colliding plates (oceanic vs continental). Students need the density distinction made explicit to explain why subduction occurs in ocean-continent but not continent-continent collisions.

nodes.label: Transform boundaries — plates sliding past each other
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe transform boundaries, explain the geological features they produce, and explain why earthquakes are concentrated there.
criteria: Describes transform boundaries as plates sliding horizontally past each other
Explains why earthquakes occur at transform boundaries (stress build-up and release)
States that transform boundaries produce earthquakes but not volcanic activity

width.minimum: Students describe transform boundaries as plates sliding horizontally past each other and state that they produce earthquakes.
width.typical: Students explain that plates grind horizontally past each other at transform boundaries; friction prevents smooth movement — stress builds and releases suddenly as earthquakes; describe strike-slip faults (e.g. San Andreas); explain that transform boundaries produce earthquakes but not volcanic activity; contrast with convergent and divergent in terms of feature type.
wider: Compare the seismic hazard at transform, convergent and divergent boundaries — which type produces the most damaging earthquakes and why?
Investigate a specific transform fault (San Andreas, Alpine Fault NZ) and explain the geological history of the boundary

modes.reason: Transform boundaries are structurally simpler than convergent but the friction-stress-release mechanism for earthquakes needs explicit explanation. Students commonly assume volcanoes occur at all plate boundaries — the contrast with convergent and divergent in terms of volcanic activity is important.

nodes.label: Evidence for plate tectonics — multiple converging lines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least three independent lines of evidence supporting the theory of plate tectonics and explain what each demonstrates.
criteria: Describes at least three distinct lines of evidence supporting plate tectonics
Explains what each evidence type demonstrates about plate movement or history
Identifies seafloor age patterns as particularly strong evidence for seafloor spreading

width.minimum: Students describe two lines of evidence and explain what each demonstrates about plate movement or history.
width.typical: Students explain: continental fit (jigsaw shapes, especially South America/Africa); matching fossil distributions across now-separated continents; matching geological formations across continental margins; seafloor age pattern — youngest at ridges, oldest at subduction zones; earthquake and volcanic activity concentrated at boundaries; construct a timeline of theory development including Marie Tharp's contribution; examine how geologist resistance to Wegener illustrates theory validation processes.
wider: Construct a timeline showing how the evidence base accumulated and why the theory was initially resisted — what changed when seafloor data became available?
Research First Nations Australians' cultural accounts that record historical earthquake or volcanic events — what geological evidence do these accounts preserve?

modes.reason: Each evidence type — continental fit, fossils, geology, seafloor age, seismic patterns — is a distinct investigative context contributing independent support for the same conclusion. Working across all types builds the 'multiple converging lines' understanding the descriptor's 'describe the scientific evidence' demand requires.

descriptors.title: Rock cycle
descriptors.description: describe the key processes of the rock cycle, including the timescales over which they occur, and examine how the properties of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks reflect their formation and influence their use
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare observable properties of rocks and minerals (AC9S3U02) and describe weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition as surface processes (AC9S5U02). Plate tectonics provides heat, pressure and uplift mechanisms (AC9S8U03). Prior learning covers surface rock identification and surface processes only — rock formation processes (igneous crystallisation, metamorphism, lithification) and the rock cycle as a system are entirely new.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the rock cycle as an interconnected system linking sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic formation, explain the geological timescales involved, and examine how each rock type's properties reflect its formation history and determine appropriate use.

nodes.label: Sedimentary rocks — weathering, transport, deposition and lithification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the formation of sedimentary rocks through the sequence of weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition and lithification, and connect observable properties to formation.
criteria: Describes the formation sequence: weathering → erosion → transport → deposition → lithification
Connects at least two observable properties of sedimentary rock to formation steps
Identifies fossils as occurring in sedimentary rocks and explains why

width.minimum: Students describe the four-step formation sequence and identify one observable property of sedimentary rock that reflects each.
width.typical: Students describe: physical and chemical weathering breaks rock into sediment; erosion and transportation carry sediment; deposition layers sediment; lithification (compaction and cementation) produces rock; explain layering as a record of deposition events; explain rounded grains as evidence of transport; explain that fossils occur in sedimentary rocks (organisms buried in sediment); identify examples (sandstone, limestone, shale, coal).
wider: Examine fossil evidence in sedimentary rock samples to predict the environment and approximate timescale of formation
Investigate First Nations Australians' selection of sedimentary rocks for specific purposes — what observable properties reflect formation and guided selection?

modes.reason: Sedimentary formation is the most connected to prior knowledge — weathering and erosion from AC9S5U02 are the first steps. Building the full formation chain from prior surface processes to completed rock is the appropriate entry point. Formation-property reasoning (rounded grains = transported; layers = sequential deposition) establishes the method used in N2 and N3.

nodes.label: Igneous rocks — magma cooling and crystallisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the formation of igneous rocks from cooling magma or lava and connect crystal size to cooling rate.
criteria: Distinguishes intrusive (underground, slow cooling) from extrusive (surface, rapid cooling) igneous formation
Explains that slower cooling produces larger crystals
Applies cooling rate reasoning to infer the formation environment of a named igneous rock
nodes.hinge_reason: Crystal size as a direct record of cooling rate is the most diagnostic formation-property link in the rock cycle. Students who grasp this reasoning can apply it independently to novel igneous samples. It also models the formation-property reasoning method that N3 and N5 extend to metamorphic rocks and uses.

width.minimum: Students distinguish intrusive from extrusive igneous formation and explain the crystal size difference using cooling rate.
width.typical: Students explain: magma cools slowly underground (intrusive) → large crystals (granite); lava cools rapidly at surface (extrusive) → small crystals or glassy texture (basalt, obsidian); explain that crystal size is a direct record of cooling rate — a key formation-property link; connect to plate tectonics — magma is produced at divergent boundaries and subduction zones; identify examples and describe properties.
wider: Investigate the relationship between cooling rate and crystal size using a salt or alum crystallisation experiment — predict and test how different cooling rates affect crystal size
Analyse igneous rock samples and infer their formation environment from crystal size alone

modes.reason: Crystal size = cooling rate is a mechanistic link students can derive rather than memorise — slower cooling allows more time for crystal growth. Making this causal chain explicit (not just 'granite has large crystals') gives students a formation-reading tool that transfers to novel samples.

nodes.label: Metamorphic rocks — heat and pressure without melting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain metamorphic rock formation through heat and pressure applied to existing rock, and describe observable properties that reflect these conditions.
criteria: Explains that metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to heat and pressure without melting
Connects banding or foliation to the directional compression of metamorphism
Identifies at least one parent rock and its metamorphic product

width.minimum: Students state that metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to heat and pressure without melting, and identify one observable property reflecting this.
width.typical: Students explain that existing rocks (any type) subjected to intense heat and pressure underground undergo recrystallisation without melting; explain banding/foliation as a result of minerals being compressed and reoriented; explain that metamorphic rocks are denser and harder than their precursors; identify parent rock and metamorphic product pairs (shale → slate → phyllite → schist; limestone → marble); connect to plate tectonics — subduction zones and mountain-building provide the heat and pressure.
wider: Examine the metamorphic series from shale → slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss and explain what increasing grade of metamorphism reveals about the conditions of formation
Compare a metamorphic rock to its parent rock and identify the structural changes produced by heat and pressure

modes.reason: Metamorphic formation is the least intuitive of the three types — heat and pressure without melting is a process with no everyday equivalent. Students need the formation conditions explained explicitly (subduction, burial, mountain building) with the observable consequences (banding, density, hardness) derived from those conditions.

nodes.label: The rock cycle — processes connecting all three types over geological time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the rock cycle as a set of interconnected processes by which rocks are continuously transformed between types, and identify the geological timescales involved.
criteria: Traces at least two complete rock cycle pathways, naming the process at each step
Compares the timescales of surface and deep rock cycle processes
Explains how plate tectonics drives the rock cycle

width.minimum: Students trace at least two complete pathways in the rock cycle, naming the process at each transformation step.
width.typical: Students describe all major pathways: weathering/erosion → sediment → sedimentary; burial/heat/pressure → metamorphic; melting → magma → igneous; uplift (any deep rock) → surface → weathering again; compare timescales: surface weathering (thousands to millions of years), burial and metamorphism (tens of millions), subduction and melting (similar); explain that plate tectonics drives the cycle by providing uplift, subduction, and heat; emphasise that no rock is permanent.
wider: Trace the journey of a specific mineral (e.g. quartz) through multiple rock cycle stages and estimate the total time elapsed
Investigate how mining of ores and minerals intersects with the rock cycle — what processes concentrate economically useful minerals, and what does extraction disrupt?

modes.reason: The rock cycle requires students to reconceptualise rock as temporary — any rock can become any other rock type given sufficient time and appropriate conditions. This is a significant conceptual shift from stable, fixed rock types.
Mineral journey tracing, timescale comparison, and mining impact analysis each illuminate different aspects of the cycle as a dynamic Earth system.

nodes.label: Rock properties, formation history and use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the properties of each rock type reflect its formation history and evaluate the suitability of specific rocks for named uses.
criteria: Explains the properties of at least two rock types in terms of their formation processes
Connects named rock properties to suitability for a specific use
Identifies how traditional rock selection practices reflect knowledge of formation-linked properties

width.minimum: Students explain the use of two rocks by connecting their properties to formation and to the demands of the application.
width.typical: Students connect: granite (interlocked large crystals, hard, weather-resistant → building, benchtops); marble (recrystallised calcite, polishable → sculpture, tiles); sandstone (layered, porous, relatively soft → building, grinding); slate (fine-grained metamorphic, splits in sheets → roofing); coal (compressed organic material → fuel); connect First Nations rock selection to observable formation-linked properties; use dichotomous keys to identify rock samples.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' quarrying practices — how were grindstones, hammerstones and cutting tools selected based on observable properties, and what does this reveal about practical knowledge of formation-linked properties?
Evaluate the environmental impact of quarrying a specific rock type and examine rehabilitation initiatives

modes.reason: This node integrates the formation-property links established in N1–N3 and the cycle understanding from N4 into practical application — properties as a consequence of formation history determining use. It is the descriptor's 'examine how properties reflect formation and influence use' demand.

descriptors.title: Energy transfer and transformation
descriptors.description: classify different types of energy as kinetic or potential and investigate energy transfer and transformations in simple systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students have encountered specific energy forms across multiple years: sound energy causes vibration (AC9S2U02), heat energy transfers between objects (AC9S3U03), light travels in straight paths (AC9S5U03), electrical energy transfers in circuits (AC9S6U03). Prior learning is energy-form specific — each form was treated in isolation. The kinetic/potential classification framework, the transfer/transformation distinction, and the concept of by-product heat are all new.
descriptors.endpoint: Students classify energy types as kinetic (movement, heat, sound, light, electrical) or potential (chemical, gravitational, elastic), distinguish energy transfer from transformation, and trace energy through multi-step systems — identifying useful outputs and by-product heat — using flow diagrams.

nodes.label: Kinetic energy — energy of active processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify kinetic energy types, explain what they share in common, and classify familiar examples.
criteria: Names at least four kinetic energy types
Explains the shared characteristic of kinetic energy forms (associated with activity or motion)
Correctly classifies novel energy examples as kinetic

width.minimum: Students list at least four kinetic energy types and state what they have in common.
width.typical: Students identify kinetic forms: movement/mechanical, thermal (heat), sound, light (radiant), electrical; explain that kinetic energy is associated with active motion or activity at particle or wave level; connect to prior knowledge — sound (AC9S2U02), heat (AC9S3U03), light (AC9S5U03), electrical (AC9S6U03) — now organised under one category; classify novel examples.
wider: Classify the energy types visible in a Rube Goldberg machine at different stages — identify all kinetic forms present
Investigate traditional fire-starting methods used by First Nations Australians — identify which kinetic energy forms are present at each stage

modes.reason: Students have met kinetic energy forms in isolation across four years. The classification step — organising familiar forms under a shared category — requires making the unifying principle (activity/motion) explicit. Without this, kinetic/potential remains two separate lists rather than a framework.

nodes.label: Potential energy — stored capacity for activity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify potential energy types, explain the stored-capacity principle, and classify familiar examples.
criteria: Names at least three potential energy types
Explains potential energy as stored capacity — not currently active
Distinguishes potential from kinetic energy and identifies the condition that determines each

width.minimum: Students name at least three potential energy types and explain what distinguishes potential from kinetic energy.
width.typical: Students identify potential forms: chemical (food, fuel, batteries), gravitational (height above ground), elastic (stretched/compressed objects); explain that potential energy is stored — not currently active but capable of being released; explain that the amount of stored energy depends on position, composition or deformation; apply the classification to everyday objects; explain that potential and kinetic energy can be interconverted.
wider: Compare the energy stored in different fuels (chemical potential) — what does energy density mean and why does it matter for transport or industry?
Investigate gravitational potential energy using a ramp — how does height relate to the kinetic energy a rolling ball has at the bottom?

modes.reason: Potential energy is less intuitive than kinetic — 'stored' energy is not visible or directly sensed. Connecting potential to the conditions that create it (height, chemical bonds, deformation) and to the kinetic energy released when conditions change is the conceptual move that makes the category coherent.

nodes.label: Energy transfer — same type, different location
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type, and give examples of thermal, mechanical and electrical transfer.
criteria: Defines energy transfer as energy moving between objects without changing type
Gives two examples of energy transfer involving different energy types
Distinguishes a transfer event from a transformation event

width.minimum: Students define energy transfer and give two examples of different energy types being transferred.
width.typical: Students describe transfer: heat flowing from hot to cold object (thermal transfer — same type, different location); sound passing from speaker to ear; electrical energy flowing through a circuit; a moving ball hitting a stationary ball (kinetic → kinetic); explain that in transfer, the energy type is preserved but moves from one object or location to another; contrast with transformation in preparation for N4.
wider: Investigate heat transfer through different materials — compare conductors and insulators in terms of transfer rate and explain using the particle model from AC9S7U05
Analyse sound energy transfer in a First Nations traditional instrument — how is energy transferred from player to air to listener?

modes.reason: Transfer and transformation are commonly confused. Transfer must be established with clear examples before transformation is introduced. The defining feature — same type, different location — needs explicit contrast with transformation (different type, same or different location) in N4.

nodes.label: Energy transformation — energy changing type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another, identify common transformation sequences, and explain by-product heat.
criteria: Defines energy transformation as energy changing from one type to another
Identifies useful output and by-product heat in at least two named transformations
Explains that by-product heat is not lost (energy is conserved) but is not the useful output
nodes.hinge_reason: By-product heat is the conceptual foundation of efficiency analysis in AC9S9U05. Students who do not understand that heat is almost always a by-product of energy transformation — and that this reduces useful output — cannot correctly identify all outputs in an efficiency calculation or construct complete Sankey diagrams.

width.minimum: Students define transformation and identify the energy type before and after in two named examples.
width.typical: Students describe common transformations: chemical → kinetic + heat (combustion); electrical → light + heat (light bulb); gravitational potential → kinetic (falling); elastic potential → kinetic + sound (stretched rubber band); explain that heat is almost always produced as a by-product in transformations — energy 'lost' to the environment; explain that by-product heat is not lost (energy conserved) but is not the useful output; connect to by-product identification in AC9S9U05 efficiency analysis.
wider: Investigate traditional fire-starting methods — trace the transformation sequence from initial stored energy (friction = mechanical → heat → chemical reaction → light + heat) and identify all by-product energy forms
Analyse a filament light bulb vs an LED: both transform electrical to light, but different proportions become by-product heat — what does this tell you about transformation efficiency?

modes.reason: By-product heat requires students to extend 'energy changes type' to include unwanted outputs alongside useful ones. Students who learn transformation examples without explicitly identifying by-product heat produce systematically incomplete energy analyses in Year 9. Making by-product heat a required component of every transformation description is the scaffold.

nodes.label: Tracing energy through multi-step systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace energy through a multi-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs.
criteria: Traces energy through a multi-step system naming all types at each stage
Identifies all transfers, transformations and by-product outputs in the trace
Distinguishes useful energy output from by-product outputs

width.minimum: Students trace energy through a two-step system, naming the energy type at each stage and identifying at least one by-product.
width.typical: Students trace: roller coaster (gravitational potential → kinetic → gravitational potential → kinetic + heat + sound); Newton's cradle (kinetic → elastic potential → kinetic + heat + sound); battery torch (chemical → electrical → light + heat); First Nations fire-starting (mechanical friction → heat → combustion chemical → light + heat); identify which outputs are useful and which are by-product; explain that tracing all outputs is the prerequisite for understanding efficiency.
wider: Observe a Rube Goldberg machine and construct a complete energy trace — identify every stage, every transfer, every transformation, and every by-product
Compare energy traces for two different systems that produce the same useful output (e.g. candle vs electric light) — identify which produces more by-product heat and what this implies

modes.reason: Each system context (mechanical, electrical, biological, traditional) exercises the energy tracing skill with a different sequence of types and outputs. Width here builds the generalised tracing capability the descriptor's 'investigate' demand requires.

nodes.label: Flow diagrams — representing and analysing energy systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct and interpret flow diagrams representing energy through a system and use these to identify where by-product outputs occur.
criteria: Constructs a flow diagram for a multi-step system with correctly labelled energy types
Includes by-product outputs at each transformation stage
Critiques a diagram for completeness — identifies any missing outputs

width.minimum: Students construct a flow diagram for a system with at least two stages, labelling input, useful output and by-product at each stage.
width.typical: Students construct flow diagrams using arrows and labelled energy types; represent both transfers and transformations correctly; include by-products at each transformation stage; critique diagrams for completeness — are all outputs accounted for?; explain that flow diagrams are the tool for efficiency analysis in Year 9.
wider: Compare flow diagrams for electricity generation from coal and from solar — what transformation stages differ and where does by-product heat appear in each?
Critique a peer's flow diagram for completeness and accuracy — identify missing outputs or incorrectly labelled transformations

modes.reason: Flow diagram construction requires applying the classification (N1–N2), transfer/transformation distinction (N3–N4) and tracing skill (N5) in a representational form. Diagrams that miss by-product outputs are a systematic error that propagates into AC9S9U05's efficiency calculations. Structured practice with completeness checking is the appropriate response.

descriptors.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
descriptors.description: classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures and compare different representations of these, including 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional models, symbols for elements and formulas for molecules and compounds
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe observable material properties (AC9SFU03), recognise physical change preserves material composition (AC9S2U03), explain solid/liquid/gas properties using a particle model (AC9S5U04), distinguish pure substances from mixtures and apply separation techniques (AC9S7U06), and describe particle arrangement, motion and attraction forces (AC9S7U05). The particle model treats particles as undifferentiated — particles have no identity (atom type). The concept of atom type, element as one atom type, and compound as chemically combined different atom types are all new. Chemical symbols and molecular formulas are new.
descriptors.endpoint: Students classify matter as elements (one atom type), compounds (two or more atom types chemically combined in fixed ratios) or mixtures (substances not chemically combined), and use chemical symbols, formulas and 2D/3D models to represent each — selecting representations based on what information each conveys.

nodes.label: Atoms and atom types — giving the particle model identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that particles in the particle model are atoms, that atoms have type (element identity), and that different substances are made of different atom types.
criteria: Explains that the particles in the particle model are atoms
States that different elements consist of different types of atoms
Explains that atom type determines element identity
nodes.hinge_reason: The atom-type extension to the particle model is the conceptual prerequisite for both elements (N2) and compounds (N3). Students who treat all particles as identical — as in the Y5/Y7 particle model — cannot understand why elements are defined by atom type or why chemically combining different atom types produces a new substance with new properties.

width.minimum: Students explain that atoms are the particles in the particle model and that different elements consist of different types of atoms.
width.typical: Students connect to AC9S7U05's particle model — those particles are atoms; explain that atom type determines what element a substance is; introduce the idea that there are ~118 known element types; explain that atoms of the same element are identical; describe atoms as the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity; note that this is a model — atoms have internal structure (introduced in AC9S9U06).
wider: Trace the historical development of the element concept from Democritus through Dalton — what changed in the model and what evidence drove each change?
Use virtual or physical models to distinguish between different atom types — what makes a carbon atom different from an oxygen atom at this level of model?

modes.reason: The shift from undifferentiated particles to typed atoms is the key conceptual move in this standard. Students need this extension made explicit — the Y7 particle model is being upgraded, not replaced. Making the upgrade visible ('you know particles exist; now we add: particles have type') prevents confusion about which model applies where.

nodes.label: Elements — one atom type, symbols and the periodic table
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define elements as pure substances consisting of only one type of atom and use chemical symbols to represent them.
criteria: Defines an element as a pure substance consisting of only one type of atom
Correctly uses symbols for at least five elements
Uses the periodic table to locate element symbols and names

width.minimum: Students define an element and correctly use symbols for at least five elements.
width.typical: Students define elements in terms of atomic composition (one type of atom only); use the periodic table as a reference for symbols; explain that symbols are internationally standardised shorthand; examine how Mendeleev arranged elements and compare to the current table; describe element properties varying across the table; connect element symbols to naming conventions (first letter capitalised, second lowercase).
wider: Examine Mendeleev's original periodic table and compare it to the current version — what principle drove the reorganisation from atomic mass to atomic number?
Investigate an unfamiliar element from the periodic table — predict its properties from its position and research whether the prediction holds

modes.reason: Elements are the simplest category — one atom type — and periodic table fluency (looking up symbols, reading position) is a tool students will use throughout secondary chemistry. The historical development of the table connects to the evidence-based nature of scientific models.

nodes.label: Compounds — different atom types chemically combined
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define compounds as substances containing two or more atom types chemically combined in fixed ratios, and use formulas to represent them.
criteria: Defines a compound as two or more atom types chemically combined in fixed ratios
Interprets a chemical formula to identify atom types and their ratios
Explains that compounds have different properties from their constituent elements
nodes.hinge_reason: The compound definition — chemically combined, new properties, fixed ratio — is the conceptual distinction that separates compounds from mixtures. Students who conflate compounds with mixtures (treating both as 'atoms of different types together') cannot understand why chemical reactions produce genuinely new substances in AC9S8U07, and cannot apply conservation of mass in AC9S9U07.

width.minimum: Students define a compound and interpret a formula (e.g. H₂O) to identify atom types and ratios.
width.typical: Students define compounds: two or more different atom types, chemically bonded, fixed ratio, new substance with different properties from constituent elements; write and interpret formulas for H₂O, CO₂, NaCl, C₆H₁₂O₆; explain subscript notation as atom ratio; contrast compound properties with constituent element properties (NaCl is edible; Na is dangerously reactive, Cl₂ is toxic); explain that chemical combination is permanent under normal conditions.
wider: Compare the properties of NaCl to its constituent elements (Na metal and Cl₂ gas) — what does the dramatic property change reveal about the nature of chemical combination?
Use virtual molecular models to build compound structures and compare the information in the formula to the 3D model

modes.reason: The NaCl vs Na + Cl₂ property comparison is the most effective way to make chemical combination concrete. Students need to encounter the dramatic property change before the compound/mixture distinction is introduced — properties are the observable evidence that chemical combination has occurred.

nodes.label: Mixtures — substances physically combined, properties retained
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define mixtures, explain that components retain their properties and can be separated by physical means, and distinguish mixtures from compounds.
criteria: Defines a mixture and gives examples of solutions, suspensions and colloids
Explains that mixture components retain their individual properties
Identifies at least two differences between a mixture and a compound

width.minimum: Students define a mixture and explain two differences from a compound.
width.typical: Students describe solutions, suspensions and colloids; explain that mixture components retain individual properties; explain variable composition (unlike fixed ratio in compounds); explain physical separability (connects to AC9S7U06 separation techniques); represent mixtures using particle diagrams — different atom types present but not bonded; contrast with compound diagram — atoms bonded in fixed arrangement.
wider: Represent the same substance (e.g. salt water) as a particle diagram and as a formula-based representation — explain what each shows and what each conceals
Investigate how indicators of mixture type are used in practical testing contexts — soil pH, water quality, medical diagnostics

modes.reason: Mixture connects directly to AC9S7U06's separation knowledge and extends it with the types classification. The key contrast with compounds — retained properties, variable composition, physical separability — must be explicitly stated. Particle diagram comparison (bonded vs unbonded atoms) makes the compound/mixture distinction visible at the model level.

nodes.label: Representations — comparing symbols, formulas and 2D/3D models
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare representations of elements, compounds and mixtures and explain what information each representation conveys and where each is most useful.
criteria: Identifies what information a symbol, formula and 3D model each convey for a named substance
Explains one advantage and one limitation of each representation type
Selects the most appropriate representation for a given purpose and justifies the choice

width.minimum: Students identify what information is shown by a symbol, a formula and a 3D model for a named substance, and explain one advantage of each.
width.typical: Students compare: symbols (identity, periodic table position — no structural info); molecular formulas (atom types and ratios, compact — no spatial info); structural formulas (bonding connections, 2D arrangement); 3D ball-and-stick/space-filling models (spatial arrangement, bond angles, relative size); particle diagrams for mixtures (relative proportions, unbonded); evaluate which representation is most useful for a given purpose; explain that no single representation captures everything.
wider: Examine multiple representations of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) — symbol, molecular formula, structural formula, 3D model — and identify what each reveals and conceals about the molecule
Compare physical and digital 3D molecular models of the same compound and evaluate each for accuracy, utility and accessibility

modes.reason: This node integrates element/compound/mixture classification (N1–N4) with the representational literacy the descriptor explicitly requires. Students evaluate representations as purpose-specific tools — the 'compare different representations' demand of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Physical and chemical changes
descriptors.description: compare physical and chemical changes and identify indicators of energy change in chemical reactions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that physical changes preserve material composition (AC9S2U03), compare reversible and irreversible changes at an observable level (AC9S6U04), use particle theory for substance properties (AC9S7U05), and classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures (AC9S8U06). AC9S6U04 provides a reversibility heuristic that mostly works but fails for dissolving. The new substance criterion — grounded in compound formation from AC9S8U06 — is new. Exothermic and endothermic as named categories of energy change in reactions are new.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare physical and chemical changes using the new substance criterion, identify observable indicators of chemical change, and explain exothermic and endothermic reactions as categories of energy change — applying all three criteria to classify and analyse unfamiliar changes.

nodes.label: Physical change at the particle level — rearrangement without new substance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain physical change as rearrangement of particles without formation of new substances, and represent this using the particle model.
criteria: Explains physical change as particle rearrangement without formation of new substances
Represents a physical change using a particle diagram showing no new substance
Explains why reversibility is a consequence of physical change, not the definition

width.minimum: Students explain physical change using the particle model — particles rearrange but atom types and bonding remain the same.
width.typical: Students describe physical changes (melting, dissolving, tearing, bending) using particle diagrams — particles change position or arrangement but no new compound is formed; connect to AC9S2U03 (physical change preserves material composition) and AC9S3U04 (state changes); explain that physical changes are typically reversible because no new substance has formed; note that reversibility is a consequence, not the definition.
wider: Represent dissolving at the particle level — show NaCl ions separating and dispersing in water — and explain why this is a physical change despite appearing to 'disappear'
Investigate which physical changes are reversible and which are difficult to reverse in practice (e.g. tearing paper) — explain using particle rearrangement

modes.reason: The particle-level representation of physical change establishes the baseline against which chemical change will be contrasted in N2. Dissolving as a physical change is important to address here — it is the case most likely to be misclassified as chemical change, and the particle diagram makes the 'no new substance' criterion visible.

nodes.label: Chemical change — new substance formation at the particle level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain chemical change as the formation of new substances through bond breaking and forming, and apply the new substance criterion to classify changes.
criteria: States that new substance formation is the criterion defining chemical change
Correctly classifies at least three changes using the new substance criterion
Explains why reversibility alone is not a reliable criterion using a named counterexample
nodes.hinge_reason: The new substance criterion replaces the unreliable reversibility heuristic from AC9S6U04. Students who retain reversibility as the primary test will misclassify dissolving (reversible but not chemical) and some reactions. The new substance criterion must be explicitly established as the correct test before indicators and energy change are introduced.

width.minimum: Students state the new substance criterion and correctly classify three unfamiliar changes as physical or chemical.
width.typical: Students explain that chemical change involves bonds breaking between atoms and new bonds forming — producing compounds with different atom arrangements and different properties; connect to AC9S8U06's compound concept — a new compound is a new substance; explain that chemical changes are typically not easily reversed because new substances have different properties from reactants; apply the new substance criterion to classify: burning (new compounds formed), rusting (iron oxide ≠ iron), cooking (proteins/starches structurally altered).
wider: Investigate an ambiguous case — is dissolving chemical or physical? Predict using the new substance criterion, test by evaporation, and evaluate the result
Analyse before-and-after property data for three unfamiliar changes and classify each using the new substance criterion — explain your reasoning

modes.reason: Explicitly confronting the reversibility heuristic failure — dissolving is reversible but not chemical; some chemical reactions can be reversed — is necessary. Students need the new substance criterion presented as a replacement, not an addition, to their prior classification tool. Particle-level diagrams showing bond-breaking and bond-forming make the criterion visible.

nodes.label: Observable indicators of chemical change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain four observable indicators of chemical change and explain why each suggests a new substance has formed.
criteria: Names four observable indicators of chemical change
Explains why each indicator suggests a new substance has formed
Distinguishes indicators (observable evidence) from the definition (new substance)

width.minimum: Students name four indicators and describe one observation demonstrating each.
width.typical: Students describe: gas production (bubbles, odour — a gaseous compound has formed); precipitate formation (solid appears in solution — an insoluble compound has formed); colour change (new compound has different light absorption); temperature change (energy released or absorbed as bonds break and form); perform or analyse simple reactions to identify indicators; explain that indicators are evidence of the criterion, not the definition — the indicator suggests a new substance may have formed.
wider: Design a reaction investigation that uses multiple indicators to confirm chemical change — which combinations give the strongest evidence?
Investigate how chemical change indicators are used in practical testing contexts — soil pH kits, water quality tests, pregnancy tests — and identify which indicator each exploits

modes.reason: Indicators are evidence of chemical change, not its definition. Students commonly invert this — classifying a change as chemical because they see a colour change. Making the evidence-criterion relationship explicit (indicator suggests new substance may have formed → confirm by checking properties) prevents systematic misclassification.

nodes.label: Exothermic reactions — energy released to surroundings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify exothermic reactions by temperature rise, explain that energy is released as bonds form in the products, and give examples.
criteria: Identifies exothermic reactions by a temperature rise in the surroundings
Explains that exothermic reactions release energy stored in chemical bonds
Gives at least two examples of exothermic reactions

width.minimum: Students identify exothermic reactions by observable temperature rise and give two examples.
width.typical: Students describe exothermic reactions (combustion, neutralisation, respiration, hand warmers); explain that when products form, the energy stored in new bonds is less than was stored in reactant bonds — the difference is released as heat; explain why temperature rises in the surroundings; connect to AC9S8U05's energy classification — chemical potential energy → thermal energy; describe applications: hand warmers, self-heating cans, fire-starting.
wider: Investigate the temperature change in a neutralisation reaction — measure the heat released and compare different acid/base combinations
Examine how exothermic reactions are exploited in hand warmers and self-heating food cans — what chemical system is used and how is the release triggered?

modes.reason: Exothermic and endothermic are most clearly understood in parallel contrast. Treating exothermic first — where the temperature rise is observable and intuitive — provides the reference point for the less intuitive endothermic in N5.

nodes.label: Endothermic reactions — energy absorbed from surroundings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify endothermic reactions by temperature drop, explain that energy is absorbed to break reactant bonds, and give examples.
criteria: Identifies endothermic reactions by a temperature fall in the surroundings
Explains that endothermic reactions absorb energy from surroundings
Gives at least two examples of endothermic reactions and distinguishes them from exothermic

width.minimum: Students identify endothermic reactions by observable temperature fall and give two examples.
width.typical: Students describe endothermic reactions (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition, dissolving ammonium nitrate); explain that the energy required to break reactant bonds exceeds the energy released in product bond formation — the difference is absorbed from surroundings as heat; explain why temperature falls in the surroundings; describe applications: cold packs; contrast with exothermic in terms of energy direction.
wider: Investigate the temperature change when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water — explain the observation using bond energy reasoning
Compare an exothermic and endothermic reaction using the same experimental setup — identify all variables that need controlling to make the comparison fair

modes.reason: Multiple endothermic reaction contexts — dissolving, photosynthesis, thermal decomposition, cold packs — each apply the same energy-absorption concept in a different domain. Breadth here is more productive than depth on a single example.

nodes.label: Comparing physical and chemical changes — integrating all criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the new substance criterion, observable indicators and energy change together to classify and analyse unfamiliar changes.
criteria: Applies the new substance criterion, observable indicators and energy change to classify an unfamiliar change
Explains why multiple converging criteria increase classification confidence
Identifies a case where a single indicator is misleading and explains using the new substance criterion

width.minimum: Students apply all three criteria to classify two unfamiliar changes and justify each classification.
width.typical: Students analyse before-and-after data (appearance, temperature, mass, properties) to classify changes; explain that multiple converging indicators increase confidence; examine cases where a single indicator is misleading — temperature change also occurs in physical processes (state change) without chemical change; connect to AC9S8U06 — chemical change produces a new compound; evaluate the claim that 'if it glows, it must be chemical' against counterexamples.
wider: Analyse a multi-step process (cooking a meal, or a First Nations food preparation technique) — identify all physical and chemical changes involved and classify each using the full criterion set
Investigate how chemical change indicators are used in environmental or medical testing — what does each indicator detect, and how is false-positive risk minimised?

modes.reason: This node integrates particle-level physical change (N1), new substance criterion (N2), indicators (N3) and energy change (N4–N5) into a complete analytical framework. Applying all criteria to novel cases — particularly cases where a single indicator could mislead — is the descriptor's full 'compare physical and chemical changes' demand.

descriptors.title: Peer review validates scientific knowledge
descriptors.description: explain how scientific knowledge is validated and refined, including the role of publication and peer review
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how scientific evidence challenges and changes our understanding of the world, and recognise that science is a human endeavour involving reasoning from evidence (AC9S7H01). They have not yet examined the formal mechanisms by which scientific claims are evaluated and accepted by the scientific community — specifically publication and peer review as institutional processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how scientific knowledge is validated and refined through the publication and peer review process — describing what peer review involves, why it is used, and how it can result in validation, revision or rejection of claims. Students can examine cases where scientific knowledge was initially rejected or revised before being accepted, and explain why consensus builds over time through accumulation of consistent evidence.

nodes.label: From evidence to accepted knowledge: the validation problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why scientific claims require validation beyond the individual scientist — identifying that bias, error and limited evidence are reasons the scientific community needs mechanisms for checking claims.
criteria: Can state at least one reason why a single scientist's findings require external validation.
Can explain that validation processes exist to reduce errors and build reliable knowledge — not just to follow rules.
Does not treat peer review as 'just getting someone else to read it' — understands its epistemically protective function.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand why validation is necessary — who see peer review as bureaucratic rather than epistemically essential — cannot explain what the process achieves or why claims may be initially rejected. The validation problem is the motivation for understanding peer review.

width.minimum: Explain at least one reason why a single scientist's findings cannot automatically be accepted as scientific knowledge (e.g. potential for error, bias, limited sample size) and state that there are community mechanisms to check this.
width.typical: Explain two or three reasons why scientific claims require validation beyond the individual scientist, and describe that the scientific community has developed processes — including peer review — specifically to address these limitations.
wider: Examine a historical case where an unchecked or fraudulent scientific claim caused harm before the validation process caught it — to build appreciation of why validation processes exist.

Connect to AC9S9I06 (assessing validity of methods and conclusions) — scientific peer review applies the same validity assessment that students apply to their own investigations, at a community level.

modes.reason: The validation problem requires reasoning about the limits of individual knowledge production: 'Even if a scientist is honest and careful, their single study may have errors, limited scope, or unrecognised assumptions. Without community checking, how do we know?' Scaffold this argument explicitly before introducing peer review as the solution.

nodes.label: The publication and peer review process
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the publication and peer review process, including how editors evaluate submitted papers, what reviewers assess, and how the process results in validation, revision or rejection.
criteria: Can describe the key steps of peer review — not just name it.
Can explain that peer review can result in revision or rejection, not just acceptance.
Can describe what reviewers are assessing — methodology, evidence, conclusions — not just 'whether it's good'.

width.minimum: Describe the key steps of peer review (submission, editor screening, reviewer assessment, revision or rejection/acceptance) and explain what reviewers are evaluating.
width.typical: Describe the publication process including pre-publication steps and the editorial/reviewer roles, and explain how peer review can result in different outcomes — acceptance, revision or rejection — and that these outcomes reflect the state of evidence, not just the individual scientist.
wider: Investigate the scale of the peer review process — e.g. a journal like Science receives around 12,000 submissions per year — as context for the volume of knowledge claims requiring evaluation and the selectivity of acceptance.
Examine the role of replication in validation — that a single peer-reviewed study is not sufficient for established knowledge, and that consensus builds from multiple independent replications.
Explore how open-access publication and pre-print servers are changing the speed and accessibility of scientific communication — and the validation challenges this creates.

nodes.label: Knowledge refined: rejection and revision cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine cases where scientific knowledge was initially rejected, revised or debated before being accepted, and explain what role evidence played in the eventual outcome.
criteria: Can describe a case where scientific knowledge was refined and explain what evidence drove the change.
Can explain that validation is not a single event — knowledge builds through accumulation of consistent evidence.
Does not describe initial rejection as simply 'scientists being wrong' — explains the epistemic reasons for caution.

width.minimum: Describe one case where a scientific claim was initially rejected and later validated (e.g. Marshall and Warren's discovery that bacteria cause peptic ulcers), explaining what evidence led to eventual acceptance.
width.typical: Examine two cases of knowledge refinement — one where initial rejection was eventually overturned by accumulating evidence, and one where scientific consensus has built over time (e.g. global warming, or consistency of evidence for the particle model of electricity from Thomson, Millikan and Rutherford) — explaining what the cases reveal about how the process works.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional fire management knowledge was initially dismissed by Western scientific institutions and later validated — examining what this case reveals about whose knowledge counts and how validation processes can be culturally biased.
Examine how Marie and Pierre Curie's discovery of new elements was validated — including the role of reproducibility and measurement precision in overcoming initial scepticism.

modes.reason: Students who understand peer review from a single case (commonly the bacteria/ulcers example) may develop a simplified picture of how rejection and validation work. Varying the cases — across time periods, knowledge types, cultural contexts — builds a more accurate understanding of validation as an ongoing, sometimes contested process.

descriptors.title: Science and technology advance together
descriptors.description: investigate how advances in technologies enable advances in science, and how science has contributed to developments in technologies and engineering
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how scientific understanding has developed through people's questions, observations and experiments (AC9S7H03, AC9S7H04). They have not yet examined the two-way relationship between science and technology specifically — where technology enables scientific discovery and scientific understanding enables technological development — as a systematic relationship rather than individual historical examples.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the two-directional relationship between science and technology — describing cases where technological advances enabled new scientific knowledge (imaging technologies, particle accelerators, digital monitoring tools) and cases where scientific understanding enabled technological development (radioactivity → medical imaging; wave-particle model → EM communications). Students can examine how this relationship has operated in Australian and global contexts.

nodes.label: Technology enabling science
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe cases where advances in technology enabled advances in scientific understanding — explaining what the technology made possible that was not possible before.
criteria: Can describe at least one example where technology enabled a scientific advance.
Can explain what the technology specifically made possible — not just that 'it helped'.
Does not treat the relationship as simply 'scientists use tools' — understands that the tool opened a previously inaccessible domain.

width.minimum: Describe one example where a technology enabled a scientific advance (e.g. development of imaging technologies enabling understanding of body system interactions; electron microscope enabling understanding of cell ultrastructure) and explain what the technology specifically made possible.
width.typical: Describe two or three cases of technology enabling science across different fields, explaining in each case what question or observation became possible with the new technology — connecting the tool to the knowledge it produced.
wider: Examine how modern technology has enabled exploration of energy conversion processes at scales previously inaccessible — from black holes to atoms to sub-atomic particles — as cases where the limits of scientific knowledge coincide with the limits of available technology.

Investigate how technological advances in monitoring greenhouse gas emissions and environmental factors have contributed to the reinstatement of traditional fire management practices — connecting remote sensing technology to both scientific knowledge and First Nations knowledge validation.

nodes.label: Science enabling technology
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe cases where scientific understanding enabled the development of new technologies or engineering solutions — explaining how the science provided the theoretical foundation for the technology.
criteria: Can describe at least one example where scientific understanding enabled a technological development.
Can explain the specific connection — what understanding made the technology possible.
Does not treat science and technology as sequential ('science first, then technology') — can recognise cases of mutual enablement.

width.minimum: Describe one example where scientific understanding directly enabled a technological application (e.g. understanding of radioactivity → radioisotope medical imaging; understanding of EM radiation properties → radar/mobile communications) and explain the specific connection.
width.typical: Describe two or three cases of science enabling technology across different content areas (biological, physical, chemical sciences), explaining in each case how understanding a mechanism or property made a specific technology possible.
wider: Investigate Australian technological contributions — cochlear implant (Graeme Clark), spray-on skin (Fiona Woods), wi-fi (O'Sullivan/CSIRO) — examining both the scientific understanding that underpinned each and how they generated new engineering knowledge.

Examine how understanding of radioactivity and radioisotopes has led to new applications and technologies — including medical diagnosis (PET scans, radioiodine therapy), industrial testing (checking welds in aircraft), and radiocarbon dating.

modes.reason: Vary the technology examples across biology, physics and materials science — Australian and international — to build genuine breadth in understanding the science-enables-technology direction. Single-domain examples (e.g. only medical technology) produce an incomplete picture.

nodes.label: The two-way relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the two-directional relationship between science and technology — recognising that the relationship is iterative, not sequential, and can examine multiple cases where each has enabled the other in a cycle of development.
criteria: Can explain what 'two-directional' means in the science-technology relationship — not just state it.
Can provide an example where both directions are visible — technology enabling science AND science enabling technology in the same domain.
Does not treat the relationship as sequential — understands it as iterative and ongoing.

width.minimum: Describe one domain where technology and science have advanced each other iteratively (e.g. medical imaging: understanding of EM radiation → X-ray technology → MRI understanding → MRI technology → new anatomical knowledge) and explain why the relationship is described as two-directional.
width.typical: Investigate two or three domains where science and technology have advanced each other across multiple iterations, and explain how scientists and engineers make machines or processes more efficient using scientific understanding as the lever.
wider: Examine how scientists and engineers make machines more energy efficient — connecting AC9S9U05 (conservation of energy, Sankey diagrams) to the applied science of engineering design.

Investigate how understanding of the nature of matter and energy has changed over time — from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics — and how each theoretical advance enabled new technologies (transistors, lasers, MRI) that in turn revealed new science.

modes.reason: The two-way relationship is the integrative claim of this descriptor. Students who have described individual cases of technology-enabling-science (Node 1) and science-enabling-technology (Node 2) need to coordinate these into a general claim: the relationship is reciprocal and iterative. The integration is conceptual — seeing the pattern across cases, not just collecting examples.

descriptors.title: Factors in science adoption
descriptors.description: analyse the key factors that contribute to science knowledge and practices being adopted more broadly by society
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how scientific knowledge and its applications affect people's lives (AC9S7H03) and examine how scientific communication shapes policy (AC9S7H04). They have not yet systematically analysed the factors that determine whether scientific knowledge or practices are widely adopted — moving from describing the relationship between science and society to analysing the conditions for adoption.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse key factors that contribute to scientific knowledge and practices being adopted more broadly by society — including evidence quality, accessibility, economic feasibility, government support, community trust, media communication and cultural alignment. Students can examine cases of adoption and non-adoption to identify which factors were decisive, including examples involving First Nations Australians' knowledge practices.

nodes.label: Adoption factors: the concept
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that scientific knowledge being valid or published is not sufficient for broad societal adoption, and identify the types of factors that affect whether adoption occurs.
