criteria: Can explain why scientific validity alone is insufficient for societal adoption.
Can identify at least two distinct categories of adoption factors.
Does not treat 'getting the word out' as the only obstacle — recognises structural, economic and cultural factors.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat scientific validity as the only adoption factor cannot meaningfully analyse the cases at Node 2 — where economically or culturally feasible practices get adopted despite mixed evidence, or where well-evidenced practices face resistance due to other factors. The multi-factor framing is prerequisite for the analysis.

width.minimum: Explain that valid scientific knowledge does not automatically get adopted by society, and identify at least two categories of factors that influence adoption (e.g. economic cost, accessibility, cultural values, government support).
width.typical: Identify multiple categories of adoption factors across scientific, economic, social and political dimensions, and explain that adoption typically requires favourable conditions across several factors simultaneously — not just evidence quality alone.
wider: Examine why citizen science projects attract public participation — connecting community engagement to the accessibility and trust factors in adoption.
Consider the adoption gap: why does significant time often pass between scientific validation and widespread adoption, and what factors close or widen this gap?

modes.reason: The claim that 'valid science is not enough' runs counter to a naive view of how knowledge works. Scaffold with a concrete counter-example first: 'We have known for decades that smoking causes cancer — why did it take so long for smoking rates to fall?' The reasoning from this case generates the factor categories students need.

nodes.label: Analysing adoption cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse specific cases of scientific knowledge or practice adoption, identifying the key factors that contributed to or inhibited adoption in each case.
criteria: Can identify at least two adoption factors in a named case and explain how each operated.
Can explain whether adoption was rapid or slow and connect this to the factor profile.
Does not simply describe what was adopted — analyses the conditions that made adoption possible.

width.minimum: Analyse one case of adoption (e.g. solar panels, vaccination, recycling, land restoration through Landcare) and identify at least two factors that contributed to adoption — explaining how each factor operated in that case.
width.typical: Analyse two adoption cases — selecting from different domains (health, environment, technology, Indigenous practices) — and for each, identify and explain the key factors, including any that inhibited adoption before it occurred.
wider: Examine how government initiatives (e.g. Landcare, renewable energy subsidies) function as adoption-enabling mechanisms — connecting policy to the economic and accessibility factors in the framework.

Investigate the adoption trajectory of solar panels and battery storage — examining how manufacturing cost reduction, government incentives and community energy concerns combined to drive adoption, and analysing why earlier periods saw low adoption despite the technology existing.

Analyse how First Nations Australians' fire management practices are being adopted in contemporary fire management — examining which factors (evidence quality, economic benefit, government recognition, cultural respect) have been operative and which have posed barriers.

modes.reason: Adoption analysis can calcify around a single case type (typically environmental technology). Varying the cases across health practices, environmental management, technology adoption, and Indigenous knowledge practices ensures students encounter the full range of factor combinations and do not over-generalise from one domain.

descriptors.title: Society shapes scientific research
descriptors.description: examine how the values and needs of society influence the focus of scientific research
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine how scientific communication shapes policy and societal responses (AC9S7H04), and have analysed adoption factors (AC9S9H03). They have not yet examined the reverse direction — how societal values and needs shape what research is funded and pursued in the first place.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how the values and needs of society influence which scientific research questions are funded, pursued and developed — identifying factors such as government priorities, economic incentives, health needs, environmental concerns, and cultural values as shapers of research focus. Students can examine cases where societal needs have directly driven scientific and technological advances, including examples where government, industry and community priorities have shaped research directions.

nodes.label: Who decides what gets researched?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that scientific research requires funding and that decisions about what research is funded reflect societal values and priorities — introducing the concept that research focus is not determined by science alone.
criteria: Can explain that research requires funding and that funding decisions reflect priorities.
Can identify at least one way societal values influence research direction.
Does not treat research focus as determined by scientific curiosity alone — understands external shaping.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that research direction is shaped by funding decisions will treat the cases at Node 2 as coincidences rather than systemic patterns. The funding-priority-values chain is the reasoning scaffold needed for meaningful examination of why particular research exists.

width.minimum: Explain that scientific research requires funding, that funding bodies (governments, industries, foundations) make decisions about which research to support, and that these decisions reflect priorities beyond scientific merit alone.
width.typical: Describe how governments, industries and research institutions determine research funding priorities, and identify examples of how these priorities reflect current societal values and needs (e.g. health concerns driving biomedical research funding; climate concern driving renewable energy research).
wider: Explore how governments determine which scientific research projects are funded — examining specific funding bodies (ARC, NHMRC in Australia) and the criteria they use.

Consider why some societally important questions receive less funding than their importance might warrant — examining how commercial viability, political priorities or cultural biases can shape funding allocation.

modes.reason: The claim that societal values shape research is not obvious — students typically think scientists choose what to investigate based on curiosity alone. Scaffold the argument: 'A scientist needs equipment, time and a lab. These require money. Money comes from funding bodies with priorities. Therefore the research that gets done reflects those priorities.' Making the causal chain explicit is the learning.

nodes.label: Examining cases of society-driven research
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine specific cases where the values and needs of society have influenced the focus of scientific research — identifying the societal driver and the resulting research direction.
criteria: Can identify the societal need or value that drove a named research direction.
Can explain the connection — not just list the case but trace the pathway from value/need to research priority.
Does not treat all research as societally driven in the same way — can distinguish government mandate, market incentive, community need and cultural value as distinct mechanisms.

width.minimum: Examine one case where a societal need or value drove a specific research direction (e.g. need to minimise greenhouse gas production leading to renewable energy research; need for food security leading to agricultural biotechnology research) and explain the connection between the societal need and the research focus.
width.typical: Examine two or three cases of society-driven research from different domains — health, environment, technology — identifying the societal driver in each and explaining how it shaped what research was done and what wasn't.
wider: Examine how Australia has developed AI systems for IVF viability prediction — connecting community health needs and values (fertility, family formation) to a specific research direction that has produced technological outcomes.

Investigate how First Nations Peoples of the Torres Strait are at the forefront of developing measures to prevent transfer of infectious diseases and pests — examining how community health sovereignty shapes the focus of this scientific work.

Examine how the need to minimise greenhouse gas production has led to scientific advances in carbon capture, renewable energy, and green chemistry — tracing the societal value to multiple research streams.
Investigate why many manufacturers are adopting green chemistry processes — examining the economic, regulatory and environmental values driving this research and development direction.

modes.reason: Single-case analysis can produce an oversimplified model of the society-research relationship. Varying cases across health, environment and technology shows that the relationship operates through different mechanisms — direct government mandate, market incentive, community advocacy, regulatory pressure — preventing any single mechanism from being treated as universal.

descriptors.title: Investigable questions, predictions and hypotheses
descriptors.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to test relationships and develop explanatory models
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop questions, make predictions and formulate methods to investigate (AC9S7I01). They have not yet developed formal hypotheses specifying a testable relationship (if-then-because structure) or developed questions targeted at testing a relationship or building an explanatory model rather than simply exploring a phenomenon.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop investigable questions that target a specific relationship between variables, write reasoned predictions, and formulate hypotheses that can be supported or refuted through evidence — in contexts requiring explanation of body systems, energy transfer or chemical reactions. Students can develop questions intended to explore an explanatory model and explain what would constitute supporting or refuting evidence.

nodes.label: What makes a question investigable?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions, and explain the criteria that make a scientific question investigable — including that it must be answerable through observable, measurable evidence.
criteria: Can identify whether a question is investigable and explain why or why not.
Can improve a vague question by making it specific about variables.
Does not treat 'interesting' as a criterion for investigability — uses testability.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what makes a question investigable will produce unfocused investigation designs at the next capability stage (AC9S9I02). A question that is too vague, not measurable, or not about a testable relationship cannot lead to a valid investigation method — the question quality determines the investigation quality.

width.minimum: Identify whether two contrasting questions are investigable or not, and explain what makes the investigable one testable (names variables, answerable by measurement or observation).
width.typical: Describe the criteria for an investigable question (observable/measurable variables, specific enough to test, not answered by opinion alone) and apply these criteria to evaluate and improve sample questions.
wider: Distinguish investigable questions from those that are philosophical, ethical or definitional — building precision about the scope of empirical investigation.
Examine how investigable questions arise from existing models — connecting the 'why does this happen?' question to an existing theoretical explanation that generates testable predictions.

modes.reason: The criteria for investigability are not self-evident. Students need the explicit reasoning: 'To be investigable, a question must name (or imply) variables that can be measured or observed. It must be answerable by data, not opinion. And it must be specific enough that one investigation could address it.' Model this evaluation with contrasting examples.

nodes.label: Reasoned predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a reasoned prediction that states an expected outcome and provides a reason based on scientific knowledge — not just a guess.
criteria: Can write a prediction that includes both an expected outcome and a scientific reason.
Can distinguish a reasoned prediction from a guess — the reason is grounded in science, not preference.
Does not omit the reason — treats the because-clause as mandatory.

width.minimum: Write a prediction for one scenario that includes an expected outcome and a reason grounded in scientific knowledge (e.g. 'I predict that increasing light intensity will increase the rate of photosynthesis because more light energy is available for the process').
width.typical: Write reasoned predictions for two or three investigable questions across different content domains, ensuring each prediction includes an expected outcome AND a scientific reason — distinguishing these from guesses or intuitions.
wider: Examine predictions that conflict with intuition — cases where scientific knowledge predicts an unexpected outcome — to build appreciation that scientific prediction differs from common sense.

Develop predictions for questions about relationships between human body systems (e.g. 'How does exercise intensity affect heart rate and breathing rate?') — connecting prediction-writing to the Y9 content.

modes.reason: Students routinely drop the reasoning component from predictions, treating them as guesses rather than evidence-based claims. Consistent practice with the expected-outcome + reason format — and correction when the reason is absent or not scientific — builds the habit before hypothesis writing.

nodes.label: Hypotheses: testable, refutable, relationship-specifying
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a formal hypothesis that specifies the predicted relationship between variables in a form that can be supported or refuted through evidence, and explain why scientific hypotheses must be refutable.
criteria: Can write a hypothesis that specifies the relationship between named variables.
Can identify what result would refute their hypothesis.
Does not write vague or circular hypotheses — the prediction must be specific enough to test.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who write unfalsifiable hypotheses (e.g. 'plants will grow differently') cannot use investigation results to either support or refute their hypothesis — the conclusion stage of the investigation collapses. Refutability is the hinge: a hypothesis that cannot be tested cannot be advanced or rejected, and the entire investigation loses its logical structure.

width.minimum: Write a hypothesis for one investigation using an if-then-because structure (or equivalent), specifying the independent variable, predicted effect on dependent variable, and a reason. Explain why the hypothesis must be refutable — what result would refute it.
width.typical: Write hypotheses for two or three investigations and evaluate each for refutability — identifying what evidence would support it and what evidence would refute it. Explain why a hypothesis that cannot be refuted is not scientifically useful.
wider: Examine the concept of a null hypothesis — the prediction that there is no effect — and explain how it is used alongside the experimental hypothesis in formal scientific investigations.

Develop hypotheses to explore an explanatory model (e.g. 'If heat energy transfers from higher to lower temperature until equilibrium is reached, then placing objects of different temperatures in contact will result in...') — connecting hypothesis writing to model testing.

modes.reason: The concept of refutability is philosophically non-trivial. Scaffold the argument: 'If no possible result could prove your hypothesis wrong, then your hypothesis doesn't actually predict anything testable — it's not a scientific hypothesis.' Concrete counter-examples (e.g. 'plants respond to their environment' — true but untestable) make this clearer than abstract explanation.

descriptors.title: Plan valid, reproducible investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct valid, reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying and controlling for possible sources of error and, as appropriate, developing and following risk assessments, considering ethical issues, and addressing key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct investigations to test predictions, identifying variables and describing methods (AC9S7I02). They have not yet explicitly focused on validity and reproducibility as criteria for method quality, or systematically identified and controlled sources of error as part of planning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct investigations that are valid (method measures what it claims to measure, variables controlled) and reproducible (method can be repeated by others to get consistent results) — systematically identifying sources of error and explaining how they are controlled. Students can develop and follow risk assessments, consider ethical issues in investigation design, and recognise responsibilities regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place.

nodes.label: Validity and reproducibility as method criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what validity and reproducibility mean as criteria for a scientific investigation method, and identify whether a described method satisfies each criterion.
criteria: Can define validity and reproducibility with precision — not just 'it works' and 'you can do it again'.
Can identify a specific feature of a method that threatens validity or reproducibility.
Does not conflate the two criteria — can explain how a method could be reproducible but not valid.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat validity and reproducibility as generic 'good science' terms without specific meaning cannot systematically identify sources of error (Node 2) or evaluate their own method quality. These criteria are the framework for all subsequent investigation planning — without them, error identification becomes arbitrary.

width.minimum: Define validity (the method measures what it claims to measure) and reproducibility (the method can be repeated by others to obtain consistent results), and apply one criterion to evaluate a described method.
width.typical: Define both validity and reproducibility, explain why each matters for scientific investigation, and evaluate a described method against both criteria — identifying specific features of the method that support or undermine each.
wider: Determine the reproducibility of a specific field investigation design — e.g. a survey of traffic passing a school — examining what features of the method determine whether another person running it would get the same result.

Distinguish internal validity (are the results due to the independent variable, not something else?) from external validity (can the results be generalised?) as two dimensions of validity relevant at Year 9.

modes.reason: Validity and reproducibility need to be operationalised as questions students ask of a method: 'Is the measurement capturing what we want to measure, or is it capturing something else?' and 'If someone else ran this, what might they do differently that would produce a different result?' These question structures need explicit modelling.

nodes.label: Identifying and controlling sources of error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify possible sources of error in an investigation method and explain how controlling or accounting for each error source increases validity and reproducibility.
criteria: Can identify at least two sources of error with specific explanations — not generic 'human error'.
Can describe a specific control strategy for each identified error source.
Can explain how uncontrolled error affects the validity of conclusions.

width.minimum: Identify at least two sources of error in a described or planned investigation and explain how each could be controlled or reduced.
width.typical: Systematically identify multiple sources of error across measurement, procedure and environmental factors, and describe specific control strategies for each — distinguishing between errors that can be eliminated and those that must be minimised and acknowledged.
wider: Examine the difference between random error (varies unpredictably) and systematic error (consistently biased in one direction), and explain how each affects data quality differently — connecting to AC9S9I06 (assessing validity of methods).

Identify possible sources of error in a method and examine whether further testing or extra variable control is needed — applying the principle that error identification should drive method refinement, not just documentation.

nodes.label: Risk assessment, ethics and Country/Place considerations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify potential hazards in an investigation, develop a risk assessment, consider ethical issues relevant to the investigation context, and describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place.
criteria: Can identify at least one investigation hazard and describe a control measure.
Can identify at least one ethical consideration relevant to a described investigation.
Can describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites in field investigation contexts.

width.minimum: Identify at least one hazard in a described investigation, describe how it would be addressed in a risk assessment, and identify one ethical consideration relevant to a described investigation type.
width.typical: Develop a risk assessment for a planned investigation (identifying hazard, likelihood, severity, and control measure), consider ethical issues relevant to the investigation (animal use, participant welfare, cultural sensitivity), and explain responsibilities regarding heritage sites when conducting field investigations.
wider: Examine ethical guidelines for animal use in scientific investigations — understanding the framework that governs care and use of animals for scientific purposes before planning any investigation involving animals.

Examine First Nations Australians' heritage laws and the public responsibility to report new sites or artefacts — describing the consequences for disturbing heritage sites on, above or below the land surface, or in waters, when planning field investigations.

descriptors.title: Select equipment and record precise data
descriptors.description: select and use equipment to generate and record data with precision to obtain useful sample sizes and replicable data, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use equipment to generate and record data (AC9S7I03). They have not yet focused on precision as a criterion for equipment selection, significant figures and scientific notation as recording conventions, or sample size justification as a design decision.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select equipment based on the precision required for the investigation, record data to the correct degree of precision using appropriate significant figures and units, consider instrument accuracy and replicability when choosing equipment, and justify sample size decisions — using digital tools where appropriate to improve collection efficiency or enable larger samples.

nodes.label: Precision in measurement and recording
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what precision means in measurement, select equipment based on required precision, and record data values to the correct number of significant figures with appropriate units.
criteria: Can select between two instruments based on required precision and explain the choice.
Can record data to the correct number of significant figures for the instrument used.
Does not record more significant figures than the instrument can provide.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who record data to arbitrary significant figures, or who cannot select equipment appropriate to the required precision, will produce data that cannot support valid conclusions at AC9S9I06. Precision errors cascade into the analysis and evaluation stages — a data set recorded to insufficient precision cannot be improved retrospectively.

width.minimum: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision in measurement, identify which of two instruments provides greater precision for a given measurement task (e.g. measuring cylinder vs. pipette), and record one data value to the correct number of significant figures.
width.typical: Select appropriate equipment based on required measurement precision across multiple scenarios, record all data values to the correct significant figures with correct units, and explain how instrument precision affects the degree of precision achievable in data recording.
wider: Examine the degree of accuracy that different instruments provide and what this means for the conclusions that can be drawn — connecting instrument precision to the limits of claim validity.
Use data loggers, examining scale settings and output representation choices — exploring how digital equipment introduces precision considerations beyond those of manual instruments.

modes.reason: Significant figure recording and unit consistency are procedural conventions requiring practice for reliable execution. Errors in these conventions are systematic and affect every data value. Students need enough practice to execute these reliably without conscious attention before they can focus on the broader investigation design.

nodes.label: Sample size and replicability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why sample size matters for the quality of scientific data and justify a sample size choice for a described investigation context — considering what constitutes a useful sample size.
criteria: Can explain why sample size affects reliability of results.
Can identify the relevant factors for determining appropriate sample size in a described investigation.
Does not default to 'more is always better' without considering practical constraints and the specific investigation context.

width.minimum: Explain why larger sample sizes produce more reliable results (reduces the effect of random variation) and describe one factor that determines what sample size is appropriate for a described investigation.
width.typical: Explain how sample size affects reliability, identify factors that influence what constitutes a useful sample size (variability in the population, required confidence, practical constraints), and justify a sample size decision for a planned investigation.
wider: Consider how the use of digital tools enables more-efficient data collection for larger sample sizes — connecting digital tool selection to sample size feasibility.

Examine how sample size decisions in real investigations are constrained by practical factors (time, cost, participant availability) and discuss how scientists balance statistical rigour with practical limitations.

descriptors.title: Select and construct appropriate representations
descriptors.description: select and construct appropriate representations, including tables, graphs, descriptive statistics, models and mathematical relationships, to organise and process data and information
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and construct tables, graphs and models to represent data (AC9S7I04). They have not yet selected among descriptive statistics as appropriate for a data type, used mathematical relationships to process data, or applied representations such as Sankey diagrams or Sankey-like proportional models.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and construct appropriate representations for organising and processing data — including tables, graphs, descriptive statistics (mean, median, range), models and mathematical relationships — and can explain the rationale for choosing one representation over another for a given data type or investigation question.

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select the most appropriate representation for a given data type or investigation question and explain the rationale for their choice.
criteria: Can select an appropriate representation and explain the rationale — not just produce the representation.
Can identify when an alternative representation would be less appropriate and explain why.
Does not default to a single graph type for all data.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who default to a single representation type (e.g. always bar graph) regardless of data type cannot process data effectively and will produce representations that obscure rather than reveal patterns. The ability to select an appropriate representation is the prerequisite for the pattern analysis at AC9S9I05.

width.minimum: Select an appropriate graph or table type for one described data set and explain why it is more appropriate than at least one alternative (e.g. why a line graph is more appropriate than a bar graph for continuous data showing a trend).
width.typical: Select appropriate representations across multiple data scenarios — including when to use tables (raw data), line graphs (trends over continuous variables), bar graphs (category comparisons), scatter plots (relationships between variables) — and explain the selection rationale for each.
wider: Examine when a mathematical relationship (formula) is more informative than a graph alone — e.g. calculating carbon storage using a formula rather than just graphing biomass data.

Compare the information provided by molecular models and balanced symbolic equations when examining conservation of mass — examining how different representations of the same data reveal different aspects (AC9S9U07 connection).

modes.reason: Representation selection requires explicit reasoning: 'What type of data is this? What question am I answering? What does this representation make visible or hide?' Students need this decision framework modelled before they can apply it independently.

nodes.label: Descriptive statistics: selecting the appropriate measure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the most appropriate descriptive statistic (mean, median or range) for a given data set and explain why — recognising that mean and median can differ and that each is appropriate in different contexts.
criteria: Can calculate mean, median and range for a small data set.
Can identify which measure is most appropriate for a described data type and explain why.
Does not default to mean for all data without considering whether it is appropriate.

width.minimum: Identify which of mean, median or range is most appropriate to summarise a described data set and give one reason for the choice (e.g. median is appropriate when the data set contains outliers that would skew the mean).
width.typical: Select the most appropriate descriptive statistics for two or three different data scenarios, explaining the rationale for each — including cases where mean and median differ significantly (skewed data) and where range is more informative than a central measure.
wider: Apply descriptive statistics to identify which sample properties are most appropriate for making generalisations from a given data set — connecting statistical choice to the validity of the scientific claim.
Examine how summarising data with only the mean can hide important features (e.g. a bimodal distribution) — building appreciation that statistical choice affects what the data says.

modes.reason: Students often apply mean by default without considering appropriateness. Practice across varied data types — including skewed and normally distributed — builds the discrimination needed for appropriate selection.

nodes.label: Constructing and using mathematical relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply mathematical relationships (formulae, ratios, proportional reasoning) to process data, and construct representations that accurately reflect quantitative relationships.
criteria: Can apply a given formula correctly to process data.
Can construct a representation where numerical values determine proportional layout (e.g. Sankey diagram).
Can explain what the processed representation reveals that raw data does not.

width.minimum: Apply one given formula or ratio to process a data set (e.g. applying a carbon storage formula to biomass measurements, or applying a ratio to construct a proportional Sankey diagram) and explain what the processed result represents.
width.typical: Apply mathematical relationships to process data across two or three investigation contexts, construct representations where numerical proportionality is required (e.g. Sankey diagrams with scaled arrows), and explain how mathematical processing transforms raw data into meaningful scientific information.
wider: Use spreadsheet software to present data in tabular and graphical forms — examining how digital tools manage the construction of accurate proportional representations that would be tedious by hand.
Apply ratios to accurately represent usable and waste energy in Sankey diagrams — connecting mathematical relationship application to the AC9S9U05 content.

descriptors.title: Analyse data for patterns and anomalies
descriptors.description: analyse and connect a variety of data and information to identify and explain patterns, trends, relationships and anomalies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify patterns and anomalies in data and explain observations using scientific knowledge (AC9S7I05). They have not yet connected data across multiple sources to support an explanation, or used proportional reasoning and extrapolation as analytical tools at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse data from their own investigations and secondary sources to identify and explain patterns, trends, proportional relationships and anomalies — connecting multiple data sources where relevant and using scientific knowledge to account for observed patterns. Students can discuss the validity of extrapolations from their data and highlight inconsistencies across data sources.

nodes.label: Identifying patterns, trends and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify patterns (repeating features), trends (directional change over a variable) and relationships (one variable changing in response to another) in data sets, using appropriate descriptive language.
criteria: Can describe a pattern or trend naming both variables and the direction of change.
Can distinguish between a trend (directional change), a pattern (repeating feature) and a relationship (covariance).
Does not use vague language like 'it goes up' — uses the variable names.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who describe patterns in vague terms ('it goes up') rather than precise relational language cannot explain them scientifically or identify anomalies against them (Node 2). The precision of pattern description determines whether the subsequent analysis is substantive.

width.minimum: Identify one pattern or trend in a described data set and describe it in specific terms — stating the direction, the variables involved, and the nature of the change (e.g. 'as X increases, Y increases proportionally').
width.typical: Identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships across two or three different data representations — using precise language to describe the nature of the relationship (proportional, inverse, non-linear) and the conditions under which it holds.
wider: Analyse data from atmospheric monitoring and ice cores to identify patterns and trends in atmospheric CO₂ — examining long-term trend vs. seasonal variation as different pattern types in the same data set.

Analyse data on heat transfer through insulating material layers to identify a proportional relationship (e.g. doubled thickness → halved heat transfer) — connecting pattern analysis to quantitative reasoning.

modes.reason: Precise pattern description is a language skill requiring practice. Students consistently drop the variable names, direction, and nature of the relationship — reverting to 'the line goes up'. Practice with feedback on language precision — specifically requiring the student to name both variables and the direction of change — builds the habit.

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining anomalies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify anomalies in data — data points that do not fit the identified pattern — and propose explanations for them in terms of measurement error, procedural variation or genuine outliers.
criteria: Can identify an anomalous data point as one that does not fit the identified pattern.
Can propose a plausible explanation for an anomaly that distinguishes between error and genuine variation.
Does not treat all anomalies the same — can evaluate whether an anomaly should be excluded or investigated.

width.minimum: Identify an anomalous data point in a provided data set and give one plausible explanation for why it differs from the pattern (measurement error, equipment malfunction, genuine variation).
width.typical: Identify anomalies and evaluate at least two possible explanations — distinguishing between errors that should be excluded and genuine outliers that may warrant further investigation — using evidence to support the preferred explanation.
wider: Compare published data with experimental data for the same measurement (e.g. sound insulation levels) and identify patterns in the differences — examining whether differences are systematic (suggesting a procedural issue) or random.

Examine tables, graphs and simulations of radioactive decay to predict changes in mass over time — using the pattern to identify which data points are anomalous and evaluating whether they reflect real decay variation or simulation error.

nodes.label: Connecting and comparing data sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect and compare data from multiple sources to identify consistencies, inconsistencies and what they mean for scientific claims — including discussing the validity of extrapolation from data.
criteria: Can identify consistency and inconsistency across two data sources on the same topic.
Can explain what an inconsistency implies for confidence in a conclusion.
Can discuss the validity of an extrapolation — identifying the assumption it requires.

width.minimum: Compare data from two sources on the same topic, identify one point of consistency and one inconsistency, and explain what the inconsistency means for the confidence of the conclusion.
width.typical: Connect data from multiple sources — primary data from an investigation and secondary published data — to evaluate whether findings are consistent, identifying inconsistencies and discussing their implications for the validity of conclusions. Discuss the validity of extrapolating beyond the data collected.
wider: Analyse representations of data from atmospheric monitoring and ice cores to highlight inconsistencies — examining how scientists deal with data from different sources that don't perfectly align.

Examine the validity of extrapolating from experimental data (e.g. extrapolating a heating curve beyond the measured range) — considering what assumptions are required and when extrapolation is or isn't justified.

modes.reason: Multi-source data connection requires integrating pattern identification (Node 1), anomaly analysis (Node 2) and validity reasoning (AC9S9I06) into a coherent analytical judgment: 'These sources agree on X; they disagree on Y; the disagreement suggests Z about the reliability of one or both.' This integration is the descriptor's analytical demand.

descriptors.title: Assess validity and evaluate conclusions
descriptors.description: assess the validity and reproducibility of methods and evaluate the validity of conclusions and claims, including by identifying assumptions, conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse methods and claims (AC9S7I06). They have not yet explicitly identified assumptions embedded in methods or conclusions, or systematically addressed conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty as dimensions of evaluation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students assess the validity and reproducibility of investigation methods by identifying specific features that support or undermine each, and evaluate the validity of conclusions and claims by identifying assumptions, conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty — including how uncertainty and conflicting evidence may support viable alternative conclusions.

nodes.label: Validity of secondary source information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what makes secondary source information valid and evaluate a secondary source against validity criteria — distinguishing credible from less credible sources.
criteria: Can apply at least two validity criteria to evaluate a named secondary source.
Can identify specific features of the source that support or undermine its credibility.
Does not treat all published sources as equally valid.

width.minimum: Identify at least two criteria for evaluating secondary source validity (e.g. peer review, author expertise, date of publication, data transparency) and apply them to evaluate one described source.
width.typical: Apply multiple validity criteria to evaluate two or three secondary sources, explaining which features of each source support or undermine credibility — and recognising that even high-quality sources can contain claims that require further scrutiny.
wider: Examine how general practitioners manage conflicting evidence to diagnose illness — using a medical decision-making context to see validity evaluation as a practical professional skill, not just an academic exercise.

Evaluate science reporting in media against the original research it claims to represent — examining where simplification, exaggeration or omission occur and what this means for the public's understanding of scientific claims.

nodes.label: Identifying assumptions in methods and conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify assumptions embedded in investigation methods and conclusions, and evaluate the impact of these assumptions on the validity of conclusions.
criteria: Can identify at least one assumption in a described method or conclusion.
Can explain the impact of that assumption being false on conclusion validity.
Does not treat methods as assumption-free — recognises that all methods contain assumptions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify assumptions cannot evaluate conclusion validity at Node 3 — they will accept or reject conclusions based on whether they 'seem right' rather than on what the evidence and method actually support. Assumption identification is the analytical foundation for conclusion evaluation.

width.minimum: Identify one assumption in a described investigation method or conclusion (e.g. 'this assumes the sample is representative of the population') and explain what would happen to the conclusion if the assumption were false.
width.typical: Identify multiple assumptions in methods and conclusions across two investigation examples, and for each, determine whether the assumption is reasonable and what impact an incorrect assumption would have on the conclusion validity.
wider: Analyse methods and conclusions to identify premises that are taken for granted, and evaluate the reasonableness of those assumptions — distinguishing between assumptions that are routinely safe (standard lab conditions) and those that require explicit justification.
Examine gaps or weaknesses in conclusions and relate these specifically to the validity and reproducibility of the method — building the link between method quality and conclusion quality.

modes.reason: Assumptions are invisible by definition — they are what is taken for granted. Students need the explicit question: 'What would have to be true for this method to work / for this conclusion to follow?' Modelling this question across examples helps students see assumptions as identifiable rather than irretrievably hidden.

nodes.label: Conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify conflicting evidence within or across investigations and explain how areas of uncertainty may support viable alternative conclusions.
criteria: Can identify an area of uncertainty or conflicting evidence in a described investigation.
Can explain how that uncertainty or evidence could support an alternative conclusion.
Does not treat all uncertainty as equally undermining — can evaluate the significance of identified uncertainty.

width.minimum: Identify one area of uncertainty or one piece of conflicting evidence in a described investigation context and explain how it could lead to an alternative conclusion.
width.typical: Identify conflicting evidence and areas of uncertainty across an investigation and evaluate whether they are sufficient to support a viable alternative conclusion — distinguishing between uncertainty that undermines the main conclusion and uncertainty that is present but does not change the conclusion significantly.
wider: Examine cases where conflicting evidence led to prolonged scientific debate before resolution — connecting evaluation skills to the human endeavour of science (AC9S9H01, H02).
Examine whether areas of uncertainty in an investigation could lead to a viable alternative conclusion — practising the explicit construction of an alternative conclusion from the same evidence set.

modes.reason: Conclusion evaluation integrates source validity (Node 1), assumption identification (Node 2) and evidence assessment into a structured judgment: 'The conclusion is/is not valid because the method [addresses/does not address] these assumptions, and there is [no/some/significant] conflicting evidence that could support an alternative conclusion.' This argument structure is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Construct evidence-based arguments ethically
descriptors.description: construct arguments based on analysis of a variety of evidence to support conclusions or evaluate claims, and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with accessing, using or citing secondary data or information
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct evidence-based arguments (AC9S7I07). They have not yet applied ethical considerations and cultural protocols specifically to secondary data use, or constructed arguments based on analysis of multiple sources — including evaluation of source credibility as part of the argument.
descriptors.endpoint: Students construct arguments based on analysis of a variety of evidence — evaluating the credibility and relevance of multiple sources to support a conclusion or evaluate a claim. Students consider ethical issues associated with accessing, using and citing secondary data, and apply cultural protocols when working with First Nations knowledges — including acknowledging contributions and the relationship between Indigenous knowledge and contemporary science.

nodes.label: Constructing multi-source arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct an argument that draws on multiple sources of evidence, evaluating the credibility of each source and explaining how the evidence collectively supports the conclusion.
criteria: Can construct an argument using at least two sources with explicit credibility evaluation.
Can explain how the evidence collectively supports the conclusion — not just list the sources.
Does not construct an argument from a single source — uses multiple independent sources.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who construct arguments from a single source — or who select evidence without evaluating credibility — cannot distinguish a well-supported argument from an opinion. The multi-source, credibility-evaluated argument structure is the capstone inquiry skill; weakness here undermines the argument quality regardless of source content.

width.minimum: Construct an argument for one claim using evidence from at least two sources, identify the credibility basis for each source, and explain how the two sources together support (or complicate) the conclusion.
width.typical: Construct an argument based on multiple sources — including at least one primary and one secondary source — evaluating the credibility, relevance and consistency of evidence, and explaining how the combined evidence supports the conclusion more strongly than any single source would.
wider: Examine secondary data to determine the credibility of the source and the validity and reproducibility of the data — applying AC9S9I06 validity criteria to the evidence selection process.
Identify multiple sources of evidence consistent with a scientific claim (e.g. the effectiveness of a vaccine) and explain why consistency across independent sources strengthens the argument.
Research methods used by scientists in studies reported in media — evaluating the validity of headlines against the original evidence to build critical media literacy as an argument skill.

modes.reason: The structure of a multi-source argument needs explicit scaffolding: 'Claim → Evidence 1 (credibility basis, how it supports) → Evidence 2 (credibility basis, how it supports) → how they work together.' Students often produce description of sources rather than an argument that uses them. Model the distinction.

nodes.label: Ethical issues in secondary data use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ethical issues associated with accessing, using and citing secondary data — including data privacy, correct attribution, and relevance to the investigation question.
criteria: Can identify at least one ethical concern in a described secondary data use scenario.
Can describe a practice that addresses the identified concern.
Does not treat ethics in data use as purely about plagiarism — recognises privacy and relevance as separate concerns.

width.minimum: Identify at least one ethical issue associated with using secondary data (e.g. data containing personal information, incorrect attribution, using data from a source with a conflict of interest) and explain why it is an ethical concern.
width.typical: Identify and explain multiple ethical issues in secondary data use — including privacy, attribution, and relevance — and describe practices that address each (anonymisation, citation, relevance checking).
wider: Examine secondary data to ensure it does not contain personal information that could harm individuals, is correctly cited and is relevant to the investigation question — applying all three criteria simultaneously to a described data set.
Examine how incorrect attribution of scientific data affects both the original researchers and the integrity of the argument that uses the data.

nodes.label: Cultural protocols with First Nations knowledges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply cultural protocols when accessing, using or citing First Nations knowledges — including acknowledging the co-contributions of Indigenous knowledge and contemporary science, and constructing arguments that recognise these relationships appropriately.
criteria: Can describe at least one cultural protocol relevant to using First Nations knowledge in a scientific argument.
Can construct an argument that appropriately acknowledges First Nations knowledge contributions.
Does not treat First Nations knowledge as merely contextual decoration — can use it as substantive evidence.

width.minimum: Describe one cultural protocol relevant to working with First Nations knowledges in a scientific context (e.g. acknowledging the source community, obtaining appropriate permission) and explain why it matters.
width.typical: Apply cultural protocols across a described scenario involving First Nations knowledge — acknowledging the relationship between First Peoples' knowledges and contemporary science, recognising co-contributions in arriving at shared understandings, and avoiding misrepresentation or extraction of knowledge without attribution.
wider: Acknowledge and construct an argument for contributions to medicine of First Nations Australians' knowledges of physiological pathways and contemporary medicinal delivery systems — demonstrating how an argument can genuinely integrate Indigenous knowledge as evidence rather than as token context.

Examine the concept of working 'both ways' — acknowledging and identifying the relationship between First Peoples' knowledges and contemporary science in arriving at shared understandings — and discuss what this means for how evidence is presented in an argument.

descriptors.title: Communicate ideas and findings effectively
descriptors.description: write and create texts to communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for identified purposes and audiences, including selection of appropriate content, language and text features, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can write and communicate scientific ideas and findings (AC9S7I08). They have not yet explicitly analysed communication choices for different purposes and audiences, or written scientific reports that include validity and reproducibility discussion as a required structural component.
descriptors.endpoint: Students write and create texts that communicate ideas, findings and arguments effectively for specific purposes and audiences — selecting appropriate content, language and text features for each context. Students can write a scientific investigation report (including background, results explanation and validity/reproducibility discussion), and produce texts for non-specialist audiences (e.g. presentations, social media campaigns, community reports) — selecting appropriate language and cultural responsiveness in all contexts.

nodes.label: Purpose, audience and communication choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse scientific texts for different purposes and audiences and explain how the author's choices — of content, language and text features — reflect the purpose and audience.
criteria: Can identify at least two communication choices in a text and connect each to the text's purpose or audience.
Can explain why different purposes or audiences require different content, language or structure.
Does not treat scientific communication as one-size-fits-all.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that communication choices are purpose- and audience-driven produce texts that are appropriate for one context when another is required. This is the planning framework for all subsequent communication tasks. Without it, students default to a single text type regardless of the brief.

width.minimum: Compare two scientific texts addressing similar topics for different audiences (e.g. a journal abstract and a magazine article on the same research) and identify at least two differences in content selection or language use that reflect the different audiences.
width.typical: Analyse two or three texts across different purposes (report, media release, community communication) and audiences (specialist, general public, specific community), identifying how content selection, language and text features shift for each combination — and explaining the rationale for each choice.
wider: Examine how culturally responsive communication differs from standard scientific communication — analysing specific texts that successfully navigate cultural sensitivity (e.g. communicating First Nations Australians' knowledges without offensive narratives or misattribution).
Compare scientific texts addressing similar topics for different purposes or audiences to build the analytical vocabulary for the communication choices students will make in their own texts.

modes.reason: Communication analysis requires an explicit framework: 'Who is the audience? What do they already know? What is the purpose — to inform, persuade, report? What content does that purpose require? What language is appropriate for that audience?' Students need this framework as a checklist before they analyse or produce texts.

nodes.label: Writing a scientific investigation report
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a scientific investigation report that includes: a background paragraph referencing relevant scientific knowledge; an explanation of results using scientific knowledge; and a discussion that considers validity and reproducibility.
criteria: Can write a background paragraph that references relevant scientific knowledge — not just describes the procedure.
Can explain results using scientific knowledge — not just state what happened.
Can write a validity/reproducibility discussion that addresses specific features of the method — not just 'it could have been more accurate'.

width.minimum: Write one component of a scientific investigation report — background, results explanation or validity/reproducibility discussion — that meets the structural requirements of that component.
width.typical: Write a complete scientific investigation report with all three components: background (introductory scientific context), results explanation (using scientific knowledge to explain what was found), and discussion (evaluating validity and reproducibility — connecting to AC9S9I02 and I06).
wider: Develop an interactive presentation that shows feedback loops in human body systems — applying the investigation report skills in a multimodal format that adds visual communication of process alongside explanatory text.

Evaluate the discussion section of a sample report against validity and reproducibility criteria — identifying where the discussion is strong or where gaps in validity analysis undermine the scientific argument.

modes.reason: Scientific report writing has structural conventions that require practice for reliable execution — particularly the results-explanation distinction (what was found vs. why it happened) and the validity/reproducibility discussion (a genuine analysis, not a procedural postscript). Students need feedback-corrected practice across multiple reports before these conventions become habitual.

nodes.label: Communicating for non-specialist audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts for non-specialist purposes and audiences — including selecting appropriate content, language and cultural sensitivity — such as social media campaigns, community reports or public presentations.
criteria: Can produce a text that is appropriate for the specified audience and purpose — as assessed against the communication choices made, not just the content.
Can adjust language from scientific register to audience-appropriate register deliberately — not just simplify randomly.
Can identify where cultural responsiveness considerations have shaped content or language choices.

width.minimum: Create one text for a non-specialist audience (e.g. a social media post, a community report section) that selects appropriate content and language for that audience and purpose.
width.typical: Create texts for two different non-specialist contexts — selecting appropriate content, language and format for each — including at least one that requires culturally responsive communication or consideration of First Nations Australian contexts.
wider: Plan a social media campaign to encourage young people to reduce their carbon footprint — applying content selection, audience-appropriate language and persuasive text features for a specific purpose.

Collaborate to prepare a written report for local government on estimated carbon storage across different local ecosystems and proposals to increase carbon storage — communicating quantitative scientific data to a policy audience with specific action implications.

Select appropriate content and language which is culturally responsive and maintains cultural protocols — considering sensitivities in communicating First Nations Australians' knowledges and managing risks of offensive narratives, language, images and attributions.

modes.reason: Non-specialist communication varies considerably by audience and purpose — a social media post, a community meeting presentation and a local government report require very different choices. Varying the communication contexts builds genuine range in communication repertoire rather than optimising for a single non-specialist format.

descriptors.title: Body systems and negative feedback
descriptors.description: compare the role of body systems in regulating and coordinating the body's response to a stimulus, and describe the operation of a negative feedback mechanism
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse structure-function relationships across cells, tissues and organs in body systems (AC9S8U02). They have not yet examined how multiple systems coordinate responses to stimuli, or modelled negative feedback as a regulatory mechanism.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare how the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate responses to stimuli — using models of receptor-command centre-effector pathways — and describe how negative feedback maintains homeostasis, including the effects of feedback system disorders.

nodes.label: Stimuli and receptors — detecting change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish internal from external stimuli and identify the receptor type involved in detecting a named stimulus.
criteria: Distinguishes internal from external stimuli with examples
Identifies an appropriate receptor for a named stimulus and describes its role
nodes.hinge_reason: Receptors are the entry point of the pathway model all subsequent nodes build on. Students who conflate stimulus with receptor, or cannot place the receptor correctly in the pathway, cannot construct the receptor → command centre → effector sequence in N2 or locate where deviation is detected in the feedback loop in N4.

width.minimum: Students identify the stimulus type (internal/external) and name an appropriate receptor for one stimulus example.
width.typical: Students sort multiple stimuli into internal/external categories; match stimuli to receptor types; explain why receptor specificity matters; distinguish sensory modalities.
wider: Investigate what happens when receptor function is impaired — e.g. sensory neuropathy, colour blindness — and predict consequences for the response pathway
Compare receptor sensitivity thresholds across modalities — why can we detect very faint sounds but not very faint tastes?

modes.reason: Students commonly treat stimulus-response as undifferentiated — 'the body just reacts.' Making the receptor explicit as a distinct, specific detection component is the scaffold that allows the pathway model to be built in N2.

nodes.label: Receptor → command centre → effector pathway
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace the receptor → command centre → effector pathway for a named stimulus, describing the role of each component.
criteria: Traces the receptor → command centre → effector pathway for a named stimulus
Describes the distinct role of each component in the response
nodes.hinge_reason: The three-component pathway is the structural scaffold N3 and N4 apply directly. Students who cannot place command centre and effector correctly cannot distinguish where nervous vs endocrine signalling differs, and cannot locate the corrective response within the feedback loop.

width.minimum: Students trace the three-component pathway for one named stimulus and describe what each component does.
width.typical: Students apply the pathway to multiple stimuli; represent pathways as correctly sequenced flow diagrams; explain why all three components are necessary; identify where signals travel between components.
wider: Compare the receptor → command centre → effector model to a technological control system (thermostat, cruise control) — identifying structural parallels and limits of the analogy
Investigate how pathway disruption at each component produces different failure modes — receptor damage vs command centre damage vs effector damage

modes.reason: Students commonly skip the command centre and treat stimulus-response as a direct receptor-to-effector connection. Making the command centre explicit — and its role in processing and directing — is the scaffold for comparing neural and endocrine coordination in N3.

nodes.label: Nervous and endocrine systems as coordination mechanisms — signal types and timescales
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the nervous and endocrine systems each implement the receptor → command centre → effector pathway, distinguishing signal type, speed, and duration.
criteria: Describes the nervous system pathway for a named stimulus, identifying electrical signalling and fast, short response
Describes the endocrine system pathway for a named stimulus, identifying hormonal signalling, bloodstream transport, and slower, sustained response

width.minimum: Students describe the nervous system as using electrical signals (fast, short duration) and the endocrine system as using hormonal signals (slower, longer duration) for one named example of each.
width.typical: Students trace the nervous and endocrine implementations of the pathway for multiple stimuli; explain why electrical signals travel faster than hormonal signals; identify glands as endocrine command centres and target organs as effectors; explain why some responses use both systems.
wider: Map a dual-system response (e.g. the stress response — adrenaline and rapid nerve signals) showing staged timelines for each system
Examine how drugs affecting synaptic transmission (local anaesthetics, nerve agents) or hormone receptors (hormone therapy, endocrine disruptors) disrupt specific points in each system's pathway

modes.reason: Students commonly treat the nervous and endocrine systems as entirely separate rather than as two implementations of the same pathway model. Explicitly mapping each system onto the receptor → command centre → effector structure builds the parallel representation needed for comparison in N4.

nodes.label: Comparing nervous and endocrine coordination
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the nervous and endocrine systems on signal type, speed, duration, and specificity, and predict which system coordinates a given stimulus.
criteria: Compares the nervous and endocrine systems on signal type, speed, and duration
Predicts which system coordinates a given novel stimulus and justifies the prediction
nodes.hinge_reason: Comparison of the two systems is the explicit demand of the descriptor's 'compare' verb and the progression endpoint. Students who cannot compare beyond surface-level listing cannot apply the model predictively or evaluate why disorders of one system produce different consequences than disorders of the other.

width.minimum: Students produce a comparison of the two systems on at least three dimensions: signal type, response speed, and response duration.
width.typical: Students compare across signal type, speed, duration, specificity, and reversibility; explain why different stimuli are coordinated by different systems or both; predict which system coordinates a novel stimulus and justify; use annotated diagrams or comparison tables.
wider: Analyse the stress response as a case where both systems coordinate simultaneously — explaining the advantage of dual coordination
Examine how imaging technologies (MRI, PET scans) have enabled real-time observation of nervous and endocrine activity — connecting technology advances to scientific knowledge (AC9S9H02)

modes.reason: Students commonly list features of each system separately rather than constructing a genuine comparison. Structured comparison tasks — same stimulus, both systems, same dimensions — build the analytical habit the descriptor requires.
Encountering the comparison across multiple stimulus types (temperature, blood glucose, stress, exercise) builds a more generalisable model than a single comparison task.

nodes.label: Negative feedback architecture — set point, deviation, corrective response, return detection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the four components of a negative feedback mechanism and explain why it maintains stability rather than amplifying change.
criteria: Labels and describes the role of each of the four components of a negative feedback loop
Explains why the mechanism is described as 'negative' — it opposes rather than amplifies deviation
nodes.hinge_reason: The four-component abstract model is the scaffold N6 applies to biological cases and N7 applies to disorder analysis. Students who cannot identify set point, deviation, corrective response, and return detection in a generic model cannot locate these elements in a specific biological system or identify which component fails in a disorder.

width.minimum: Students label and describe the role of each of the four components in a negative feedback loop using a generic or diagrammatic model.
width.typical: Students represent negative feedback as a complete flow diagram; explain why the mechanism is called 'negative'; distinguish negative from positive feedback; explain why homeostasis is essential for cell function.
wider: Compare negative and positive feedback — identifying where positive feedback is used in biological systems (childbirth, blood clotting) and why amplification is appropriate in those contexts
Model the feedback architecture using a non-biological analogy and evaluate the strengths and limits of the analogy

modes.reason: Students commonly understand feedback from examples without being able to articulate the abstract architecture. Making the four components explicit — and distinguishing 'negative' as opposing rather than bad — is the scaffold that allows transfer to novel biological cases in N6 and disorder analysis in N7.

nodes.label: Negative feedback in canonical biological cases — tracing complete loops
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace a complete negative feedback loop for at least two named biological examples, correctly identifying all four components in each.
criteria: Traces a complete negative feedback loop for a named biological example, correctly identifying all four components
Names at least two biological examples of negative feedback and identifies the set point in each

width.minimum: Students trace the complete negative feedback loop for one biological example (temperature regulation or blood glucose), identifying all four components.
width.typical: Students trace feedback loops for multiple homeostatic systems (temperature, blood glucose, blood pressure, hydration); explain why homeostasis is essential for cell function; use annotated flow diagrams with correct directionality.
wider: Develop a model, animation or presentation representing a named feedback loop — applying digital communication skills to represent dynamic biological processes (AC9S9I08)
Investigate how pharmaceutical interventions target specific points in the feedback loop — e.g. beta blockers reducing heart rate response, metformin improving glucose uptake

modes.reason: Tracing complete loops with all four components correctly placed requires precision. Common errors — confusing set point with corrective response, omitting return detection — are worth targeted practice before disorder analysis in N7.
Encountering the same four-component architecture across temperature, blood glucose, and blood pressure builds transferability to novel cases and disorder analysis.

nodes.label: Feedback system disorders — locating failure in the loop
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a disorder of a feedback system disrupts homeostasis by identifying which component of the loop has failed and describing the consequence.
criteria: Identifies which component of the feedback loop fails in a named disorder
Explains the homeostatic consequence of that failure

width.minimum: Students explain one feedback system disorder, identifying the affected component (receptor, command centre, effector, or return detection) and describing the homeostatic consequence.
width.typical: Students analyse multiple disorders (type 1 diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypertension) by locating the failure point in the loop; explain why the same disorder produces different consequences depending on which component fails; connect disorder analysis to treatment approaches.
wider: Investigate how medical devices (insulin pumps, pacemakers, CPAP machines) artificially replace or supplement the failed component — mapping device function onto the four-component architecture
Evaluate claims about a health product using the feedback model as a diagnostic lens — identifying what feedback mechanism the product claims to support and whether the claim is coherent

modes.reason: Students commonly describe disorders as 'the body not working' without locating the failure within the loop architecture. Explicitly asking 'which component has failed?' applies the four-component model diagnostically and consolidates N5 understanding.

Analysing multiple disorders across different systems reinforces that the same feedback architecture underlies all homeostatic regulation, and that failure at different components produces predictably different consequences.

descriptors.title: Reproduction and species survival
descriptors.description: describe the form and function of reproductive cells and organs in animals and plants, and analyse how the processes of sexual and asexual reproduction enable survival of the species
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how structural features and behaviours are adaptations enabling survival in particular habitats (AC9S5U01) and analyse how physical conditions affect organism survival (AC9S6U01). They can recognise cells as basic units of living things and describe specialised cell structures (AC9S8U01). They have not yet examined reproductive organs and cells as systems with specific forms matched to function, or analysed sexual vs asexual reproduction in terms of variation and species survival trade-offs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the form and function of reproductive cells and organs in animals and plants, and analyse how sexual reproduction generates variation and how asexual reproduction enables rapid colonisation — connecting each strategy to survival in different environmental contexts.

nodes.label: Reproductive cells — form matched to function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structural features of male and female gametes and explain how each feature relates to the gamete's reproductive function.
criteria: Describes at least two structural features of sperm and two of egg cells
Explains how each feature relates to the gamete's function
Identifies plant equivalents (pollen, ovule) and describes one form-function relationship in each
nodes.hinge_reason: Form-function relationships in gametes are the foundation for understanding reproductive organ systems (N2) and fertilisation success (N3). Students who treat gametes as interchangeable undifferentiated cells cannot explain why reproductive organs are structured as they are, or why gamete ratios (millions of sperm, one egg) are adaptive.

width.minimum: Students describe two structural features of a sperm cell and two of an egg cell and explain how each feature serves its function.
width.typical: Students compare sperm and egg across size, motility, energy stores and quantity; explain why sperm are numerous and motile while eggs are large and energy-rich; apply the structure-function principle from AC9S8U01 to gametes; describe pollen and ovules as the plant equivalents.
wider: Compare gamete form across animal groups — external vs internal fertilisers — and explain how gamete number and size reflect fertilisation strategy
Investigate how the form of pollen grains reflects their dispersal mechanism (wind vs insect pollination)

modes.reason: Students enter with a general structure-function principle from AC9S8U01 but have not applied it to gametes. Making the form-function link explicit for each gamete feature — rather than listing features as facts — is the scaffold the organ system analysis in N2 requires.

nodes.label: Reproductive organs — systems supporting gamete production and fertilisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the key structures of male and female reproductive systems in animals and plants and explain how these work collectively to support gamete production, transfer and fertilisation.
criteria: Names key structures of animal reproductive systems and explains the role of each
Describes plant reproductive structures (stamen, carpel) and their roles in pollination and fertilisation
Explains how reproductive organ structures collectively support fertilisation

width.minimum: Students name the key structures of one reproductive system (animal or plant) and explain the role of each in gamete production or transfer.
width.typical: Students describe male and female animal reproductive systems as integrated structures; explain how each structure supports gamete production, transport or fertilisation; describe equivalent plant structures (stamen, carpel, ovary); explain how flower structure supports pollination and fertilisation; connect organ form to the gamete form established in N1.
wider: Compare reproductive organ complexity across animal groups — fish, frog, mammal — and connect structural differences to internal vs external fertilisation strategies
Investigate how First Nations Australians' knowledge of plant reproductive cycles informed seasonal harvesting practices

modes.reason: Reproductive systems are most clearly understood as integrated wholes — each structure serving a step in a sequence — rather than as lists of parts. Tracing the gamete pathway through the system (production → maturation → transport → fertilisation) gives structure to organ function descriptions.

nodes.label: Sexual reproduction — fertilisation, variation and survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how sexual reproduction produces variation among offspring and analyse how this variation supports species survival.
criteria: Explains how random combination of gametes produces genetic variation among offspring
Connects variation to survival advantage — some offspring are more likely to survive changed conditions
Explains the trade-off between offspring number, parental care and reproductive strategy in a named example
nodes.hinge_reason: The variation-survival link is the conceptual core of the descriptor's 'analyse how reproduction enables survival' demand, and it is the direct prerequisite for the sexual vs asexual comparison in N4. Students who understand reproduction only as a mechanism for producing offspring — without the variation-survival connection — cannot analyse the adaptive significance of either strategy.

width.minimum: Students explain that sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents and state that this produces variation among offspring.
