width.typical: Students explain that variation arises from random gamete combination; describe how variation increases the likelihood that some offspring survive changed conditions; explain that sexual reproduction is slower and costlier than asexual but produces genetically diverse offspring; connect to parental care and offspring number trade-offs in different animal groups.
wider: Analyse how the reproductive strategies of different animals (number of offspring, parental care, internal vs external fertilisation) reflect survival trade-offs in their environments
Investigate how sexual reproduction in plants involves both pollination and fertilisation — trace the full pathway from pollen to seed

modes.reason: Students commonly understand that sexual reproduction produces variation but treat variation as a byproduct rather than as the adaptive advantage. Making the variation-survival link explicit — variation is the mechanism by which a species hedges against environmental change — is required before the comparison with asexual reproduction in N4 is meaningful.

nodes.label: Asexual reproduction — strategies, speed and survival contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe asexual reproductive strategies in plants and animals and explain when asexual reproduction is advantageous for species survival.
criteria: Describes at least two distinct asexual reproductive strategies with examples
Explains why asexual reproduction is advantageous in stable environments or for rapid colonisation
Identifies the key limitation of asexual reproduction — genetic uniformity and vulnerability to change

width.minimum: Students describe two asexual reproductive strategies and explain one context in which asexual reproduction confers a survival advantage.
width.typical: Students describe binary fission, budding, fragmentation and vegetative reproduction in plants; explain that asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring rapidly; explain why asexual reproduction is advantageous in stable environments or for rapid colonisation; identify the limitation — no variation means vulnerability if conditions change.
wider: Investigate asexual and sexual reproductive strategies in plants (runners, bulbs, seeds) and explain which strategy dominates in which ecological context
Compare asexual reproduction in bacteria (binary fission) to vegetative reproduction in plants — what structural differences underlie the same functional strategy?

modes.reason: Asexual reproduction strategies vary significantly across organism types — bacterial, fungal, plant, animal — and each context illuminates a different aspect of the speed vs variation trade-off. Multiple contexts build the comparative understanding the 'analyse' demand requires.

nodes.label: Comparing reproductive strategies — analysing survival trade-offs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare sexual and asexual reproduction and analyse how each strategy enables species survival in different environmental contexts.
criteria: Compares sexual and asexual reproduction across variation, speed and resource cost
Analyses the survival advantage of each strategy in a specific named environmental context
Explains why some species use both strategies depending on conditions

width.minimum: Students compare sexual and asexual reproduction across at least two dimensions (variation, speed, cost) and explain which strategy is advantageous in a named context.
width.typical: Students construct a comparative analysis of both strategies; explain that many organisms use both strategies depending on conditions; analyse specific examples where strategy choice reflects environmental pressure; connect reproductive strategy to organism complexity and parental investment; explain how reproductive strategy relates to species survival over evolutionary time.
wider: Analyse a species that uses both sexual and asexual reproduction (e.g. strawberry plants, coral, Daphnia) — predict which strategy dominates under what conditions and why
Evaluate how human agricultural practices exploit asexual reproduction (cloning, cuttings) and discuss the genetic diversity implications

modes.reason: This node integrates gamete form (N1), organ systems (N2), sexual reproduction and variation (N3), and asexual strategies (N4) into a comparative analysis of survival strategy. It is the descriptor's 'analyse how the processes enable survival' demand applied to both reproduction types simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Carbon cycle and Earth's spheres
descriptors.description: represent the carbon cycle and examine how key processes including combustion, photosynthesis and respiration rely on interactions between Earth's spheres (the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe Earth's surface changes (AC9S5U02), model how Earth's tilt and revolution produce seasonal change (AC9S6U02), and compare reversible and irreversible changes including combustion (AC9S6U04). They can use food web models to represent matter and energy flow through ecosystems (AC9S7U02) and explain plate tectonics and rock cycle processes (AC9S8U03, AC9S8U04). They have not yet encountered Earth as a system of interacting spheres, or carbon as a substance that cycles through those spheres via identifiable chemical and biological processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent the carbon cycle using diagrams or models and explain how combustion, photosynthesis and respiration each move carbon between Earth's spheres — including how human activity through combustion perturbs the natural cycle.

nodes.label: Earth's spheres — geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and describe Earth's four spheres and give examples of matter or processes found in each.
criteria: Names all four of Earth's spheres and describes what each contains
Gives at least one example of matter and one process located in each sphere
Explains that Earth functions as a system where spheres interact
nodes.hinge_reason: The four-sphere framework is the structural scaffold the carbon cycle diagram depends on. Students who cannot locate processes (photosynthesis, combustion, respiration) in specific spheres cannot represent carbon movement between spheres in N3–N5, and cannot explain what 'sphere interaction' means when examining each process.

width.minimum: Students name all four spheres and give one example of matter or a process in each.
width.typical: Students describe the composition and location of each sphere; give multiple examples of matter and processes in each; describe the boundaries between spheres as zones of interaction; explain that Earth functions as a system where spheres influence each other.
wider: Map a familiar phenomenon — a rain event, a bushfire — across all four spheres and identify which sphere interactions are involved
Investigate First Nations Australians' firestick farming as a practice that deliberately manages interactions between the biosphere and atmosphere

modes.reason: Students have prior knowledge of individual Earth systems (rock cycle, water cycle, ecosystems) but not the integrating four-sphere framework. Establishing the framework explicitly — with clear examples in each sphere — is the orientation node the rest of the standard builds on.

nodes.label: Carbon as a substance cycling through Earth's spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where carbon is stored in each of Earth's spheres and explain that carbon moves between these stores.
criteria: Identifies carbon stores in at least three of Earth's four spheres with examples
Explains that carbon moves between stores rather than being created or destroyed
Distinguishes fast-cycling carbon stores (atmosphere, living organisms) from slow stores (fossil fuels, carbonate rock)

width.minimum: Students identify carbon stores in at least three spheres (e.g. CO₂ in atmosphere, organic matter in biosphere, carbonate rocks in geosphere) and state that carbon moves between stores.
width.typical: Students describe carbon stores in all four spheres (atmospheric CO₂, dissolved carbon in oceans, organic carbon in living and dead matter, fossil fuels and carbonate rocks in geosphere); explain that carbon is neither created nor destroyed — it moves between stores; introduce carbon cycle as the map of those movements.
wider: Investigate carbon sequestration in a local ecosystem — what stores exist and how large are they relative to atmospheric CO₂?
Compare timescales of carbon movement: carbon in a leaf vs carbon in a coal seam — why does geological storage matter for climate?

modes.reason: Students need to understand carbon as a substance with identifiable locations before they can trace its movement in the cycle. The 'stores and flows' framing — familiar from food web energy flow in AC9S7U02 — is the conceptual bridge to carbon cycle representation.

nodes.label: Photosynthesis and respiration — carbon movement through the biosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how photosynthesis and respiration move carbon between the atmosphere and biosphere, and represent these as flows in the carbon cycle.
criteria: Explains that photosynthesis moves carbon from the atmosphere to the biosphere
Explains that respiration and decomposition move carbon from the biosphere to the atmosphere
Represents both processes as directional arrows between spheres in a diagram
nodes.hinge_reason: Photosynthesis and respiration are the biological processes that dominate carbon cycling between biosphere and atmosphere. Students who cannot represent these as directional flows cannot construct a correct carbon cycle diagram in N5, and cannot explain why deforestation or ecosystem loss accelerates CO₂ accumulation in the atmosphere.

width.minimum: Students state that photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere and stores carbon in organic matter, and that respiration releases CO₂ back to the atmosphere.
width.typical: Students describe photosynthesis and respiration as complementary processes; explain that photosynthesis moves carbon from atmosphere to biosphere and respiration does the reverse; connect to food web energy flow from AC9S7U02; represent both processes as arrows in a carbon cycle diagram; explain that decomposition is also a form of respiration returning carbon to the atmosphere.
wider: Investigate how carbon moves through a food web — trace a carbon atom from CO₂ through photosynthesis, herbivore, carnivore and decomposer back to atmosphere
Investigate First Nations Australians' fire management regimes and explain how controlled burning affects the photosynthesis-respiration balance in an ecosystem

modes.reason: Students often know photosynthesis and respiration as chemical equations without locating them as sphere-exchange processes. Reframing both processes as carbon-flow arrows between specific spheres — the representation the descriptor demands — requires an explicit conceptual shift from 'what happens in a cell' to 'how carbon moves between stores'.

nodes.label: Combustion — carbon release from geosphere to atmosphere
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how combustion of fossil fuels moves carbon from the geosphere to the atmosphere and describe the impact of human activity on this flow.
criteria: Explains that combustion of fossil fuels moves carbon from geosphere to atmosphere
Describes why this represents a net addition to the atmospheric carbon store (geological timescale of sequestration vs rapid release)
Connects increased atmospheric CO₂ to the greenhouse effect and its role in heat retention

width.minimum: Students explain that combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon stored in the geosphere as CO₂ into the atmosphere.
width.typical: Students connect fossil fuel formation to ancient carbon sequestration (geological timescale); explain that combustion rapidly releases carbon that took millions of years to sequester; describe human industrial and transport combustion as the dominant driver; connect to the greenhouse effect elaboration — increased atmospheric CO₂ affects heat retention; calculate or estimate an individual's carbon footprint.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' firestick farming as a controlled combustion practice — how does this differ from fossil fuel combustion in terms of carbon cycle impact?
Model the carbon cycle perturbation: if combustion adds X tonnes of CO₂ to the atmosphere annually, and photosynthesis + ocean absorption removes Y, what happens to the atmospheric store over time?

modes.reason: The elaborations name multiple combustion contexts — industrial, transport, firestick farming, carbon capture — each of which illuminates a different aspect of the combustion-cycle interaction. Varied contexts build the system-level understanding required for carbon cycle representation.

nodes.label: Representing the carbon cycle — integrating processes across all spheres
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct or annotate a carbon cycle diagram that represents all key processes (photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition) as flows between Earth's spheres.
criteria: Constructs or correctly annotates a carbon cycle diagram with at least four labelled flows between named spheres
Identifies which flows are biological, which are geological, and which are human-driven
Explains how human combustion has altered the balance of the natural carbon cycle

width.minimum: Students correctly label a carbon cycle diagram showing at least four carbon flows between named spheres.
width.typical: Students construct a complete carbon cycle diagram from memory or annotate a template with all major flows; explain the direction and mechanism of each flow; identify where human activity has altered natural flow rates; explain how carbon sequestration (natural or technological) works within the cycle; describe the cycle as a system in approximate balance before industrialisation.
wider: Evaluate a carbon sequestration strategy (reforestation, biochar, ocean fertilisation) using the carbon cycle diagram — which flows does it target and what are the risks?
Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional fire management reduces net greenhouse gas emissions — map the mechanism onto the carbon cycle diagram

modes.reason: This node integrates the four-sphere framework (N1), carbon stores (N2), photosynthesis and respiration flows (N3), and combustion (N4) into a single representative model. Constructing the diagram is the descriptor's 'represent the carbon cycle' demand — the integration point for all prior nodes.

descriptors.title: Wave and particle models
descriptors.description: use wave and particle models to describe energy transfer through different mediums and examine the usefulness of each model for explaining phenomena
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how light travels in straight paths and describe reflection and refraction (AC9S5U03). They can explain energy transfer and transformation in electrical circuits (AC9S6U03) and classify energy as kinetic or potential (AC9S8U05). They can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances (AC9S7U05). They have encountered both particle and wave ideas separately but have not yet applied them as competing or complementary models for explaining energy transfer, or evaluated which model is more useful for a given phenomenon.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use wave and particle models to describe how energy is transferred through different mediums — including sound, heat and light — and examine the usefulness and limitations of each model for explaining phenomena including electromagnetic radiation.

nodes.label: The particle model of energy transfer — conduction and convection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain conduction and convection using the particle model, describing how particle motion and collisions transfer energy through matter.
criteria: Explains conduction using particle collisions as the transfer mechanism
Explains convection using bulk particle movement driven by density differences
Applies the particle model to explain why a named material is a good conductor or insulator

width.minimum: Students explain conduction as energy transfer through particle collisions in a solid, and convection as bulk movement of particles carrying energy in a fluid.
width.typical: Students apply the particle model to explain why metals conduct heat well (closely packed particles, efficient collision transfer) while insulators do not; explain convection currents as density-driven particle movement; connect to AC9S7U05's particle theory; describe how First Nations Australians' traditional clothing and bedding exploit or minimise conduction and convection.
wider: Investigate insulation designs from First Nations Australians' clothing and bedding across different climate regions — what particle-level mechanisms do the materials exploit?
Design a fair test comparing the insulating properties of two materials and explain the results using the particle model

modes.reason: Students have prior particle theory (AC9S7U05) applied to physical properties but not to energy transfer. Explicitly connecting particle motion to energy transfer — collision as the mechanism, not just 'heat moves through the material' — establishes the particle model as an explanatory tool before the wave model is introduced.
Conduction and convection in varied material and cultural contexts build the model's explanatory range before it is compared with the wave model.

nodes.label: The wave model of energy transfer — sound
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe sound as a wave and explain how sound energy is transferred through a medium using the wave model, including the relationship between wave properties and sound characteristics.
criteria: Describes sound as a longitudinal wave requiring a medium
Uses compression and rarefaction to explain how sound energy is transferred
Relates frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness with examples
nodes.hinge_reason: The wave model of sound is the first full application of wave properties (frequency, amplitude, wavelength, medium-dependence) as a coherent framework. Students who do not secure the wave model for sound cannot extend it to electromagnetic radiation in N4, and cannot evaluate which model is more useful for which phenomenon — the descriptor's core analytical demand.

width.minimum: Students describe sound as a longitudinal wave and explain that it requires a medium, using compression and rarefaction to describe how energy is transferred.
width.typical: Students relate frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness; model wave transfer using a slinky spring; explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum; describe how the medium's properties affect sound transmission speed; investigate sound transmission in First Nations traditional instruments.
wider: Investigate how material selection affects sound energy transfer in a First Nations traditional instrument — explain the design choices using the wave model
Compare sound transmission speed in air, water and solids and explain the differences using particle spacing and bonding

modes.reason: Students have encountered sound in everyday contexts but not as a formal wave model with defined properties. Establishing wave properties (frequency, amplitude, wavelength, medium-dependence) through sound — the most concrete wave context — is the scaffold for the more abstract electromagnetic wave model in N4.

nodes.label: The particle model of electricity — static charge and current
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain static electricity and electrical current using the particle model of charge, and connect particle behaviour to concepts of voltage, conductors and insulators.
criteria: Explains static electricity as electron transfer between materials producing charge imbalance
Describes electrical current as directed electron flow through a conductor
Distinguishes conductors from insulators using the particle model (free vs bound electrons)

width.minimum: Students explain static electricity as the accumulation of charge due to electron transfer, and electrical current as the flow of electrons through a conductor.
width.typical: Students explain charging by friction, induction and contact using electron transfer; describe current as directed electron flow driven by voltage; explain conductors as materials with free electrons and insulators as materials without; connect to electrical circuit concepts from AC9S6U03; explain electrostatic discharge as rapid electron movement to neutralise charge imbalance.
wider: Investigate an electrostatics phenomenon (lightning, Van de Graaff generator) and explain it fully using the particle model of charge
Examine how semiconductor materials — with intermediate conductivity — challenge the simple conductor/insulator binary, and explore applications in electronics

modes.reason: Students have prior knowledge of circuits (AC9S6U03) but at the observable level — components, connections, current as a functional concept. The particle model reframes current as electron flow and extends the model to static electricity, which has no circuit equivalent. This is a model extension, not revision.

nodes.label: The wave model of light and electromagnetic radiation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe light and electromagnetic radiation as waves and explain how the wave model accounts for phenomena including reflection, refraction and the electromagnetic spectrum.
criteria: Describes light as a transverse wave and the EM spectrum as a family of waves differing in frequency and wavelength
Uses the wave model to explain reflection and refraction
Explains how wave frequency relates to energy across the electromagnetic spectrum

width.minimum: Students describe light as a transverse wave and use the wave model to explain reflection and refraction.
width.typical: Students describe the electromagnetic spectrum as a family of transverse waves varying in frequency and wavelength; explain that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; connect wave frequency to energy (radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma); explain how EM wave properties determine their use in communication technologies; apply the wave model to explain reflection and refraction from AC9S5U03.
wider: Investigate the forms of electromagnetic radiation used in different modern communication technologies — what wave properties make each suitable for its application?
Examine how the wave model explains UV damage to skin and X-ray imaging — what wave property is the key variable?

modes.reason: Applying the wave model across the full EM spectrum — from radio to gamma — and to real communication and medical technologies builds the model's explanatory range needed for the 'usefulness' evaluation in N5.

nodes.label: Evaluating model usefulness — wave vs particle for different phenomena
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the usefulness of wave and particle models for explaining different energy transfer phenomena and identify where each model succeeds or fails.
criteria: Evaluates the usefulness of each model for at least two distinct phenomena
Identifies at least one phenomenon where the wave model is more useful and one where the particle model is more useful
Explains that scientific models are tools with domains of usefulness rather than literal descriptions of reality

width.minimum: Students identify one phenomenon better explained by the wave model and one better explained by the particle model, and explain why in each case.
width.typical: Students systematically evaluate wave and particle models against phenomena: sound (wave model — medium required, wave properties), conduction (particle model — collision mechanism), light (wave model accounts for diffraction, reflection, refraction; particle model explains photoelectric effect); introduce the concept of photons as a case where neither model alone is sufficient; explain that models are tools with domains of usefulness, not literal descriptions.
wider: Research the wave-particle duality of light — what experimental evidence supports each model, and how does the concept of photons attempt to reconcile them?
Evaluate the particle model of light (photons) for explaining the photoelectric effect and discuss what this reveals about the limits of classical models

modes.reason: This node is the descriptor's 'examine the usefulness of each model' demand. Students bring both models — particle (N1, N3) and wave (N2, N4) — into comparative evaluation across phenomena. The key conceptual move is recognising that models are domain-specific tools, not universal truths.

descriptors.title: Conservation of energy and efficiency
descriptors.description: apply the law of conservation of energy to analyse system efficiency in terms of energy inputs, outputs, transfers and transformations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can classify energy as kinetic or potential and explain energy transfers and transformations in simple systems (AC9S8U05). They can explain energy transfer and transformation in electrical circuits (AC9S6U03). They have qualitative understanding of energy transformation but have not yet applied conservation of energy as a quantitative law, or analysed system efficiency — the proportion of useful output energy — as a calculated quantity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply the law of conservation of energy to account for all energy inputs and outputs in a system, calculate efficiency as useful output divided by total input, and use Sankey diagrams to represent energy flow — applying this analysis to real systems including electricity generation and appliances.

nodes.label: Conservation of energy — total energy is maintained in any system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state the law of conservation of energy and apply it to account for all energy in a system — including energy that is transferred as heat or sound rather than as useful output.
criteria: States the law of conservation of energy correctly
Explains that 'wasted' energy is transferred to the environment, not destroyed
Accounts for all energy outputs (useful + wasted) in a simple system
nodes.hinge_reason: Conservation of energy is the law the entire standard applies. Students who believe energy is 'used up' or 'disappears' in a system cannot correctly identify all outputs when calculating efficiency in N2, and will misinterpret Sankey diagrams as showing energy loss rather than energy redistribution. This misconception is common and must be resolved before efficiency analysis is introduced.

width.minimum: Students state that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, and apply this to explain why the total energy in a closed system remains constant.
width.typical: Students apply conservation of energy to trace all energy outputs in a system (useful + wasted); explain that 'wasted' energy is not lost — it is transferred to the environment, typically as heat or sound; connect to prior kinetic/potential energy knowledge from AC9S8U05; explain that conservation of energy applies even when energy appears to disappear.
wider: Investigate the energy transformations in a bouncing ball — where does the kinetic energy go at each bounce, and can you account for all of it?
Apply conservation of energy to a pendulum system — trace energy between kinetic and potential forms over multiple swings and explain why the pendulum eventually stops

modes.reason: The misconception that energy is 'used up' or 'lost' in a transformation is persistent and directly blocks efficiency analysis. Students must explicitly encounter and resolve this before N2 — efficiency only makes sense as a ratio if total energy is conserved.

nodes.label: Efficiency — useful output as a proportion of total input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define efficiency, calculate it as a ratio of useful output to total input energy, and explain why no real system achieves 100% efficiency.
criteria: Calculates efficiency as useful output ÷ total input with correct units
Explains why no real system achieves 100% efficiency
Compares efficiency values across two systems and interprets the difference
nodes.hinge_reason: Efficiency as a calculated ratio is the quantitative core of the descriptor's 'analyse system efficiency' demand. Students who cannot apply the formula correctly — particularly students who confuse efficiency with output quantity rather than proportion — cannot use Sankey diagrams quantitatively in N3 or compare real systems in N4.

width.minimum: Students calculate efficiency using efficiency = useful output ÷ total input and explain why real systems are less than 100% efficient.
width.typical: Students apply the efficiency formula across multiple contexts (light bulb, engine, solar panel); explain that inefficiency results from energy being transferred in non-useful forms (heat, sound, light); explain why 100% efficiency is unachievable in practice; connect to energy star ratings on appliances; compare efficiency values to evaluate system performance.
wider: Investigate the efficiency of ground ovens used by First Nations Australians — estimate energy input and useful thermal output and compare to a modern equivalent
Compare the efficiency of electricity generation from coal, nuclear, hydroelectricity, gas, solar and wind using published data — what does the variation reveal about energy conversion processes?

modes.reason: Efficiency calculation requires procedural precision — identifying useful output correctly, applying the ratio, interpreting the result as a proportion. Students need structured practice before the Sankey diagram representation in N3.

Multiple efficiency contexts — appliances, generation sources, traditional technologies — build the comparative analytical capability the descriptor's 'analyse' demand requires. Each context has a different energy input/output profile.

nodes.label: Sankey diagrams — representing energy inputs, outputs and losses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct and interpret Sankey diagrams to represent energy flow through a system, reading off efficiency and identifying where energy losses occur.
criteria: Reads efficiency and identifies major energy losses from a given Sankey diagram
Constructs a Sankey diagram from energy data with correctly proportioned arrows
Critiques a Sankey diagram — identifies what it represents well and any limitations

width.minimum: Students correctly read efficiency and identify the largest energy loss from a given Sankey diagram.
width.typical: Students construct Sankey diagrams for simple systems from energy data; interpret the width of arrows as proportional to energy quantity; identify which transformation stage is least efficient; evaluate the diagram as a representation — what it shows clearly and what it obscures; critique diagrams for accuracy.
wider: Construct a Sankey diagram for a multi-stage energy system (e.g. coal → electricity → light) and calculate the overall efficiency as a product of stage efficiencies
Evaluate the claim that Sankey diagrams are more informative than efficiency percentages alone — when is the diagram more useful, and when is a number sufficient?

modes.reason: Sankey diagrams encode both qualitative (direction, type) and quantitative (width = energy quantity) information simultaneously. Students need explicit instruction on reading the representation — particularly that arrow width is proportional to energy, not just indicating flow direction — before they can use diagrams to analyse real systems.

nodes.label: Applying conservation of energy and efficiency to real systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the law of conservation of energy and efficiency analysis to evaluate real energy systems and identify where improvements could be made.
criteria: Applies conservation of energy to account for all energy inputs and outputs in a real system
Calculates efficiency for a real system and interprets the result
Identifies where energy losses occur and suggests a practical improvement

width.minimum: Students apply conservation of energy and calculate efficiency for one real system and suggest one improvement based on the analysis.
width.typical: Students analyse electricity generation systems (coal, solar, hydro) using efficiency data; evaluate appliance energy star ratings; apply efficiency analysis to sporting contexts (pole vault, archery) to explain how technique improvements reduce energy loss; connect efficiency improvement to reduced resource use and environmental impact.
wider: Compare the efficiency of traditional First Nations ground ovens to modern cooking technologies — account for all energy inputs and outputs in both systems
Evaluate a proposed efficiency improvement in a named energy system — use conservation of energy to predict the impact on total energy use and waste heat

modes.reason: This node integrates conservation of energy (N1), efficiency calculation (N2) and Sankey representation (N3) into analysis of real systems — the descriptor's full 'apply the law of conservation of energy to analyse system efficiency' demand. Students bring all three tools to bear on novel systems.

descriptors.title: Atomic model and radioactive decay
descriptors.description: explain how the model of the atom changed following the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons and describe how natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances (AC9S7U05) and classify matter as elements, compounds and mixtures using symbols and formulas (AC9S8U06). They have a functional particle model but it is the simple undifferentiated particle model — particles have no internal structure. They have not yet encountered subatomic particles, the historical development of atomic models, or the concept of nuclear instability and radioactive decay.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how experimental evidence drove the development of the nuclear model of the atom through the discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons, and describe how unstable isotopes undergo radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) to produce stable atoms — including half-life as a measure of decay rate.

nodes.label: The nuclear model of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structure of the nuclear atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons, and use atomic number and mass number to describe specific atoms.
criteria: Describes the nuclear atom: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells
Uses atomic number and mass number to determine proton, neutron and electron counts
Describes the relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.hinge_reason: The nuclear model is the structural foundation all subsequent nodes require. Students who cannot correctly assign protons, neutrons and electrons to an atom from its atomic and mass numbers cannot define isotopes in N2, understand why some isotopes are unstable in N3, or follow decay sequences in N4.

width.minimum: Students describe the nucleus as containing protons and neutrons, with electrons surrounding it, and use atomic number to identify an element.
width.typical: Students describe the relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons; explain that atomic number equals proton number and determines the element's identity; explain that mass number equals protons plus neutrons; describe electrons as occupying shells around the nucleus; connect to the prior undifferentiated particle model as a simplification that is now being replaced.
wider: Compare the mass and charge of subatomic particles quantitatively — what does the near-zero mass of the electron reveal about where most atomic mass is located?
Examine how the discovery of the nucleus changed scientific understanding — what did Rutherford's gold foil experiment show that Thomson's plum pudding model could not explain?

modes.reason: Students enter with a functional but structure-free particle model. Introducing internal atomic structure requires the prior model to be explicitly extended — particles now have constituent parts. The historical transition from Thomson to Rutherford's model is the elaboration's evidence-based framing for this conceptual shift.

nodes.label: Isotopes — same element, different neutron numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and explain why some isotopes are unstable.
criteria: Defines isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Identifies that some isotopes are unstable and undergo radioactive decay
Uses isotope notation (e.g. carbon-14) correctly

width.minimum: Students define isotopes correctly and identify that unstable isotopes undergo radioactive decay.
width.typical: Students describe naturally occurring isotopes of common elements (carbon-12/13/14, uranium-235/238); explain that isotopes have the same chemical properties (same proton number) but different masses; explain that neutron-to-proton ratio affects nuclear stability; describe unstable isotopes as those with configurations that tend toward decay; connect carbon-14 specifically to radiocarbon dating.
wider: Investigate how radiocarbon dating has been used to establish that First Peoples of Australia have been present for more than 60,000 years — what does the carbon-14 decay rate reveal about sample age?
Compare stable and unstable isotope distributions for a named element and identify what neutron-to-proton ratios characterise stability

modes.reason: Isotopes require students to understand that atomic identity is determined by proton number alone — same protons, different neutrons, same element. This is the prerequisite for understanding why only some atoms decay (unstable neutron-to-proton ratios) in N3.

nodes.label: Types of radioactive decay — alpha, beta and gamma
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe alpha, beta and gamma decay in terms of what is emitted and how each changes the nucleus, and compare their penetrating power.
criteria: Describes what is emitted in alpha, beta and gamma decay
Explains how alpha and beta decay change the atomic number and mass number of the nucleus
Compares the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation
nodes.hinge_reason: The three decay types are the mechanistic content of the descriptor's 'describe how natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms' demand. Students who cannot distinguish decay types — particularly students who conflate alpha/beta emission with gamma, or who cannot track changes to atomic and mass numbers — cannot follow decay sequences toward stability in N4 or understand why different isotopes have different applications.

width.minimum: Students describe what is emitted in each decay type (alpha particle, beta particle, gamma ray) and state one difference in their penetrating power.
width.typical: Students describe alpha decay as emission of a helium nucleus (reducing atomic number by 2, mass number by 4); describe beta decay as emission of an electron from the nucleus (increasing atomic number by 1); describe gamma emission as release of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with no change to atomic number or mass; compare penetrating power (alpha — stopped by paper, beta — by aluminium, gamma — reduced by lead/concrete); describe applications in medicine and industry.
wider: Investigate the use of radioactive isotopes in medicine — how is the type of decay and half-life matched to the diagnostic or treatment application?
Examine how gamma radiation is used to check for faults in aircraft and spacecraft materials — what property of gamma makes it suitable for this application?

modes.reason: Alpha, beta and gamma are qualitatively different in emission type, effect on nucleus, and penetrating power. Students need a clear comparison framework — what is emitted, what changes in the nucleus, how far it penetrates — before applying decay to stability sequences.

Medical imaging, cancer treatment, materials testing, and radiocarbon dating are each a distinct application context that requires matching decay type to purpose. These contexts build genuine understanding of why decay type matters beyond identification.

nodes.label: Half-life — rate of radioactive decay
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define half-life, use half-life data to calculate remaining activity after a given number of half-lives, and explain how half-life determines the suitability of isotopes for different applications.
criteria: Defines half-life as the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay
Calculates the remaining quantity of a radioisotope after a given number of half-lives
Explains why half-life determines the suitability of an isotope for a named application

width.minimum: Students define half-life as the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay and calculate remaining quantity after two half-lives.
width.typical: Students apply half-life calculations across multiple timescales (carbon-14 at 5,730 years, uranium-238 at 4.5 billion years); interpret decay curves graphically; explain why short-lived isotopes are suitable for medical imaging and long-lived ones for geological dating; explain that half-life is constant and unaffected by physical or chemical conditions.
wider: Simulate radioactive decay using digital tools or physical models (dice) and compare the simulated decay curve to the mathematical model
Investigate how uranium-238 half-life data is used in geological dating — what assumptions must be true for radiometric dating to give accurate ages?

modes.reason: Half-life is a probabilistic concept — it describes the behaviour of large populations of nuclei, not individual atoms. Students commonly expect individual atoms to decay at half-life intervals. Making the probabilistic nature explicit, and connecting the constant half-life to practical application matching, completes the decay model.

nodes.label: Decay sequences — how unstable isotopes reach stability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how a series of decay events transforms an unstable isotope into a stable one, and explain the relationship between the descriptor's descriptor claim that 'natural radioactive decay results in stable atoms'.
criteria: Traces a named decay sequence and identifies the stable end product
Tracks changes to atomic number and mass number at each decay step
Explains how the sequence of decay events moves the nucleus toward stability

width.minimum: Students trace a simple one or two-step decay sequence (e.g. radon-222 → polonium-218 via alpha decay) and identify the stable end product.
width.typical: Students trace multi-step decay chains (e.g. uranium-238 → lead-206); track changes to atomic number and mass number at each step; explain that each decay step moves the nucleus toward a more stable neutron-to-proton ratio; connect to the historical development of atomic theory — decay provided early evidence for nuclear structure.
wider: Investigate how mass and energy are connected in nuclear reactions — what happens to the 'missing mass' in a decay event? (binding energy / E=mc² at a qualitative level)
Examine how the discovery of radioactive decay changed the understanding of the atom's internal structure — what did natural transmutation reveal that the earlier model could not explain?

modes.reason: This node brings together the nuclear model (N1), isotope instability (N2), decay types (N3) and half-life (N4) into a complete account of how decay sequences produce stable atoms — the descriptor's explicit endpoint. Tracing a decay chain exercises all prior nodes in sequence.

descriptors.title: Chemical equations and conservation of mass
descriptors.description: model the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions using a range of representations, including word and simple balanced chemical equations, and use these to demonstrate the law of conservation of mass
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare physical and chemical changes and identify indicators of energy change in chemical reactions (AC9S8U07). They can classify matter as elements, compounds and mixtures and use chemical symbols and formulas (AC9S8U06). They can compare reversible and irreversible changes (AC9S6U04). They have not yet modelled atom rearrangement as the mechanism of chemical change, written balanced symbolic equations, or applied conservation of mass as a quantitative principle to chemical reactions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students model chemical reactions as atom rearrangement using word equations, molecular models and balanced symbolic equations, and use conservation of mass — demonstrated through atom counting — to explain why equations must be balanced.

nodes.label: Reactants and products — identifying what changes in a chemical reaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify reactants and products in a chemical reaction and describe the change in terms of new substances being formed.
criteria: Identifies reactants and products in a named chemical reaction
Explains that chemical reactions produce new substances with different properties
Connects reactant-product change to prior indicators of chemical change (AC9S8U07)

width.minimum: Students correctly identify reactants and products in a named reaction and state that new substances with different properties are formed.
width.typical: Students identify reactants and products in multiple reaction types; connect to prior physical vs chemical change knowledge from AC9S8U07 — new substances with different properties are the defining feature; explain that chemical change involves bond breaking and forming; describe observable evidence (colour change, gas production, precipitate, energy change) as indicators of product formation.
wider: Investigate why most elements are not found in their elemental state — what does their chemical reactivity tell us about the products formed in natural reactions?
Examine a combustion reaction in terms of reactants and products — identify all products, including water vapour, not just CO₂

modes.reason: Students have prior knowledge of chemical change indicators but not the reactant-product framing as a formal input-output model. Establishing this framing — reactants consumed, products formed — is the conceptual orientation for the atom rearrangement model in N2.

nodes.label: Atom rearrangement — chemical reactions as atomic-level redistribution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can model a chemical reaction as the rearrangement of atoms using molecular models or diagrams, showing that atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
criteria: Uses a molecular model or diagram to represent a simple reaction showing atoms before and after
Counts atoms on each side of a representation and confirms they match
Explains that atoms are rearranged — not created or destroyed — in chemical reactions
nodes.hinge_reason: Atom rearrangement is the mechanistic foundation of the conservation of mass principle and the conceptual basis for why equations must be balanced. Students who understand chemical change only at the observable level — new substance formed — cannot understand why balancing an equation is a meaningful scientific constraint rather than an arbitrary rule.

width.minimum: Students use a molecular model or diagram to represent a simple reaction (e.g. hydrogen + oxygen → water) showing the same atoms before and after.
width.typical: Students model multiple reactions using molecular models, structural diagrams, or ball-and-stick representations; count atoms on each side to verify they match; explain that bonds between atoms break and reform to produce new arrangements; explain that the type and number of atoms is unchanged — only their arrangement changes; connect this to why mass is conserved.
wider: Investigate a reaction in a closed system (sealed container) and demonstrate conservation of mass by weighing before and after — relate the result to the atom rearrangement model
Use molecular modelling software to build reactant and product structures for a named reaction and confirm atom count matches

modes.reason: Students commonly treat balancing equations as a procedural task without understanding why it is required. Making atom rearrangement explicit — same atoms, new arrangement — is the conceptual move that makes conservation of mass a necessary consequence rather than an imposed rule.

nodes.label: Word equations — naming reactants and products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write correct word equations for named chemical reactions, correctly identifying all reactants and products.
criteria: Writes a correct word equation for at least two named reactions, including all products
Uses correct arrow notation (reactants → products)
Explains what word equations show and what they do not (no quantities, no atom counts)

width.minimum: Students write a correct word equation for two named reactions.
width.typical: Students write word equations for combustion, neutralisation, and displacement reactions; include all products (including water in combustion); use correct arrow notation; explain the limitation of word equations — they name substances but do not show quantities or atom counts.
wider: Write word equations for First Nations Australians' chemical processes — e.g. reactions used to convert toxic plants into edible food — and identify reactants and products
Investigate green chemistry principles — examine a reaction used in industry and write the word equation, identifying any wasteful products and suggesting alternatives

modes.reason: Word equations require correct identification of all reactants and all products — a common error is omitting water or CO₂ in combustion. Structured practice with self-correction at the word equation level is the prerequisite for symbolic equation writing in N4.

nodes.label: Balanced symbolic equations — demonstrating conservation of mass
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and balance simple symbolic chemical equations and explain why balancing demonstrates the law of conservation of mass.
criteria: Balances a simple symbolic equation by adjusting coefficients (not subscripts)
Verifies a balanced equation by counting atoms of each element on both sides
Explains that a balanced equation demonstrates conservation of mass — same atoms, same total mass, on both sides
nodes.hinge_reason: Balancing symbolic equations is the procedural and conceptual endpoint of the descriptor — it is the representation through which conservation of mass is demonstrated. Students who cannot balance equations cannot demonstrate conservation of mass, and persistent errors (changing subscripts, wrong atom counting) are systematic and require explicit correction before the law can be applied.

width.minimum: Students correctly balance a simple symbolic equation by adjusting coefficients (not subscripts) and verify by atom counting.
width.typical: Students balance symbolic equations for multiple reaction types; explain the rule that subscripts cannot be changed (they define the substance) while coefficients can; verify balance by atom counting on both sides; explain that a balanced equation is a model demonstrating conservation of mass; connect to the atom rearrangement model from N2 — balanced equations show the same atoms before and after.
wider: Write and balance symbolic equations for reactions used to obtain elements from their compounds (e.g. metal extraction) and explain what the balanced equation reveals about mass relationships
Apply conservation of mass quantitatively — given the mass of one reactant, predict the mass of product formed using the molar ratios in a balanced equation (introductory level)

modes.reason: Balancing equations requires procedural precision across two constraints simultaneously: identifying which atoms need balancing, and adjusting only coefficients. Systematic errors — changing subscripts, miscounting polyatomic groups — are common and propagate into all subsequent chemistry work (AC9S10U07).

nodes.label: Conservation of mass — connecting representation to empirical evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use balanced equations to explain the law of conservation of mass, and connect this to experimental evidence from reactions in closed and open systems.
criteria: Explains why total mass is conserved in a closed system chemical reaction
Explains apparent mass changes in open system reactions using conservation of mass
Uses a balanced equation to connect the symbolic representation to the empirical mass conservation result

width.minimum: Students explain why a reaction in a closed system shows no change in total mass, and why an open system may appear to lose or gain mass.
width.typical: Students investigate or analyse data from closed system reactions to confirm mass conservation; explain apparent mass changes in open systems (gas escaping or being absorbed from air); use balanced equations to predict mass of products from known reactant masses; evaluate the claim that 'mass is conserved in chemical reactions' against experimental data.
wider: Investigate green chemistry principles — if mass is always conserved, why does green chemistry focus on waste? Reconcile atom economy with conservation of mass
Examine a reaction where mass appears to change in an open system and explain the discrepancy using conservation of mass — what left or entered the system?

modes.reason: This node integrates atom rearrangement (N2), word equations (N3) and balanced symbolic equations (N4) into an empirically grounded account of conservation of mass. Connecting the symbolic model to experimental data — particularly explaining open vs closed system discrepancies — is the descriptor's 'demonstrate the law of conservation of mass' demand.

descriptors.title: Genetics and inheritance
descriptors.description: explain the role of meiosis and mitosis and the function of chromosomes, DNA and genes in heredity and predict patterns of Mendelian inheritance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe reproductive structures and processes in animals and plants and analyse how sexual and asexual reproduction enable species survival (AC9S9U02). They can recognise cells as the basic units of living things and describe specialised cell structures (AC9S8U01). They have not yet examined the molecular basis of heredity — chromosomes, DNA and genes as functional units — or the mechanics of meiosis and mitosis as cell division processes, or Mendelian inheritance as a predictive model.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles of meiosis and mitosis in heredity, describe the structural relationship between chromosomes, DNA and genes, and predict genotype and phenotype ratios in monohybrid crosses including dominant/recessive and sex-linked patterns.

nodes.label: Chromosomes, DNA and genes — the structural hierarchy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structural relationship between chromosomes, DNA and genes, and explain how genetic information is organised and stored.
criteria: Describes chromosomes as structures made of DNA
Explains that genes are segments of DNA that code for heritable characteristics
Distinguishes genotype (genetic information) from phenotype (expressed characteristic)
nodes.hinge_reason: The structural hierarchy is the conceptual foundation all subsequent nodes require. Students who cannot locate genes on chromosomes, or who conflate DNA with chromosomes, cannot follow how meiosis separates chromosome pairs (N2), how alleles are transmitted (N4), or how sex-linked inheritance depends on chromosome identity (N6).

width.minimum: Students describe that chromosomes are made of DNA and that genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for heritable characteristics.
width.typical: Students represent the chromosome → DNA → gene hierarchy using diagrams or models; explain that humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; describe that genes code for proteins and that proteins determine characteristics; distinguish genotype from phenotype.
wider: Investigate how mutations — changes in DNA sequence — can alter gene function and connect to real genetic conditions (cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia)
Explore First Nations Australians' knowledges of heredity as evidenced by kinship and marriage laws — what observations about inheritance do these systems encode?

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate DNA, genes and chromosomes as interchangeable terms. Making the containment hierarchy explicit — chromosome contains DNA; gene is a segment of DNA — is the scaffold the transmission model in N4 requires. Diagrams that show the same information at multiple scales are effective here.

nodes.label: Mitosis — cell division for growth and repair
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the outcome of mitosis and describe its role in growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
criteria: States that mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells
Explains that chromosome number is maintained through mitosis
Identifies growth and repair as the biological purposes of mitosis

width.minimum: Students state that mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell and explain its role in growth or repair.
width.typical: Students describe that mitosis copies all chromosomes before division to maintain chromosome number; explain why genetic identity is preserved; connect to asexual reproduction from AC9S9U02; distinguish mitosis from meiosis in terms of purpose and outcome.
wider: Investigate how uncontrolled mitosis is the basis of cancer — what goes wrong, and how do treatments target dividing cells?
Compare mitosis-based asexual reproduction (identical offspring) to sexual reproduction — what are the evolutionary trade-offs?

modes.reason: Mitosis is primarily a contrast node — its value is in establishing what meiosis is NOT. Students need a clear outcome model (two identical cells, chromosome number preserved) before the reduction and recombination logic of meiosis in N3 is meaningful.

nodes.label: Meiosis — halving chromosome number and generating variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes and describe how meiosis generates genetic variation.
criteria: Explains that meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes
Describes that each gamete receives one chromosome from each homologous pair
Explains how meiosis contributes to genetic variation in offspring
nodes.hinge_reason: Meiosis is the mechanistic foundation of the inheritance model. Students who cannot explain why gametes carry one allele of each gene pair cannot construct Punnett squares correctly in N4, cannot explain why offspring ratios are probabilistic, and cannot account for sex-linked inheritance in N6 (where the sex chromosomes are the relevant pair being separated).

width.minimum: Students explain that meiosis produces four genetically unique cells with half the chromosome number, and that this enables fertilisation to restore the full number.
width.typical: Students explain chromosome separation during meiosis; describe that homologous pairs are separated so each gamete receives one chromosome from each pair; explain how random assortment and crossing over during meiosis generate variation; connect gamete formation to the inheritance model in N4.
wider: Investigate errors in meiosis (non-disjunction) and connect to chromosomal conditions such as Down syndrome or Klinefelter syndrome
Compare the variation generated by meiosis + fertilisation to asexual reproduction — why does sexual reproduction produce more variation, and what are the costs?

modes.reason: The logic of meiosis — homologous pairs separating so each gamete gets one from each pair — is the mechanism that makes Punnett squares work. Students who learn Punnett squares without this foundation produce correct ratios by rote without understanding why the probabilities hold. This must be established before N4.

nodes.label: Alleles and Mendelian inheritance — dominant and recessive
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain dominant and recessive allele relationships and use Punnett squares to predict genotype and phenotype ratios in monohybrid crosses.
criteria: Constructs a Punnett square for a monohybrid cross and states correct genotype and phenotype ratios
Uses correct allele notation and correctly forms gametes from each parental genotype
Interprets a pedigree diagram to identify phenotypes and infer genotypes for dominant/recessive traits
nodes.hinge_reason: Mendelian prediction is the core quantitative demand of the descriptor. Students who cannot correctly assign alleles to gametes via Punnett squares — the most common failure point — produce incorrect ratios throughout and cannot extend to sex-linked patterns in N6 or pedigree interpretation. Punnett square errors typically stem from unresolved meiosis logic from N3.

width.minimum: Students correctly construct a Punnett square for a monohybrid cross involving dominant and recessive alleles and state the expected phenotype ratio.
width.typical: Students apply Punnett squares to multiple cross types (PP × pp, Pp × Pp, Pp × pp); predict and explain genotype and phenotype ratios; use correct notation (capital/lowercase); connect allele pairs to the chromosome pairs separated by meiosis; interpret pedigree diagrams for dominant and recessive traits.
wider: Investigate a real genetic condition (e.g. cystic fibrosis or haemochromatosis) using pedigree analysis — identify carriers and predict risk for offspring
Explore First Nations Australians' kinship systems as evidence of observed heredity patterns — what inheritance regularities do marriage laws reflect?

modes.reason: Punnett square construction requires procedural precision — correct allele assignment, correct gamete formation from each parent, correct offspring reading. Errors are systematic and students need structured practice with self-correction before moving to sex-linked patterns.

Pedigree diagrams, real genetic conditions, and kinship structure examples each apply the Mendelian model to a different representational and cultural context. This is genuine width — the model is the same, the context and representation vary.

nodes.label: Fertilisation and heredity — connecting meiosis to offspring variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how meiosis and fertilisation together determine heredity and account for variation among siblings from the same parents.
criteria: Traces the pathway from parent genotypes through meiosis, gametes and fertilisation to offspring genotype
Explains why siblings from the same parents can have different genotypes and phenotypes
Connects Punnett square probability ratios to the random combination of gametes at fertilisation

width.minimum: Students explain that fertilisation combines one gamete from each parent to restore the full chromosome number, and that random gamete combination produces variation among offspring.
width.typical: Students trace the full pathway from parent genotypes → meiosis → gametes → fertilisation → offspring genotypes; explain why siblings from the same parents differ genetically; connect Punnett square probabilities to the randomness of fertilisation; explain that genetic information from both parents is represented in all offspring.
wider: Investigate how genetic information from both parents is passed to offspring and analyse how this increases species variation compared to asexual reproduction
Explore environmental and other factors that cause mutations and explain how mutations introduce new variation not explained by Mendelian inheritance alone

modes.reason: This node integrates N1 (DNA/chromosomes), N3 (meiosis) and N4 (Mendelian ratios) into a coherent account of heredity. Students who can construct a Punnett square but cannot explain why the probabilities hold need this connective node before sex-linked inheritance is introduced.

nodes.label: Sex-linked inheritance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain sex determination by sex chromosomes and predict genotype and phenotype ratios for sex-linked traits using Punnett squares.
criteria: Explains that sex is determined by the X and Y chromosome pair
Uses correct X-linked allele notation in a Punnett square and predicts phenotype ratios for males and females
Identifies why X-linked recessive conditions are more frequently expressed in males than females

width.minimum: Students explain that sex is determined by X and Y chromosomes and correctly apply a Punnett square to predict phenotype ratios for one sex-linked trait.
width.typical: Students explain why sex-linked conditions (e.g. colour blindness, haemophilia) affect males and females differently; apply X-linked notation correctly; predict carrier status in females; interpret pedigrees for X-linked traits; explain why Y-linked traits pass only father to son.
wider: Analyse a pedigree for an X-linked condition across three generations — identify carriers, predict risk for specific family members
Compare rates of sex-linked condition expression in males vs females using probability analysis — why are males more frequently affected by X-linked recessive conditions?

modes.reason: Sex-linked inheritance requires students to adapt the Punnett square notation they established in N4 — alleles are now carried on chromosomes of different sizes, and males have only one copy of X-linked genes. The logic extension from N4 must be made explicit, not assumed.

Multi-generational pedigrees for X-linked conditions (haemophilia, colour blindness) provide genuine width — students apply the sex-linked model to varied family structures and predict carrier and affected status. This is the elaboration's explicit expectation.

descriptors.title: Evolution by natural selection
descriptors.description: use the theory of evolution by natural selection to explain past and present diversity and analyse the scientific evidence supporting the theory
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how specific structural features and behaviours are adaptations enabling survival in particular habitats (AC9S5U01), analyse how physical conditions affect organism survival (AC9S6U01), and explain classification systems and biodiversity (AC9S7U01). They understand sexual and asexual reproduction and the role of variation in species survival (AC9S9U02). They have not yet encountered natural selection as a mechanistic explanation for how populations change over time, or engaged with the evidence base — fossil record, anatomical and chemical similarities, geographical distribution — that supports the theory.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the theory of evolution by natural selection to explain both past and present biological diversity, and analyse multiple lines of scientific evidence — fossil record, anatomical and chemical similarities, geographical distribution — that support the theory.

nodes.label: Variation within populations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that individuals within a population vary in heritable characteristics and identify the sources of that variation.
criteria: Explains that individuals within a population vary in heritable characteristics
Distinguishes heritable from non-heritable variation
Identifies mutation and sexual reproduction as sources of heritable variation
nodes.hinge_reason: Natural selection cannot operate without heritable variation — it is the raw material the mechanism acts on. Students who treat all individuals in a population as identical, or who do not understand that variation must be heritable to be selected, cannot construct the selection mechanism in N2 or explain why advantageous traits accumulate over generations.

width.minimum: Students state that individuals in a population vary and that some variation is heritable, giving one example.
width.typical: Students distinguish heritable from non-heritable variation; connect heritable variation to meiosis and sexual reproduction (AC9S10U01); explain that mutation introduces new variation; describe variation across a population as a distribution rather than a binary.
wider: Investigate variation in a measurable characteristic across a sample population and represent the distribution graphically — what does the shape of the distribution suggest?
Connect to AC9S10U01 — how does the genetic recombination from meiosis generate the heritable variation that natural selection acts on?

modes.reason: Students commonly accept that 'animals adapt to their environment' as a process that happens to individuals, not populations over generations. Establishing that variation is the starting condition — present in every population before any selection pressure exists — is the prerequisite for understanding selection as a filter, not a creator.

nodes.label: Natural selection as a mechanism — variation, selection pressure, differential survival
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the mechanism of natural selection: how a selection pressure acts on heritable variation to produce differential survival and reproduction, leading to population change over generations.
criteria: Describes the mechanism of natural selection as variation → selection pressure → differential survival/reproduction → inherited by offspring
Applies the mechanism correctly to a named example
Distinguishes natural selection from the Lamarckian view that individuals adapt during their lifetime
nodes.hinge_reason: The mechanism of natural selection is the core explanatory tool the descriptor demands. Students who conflate natural selection with individual adaptation (Lamarckism) or who cannot articulate the variation → differential survival → inherited by offspring chain cannot explain either past diversity (N4) or present diversity (N5), and cannot evaluate any evidence for the theory (N3).

width.minimum: Students describe that individuals with advantageous traits are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those traits to offspring, with one named example.
width.typical: Students apply the mechanism across multiple examples including predation, disease and environmental change as selection pressures; explain why traits accumulate in populations over generations; distinguish natural selection from Lamarckian 'use and disuse'; describe artificial selection as a human-directed application of the same mechanism.
wider: Investigate natural selection in a specific documented case — e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria, or industrial melanism in peppered moths — and trace each step of the mechanism
Compare natural selection to artificial selection in breeding programmes — what are the structural similarities and what is different?

modes.reason: The Lamarckian misconception — that individuals change during their lifetime to suit the environment and pass those changes on — is persistent and must be explicitly addressed. Students need to reconstruct the selection mechanism step by step, identifying where Lamarck's account differs at each step.

Applying the selection mechanism to varied, well-evidenced cases builds the explanatory fluency needed to use the theory as an analytical tool in N4 and N5. Each case exercises the same mechanistic reasoning in a new context.

nodes.label: Evidence for evolution — multiple lines of support
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and explain multiple lines of evidence that support the theory of evolution by natural selection, including the fossil record, anatomical and chemical similarities, and geographical distribution.
criteria: Describes at least three distinct lines of evidence for evolution
Explains what each evidence type demonstrates about common descent or change over time
Identifies that multiple independent evidence types support the same conclusion

width.minimum: Students describe at least two distinct lines of evidence for evolution and explain what each line demonstrates.
width.typical: Students explain the fossil record as evidence of change over time and species extinction; describe homologous structures as evidence of common ancestry; explain chemical similarities (DNA, protein sequences) as evidence of evolutionary relationships; describe geographical distribution patterns (island species, marsupial distribution) as evidence consistent with common descent; explain how each evidence type supports the theory independently.
wider: Analyse a specific cladogram or phylogenetic tree using DNA sequence data — what does the branching pattern indicate about evolutionary relationships?
Investigate how the discovery of gravitational waves or other recent scientific advances parallel the process by which evolutionary evidence accumulates and gets validated

modes.reason: Each evidence type — fossil record, anatomical homology, chemical similarity, geographical distribution — is a distinct line of reasoning. Students encountering only one type often believe the theory rests on that single line. Working across all four types builds the 'multiple independent lines' understanding the descriptor's 'analyse' demand requires.

nodes.label: Using natural selection to explain past diversity — speciation and extinction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the theory of natural selection to explain how past populations diverged into new species and how extinction results from failed adaptation to selection pressures.
criteria: Explains how geographic isolation and different selection pressures can lead to speciation
Uses natural selection to explain why species go extinct when selection pressures change
Connects fossil record evidence to the timeline of species appearance and disappearance

width.minimum: Students explain that populations isolated from each other face different selection pressures and can diverge over time, and describe extinction as the failure to adapt to changed conditions.
width.typical: Students explain speciation as the result of geographic isolation, different selection pressures and accumulated variation over time; connect to the fossil record evidence from N3; explain mass extinctions as large-scale selection events; describe how evolutionary history is reconstructed from fossil and molecular evidence.
wider: Examine the adaptive radiation of a species group — e.g. Darwin's finches or Australian marsupials — and explain the diversity using natural selection and geographic isolation
Investigate some structural and physiological adaptations of First Nations Australians to the Australian environment and discuss how evolutionary and cultural adaptation interact

modes.reason: This node applies the selection mechanism (N2) and evidence base (N3) to explain deep time patterns. Students synthesise the mechanism, evidence and timescale into an account of how present biodiversity arose from past populations — the 'past diversity' demand of the descriptor.

nodes.label: Using natural selection to explain present diversity and current change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the theory of natural selection to explain current patterns of biodiversity and analyse examples of evolution occurring in present populations.
criteria: Applies natural selection to explain a current example of observable population change
Explains present biodiversity as the product of ongoing evolutionary processes
Analyses how a current selection pressure is affecting a named population

width.minimum: Students apply natural selection to explain one current example of population change (e.g. antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance) and connect it to present biodiversity patterns.
width.typical: Students explain that evolution is ongoing; analyse present cases of rapid selection (antibiotic resistance, introduced species, climate-driven range shifts); explain biodiversity as the cumulative product of evolutionary history; connect to AC9S7U01's classification systems as a map of evolutionary relationships; discuss how human activity is a current selection pressure.
wider: Examine biodiversity data for a specific ecosystem and explain current distribution patterns using evolutionary history and present selection pressures
Analyse how climate change is acting as a current selection pressure — what traits are being selected for or against in a named species?

modes.reason: This is the descriptor's full demand: using the theory as an explanatory and analytical tool across past and present diversity. Students bring the mechanism (N2), evidence types (N3), and historical account (N4) together to analyse present patterns — completing the 'use the theory to explain' requirement.

descriptors.title: Big Bang theory
descriptors.description: describe how the big bang theory models the origin and evolution of the universe and analyse the supporting evidence for the theory
descriptors.knowledge: Students can model and explain how Earth-sun-moon positions cause eclipses, seasons and tides (AC9S7U03) and describe daily and seasonal environmental changes (AC9S1U02, AC9S2U01). They have scale and cyclic-phenomenon understanding at the solar system level. They have not yet encountered cosmological scale (galaxies, light-years, astronomical units), the origin and timeline of the universe, or the evidence base for the big bang — cosmic microwave background radiation, redshift of galaxies, or Hubble's observations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how the big bang theory models the origin and evolution of the universe — including its major stages and the formation of stars and galaxies — and analyse the supporting evidence including redshift, cosmic microwave background radiation and the observed proportions of matter.

nodes.label: Scale and structure of the universe
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the major structural components of the universe using appropriate scale and units, and place Earth within the cosmic hierarchy.
criteria: Names the major structural components of the universe in order of scale
Uses light-years or astronomical units correctly in a distance context
Uses scientific notation to express cosmological distances or ages

width.minimum: Students name the major components of the universe in order of scale (planet, star, solar system, galaxy, universe) and use at least one appropriate unit (light-year or astronomical unit) correctly.
width.typical: Students describe the scale of the universe using scientific notation and appropriate units; compare distances within the solar system (AU) to intergalactic distances (light-years); describe galaxies as collections of billions of stars; explain that the observable universe contains billions of galaxies; compare the age of the universe to the age of Earth.
wider: Construct a scaled timeline or distance model of the universe and reflect on the limits of human intuition at cosmological scales
Explore First Nations Australians' knowledges of celestial bodies and origin stories — what observational knowledge of the night sky underlies these accounts?

modes.reason: Students enter with solar system scale understanding but without cosmological scale. Establishing the size and structure of the universe is prerequisite orientation — students cannot interpret redshift data or the CMB without understanding that observations involve enormous distances and timescales. Scientific notation and unit fluency are required for all subsequent elaboration contexts.

nodes.label: The big bang model — origin and timeline of the universe
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the big bang theory as a model of the origin and evolution of the universe and outline the major stages from the initial singularity to the formation of stars and galaxies.
